That's why a resolved promise's then runs before a setTimeout with zero delay.

The practical lesson: long synchronous code blocks everything, because nothing else can run while the stack is busy. In the browser the UI freezes, and in Node every request waits. So heavy CPU work goes to Web Workers or worker threads.
On the front end, I watch for a few main categories of security issues.

First, cross-site scripting, XSS. React escapes values by default, which protects us, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, or putting user input into URLs like javascript links, bypasses that, so I avoid it or sanitise with DOMPurify. A Content Security Policy adds another layer. Second, token storage. Tokens in localStorage can be stolen by any XSS, so I prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, or keeping tokens in memory. Third, reverse tabnabbing. Links with target blank used to give the new page access to window.opener, so it could redirect our original tab to a phishing page. The fix is rel noopener noreferrer. Fourth, never trusting the front end for security. Hiding a button isn't authorization; the API must check everything. And fifth, dependency vulnerabilities, checked with npm audit in the pipeline.

The tabnabbing one is a real fix I did in IRT. A security scan flagged it, and I updated about 40 external links, added a shared link component that sets rel by default, and a lint rule so it can't come back.
Node.js runs JavaScript on a single main thread with an event loop, and uses non-blocking I/O through a library called libuv.

When a request needs a database query or an HTTP call, Node doesn't wait. It starts the operation, moves on to other requests, and runs the callback when the result arrives. So one process can handle thousands of concurrent connections with very little memory, because there's no thread per request. Things like file system operations and DNS run on a small libuv thread pool behind the scenes.

That makes Node a great fit for I/O-heavy work: APIs that mostly call databases and other services, backend-for-frontend layers, real-time apps with WebSockets, and developer tooling. Sharing TypeScript with the front end is also a productivity win. It's a weak fit for CPU-heavy work, like large calculations or image processing, because that blocks the event loop and every request waits. For those, worker threads or a different service are better. And in production, you run several processes or containers to use all CPU cores.
In my work, I've used Node and TypeScript for internal tooling and integration services, while the core domain logic stays in .NET.
I structure a Node.js TypeScript microservice much like a .NET one: clear layers, typed contracts, and the same operational basics.

The layers are: routes or controllers that handle HTTP, services that hold the business logic, and repositories or clients that talk to databases and other services. Request and response shapes are typed, and inputs are validated at the edge with something like zod, so the rest of the code can trust the types. I use Express for simple services, or NestJS when I want more structure, since NestJS has modules and dependency injection very similar to ASP.NET Core. Errors go through a central error-handling middleware that returns a consistent error format, and async errors are captured properly.

Operationally: configuration from environment variables, validated at startup; structured JSON logging with pino, including a correlation id; a health endpoint; and graceful shutdown on SIGTERM. Then Jest tests, ESLint, a Dockerfile with a small base image, and the same CI/CD pipeline template as our .NET services.
Keeping that consistency means any engineer can work on any service, whatever the language.
FastAPI and Flask are both popular Python web frameworks, but they're built for different eras of Python.

Flask is a minimal micro-framework, built on WSGI, and synchronous by default. It's simple, very flexible, and has a huge ecosystem, but you add things like request validation and API documentation yourself with extensions. FastAPI is newer and async-first, built on ASGI. It uses Python type hints with Pydantic models, so request bodies are validated and converted automatically, and invalid input returns a clear 422 error. It generates OpenAPI documentation and Swagger UI from the code, it has built-in dependency injection with Depends, and it's one of the fastest Python frameworks.

So for a new typed REST service, I choose FastAPI. It feels quite close to ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, with typed models and automatic docs. Flask still makes sense for very simple apps, or existing Flask codebases where there's no reason to rewrite.
I've built REST services with both. In practice, the type-driven validation in FastAPI removed a lot of hand-written checking code, and the automatic docs made integration with other teams easier.
FastAPI is built on ASGI, so it supports async natively, and it uses Pydantic for validation.

For async: if I declare an endpoint with async def, it runs on the event loop. That's efficient for I/O, but only if everything inside is also async, using libraries like httpx for HTTP calls and asyncpg or async SQLAlchemy for databases. If I call blocking code inside an async def, it blocks the whole event loop and every request waits. If I have to use blocking libraries, I declare the endpoint with plain def, and FastAPI runs it in a thread pool instead. That's a common mistake to watch for.

For validation, I define Pydantic models with type hints and constraints. FastAPI automatically parses and validates the request body, query and path parameters against them, and returns a 422 with detailed errors if they're invalid. Response models filter and serialise the output, so internal fields aren't leaked. Depends provides dependency injection for database sessions, authentication and configuration.
In production, I run it with uvicorn workers, behind a load balancer, in a container. It's conceptually very similar to ASP.NET Core model binding plus DI.
Spring Boot and ASP.NET Core are very similar in concept, so moving between them is mostly learning new names.

Both have a built-in dependency injection container with constructor injection, use annotations or attributes to declare routes, run on an embedded web server, support configuration profiles per environment, and have a mature ORM. The mapping is quite direct. RestController in Spring is like a controller with ApiController. Constructor injection works the same way. JPA with Hibernate is like EF Core. application.yml is like appsettings.json, Spring profiles are like ASP.NET Core environments, and Maven or Gradle play the role of NuGet and the dotnet CLI. Spring filters and interceptors are similar to middleware and filters.

The differences are more about ecosystem and style. Spring has a very large ecosystem, like Spring Security, Spring Cloud and Spring Data, and relies heavily on annotations and auto-configuration, which can feel magical. ASP.NET Core is a bit more explicit, with configuration in Program.cs, and it's very fast in benchmarks.
Because the concepts transfer, I'm comfortable reading and contributing to Spring Boot services, and the design principles I use in .NET apply directly.
When a team uses several languages, consistency comes from shared contracts and conventions, not from the language.

First, contracts. Every API is designed contract-first with OpenAPI, uses the same error format, based on ProblemDetails, and follows the same versioning rules. So a consumer can't tell which language a service is written in. Second, operational conventions. Every service uses correlation ids, structured JSON logs to CloudWatch, health endpoints, and metrics to Grafana, so support works the same way everywhere. Third, the delivery pipeline. The same CI/CD template builds, tests, runs a SonarQube quality gate, builds a container image, and deploys with infrastructure as code, whatever the language. Each language has a service template with all of this ready, so a new service starts consistent.
And I choose the language by fit, not taste. .NET for core domain services, Node and TypeScript for I/O glue and tooling, and Python for data and AI scripting.
The correlation-id work is a good example. I wrote it for .NET first, then we added the same header convention in Node and Python, so one query traces a request across all of them.
In both ecosystems, the goal is the same: reproducible builds, controlled updates, and catching vulnerable packages early.

In Node, package.json declares dependencies with version ranges, and the lock file, package-lock.json, records the exact versions of everything, including transitive dependencies. The lock file is always committed. In CI, I use npm ci instead of npm install, which installs exactly what's in the lock file and fails if it's out of sync. npm audit, or a tool like Dependabot, checks for known vulnerabilities. In Python, I use a virtual environment per project, so dependencies don't clash, and pin exact versions, either in requirements.txt or with a lock file from Poetry or uv. pip-audit checks for vulnerabilities.
For both, Docker images pin versions too, including the base image, and updates happen regularly through small pull requests, so we never face one huge risky upgrade.
It's the same idea as NuGet with central package management in .NET, which I introduced during our .NET 10 upgrade after a version conflict.
I choose the language for a new microservice based on fit and on what the team can support, not on personal preference.

First, team skills and the existing ecosystem in that domain. If the team and all neighbouring services are .NET, there needs to be a strong reason to introduce something else, because every new language adds maintenance, hiring and support cost. Second, the workload. Complex domain logic or CPU-heavy work suits .NET or Java. I/O-heavy glue, backend-for-frontend layers and tooling suit Node and TypeScript. Data processing, machine learning and AI scripting suit Python. Third, libraries. Sometimes the best library decides, for example mature commercial SFTP providers in .NET, or the newest LLM SDKs often appearing first in Python and TypeScript. Fourth, operations: can we monitor, secure, test and deploy it with our existing templates and pipelines?
So in practice, our core IRT services are .NET, and other languages appear where they clearly fit better.
The decision should be written down, for example in an architecture decision record, so the next person knows why.
EC2, ECS and Lambda are three levels of compute on AWS, from most control to least management.

EC2 gives you virtual machines. You choose the instance type and operating system and manage everything on it: patching, scaling, software. It's the right choice for legacy applications, special software that needs OS-level access, or workloads that don't fit containers. ECS runs Docker containers as long-running services, either on EC2 instances or on Fargate, where you don't manage servers at all. It's a great fit for web APIs and background workers with steady traffic, because containers are always running, start consistently, and you control the runtime. Lambda runs functions in response to events, like an HTTP request, a file in S3, or a message in a queue. You pay only per invocation and duration, and it scales automatically, even to zero. But each run is limited to 15 minutes, and cold starts add latency.
So my rule: Lambda for event-driven glue, scheduled jobs and spiky or low traffic. ECS for core APIs and workers with steady load. EC2 only when I need that level of control.
Our IRT platform follows exactly that: the .NET services and RabbitMQ consumers run on ECS, and Lambda handles event-driven pieces like reacting to files in S3.
ECS has a small set of building blocks, and once you know them, the rest is straightforward.

A cluster is a logical group of capacity where tasks run, either EC2 instances you manage, or Fargate, where AWS manages it. A task definition is the blueprint, a bit like a docker-compose file. It specifies the container image, CPU and memory, environment variables and secrets, port mappings, the IAM task role the app uses to call AWS services, the execution role ECS uses to pull images and secrets, and the logging configuration. A task is a running instance of that definition, one or more containers running together. A service keeps a desired number of tasks running, for example three. It replaces unhealthy or stopped tasks, registers them with a load balancer target group, handles rolling deployments when you update the task definition, and integrates with autoscaling.
There are also capacity providers, which decide where tasks run, like Fargate or Fargate Spot.

In our platform, each .NET service has its own task definition and ECS service, behind an ALB target group, with a task role scoped to just what it needs. Deployments simply register a new task definition revision.
API Gateway is a managed front door for APIs. Clients call it, and it routes requests to the backend, like Lambda functions, HTTP services on ECS, or directly to other AWS services.

Its value is everything it handles before the request reaches your code. Authentication: JWT and Cognito authorisers, custom Lambda authorisers, or IAM. Throttling and quotas, including usage plans with API keys per client, so one partner can't overload the system. Request validation against a schema, CORS, and request and response transformation. It also supports stages, like dev and prod, custom domains, caching, and logging and metrics in CloudWatch. There are three types: REST APIs, the most feature-rich; HTTP APIs, which are simpler, faster and cheaper; and WebSocket APIs for real-time two-way communication.
Limits to remember: a default 29-second integration timeout, and payload size limits, so it's not for long-running or large requests.
In our platform, partner-facing APIs go through API Gateway, which gives us per-partner throttling and keys, while internal UI traffic goes through the ALB directly to ECS.

A cold start happens when Lambda has to create a new execution environment to handle a request. That means downloading the code, starting the runtime, and running your initialisation code, before the function itself runs. Later requests reuse the warm environment and are fast.

Cold starts happen on the first request, after a period of inactivity, and when scaling up, because each new concurrent execution needs its own environment. For .NET, cold starts have traditionally been longer than for Node or Python, because of runtime startup and JIT compilation, sometimes over a second.

To reduce them: keep the deployment package small and trim dependencies. Use native AOT compilation, which removes JIT and makes .NET start much faster, or ReadyToRun as a lighter option. Use SnapStart where supported, which restores a snapshot of an initialised environment. Keep initialisation code light, and lazily create heavy clients. Allocating more memory also gives more CPU, which speeds up startup. And for latency-critical functions, provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm, at an extra cost.

Often the simplest answer is architecture: if a path is latency-critical and constant, a container on ECS may suit it better. Our Lambdas are event-driven background tasks, where a cold start doesn't hurt users.
DynamoDB modelling is the opposite of relational modelling. Instead of starting from entities and normalising, you start from the access patterns.

First, I list every query the application needs, like "get a shipment by id", "list shipments for a site by date", or "get all events for a shipment". Then I design keys to serve them. The partition key must have high cardinality, like a shipment id rather than a status, so data and traffic spread evenly and we avoid hot partitions. The sort key allows range queries within a partition, with conditions like begins_with or between, for example a sort key of "EVENT#" plus a timestamp. Extra access patterns are served with global secondary indexes. Single-table design goes further, storing related item types in one table with generic key names, so one query can fetch a shipment and its events together.
Other tools I use: conditional writes for optimistic concurrency and uniqueness, TTL to expire old items automatically, and Streams to react to changes.

The trade-off is that unplanned queries are expensive, so this works best when access patterns are stable. In our platform, DynamoDB holds simpler, high-volume status and event data, designed exactly this way.
Caching strategies differ mainly in when the cache and the database are written, and which one you read first.

Cache-aside, or lazy loading, is the most common. The application reads from the cache; on a miss, it reads from the database and stores the result in the cache with an expiry. It only caches data that's actually requested, and the cache can fail without breaking anything, but the first read is slower and data can be stale until it expires. Write-through writes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always up to date for reads, at the cost of slower writes and caching data that may never be read. Write-behind writes to the cache first and flushes to the database later. It's very fast, but risky, because data can be lost if the cache fails.

Whatever the strategy, a few rules apply: set TTLs, invalidate or update the cache when data changes, add jitter to expiries, and protect against cache stampedes, where many requests miss at once, with locking or HybridCache. And never treat the cache as the source of truth.
In our platform, ElastiCache Redis uses cache-aside for reference data, like depots and country rules, with short TTLs and eviction on change.
Both distribute traffic across targets, but they work at different network layers.

The Application Load Balancer works at layer 7, the HTTP level. It understands HTTP and HTTPS, so it can route based on the URL path, the host name, headers or query strings. For example, /api/shipments goes to one service and /api/sites to another. It terminates TLS, integrates with AWS WAF for web protection, supports WebSockets and HTTP/2, can authenticate users with OIDC, and works directly with ECS target groups. The Network Load Balancer works at layer 4, TCP and UDP. It doesn't look inside the request, so it's extremely fast, with very low latency, handles millions of requests per second, and provides static IP addresses, which some partners need for firewall allow-lists. It also supports non-HTTP protocols.
Both perform health checks and spread traffic across availability zones.

So for web APIs and microservices, the ALB is the default. I use an NLB when I need static IPs, extreme performance, or non-HTTP traffic, like an SFTP endpoint or a TCP service. In our platform, the ALB fronts all our ECS services, with path-based routing to each service.
S3 is AWS's object storage. It stores files, called objects, in buckets, with extremely high durability, eleven nines, and practically unlimited capacity.

It's used for all kinds of things: uploaded files and exports, backups, static websites, build artifacts, data lakes and logs. Storage classes trade cost against access speed, from S3 Standard for frequently accessed data, to Infrequent Access, to Glacier for archives. Lifecycle rules automatically move objects to cheaper classes or delete them after a period.

A presigned URL gives temporary access to one specific object, for upload or download, without giving the client any AWS credentials. Our backend, which has permission, generates a URL signed with its credentials, valid for a short time, like five minutes. The client uses that URL directly with S3. This is very useful for large files, because the upload goes straight to S3 instead of through our API, which saves bandwidth and memory, and avoids API Gateway size limits.

Security basics always apply: Block Public Access, encryption, least-privilege policies. In our platform, CSV imports and exports use presigned URLs, and our API only receives the object key after the upload completes.
Least privilege means every identity gets only the permissions it needs to do its job, nothing more. In AWS, I apply it in a few concrete ways.

First, every service gets its own IAM role: an ECS task role, or a Lambda execution role. No shared "app" role with everything. Second, policies are specific: specific actions, like s3:GetObject rather than s3:*, and specific resource ARNs, like one bucket and prefix, or one secret, never a wildcard on everything. Conditions can narrow it further, for example requiring requests to come through our VPC endpoint, or requiring encryption. Third, no long-lived access keys in code or configuration. Services use roles with temporary credentials, and people use SSO. Fourth, separate AWS accounts for environments, so a mistake in development can't touch production. And fifth, review regularly: IAM Access Analyzer finds unused permissions and resources shared externally, so we can tighten policies over time.
Starting broad and planning to tighten later rarely happens, so I start tight and add permissions when needed.
In our platform, the vendor exchange service's role can only read its own Secrets Manager entries and write to one S3 prefix. If it were compromised, the blast radius is small.
A typical layout uses one VPC spread across at least two availability zones, so losing one data centre doesn't take the system down.

In each availability zone, there are public and private subnets. Public subnets hold only what must face the internet: the Application Load Balancer, and NAT Gateways for outbound traffic. Private subnets hold everything else: ECS tasks, Lambdas that need VPC access, RDS databases and ElastiCache. Often the databases are in a separate, more restricted data subnet tier. Nothing in a private subnet has a public IP.

Security groups control traffic between layers, by reference. The ALB accepts 443 from the internet, the services accept traffic only from the ALB's security group, and the database accepts connections only from the services' security groups. VPC endpoints for S3, DynamoDB, ECR and Secrets Manager keep AWS traffic private and avoid NAT costs. In front, Route 53 for DNS and WAF on the ALB. Flow logs record traffic for troubleshooting and audits.

That's essentially how our IRT environment is set up, with each environment in its own account and VPC. It gives defence in depth: even a compromised container can't reach the database unless its security group allows it.
Infrastructure as code means defining cloud resources, like networks, databases, load balancers and permissions, in versioned files, instead of creating them by clicking in a console.

Tools like CloudFormation and Terraform read those files and create or update the real infrastructure to match. That brings the same benefits we get with application code. Repeatability: every environment, development, validation and production, is built from the same definitions, so they don't drift apart. Code review: infrastructure changes go through pull requests, and a plan shows exactly what will change before it happens. Audit trail: git history shows who changed what, when and why. Drift detection: we can find manual changes. And recovery: an entire environment can be rebuilt quickly, which is essential for disaster recovery.
In regulated work like ours, that traceability is very important. Auditors want to see that every production change was reviewed, approved and reproducible, and IaC gives that evidence naturally.
Changes flow through the same pipeline as code: pull request, plan, review, approval, apply. Nobody changes production infrastructure by hand.
Both are infrastructure-as-code tools, with different strengths.

CloudFormation is AWS's native service. You write templates in JSON or YAML, and AWS manages them as stacks, including the state, so there's no state file for you to manage. It supports change sets to preview changes, and automatically rolls back if a deployment fails. New AWS features are usually supported quickly, and it's free. Its limit is that it's AWS only. AWS CDK lets you write CloudFormation in real programming languages, like C# or TypeScript. Terraform, from HashiCorp, uses its own language, HCL, and works across many providers: AWS, Azure, GCP, and also things like GitHub, Datadog or Kubernetes. It has an explicit plan and apply workflow, and a large ecosystem of reusable modules. But you manage the state file yourself, securely and with locking. OpenTofu is the open-source fork.
So I'd choose CloudFormation or CDK for an AWS-only organisation that wants the native, managed experience. Terraform for multi-cloud, or when managing non-AWS resources with the same tool.
The principles matter more than the tool: everything in code, reviewed, deployed by pipelines.
Terraform state is a file that maps the resources defined in your code to the real resources in the cloud, along with their attributes, like IDs and ARNs.

Terraform needs it to know what it's managing. When you run plan, it compares your code, the state, and the real infrastructure, and works out what to create, change or destroy. Without state, it wouldn't know that a bucket in your code is the bucket that already exists.

Managing it properly is critical. It should be stored remotely, never on a laptop and never in git, because it can contain sensitive values. On AWS, the common setup is an S3 backend with encryption and versioning, plus locking, traditionally through a DynamoDB table, or with S3 native locking in newer versions. Terraform Cloud is another option. Locking prevents two people or pipelines from applying at the same time and corrupting it. I keep separate state per environment, and often per component, like network and application, so a mistake has a small blast radius. And I use terraform import to bring existing resources under management, and moved blocks or state commands carefully when refactoring.
The golden rule is: never edit the state by hand, and only change infrastructure through Terraform.
The Terraform workflow is write, plan, review and apply, ideally all through a pipeline.

First, I write or change the configuration in HCL, usually using modules for reusable pieces. Then terraform init downloads the provider plugins and modules and configures the backend where state is stored. terraform fmt and validate check formatting and syntax. Next, terraform plan compares the code with the state and the real infrastructure, and shows exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed. That plan is the key review artifact. In a pull request, the pipeline posts the plan, and reviewers check it carefully, especially anything marked "destroy" or "replace", which can mean data loss. After approval, terraform apply makes the changes, ideally applying the exact saved plan that was reviewed.

Important practices: run it from the pipeline, not from laptops, so there's one controlled identity with the right permissions and a full log. Use state locking. And detect drift by running a scheduled plan, which alerts if real infrastructure no longer matches the code.
For regulated environments, the saved plan and the approval become part of the change evidence.

Drift is when the real infrastructure no longer matches what's defined in the code. It usually happens because someone made a manual change in the console, often during an incident, like opening a security group port or resizing a database, and never put it back into code.

Drift is dangerous for several reasons. Environments stop being identical, so something works in UAT but not in production. The next deployment may silently undo the manual fix, or fail. And in a regulated environment, an untracked change is an audit finding.

To detect it: CloudFormation has built-in drift detection, and with Terraform, I run a scheduled terraform plan in the pipeline, which alerts if it shows any changes when the code hasn't changed. AWS Config rules can also flag non-compliant resources.

To prevent it: restrict console write access in production, so people have read-only access by default and changes go through pipelines. Allow emergency break-glass access, but with logging and a rule that any emergency change is put into code right after. Tag resources managed by IaC so everyone knows not to touch them manually.
The culture part matters most: the fix isn't done until it's in code.

An image is an immutable, read-only template that contains everything needed to run an application: the base operating system layer, the runtime, dependencies, and the application itself. A container is a running instance of an image, with its own process, a thin writable layer, and its own isolated view of the network and file system. One image can run as many containers.

A Dockerfile is the recipe that builds an image. It's a list of steps: start FROM a base image, set the working directory, COPY files in, RUN commands like restoring packages and building, set environment variables, EXPOSE a port, and define the ENTRYPOINT that starts the app.

Each instruction creates a layer, and layers are cached. If a layer hasn't changed, Docker reuses it. So the order matters: put things that change rarely first, like the base image and dependency restore, and things that change often last, like copying source code. That makes rebuilds much faster.

Containers also share the host's kernel, which makes them much lighter and faster to start than virtual machines. In our platform, every .NET service is built into an image in the pipeline, and the same image goes from validation to production.
A production Dockerfile for .NET should produce a small, secure image, and build quickly with good caching.

I use a multi-stage build. The first stage uses the full .NET SDK image to restore and publish. I copy the csproj files first and run dotnet restore, before copying the rest of the source. Because the project files rarely change, that restore layer stays cached, and rebuilds only recompile code. Then dotnet publish in Release configuration. The final stage starts from the much smaller ASP.NET runtime image, or even a chiseled Ubuntu image, which has no shell or package manager, and copies only the published output. The SDK and source code never reach production.

For security and operations: run as a non-root user, which the newer .NET images support with the app user. Expose the port, set the entrypoint, and make sure the app has a health endpoint. Never put secrets in the image, because anyone with the image can read them; they come from Secrets Manager at runtime. Then scan the image for vulnerabilities, and tag it with the version and commit.
When we upgraded to .NET 10, we moved our images to the new runtime base images and scanned them with Trivy before release.

A pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It's one or more containers that run together on the same node, share the same network address and can share storage volumes. Usually it's one application container, sometimes with a sidecar, like a log shipper or proxy. Pods are disposable: they get replaced, not repaired.

Around pods, there are a few main objects. A Deployment declares how many replicas of a pod you want and manages rolling updates and rollbacks, through ReplicaSets. A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances across the pods, because pod IPs keep changing. An Ingress, or the newer Gateway API, routes external HTTP traffic to services by host and path. ConfigMaps and Secrets hold configuration and sensitive values. A Namespace separates teams or environments within a cluster. And for special cases: a StatefulSet for stateful apps that need stable identities and storage, a DaemonSet to run one pod per node, and Jobs and CronJobs for batch and scheduled work. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales replicas.
The core idea is declarative: you describe the desired state, and Kubernetes continuously works to make reality match it.
Our platform uses ECS, but the concepts map directly: an ECS task is like a pod, and an ECS service is like a Deployment plus a Service.
A Kubernetes Deployment YAML describes the desired state of an application: what to run, how many copies, and how to update it.

At the top, apiVersion apps/v1, kind Deployment, and metadata with a name and labels. In the spec, replicas sets how many pods, for example three. The selector says which pods this Deployment manages, by matching labels. Then the template describes the pod itself: its labels, which must match the selector, and the containers. For each container: the image with a specific version tag, never latest; the container port; environment variables, often from ConfigMaps and Secrets; and resources, with requests, which the scheduler uses to place the pod, and limits, which cap usage. Then the probes: readiness, liveness and startup, usually pointing to health endpoints. Finally, the update strategy: RollingUpdate, with maxSurge and maxUnavailable controlling how many pods are replaced at a time.
Production extras include a security context to run as non-root with a read-only file system, a service account, pod anti-affinity to spread replicas across nodes, and a PodDisruptionBudget.
The YAML usually lives in a Helm chart or Kustomize overlay, deployed by the pipeline.
Kubernetes uses three kinds of probes to understand the health of a container, and each one triggers a different action.

The readiness probe asks: is this pod ready to receive traffic right now? If it fails, Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service's endpoints, so no requests are sent to it, but it doesn't restart it. That's useful during startup, or when a dependency is temporarily unavailable. The liveness probe asks: is this container stuck or broken beyond recovery? If it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes kills and restarts the container. That's for deadlocks or hung processes. The startup probe gives slow-starting applications time to start. While it's running, liveness and readiness checks are paused, so a slow startup isn't mistaken for a hang.

The common mistake is making the liveness probe check dependencies, like the database. If the database has a brief problem, every pod fails liveness, and Kubernetes restarts all of them at once, which makes the outage worse. So liveness should be cheap, checking only the process itself, while readiness can check critical dependencies.
In ASP.NET Core, I expose /health/live and /health/ready with health checks tagged accordingly. Our ECS services use the same split with ALB health checks.
Both hold configuration for containers in Kubernetes, separated by sensitivity.

A ConfigMap holds non-sensitive configuration, like URLs, feature settings, timeouts or a whole appsettings file. A Secret holds sensitive values, like passwords, API keys and certificates. One important detail: Secrets are only base64-encoded by default, not encrypted, so anyone with read access to them can decode them. In production, you enable encryption at rest in etcd, restrict access with RBAC, or better, use an external store like AWS Secrets Manager with the External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver, so secrets are synced or mounted from the vault.
Both can be injected into containers as environment variables or as mounted files. Mounted files can be updated without restarting the pod, while environment variables only change on restart.

The key principle is build once, configure per environment: the same image runs everywhere, and only ConfigMaps and Secrets differ between environments, managed through infrastructure as code. In ASP.NET Core, environment variables and mounted files plug straight into the configuration system, and the Options pattern with ValidateOnStart catches missing values. On ECS, we do the same with task definition environment variables and secrets from Secrets Manager.
Autoscaling in both platforms adds capacity when load increases and removes it when load drops, but the mechanisms differ.

In Kubernetes, there are two levels. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales the number of pod replicas based on metrics, like average CPU or memory, or custom metrics such as requests per second or queue length, using tools like KEDA. Then, if there's no room on existing nodes for the new pods, the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes to the cluster, and removes underused ones. For HPA to work well, pods need accurate resource requests, because CPU utilisation is calculated against the request.

In ECS, Service Auto Scaling adjusts the desired task count. The most common policy is target tracking, for example keeping average CPU at 60 percent, or a target number of requests per task from the ALB. Step scaling reacts to CloudWatch alarms, and scheduled scaling handles predictable patterns. With Fargate, there are no nodes to scale, which removes the second level entirely.
In both cases: scale out quickly, scale in slowly, and make sure apps start fast and shut down gracefully. Our ECS services use target tracking on CPU and request count, with a minimum of two tasks.
These three are often mentioned together, but they solve different problems.

Docker is the tool for building and running containers on a single machine. You write a Dockerfile, build an image, and run containers from it. It's perfect for development and for packaging, but by itself it doesn't manage containers across many machines, or restart them when a machine fails. Kubernetes is a container orchestrator. It runs containers across a cluster of machines, and handles scheduling, self-healing, scaling, rolling updates, service discovery and configuration. It's very powerful and portable across clouds, but complex to operate, with many concepts to learn. ECS is AWS's own container orchestrator. It does the same core job as Kubernetes: scheduling, healing, scaling and deployment, but it's simpler, deeply integrated with IAM, ALB and CloudWatch, and with Fargate there are no servers to manage. The trade-off is that it's AWS only.
So they work together: Docker builds the images, and Kubernetes or ECS runs them in production.

In our platform, we build images with Docker in the pipeline, push them to ECR, and ECS on Fargate runs them. For a product team on AWS, ECS gives most of the benefits with much less operational work.
These three describe how far automation goes in the path from a code change to production.

Continuous integration means every change merged into the main branch is automatically built and tested, many times a day. Problems are found within minutes, while the change is still fresh in the developer's mind, instead of in a painful integration phase later. Continuous delivery goes further: every change that passes the pipeline is in a releasable state, and deploying it to production is a simple, automated action, but a human decides when, usually with an approval. Continuous deployment removes that last manual step: every change that passes all automated checks goes to production automatically, with no human approval.
Continuous deployment needs very strong automated testing, monitoring, and feature flags, because there's no human gate.

In a regulated GxP environment like ours, we practise continuous integration and continuous delivery, but not continuous deployment. Every change is built, tested and scanned automatically, and the same artifact is promoted through FV, TechOps, UAT and production. But each release to validated environments needs formal approvals and test evidence. Automation makes those releases fast and repeatable, while the approvals satisfy compliance.

Our pipelines run on an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, inherited from CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, before IQVIA acquired it, and they deploy to both our on-premise nodes and AWS. The flow is split into a build that runs on every change and a release that promotes one artifact through environments.

The build pipeline is written in YAML and lives in the repository. On every pull request and merge, it restores packages, builds, runs unit tests and collects code coverage, then runs SonarQube analysis. If the quality gate fails, for example low coverage on new code or a new vulnerability, the build fails and the pull request can't be merged. On success, it publishes versioned artifacts and Docker images, tagged with the version and commit.

The release then deploys that exact same artifact through our environments: FV for formal verification, TechOps, UAT for user acceptance, and finally production. We never rebuild between environments, so what was tested is exactly what goes live. Each stage has approvals, automated smoke tests, and release evidence attached, like test results and the change record, which matters in a GxP product.
My part is integration and release coordination across about 5 scrum teams: making sure each team's changes are in the right release branch, versions are tagged, and environments are verified.
Both define how code is built and deployed in Azure DevOps, but they're managed very differently.

YAML pipelines are defined as code, in a file in the repository. That means they're versioned with the application, reviewed in pull requests, and can be branched and rolled back like code. They support multi-stage pipelines covering build and deployment in one definition, reusable templates shared across many repositories, and environments with approvals and checks, like business hours or required reviewers. Classic release pipelines are configured in the web UI. They have a visual designer with stages, tasks and pre- and post-deployment approvals, which is easy to understand at a glance and still common, especially on older on-premises Azure DevOps Server installations. But changes aren't versioned with the code, they're harder to review, and harder to reuse across projects.
Microsoft's direction is YAML, and new features arrive there first.

In our environment, we have both, because our on-premise Azure DevOps Server grew out of Cenduit's Team Foundation Server. Builds are YAML pipelines with shared templates, and some release flows still use classic releases with their visual approval stages, which our validation team is used to. Moving releases to YAML environments with checks is a gradual migration.
Our branching and tagging strategy is designed for controlled releases and full traceability, which matters in a regulated product.

Developers work on short-lived feature branches created from the main development branch. Every change goes through a pull request with at least one review, a linked work item, and build validation, so tests and the SonarQube gate must pass before merging. When we prepare a release, we cut a release branch for that version. Only fixes for that release go into it, while new features continue on main. If production needs an urgent fix, we create a hotfix branch from the release tag, fix it, release it, and merge the fix back to main so it isn't lost.

Tags are essential. Every build that's deployed gets a tag with its semantic version, so we can always tell exactly which code is running in each environment. Auditors rely on that, and so does support when investigating a production issue.

My role here is release integration: I coordinate which changes from about 5 scrum teams go into each release branch, check merges and versions, and make sure the tags and release notes match what was deployed.

Ansible is an automation tool for configuring servers and deploying software. It's agentless: it connects over SSH to Linux machines, or WinRM to Windows, and runs tasks defined in YAML playbooks, organised into reusable roles.

In our environment, we used Ansible together with Python and Shell scripts to install releases across multiple nodes: copying artifacts, stopping and starting services, updating configuration, and running checks, in the same way on every server. That replaced manual, step-by-step installations, which were slow and error-prone across many machines.

Idempotency is a core Ansible idea. An idempotent task can run many times and always leaves the system in the same final state. For example, "ensure this package is installed" or "ensure this file has this content". If it's already in that state, Ansible does nothing and reports "ok", instead of "changed". That means you can safely rerun a playbook after a partial failure, and it only fixes what's needed. Modules like package, copy and template are idempotent by design. Raw shell commands aren't, so you have to add conditions like "creates" or "when" to make them safe.
That safe-rerun property made our multi-node deployments much more reliable.
These are three strategies for releasing a new version with minimal risk and downtime.

A rolling deployment replaces instances gradually: start a new instance, wait until it's healthy, then stop an old one, and repeat. It needs little extra capacity and it's the default on ECS and Kubernetes. The downside is that old and new versions run side by side for a while, so they must be compatible, and rolling back means another rolling deployment. Blue-green runs two complete environments. Blue serves production, and you deploy the new version to green, test it there, then switch all traffic at once, usually at the load balancer. Rollback is instant, just switch back. The cost is double the resources during the switch, and database changes must work for both. Canary sends a small percentage of real traffic to the new version, like 5 percent, while monitoring error rates and latency. If metrics stay healthy, you increase gradually to 100 percent. If not, you roll back, and only a small share of users were affected.
My choice depends on risk: rolling for routine changes, blue-green for instant rollback, and canary for high-risk changes with good metrics.
Our ECS services use rolling deployments with health checks and automatic rollback.
Rollback with database changes is tricky because you can redeploy old code in minutes, but you can't easily "undeploy" a schema change, especially if new data was written.

So the main strategy is to make rollback of the code always possible, by keeping schema changes backward compatible. That's the expand and contract pattern. In the first release, we only expand: add new columns or tables, nullable or with defaults, and never remove or rename anything the old version uses. The new code uses the new structure. If we roll back, the old code still works, because everything it needs is still there. Only in a later release, once the new version is proven, do we contract, removing old columns.

Other safeguards: keep the previous artifact and release tag ready to redeploy. Use feature flags, so new behaviour can be switched off without a deployment. Take a backup or snapshot before risky migrations. Have tested down scripts for changes that really need reversing. And document the rollback plan in the release, with clear decision criteria and who decides.

In a GxP release, the rollback plan is part of the change record, reviewed before release. In practice, with expand and contract, we've never needed to reverse a schema change; rolling back code was enough.
In a regulated GxP environment, a release has to be not only correct, but provably controlled, because the software affects clinical trials and patient safety.

That adds several things. Every change links to a requirement or a defect, with an impact assessment that decides what must be retested. There are formal environments with sign-offs: FV for formal verification, TechOps, UAT for user acceptance, and then production, each with documented test results. Segregation of duties: the person who writes the code isn't the one who approves or deploys it to production. Deployments use validated, repeatable scripts, not manual steps, and there's an audit trail of who deployed what, when, and with which approval. Releases come with release notes, traceability matrices and evidence that auditors can review. And any deviation, like a failed step or an emergency fix, is documented and assessed.
This sounds slow, but automation makes it manageable. Pipelines produce much of the evidence automatically, like test reports, quality gates and deployment logs.

I coordinate integration and releases across about 5 scrum teams, so I see this every release: checking every change is approved and traced, the tagged artifact matches what was tested, and the evidence is complete before production.
Logs, metrics and traces are the three pillars of observability. Each answers a different question about a running system.

Logs are detailed records of individual events: "shipment 123 failed validation", with context like the user, the correlation id and the error. They answer "what exactly happened?" They're best as structured JSON, so they can be searched and filtered, and in our case they go to CloudWatch Logs. Metrics are numbers measured over time: request rate, latency percentiles, error rate, CPU, memory, queue depth. They're cheap to store and fast to query, so they're what dashboards and alarms are built on. They answer "is something wrong, and how bad is it?" Traces follow a single request across all the services it touches, with timing for each step. They answer "where in the chain is the problem?", like which service or database call made a request slow.
They work best together. An alarm on a metric tells me error rates are up. A trace shows which service is failing. And the logs for that request, found by its correlation id, show the actual error.
In our platform, CloudWatch and Grafana cover metrics and dashboards, and our correlation-id work links logs across services.
We use CloudWatch as the main source of logs and metrics in AWS, and Grafana as the place where we look at everything together.

In CloudWatch, our services send structured JSON logs to CloudWatch Logs, and we use Logs Insights to query them, for example filtering by correlation id, or counting errors by type over the last hour. AWS services publish metrics automatically: ECS CPU and memory, ALB request counts, latency and 5xx errors, RDS CPU and connections, Lambda errors and duration. We add custom metrics for business events, like shipments processed. CloudWatch alarms watch the important metrics and notify the team through SNS when thresholds are breached.

Grafana then combines CloudWatch and other sources into dashboards: one per service, showing the golden signals, and one per business flow, like the shipment pipeline from request to vendor confirmation. During releases, we watch a release dashboard to compare error rates and latency before and after deployment.

For background work, like scheduled jobs, vendor files and dead-letter queues, I also built AlertWatchDog, a small Azure Functions tool that checks them every few minutes and alerts the team in Teams, escalating if nobody responds. The principle I follow is alert on symptoms users feel, like errors and latency, not on every internal metric. For example, after fixing our slow shipment query, we added a latency alarm and a dashboard panel for that endpoint, so any regression shows up immediately.
The golden signals are four metrics, from Google's SRE practices, that tell you whether a service is healthy from the user's point of view.

Latency is how long requests take. I track percentiles, like p95 and p99, not just the average, because the average hides the slow requests that users actually complain about. It's also worth separating the latency of successful and failed requests, since fast errors can make latency look good. Traffic is how much demand the system is handling, like requests per second, or messages per second for a queue consumer. Errors is the rate of failing requests: 5xx responses, exceptions, and for messaging, dead-lettered messages. Saturation is how full the system is: CPU, memory, database connection pool usage, thread pool queues, or queue depth. Saturation often warns you before latency and errors get worse.
Together, they give a quick, reliable picture of any service, and they're a good basis for alerts and service level objectives.
In our Grafana dashboards, every service has these four at the top. For RabbitMQ consumers, saturation means queue depth and consumer lag, which is what warned us early in later broker issues.
Root-cause analysis has two phases: first stabilise the system, then understand why it happened, so it doesn't happen again.

Stabilise first. Mitigate the user impact as quickly as possible, by rolling back a deployment, scaling out, failing over, or disabling a feature with a flag, and keep stakeholders informed. The full investigation can wait; users can't. Then gather evidence: build a timeline of when it started, what changed just before, like a deployment, configuration or traffic pattern, and what the dashboards, logs and traces show. Logs filtered by correlation id from affected requests are very useful. Then form hypotheses and test them against the evidence, instead of jumping to conclusions. I use the 5 Whys technique to go past the symptom. For example, the API timed out; why? The database was slow; why? A query was scanning; why? A new filter was non-SARGable; why wasn't it caught? No performance check for that query. The last answer is usually the real fix.
Finally, fix the root cause, add monitoring or tests so it can't recur silently, and write a blameless post-incident review with clear actions and owners.
Our RabbitMQ incident in mid-2024 followed exactly this path, ending in publisher confirms and new alerts.
A good alert is one that someone should act on, right now, and knows how to act on.

First, it must be actionable. When it fires, there's a clear action, ideally documented in a linked runbook: what it means, how to check, and how to mitigate. If the honest response is "ignore it", it shouldn't be an alert. Second, it's based on user impact, not internal noise. Alert on symptoms, like error rate or latency above a threshold, sustained for several minutes, rather than on a single CPU spike that resolves on its own. Third, it's routed to the right owner with the right severity. A critical production issue pages the on-call person, while a warning goes to a team channel or a ticket. Fourth, alerts are reviewed regularly. If an alert fires often and nobody acts, it's either tuned or deleted, because alert fatigue makes people ignore the important ones.
A few alerts that are almost always worth having: high error rate, high latency, messages in a dead-letter queue, and a business flow suddenly dropping to zero.

That last one came from our RabbitMQ incident in mid-2024: we added an alert when the incoming shipment update rate drops to zero during business hours, because silence was the symptom. The same idea drives AlertWatchDog, the Azure Functions monitoring tool I built: it alerts when an expected job run or vendor file doesn't happen.
RabbitMQ and Kafka are both used for messaging, but they're built on different models.

RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker. Producers publish to exchanges, which route messages to queues using bindings and routing keys. Consumers take messages from queues, acknowledge them, and then the message is removed. It has very flexible routing, per-message acknowledgements, priorities, and dead-letter queues, so it's excellent for task queues, commands, and work distribution, where each message should be processed once by one worker. Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, append-only log. Producers write events to topics, and the events are kept for a retention period, whether they've been read or not. Consumers track their own position, called the offset, so many independent consumer groups can read the same events, and you can replay history. It provides ordering within a partition and very high throughput.
So I choose RabbitMQ for commands and work queues with complex routing, and Kafka for event streaming, when several services need the same events, or replay, retention and high volume matter.
In our platform, RabbitMQ handles service-to-service workflows like shipment processing.
These are the three core concepts that give Kafka its scalability and ordering.

A topic is a named stream of events, like "shipment-events". Each topic is split into partitions. A partition is an ordered, append-only log, where each event gets a sequential offset. Partitions are spread across brokers, which is how Kafka scales. When producing, the producer chooses the partition, usually by hashing the message key. So all events with the same key, like the same study id or shipment id, always go to the same partition, and stay in order. Ordering is only guaranteed within a partition, not across the whole topic.

A consumer group is a set of consumers that share the work of reading a topic. Each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group at a time. So if a topic has six partitions, up to six consumers in a group can work in parallel; a seventh would sit idle. The partition count therefore limits parallelism. Different consumer groups read the same topic independently, each with its own offsets. When consumers join or leave, Kafka rebalances partitions among them.
Consumers commit offsets after processing, so after a restart they continue where they left off.
In RabbitMQ, producers never publish directly to a queue. They publish to an exchange, and the exchange type decides how messages are routed to the queues bound to it.

A direct exchange routes by exact match. A message with routing key "shipment.created" goes to queues bound with exactly that key. It's good for commands and simple point-to-point routing. A topic exchange routes by pattern. Routing keys are dot-separated words, and bindings can use wildcards: a star matches exactly one word, and a hash matches zero or more. For example, a queue bound with "shipment.*.created" gets created events from any region. It's the most flexible and the one I use most. A fanout exchange ignores the routing key and copies every message to all bound queues, which is a simple broadcast, like notifying several services that reference data changed. A headers exchange routes based on message header values instead of the routing key, which is rarely needed.
There's also the default exchange, which routes to a queue with the same name as the routing key.
In our platform, we use topic exchanges for domain events, like shipment status changes, so each consuming service binds only to the event patterns it cares about.

Situation: In mid-2024, our RabbitMQ broker hit its memory high watermark during a busy period. When that happens, RabbitMQ blocks publishing connections, and some connections were dropped. The problem was that our services published shipment status updates without publisher confirms, which is fire-and-forget. So for about 40 minutes, about 1,200 status updates simply vanished, with no errors in our logs. We found out when study teams reported shipments stuck in the wrong status.
Task: I was on support duty, so my job was to restore the missing data first, and then make sure messages could never be lost silently again.

Action: For recovery, I replayed the vendor status files for that window. That was safe because our consumers upsert, so reprocessing was idempotent. For the permanent fix, I enabled publisher confirms. The channel is put into confirm mode, and the broker acknowledges each message once it's safely stored, or sends a negative acknowledgement. In RabbitMQ.Client 7, BasicPublishAsync then waits for the confirm and throws on failure, so we can retry. Messages are persistent, queues are durable, and consumers use manual acks with dead-letter queues. We also tuned memory, and added alerts on memory, blocked connections, and the incoming update rate dropping to zero during business hours.
Result: Throughput cost was about 5 percent, and since then we haven't lost a message.

messages.note: No ack or a nack within timeout: retry or alert

s: These are the three delivery guarantees a messaging system can offer, and each is a trade-off between losing messages and duplicating them.

At-most-once means a message is delivered once or not at all. There are no retries, so if something fails along the way, the message is lost. It's only acceptable for data where loss doesn't matter, like some metrics. At-least-once means the system keeps retrying until the message is acknowledged, so nothing is lost. But if a consumer processes a message and crashes before acknowledging, it will receive it again, so duplicates are possible. That's why consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once means no loss and no duplicates. It's only truly available within limits, like Kafka transactions for read-process-write inside Kafka. Across different systems, like a broker and a database, it's achieved "effectively" through at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
In practice, at-least-once with idempotent consumers is the standard choice for business data.

That's how our platform works. Publishing uses confirms, so the broker definitely has the message, consumers acknowledge only after successful processing, and every message has an id, which consumers use to skip duplicates.
An idempotent consumer produces the same result whether it processes a message once or several times. With at-least-once delivery, duplicates will happen, so this is essential.

There are a few techniques, and I often combine them. First, every message carries a unique message id. The consumer keeps an inbox table of processed ids, and skips any message it has already seen. The key detail is that the insert into the inbox table and the business update happen in the same database transaction, so either both are saved or neither is. Second, natural idempotency: design operations so repeating them is harmless. "Set shipment status to Delivered" is idempotent, while "increment delivered count" isn't. Upserts instead of inserts, and unique constraints, help too. Third, for ordering problems, a version or timestamp check, so an older event can't overwrite newer data.
Then the failure path: retry transient errors with backoff, and after a few attempts move the message to a dead-letter queue, instead of retrying forever.
This property saved us in our RabbitMQ incident in mid-2024. Because consumers upsert, I could safely replay a whole window of vendor files without creating duplicates.
A dead-letter queue, or DLQ, is a separate queue where messages go when they can't be processed successfully, so they don't block the main queue or get lost.

Messages typically end up there for three reasons: processing keeps failing after a set number of retries, for example because of bad data or a bug; the message is explicitly rejected; or it expires. Without a DLQ, a "poison message" that always fails can be retried forever, blocking other messages or burning resources. With a DLQ, it's moved aside, and normal processing continues.

In RabbitMQ, you configure a dead-letter exchange on the queue, and rejected or expired messages are routed there. With quorum queues, you can also set a delivery limit. In Kafka, there's no built-in DLQ, so the consumer publishes failed messages to a retry topic or a dead-letter topic itself. In AWS SQS, you configure a redrive policy with a maximum receive count.

The most important rule is that a DLQ must never be silent. We alert on any message in a DLQ, someone inspects it, fixes the cause, and then replays the messages back to the main queue. Our consumers are idempotent, so replaying is safe.
The transactional outbox pattern solves a very common reliability problem in microservices: updating your database and publishing an event as one reliable step.

The problem is that the database and the message broker can't share one transaction. If you save the change and then publish, the publish might fail after the commit, and other services never hear about it. If you publish first and then the save fails, other services react to something that never happened. Either way, systems disagree.

The outbox pattern fixes this. In the same database transaction as the business change, you also insert a row into an outbox table, containing the event. Because it's one local transaction, either both are saved or neither is. Then a separate background relay reads unpublished rows from the outbox, publishes them to RabbitMQ or Kafka, and marks them as published. If publishing fails, it simply retries later. This gives at-least-once publishing, so consumers must be idempotent. The relay can poll the table, or use change data capture with a tool like Debezium.
In our shipment flow, the shipment update and its outbox event are saved together, and a background service publishes them with publisher confirms. If the broker is down, events just wait.
Authentication and authorization are two separate questions, and they always happen in that order.

Authentication answers "who are you?" It's proving identity, like logging in with single sign-on, or an API validating a token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry, and then knowing the user's identity and claims. Authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" It's checking permissions, through roles, claims, policies, and resource-level checks, like "can this user see this specific study?"

In ASP.NET Core, they're two middleware: UseAuthentication runs first and sets HttpContext.User, then UseAuthorization evaluates the Authorize attributes and policies on the endpoint. The status codes reflect the difference too. 401 Unauthorized actually means not authenticated: no valid token. 403 Forbidden means authenticated, but not allowed.

In our clinical system, authorization is the harder and more important part. A user with a valid login and the right role still mustn't see data from a study they're not assigned to. So beyond roles, we have resource-based checks on every request that touches study data. Missing that kind of check is the number one API risk in the OWASP list.
A JWT, or JSON Web Token, is a compact, signed token that carries claims about a user. It has three parts, separated by dots, each base64url-encoded.

The header says which algorithm was used to sign it, like RS256, and which key. The payload contains the claims: sub for the user id, roles or scopes, iss for who issued it, aud for which API it's meant for, exp for when it expires, and so on. The signature is created by the identity provider with its private key, over the header and payload.

To validate it, the API checks the signature using the issuer's public key, usually downloaded from its JWKS endpoint, which proves the token wasn't tampered with and came from the trusted issuer. Then it checks the issuer and audience match what's expected, and that the token isn't expired or used before its not-before time, allowing small clock skew. Only then are the claims trusted.

Two important points. A JWT is signed, not encrypted, so anyone can read the payload; never put secrets or personal data in it. And because it's validated without a server call, it can't be revoked easily. That's why we keep access tokens short, 15 minutes, and added a denylist for logout.
The authorization code flow with PKCE is the recommended way for apps to log users in with OpenID Connect and get tokens to call APIs.

First, the app creates a random secret called the code verifier, and sends a hashed version of it, the code challenge, when it redirects the user to the identity provider's login page. The user logs in there, through single sign-on, and the app never sees their password. The identity provider then redirects back to the app with a short-lived, one-time authorization code. The app exchanges that code at the token endpoint, sending the original code verifier. The provider checks that the verifier matches the challenge, which proves the same app that started the login is finishing it, so a stolen code is useless. It then returns tokens: an access token, which is the OAuth part, for calling APIs; an ID token, which is the OpenID Connect part, saying who the user is; and often a refresh token.
PKCE was originally for mobile and single-page apps that can't keep a client secret, but it's now recommended for all clients, and it replaces the old implicit flow.
Our web apps use this flow with our corporate identity provider, and our APIs validate the access tokens.

Situation: In 2024, a security review found that in one of our IRT modules, a user's token still worked for up to 60 minutes after they clicked logout. That's because JWTs are validated statelessly: the API checks the signature and expiry, but never asks a server whether the user has logged out. In a clinical system, a stolen or shared token staying valid after logout was not acceptable.
Task: I was asked to make logout effective immediately, without making every API call a heavy round trip to the identity provider.

Action: I did it in layers. First, I reduced the access token lifetime to 15 minutes, so any leaked token has a small window. Second, on logout, we revoke the refresh token on the server, clear the cookies, and end the identity provider session. Third, for the remaining minutes, I added a denylist. When a user logs out, the token's unique id, the jti claim, goes into ElastiCache Redis, with a time-to-live equal to the token's remaining lifetime, so the list stays tiny. In the JWT bearer OnTokenValidated event, every API checks that list. If Redis is unavailable, we fail closed. We also revoke on password change or role removal. I added a Playwright test that replays an old token after logout and expects a 401.
Result: Old tokens are now rejected immediately, the check adds only about 1 ms per request, and the APIs stay essentially stateless.

Situation: Some users of our IRT system started getting a 400 error, "request header too long", and couldn't use the application at all. We had about 30 support tickets, and the pattern was clear: it only affected users assigned to many studies.
Task: I picked up the investigation, with the goal of fixing it properly, not just for the current users.

Action: I reproduced it with a test user in many groups. Browsers send all cookies for a domain on every request, and servers cap the total header size, about 16 KB in our setup. Our SSO authentication cookie stored every role and group claim, so for these users it was split into several chunked cookies totalling about 13 KB, and with other cookies on the domain, it went over the limit. Raising the server limit would only postpone the problem, and every request would still carry kilobytes of cookie. So I moved the authentication ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, backed by ElastiCache Redis, so the cookie only holds a small session key. Study permissions are now loaded per request through a cached claims transformation. I also narrowed the cookie domain and path. It went through our regulated release process.
Result: The cookie dropped from about 13 KB to under 1 KB, the tickets stopped, and users noticed nothing except that it worked.
Reverse tabnabbing is a phishing attack that abuses links opening in a new tab.

When a page opens a link with target equals blank, historically the new page got a reference back to the original page through window.opener. A malicious or compromised external site could then use window.opener.location to silently redirect the original tab, for example to a fake login page that looks exactly like ours. The user finishes reading the new tab, goes back to what they think is our app, sees "your session expired, please log in", and enters their credentials into the attacker's page.

The fix is to add rel equals noopener noreferrer to links with target blank. noopener removes the window.opener reference, and noreferrer also stops the referrer header from leaking our URL. For links opened in JavaScript, use window.open with the noopener feature. Modern browsers now treat target blank as noopener by default, but being explicit is still best practice, and security scanners flag it. A Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header adds another layer.
I fixed this in IRT. A security scan flagged it, and I updated about 40 external links, created a shared link component that sets rel by default, and added a lint rule so it can't come back.
For APIs, the OWASP API Security Top 10 is the most relevant list, and a few risks matter most in practice.

Broken access control is the number one risk, especially broken object-level authorization: a user changes an id in the URL and gets someone else's data. Prevention is checking authorization for every specific resource, not just at the endpoint level. In our clinical system, that means checking study assignment on every request. Next, broken authentication: weak token validation, long-lived tokens, or no logout. We validate tokens fully, keep them short, and have a denylist. Injection: prevented with parameterised queries through EF Core, and input validation. Excessive data exposure and mass assignment: prevented with DTOs for input and output. Lack of rate limiting: prevented with rate limiting middleware and gateway throttling. Security misconfiguration: verbose errors, open CORS, default settings, prevented with secure defaults and reviews. And vulnerable components: dependency scanning and SonarQube in the pipeline.
Plus logging and monitoring, so attacks are actually noticed, without logging sensitive data.
These are part of our code review checklist for every new endpoint, which catches most problems before they ship.
XSS and CSRF are both browser-based attacks, but they work in opposite directions.

XSS, cross-site scripting, is when an attacker manages to run their own JavaScript inside your site, usually by injecting it through user input that's displayed without proper encoding, like a comment or a name field. That script runs with your site's privileges, so it can read data on the page, steal tokens from localStorage, or act as the user. Prevention: encode output, which React does by default; sanitise any HTML you must render, with DOMPurify; use a Content Security Policy to block inline and unknown scripts; and keep session cookies HttpOnly, so scripts can't read them.

CSRF, cross-site request forgery, is when an attacker's website makes the user's browser send a request to your site, and the browser automatically includes the user's cookies, so the request looks legitimate. For example, a hidden form that submits a change. Prevention: SameSite cookies, which stop cookies being sent on cross-site requests, anti-forgery tokens in forms, which ASP.NET Core supports built in, and checking the Origin header.
APIs using bearer tokens in headers, not cookies, aren't vulnerable to CSRF, but they are to XSS if tokens sit in localStorage.
My rule for secrets is simple: they never appear in source code, configuration files in git, container images or logs.

Secrets live in a managed store. On AWS, that's Secrets Manager for credentials that should rotate, and Parameter Store SecureString for others, encrypted with KMS. In Azure, Key Vault, and in pipelines, secret variables. Services read them at runtime using their IAM role, so there are no keys to bootstrap the keys. Access follows least privilege: each service can read only its own secrets, per environment, and access is audited through CloudTrail. Secrets are rotated regularly. For RDS, Secrets Manager does it automatically, and apps re-read the secret if a connection fails. For local development, developers use .NET user secrets or a local file that's excluded from git.
Detection matters too: secret scanning in CI and pre-commit hooks, like gitleaks, so if someone accidentally commits a key, it's caught and rotated immediately. And logs mask sensitive values.

The same principle applies to tools I've built. In our CIRT MCP server, each user's Azure DevOps personal access token comes from their own environment, never from a file in the repository, and the server acts with that user's own permissions.

The Model Context Protocol, MCP, is an open protocol that standardises how AI applications connect to external tools and data. A good way to think of it is like USB-C for AI: one standard connector instead of a custom integration for every pair of tools.

There are three roles. The host is the AI application, like Claude, Cursor or GitHub Copilot. Inside it, an MCP client connects to MCP servers. An MCP server exposes capabilities: tools, which are actions the model can call, like "queue a build"; resources, which are data the model can read; and prompts, which are reusable templates. The client discovers what the server offers, including each tool's name, description and input schema, and the model decides when to call a tool based on the user's request. Communication uses JSON-RPC, over stdio for local servers, or HTTP for remote ones.
The benefit is that you build an integration once, and it works with any MCP-compatible host. Before MCP, every AI tool needed its own plugin format.

I built the CIRT MCP server, with about 77 tools, which lets AI agents run builds, releases and multi-node deployments on our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. It cut deployments from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.

The CIRT MCP server lets AI agents run build, release and multi-node deployment operations on our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. I designed it around one idea: the model should always be able to pick the right tool and use it correctly.

The about 77 tools are grouped by domain: roughly 15 for builds, 20 for releases and approvals, 25 for multi-node deployments, and 17 for information, like logs, artifacts and environment checks. Names follow a verb-noun convention, like queue_build, get_release_status and deploy_release_stage, so the model chooses correctly. Each description says when to use the tool and what it returns, and parameters are typed with enums and examples, like the environment names FV, TechOps, UAT and Prod. Outputs are short, structured summaries, like status, failing step and a link, not raw JSON dumps, to save the model's context. Long operations return an id, and a separate status tool polls, so nothing blocks for hours. A few composite tools, like deploying to an environment and verifying versions on all nodes, reduce multi-step mistakes.
It's built in C# with the official MCP SDK, runs locally over stdio, and calls Azure DevOps with each user's own permissions.
The result: deployments went from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.
An MCP server lets an AI model take real actions, so safety has to be designed in, not added later. I think about it in a few layers.

First, identity and least privilege. The server acts with the calling user's own credentials and permissions, never a shared admin token. So the AI can never do more than that user could do manually. Second, separating risk. Read-only tools, like getting status or logs, are separate from write tools, like queuing a build or deploying. Destructive or production-affecting actions require explicit confirmation, and our existing human approval gates in Azure DevOps stay in place. The AI doesn't bypass the GxP process. Third, input validation. Every input is validated against a schema, with allow-lists for things like environment names, so a model can't pass something unexpected. Fourth, auditability. Every tool call is logged with who, what, parameters and result. Fifth, protection against prompt injection. Content returned from tools, like logs, is treated as data, not instructions, and tools never execute arbitrary commands.
