And clear errors, so the model reports a failure instead of guessing.
In our CIRT MCP server, these choices were what made teammates comfortable using it on real UAT deployments.
A good tool definition makes it easy for the model to choose the right tool and call it correctly the first time. It's really API design, but the consumer is an AI model.

The name should be specific and verb-first, like queue_build or get_release_status, not something vague like "build" or "helper". The description is the most important part: it should say what the tool does, when to use it, and when not to, what it returns, and maybe a short example. The model reads it to decide. The input schema should be small and typed, with enums for fixed choices, like environment names, sensible defaults, and only truly required fields marked as required. Fewer, clearer parameters mean fewer mistakes. The output should be compact and structured, like a status, the key fields and a link, instead of huge raw responses that waste the model's context. And errors should be clear and actionable, like "environment UAT2 doesn't exist; valid values are FV, TechOps, UAT, Prod", so the model can correct itself.
Also, avoid overlapping tools that do almost the same thing, because the model will pick the wrong one.
These rules came directly from building our CIRT MCP server with about 77 tools.
I use GitHub Copilot and Cursor every day as a productivity tool, but I treat their output like code from a new teammate: useful, but always reviewed.

Inline completions handle repetitive code very well: DTO mappings, boilerplate, simple tests and LINQ queries. Chat helps me understand unfamiliar code quickly, like an older module or a library I haven't used before. In Cursor, agent mode is great for multi-file changes, refactors and upgrade chores, like updating packages or replacing an API across a solution. We use project rules, so it follows our conventions, like our logging and error handling patterns. I also use it to generate unit tests and test data, to draft SQL and pipeline YAML, and to write documentation and pull request descriptions.

What I don't do is accept large changes without reading them, or let it touch security-sensitive code without careful review. Everything still goes through compilation, tests, SonarQube and code review.
The biggest impact for me was in building the CIRT MCP server, where the AI tools sped up writing the tool wrappers, and the server itself now lets those same tools run our deployments.
I review AI-generated code with the same standards as any pull request, and in some areas, more strictly, because it can look very confident while being wrong.

For accuracy, I read the logic carefully: edge cases, null handling, error handling, and async correctness, like missing awaits or blocking calls. I check that it actually does what I asked, not something similar. I check APIs and packages against official documentation, because models sometimes invent methods, use outdated APIs, or suggest packages that don't exist, which can even be a supply-chain risk if someone registers that name. For security, I look for injection risks, missing authorization checks, hard-coded secrets, unsafe deserialisation, and sensitive data in logs.

Then I verify, not trust. It must compile without warnings, pass unit tests, which I often write or review myself, pass SonarQube and security scans, and actually run. For important logic, I ask for or write tests for the edge cases first.
And the final rule: I only commit code I understand well enough to explain in a code review, and maintain later. If I can't explain it, it doesn't go in.
Good prompting is mostly about giving the model the same context and clarity you'd give a new colleague.

First, context and goal: the role, the relevant code or files, the exact outcome I want, and constraints, like ".NET 10, use our existing logging pattern, don't add new packages". Vague prompts get generic answers. Second, examples: if I want a particular format or style, I show one or two examples of input and output, which is called few-shot prompting. Third, decomposition: for complex tasks, I ask for a plan first, review it, and then ask for the implementation step by step, instead of one huge request. Fourth, an explicit output format, like JSON with given fields, or "only the changed method". Fifth, iteration with real feedback: I paste the actual compiler error or failing test output back to the model, which is much more effective than saying "it doesn't work".
For tools and agents, the same ideas apply to system prompts and tool descriptions: be specific about when to do something and when not to.
When I introduced our MCP server to the team, I wrote 10 example prompts in the README, and good examples were one of the biggest factors in people succeeding on their first try.
RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is a way to make a language model answer questions using your own, up-to-date documents, instead of relying only on what it learned during training.

It has two phases. Ingestion: you take your documents, like wikis, runbooks or specifications, split them into chunks, create an embedding for each chunk, which is a vector that represents its meaning, and store them in a vector index. Querying: when a user asks a question, you embed the question, search the index for the most similar chunks, often combined with keyword search, and put those chunks into the prompt with instructions like "answer using only this context and cite sources". The model then answers grounded in that content.

The benefits are that answers use current and private information, without retraining the model, and they can cite sources, so users can verify them, which reduces hallucinations. The quality depends heavily on retrieval: chunk size, good metadata, hybrid search, and re-ranking. And access control matters: users must only retrieve documents they're allowed to see.
For example, a RAG assistant over our release runbooks and deployment logs could answer "why did the last UAT deployment fail" with links.

An AI agent is a language model running in a loop: it plans what to do, calls a tool, observes the result, and decides the next step, repeating until the goal is reached. Agentic orchestration is how you coordinate that loop, or several agents, safely and reliably.

Orchestration covers a few things. Which agents exist and their roles, for example a planner that breaks down the task, an executor that calls tools, and a reviewer that checks the result. Which tools each agent can use. And the limits: a maximum number of steps, cost or time budgets, permissions, and points where a human must approve. AutoGen, from Microsoft, is a framework for building multi-agent conversations, where agents with different roles talk to each other to solve a task. Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that works in your repository and terminal: it reads files, runs commands, edits code and runs tests, in that same plan-act-observe loop.
The key engineering concerns are reliability and safety: clear tool definitions, good error messages so agents can recover, logging every step, and human approval for risky actions.
Our CIRT MCP server is the tool layer that agents like Claude and Cursor use for deployments, with approvals kept for production.
Both give you access to powerful language models, but Azure OpenAI wraps them in enterprise controls.

With Azure OpenAI, the models run inside the company's own Azure tenant. You get enterprise security and identity, with Microsoft Entra ID authentication and role-based access, private networking through private endpoints, so traffic doesn't cross the public internet, data residency in chosen regions for compliance, and contractual commitments that your prompts and data aren't used to train models. It also integrates with Azure monitoring, content filtering and governance. Using a model provider's API directly is simpler to start with, may get the newest models and features sooner, and is great for prototypes, but the security, compliance and data agreements depend on that provider's terms and need separate review.

For a regulated healthcare company, the enterprise controls usually decide it. Clinical and personal data must be protected, so private networking, data residency and clear data-use terms are often requirements, not preferences.

My approach would be to prototype quickly, but build production features on the enterprise-approved platform, and design the code behind an abstraction, so we can switch models without rewriting the application.
Hallucinations can't be eliminated completely, so I reduce them at every layer and design the feature so that mistakes are caught.

First, ground the model in facts. Use RAG to supply relevant documents, and tool calls to fetch real data, like a release status, instead of letting the model guess. Instruct it clearly to say "I don't know" when the context doesn't contain the answer, and to cite sources. Second, constrain the output. Use structured outputs or function calling with a schema, and validate the result in code, like checking that an environment name or id actually exists, before acting on it. Third, evaluate systematically. Keep a test set of realistic questions with expected answers, run it whenever the prompt or model changes, and review samples by hand. Log prompts and outputs, with sensitive data protected, to find failure patterns. Fourth, keep a human in the loop for high-impact actions, like production deployments, and show users the sources so they can verify.
Lower temperature and smaller, focused tasks also help.
In our CIRT MCP server, the model never invents a status. It always calls a tool for real data, and production steps still need human approval.

Situation: After I built the CIRT MCP server, it could clearly save time, but teammates kept using the old manual, multi-person deployment process. It wasn't resistance to the idea. It was habit, and caution, because deployments to validated environments are serious in a GxP product.
Task: I wanted the team to adopt it because it genuinely helped, not because it was mandated.

Action: I started with their concerns. The server uses each person's own permissions, risky steps need confirmation, existing approval gates are unchanged, and every action is logged. Then I made it easy to try. I ran a 30-minute live demo on a real UAT deployment, wrote a README with 10 example prompts, and paired with the first 4 engineers on their first real runs. We started in lower-risk environments, FV and TechOps, before UAT and production. I set up a chat thread for questions and added the tools people asked for. For example, the tool to fetch logs for a failed step came from a teammate's request. And I measured the results, comparing 8 deployments with it and 8 without, so the value was visible, not just my opinion.
Result: Within about two months, most release deployments used it. Deployment time went from 6 hours to 2, and people needed from 6 to 1. The first users became champions who helped others.
The main difference is how the application is built and deployed: as one unit, or as many independent services.

A monolith is a single deployable application. All features share one codebase, one process and usually one database. It's simple to develop, test and debug, calls between parts are fast in-process calls, transactions are easy, and there's one thing to deploy and monitor. The downsides appear at scale: the codebase can become tangled, one team's change requires redeploying everything, you can only scale the whole application, and one bug can take everything down. Microservices split the application into independent services, each owning one business capability and its own data. Teams can deploy and scale their services independently, failures can be isolated, and each service can use the best technology. But you pay for that with network calls and their failures, distributed data and eventual consistency, and much more DevOps and observability work.
My view is that a well-structured modular monolith is often the right start, and microservices make sense when teams and parts of the system really need independence.
Our IRT platform is microservices, because many teams, about 5 per release, work on clearly separate areas like randomisation, supply and shipments.

I'd design randomisation around one absolute rule: every subject must get exactly one correct assignment, and two sites can never get the same slot, because errors here affect the trial's validity and patient safety.

The API would be a POST to studies, subject id, randomise, callable only by authorised users at that subject's site, with an idempotency key, so a retry after a timeout returns the same result instead of randomising twice. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. The service checks eligibility, then loads the study's randomisation scheme, which might be a pre-generated blocked list, or stratified by factors like age group or country. It allocates the next available slot for that stratum inside a database transaction, with locking, so concurrent requests from different sites can't take the same slot. In the same transaction, it records the assignment, writes a full audit record, and adds an outbox event. Then events trigger the rest asynchronously: kit assignment, supply checks and notifications.

Blinding is critical: the treatment arm is never returned to blinded users, and access to unblinded data is strictly separated and audited. Strong consistency matters more than availability here, so I'd choose SQL Server with proper transactions.
This reflects how IRT systems work, which is my domain.
I'd split this into a few services around clear responsibilities, connected by events.

An inventory service tracks stock at depots and sites, by kit type, lot and expiry date. A resupply service applies rules, like "when a site has fewer than five kits of a type, or kits are about to expire, create a shipment request", and it's triggered by events rather than polling. A shipment service owns the shipment lifecycle: requested, approved, dispatched, in transit, delivered, received, with every status change recorded. A vendor integration service exchanges data with depot vendors, which in practice is often SFTP files or partner APIs. The services communicate through events over RabbitMQ or Kafka, like KitAssigned, StockLow, ShipmentCreated and ShipmentDelivered, using the outbox pattern, and consumers are idempotent.

Key concerns: strong consistency when allocating scarce stock, cold-chain and temperature excursion handling, full audit trails for GxP, and reconciliation jobs that compare our data with vendor data. Dashboards show shipments stuck in a status too long.

This is close to what I work on. Our vendor exchange uses an ISftpClient abstraction over three libraries, and after our mid-2024 RabbitMQ incident, publishing uses confirms, so status updates can't be lost silently.
I'd design the CSV import as an asynchronous job, so large files don't block the API, and users get clear, complete feedback.

The upload goes to S3 through a presigned URL, or directly to the API for small files, with a size limit, like 5 MB, about 10,000 rows. The API creates an import job and immediately returns 202 Accepted with a job id. A background worker picks up the job, streams the file row by row, so memory stays flat, and validates in two passes: the structure, like headers, types and required fields, and then business rules, like "this site exists and is active in this study". A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. It collects every error with its row number, instead of stopping at the first one. Then, depending on the requirement, it either rejects the whole file if anything fails, which is usually right for clinical data, or imports valid rows. Valid rows are written in batches inside transactions. The client polls a status endpoint, or gets a notification, and can download an error report.
Safeguards: a file hash to block importing the same file twice, a limit of 2 concurrent imports per user, and a full audit record.
This is basically the CSV bulk import I designed and mostly built for IRT.
The API gateway pattern puts a single entry point in front of a set of microservices, so clients don't need to know about each individual service.

The gateway handles cross-cutting concerns in one place: routing requests to the right service, authentication and token validation, rate limiting and throttling, TLS termination, CORS, logging, and sometimes caching and request aggregation, where it combines several service calls into one response for the client. Backend-for-frontend, or BFF, takes that further: instead of one general gateway, each type of client gets its own thin backend. For example, the web app's BFF returns exactly what the web screens need, and the mobile BFF returns smaller payloads optimised for mobile. The front-end team often owns its BFF, so they can change it without affecting other clients. A BFF is also a good place to keep tokens server-side, instead of in the browser.
The important rule is to keep business logic out of the gateway. It should route and protect, not make business decisions, or it becomes a new monolith.
On AWS, that's API Gateway or an ALB. In our platform, the ALB routes to our services by path, and API Gateway provides per-partner throttling for external APIs.

The CAP theorem says that in a distributed system, when there's a network partition, meaning parts of the system can't talk to each other, you have to choose between consistency and availability. You can't fully have both.

Consistency means every read gets the most recent write, or an error. Availability means every request gets a response, even if it might be stale. Partition tolerance isn't really optional, because networks do fail. So the real choice is how the system behaves during a partition. A CP system refuses or delays some requests to stay correct. An AP system keeps answering, possibly with stale data, and reconciles later. When there's no partition, you can have both, and the trade-off becomes latency versus consistency, which is the PACELC extension.

The useful insight is that you choose per feature, not for the whole system. In clinical trials, allocating limited drug kits or a randomisation slot must be consistent, so it's CP: better to fail and retry than to promise the same kit to two sites. But dashboards, notifications and reports can be AP: slightly stale data is fine, and availability matters more.
That's exactly how our IRT platform is designed: transactional SQL for allocation, eventually consistent events for everything around it.
The saga pattern handles business transactions that span several microservices, where a single database transaction isn't possible.

The long transaction is split into a sequence of local transactions. Each service does its part in its own database, and then publishes an event or triggers the next step. If a step fails, the saga runs compensating actions to undo the earlier steps. For example: reserve kits, create a shipment, notify the vendor. If the vendor rejects the shipment, compensations cancel the shipment and release the reserved kits. Compensations are business actions, not database rollbacks, and they must be idempotent too.

There are two styles. Choreography: there's no central coordinator; each service listens for events and reacts, publishing its own events. It's simple for short flows, but the overall process becomes hard to see and change. Orchestration: a central orchestrator tells each service what to do next and tracks the state of the saga. It's easier to understand, monitor and change for complex flows, but the orchestrator is an extra component. AWS Step Functions or a durable workflow engine can play that role.
Sagas need the outbox for reliable events, idempotent consumers, and clear statuses so users see "pending" rather than inconsistent data.
In a GxP system, the audit trail is a regulatory requirement, under rules like FDA 21 CFR Part 11, so it must be complete, trustworthy and easy to review.

For every create, update and delete of regulated data, I'd record who did it, their user id and name; what changed, with the entity, old values and new values; when, with a synchronised UTC timestamp; where, like the source system or IP; and why, a reason for change where the process requires it. The audit store is append-only and tamper-evident: no user, not even admins through the application, can edit or delete audit records, and techniques like hash chaining or write-once storage can prove nothing was altered.

To capture changes consistently, I'd use an EF Core SaveChanges interceptor that inspects the change tracker and writes audit entries in the same transaction, so a change can't be saved without its audit. Business events, like "subject randomised", are audited explicitly too. Bulk operations that bypass the change tracker need their own auditing. The audit data is stored separately, with retention matching regulatory requirements, and there's a search UI for auditors.
Our correlation id is also stored in audit records, which links an audit entry to the exact request and logs.
I'd design rate limiting by deciding what to protect, who to limit, and where to enforce it.

First, the algorithm. Fixed window is the simplest, like 100 requests per minute, but allows bursts at window edges. Sliding window smooths that out. Token bucket allows short bursts, while enforcing an average rate, which suits most APIs. And concurrency limits cap how many requests run at the same time, which is good for expensive operations. Second, the key: per user, per API key or client, per IP address for anonymous traffic, or per tenant. Third, where. At the edge, API Gateway throttling and WAF rate rules stop abuse before it reaches services. In the application, ASP.NET Core's rate limiting middleware applies finer, per-endpoint policies. With multiple instances, in-app limits are per instance, so for a true global limit, I'd use a shared store, like Redis, with atomic counters.
And the response: return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header, and well-behaved clients back off. Monitor rejections, so limits are tuned rather than guessed.
In our platform, partners get per-key limits at API Gateway, and our CSV import has a concurrency limit of 2 imports per user.
I'd frame it as a system design for deployment automation driven by AI agents, which is the CIRT MCP server I built.

The requirements were: reduce our deployments from 6 hours and 6 people, keep all GxP approval gates, and work with our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. The clients are AI hosts, like Cursor, Claude or Copilot, which talk MCP to the server, running locally on each user's machine over stdio. The server has a tool layer of about 77 tools, an Azure DevOps client with timeouts and retries, a deployment plan model per environment, a status poller, and an audit logger. Azure DevOps remains the source of truth and does the actual work; the server orchestrates it.

The design choices: long-running work never blocks. Starting a deployment returns an id, and a status tool polls it. Steps are idempotent, so a failed deployment can resume from the failed step. Failures produce a clear, human-readable report. For safety, each user's own credentials are used, production still needs human approval, and every action is logged. For scaling, each user runs their own instance, so there's no shared server to become a bottleneck.
The result: 6 hours down to 2, and 6 people down to 1.
High availability means the system keeps working when individual components fail. The core idea is removing single points of failure at every layer.

For compute: run multiple instances of every service, spread across at least two availability zones, behind a load balancer that health-checks them and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones. The orchestrator, like ECS, automatically replaces failed tasks. Services are stateless, so any instance can handle any request. For data: managed databases with Multi-AZ, where a synchronous standby takes over automatically if the primary fails, plus automated backups and point-in-time recovery. Caches and brokers are clustered too. For the application: timeouts, retries and circuit breakers between services, queues to absorb failures, and graceful degradation, so non-critical features can fail without taking down core ones. For deployments: rolling or blue-green, with health checks and automatic rollback, because many outages come from changes.
And then test it: failover drills, chaos experiments like killing instances, and monitoring with alerts, so you know availability is real, not assumed.
In our IRT platform, every service runs at least two tasks across two availability zones, and RDS SQL Server is Multi-AZ, because sites in many countries need the system around the clock.

Let me explain it with a simple picture. When a new medicine is tested, thousands of patients in hospitals around the world take part. Each patient is randomly given either the new medicine or a comparison treatment, and nobody, not the doctor and not the patient, should know which one. That's what keeps the trial fair.

IRT is the system that makes that random choice fairly and secretly. When a site enrols a patient, IRT decides the treatment group and tells the site which numbered drug kit to give, so the kit number hides what's inside. It also acts like an automatic stock manager: it watches the stock at every hospital, sends shipments from depots before they run out, and tracks those shipments. It also supports electronic consent, and it tracks every kit that patients return, which we call drug accountability. Each trial is set up in IRT as a study, by our internal team using a tool called the Admin console: the hospitals, the treatment groups, the visit plan and the medicine kits.

Because mistakes here can affect patient safety and the trial results, it's a regulated, GxP system. Every change we make is tested, validated and approved, and every action is recorded in an audit trail.
So in one line: a fair, secret lottery plus a global pharmacy stock manager.

Why: our deployments ran on an on-premise Azure DevOps Server across many nodes, and they were largely manual. That server is a legacy of CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, which IQVIA acquired: new services moved to AWS, but validated builds and releases stayed on-premise, where AI assistants like Copilot and Cursor couldn't reach. A typical deployment took about 6 hours and needed about 6 people on a call, following steps, checking each node and copying logs around. It was slow, expensive and error-prone.

What: I built the CIRT MCP server. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, lets AI tools like Cursor, Claude Code and Copilot call external tools. My server exposes about 77 typed tools for builds, releases, approvals and multi-node deployments, wrapping the Azure DevOps APIs and our install scripts. So an engineer can say "deploy release 4.2 to UAT and verify all nodes", and the agent runs the right steps.

How: it's written in C# with the official MCP SDK, runs locally over stdio, and is packaged as a .NET global tool. Tools are grouped by domain with clear names and schemas, long operations return an id with a status tool to poll, and outputs are short structured summaries. For safety, it uses each user's own token, separates read and write tools, asks for confirmation on risky steps, keeps the existing approval gates, and logs every call.
Impact: measured on 8 vs 8 comparable deployments, time went from 6 hours to 2, and people from 6 to 1.

Situation: After the CIRT MCP server was in use, my lead asked a fair question: is the improvement real, or does it just feel faster? Claims like "6 hours to 2" need evidence, especially when you're asking a whole team to change how they work.
Task: I needed a like-for-like comparison, based on data from the system of record, not memory or estimates.

Action: I took 8 deployments from the two release cycles before the tool, and 8 similar deployments from the next two cycles using it. I matched them on the same environments and the same number of nodes, 4 to 6, and similar release sizes, so the comparison was fair. For duration, I used the release start and end timestamps from Azure DevOps. For people, I used the attendee lists of the deployment calls. I was also honest about the limits: it's a small sample, and part of the improvement came from cleaning up our install scripts while building the tools. And I was clear that approvals and validation still need humans.

Result: The average deployment time went from about 6 hours to about 2, and the people involved from 6 to 1. In business terms, that's roughly 20 person-hours down to 2 per deployment. Having real numbers made it much easier to get the rest of the team, and management, behind it.
Honestly, the hardest part wasn't the code. It was designing the tools so the AI reliably picked the right one out of about 77.

Early on, the model sometimes chose the wrong tool, or passed slightly wrong parameters, because some tools overlapped or had vague descriptions. I fixed that with a strict verb-noun naming convention, like queue_build and get_release_status, descriptions that say "use this when", enums for environment names instead of free text, and by removing overlapping tools. Outputs also mattered: returning raw JSON logs filled up the model's context, so I switched to short structured summaries with a link to the full details.

The second challenge was long-running deployments. A deployment can take an hour, and a tool call can't block that long. So start tools return an id, and status tools poll. The third was the on-premise Azure DevOps Server API. It differs from the cloud documentation in versions and authentication details, so I tested every call against our actual server. And throughout, I had to keep humans in control: read-only tools first, write tools with confirmation, and production only through existing approvals.
The lesson is that for AI tools, interface design matters more than implementation.

Situation: The first version of the CIRT MCP server ran from my own clone of the repository. When a couple of teammates started using it, they cloned it too, and their copies quickly got out of sync with mine. People were running different versions, and setup took about an hour of building and configuring.
Task: I wanted installation to be a single, repeatable step, with everyone on the same version, and no secrets anywhere in files.

Action: I packaged it as a .NET global tool, using PackAsTool and a tool command name in the project file, with semantic versioning and release notes. I created its own pipeline that builds, tests and publishes it to our internal Azure Artifacts feed on every tag. To install, a teammate runs one dotnet tool install command, and adds one entry to their Cursor or Claude Code MCP configuration. The server URL and each person's personal access token come from environment variables, never from config files or the repository. Updates are just dotnet tool update. I also added a health_check tool that confirms connectivity and permissions, so if something's wrong, the first run tells you exactly what.

Result: Setup went from about an hour to about 10 minutes, everyone runs the same version, and support questions about setup almost disappeared. That ease of installation was a big part of why adoption spread.

IRT exchanges data files with external vendors, like depot and logistics partners, over SFTP. Things like shipment requests, status updates and inventory files. I owned the component that handles those transfers.

Its key design is one abstraction over three libraries. The ISftpClient interface defines connect, upload, download, list and delete. Behind it, there are three providers: ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex. A factory reads each vendor's configuration and returns the right provider, using keyed services in DI. So the calling code, like the vendor exchange service, never changes, whichever library is used. A base class holds the shared behaviour: retry with backoff for transient network errors, consistent logging with the vendor and file name, and mapping every library's exceptions into our own SftpTransferException, so callers handle errors the same way.

Each provider passes the same set of contract tests, for things like overwriting existing files, timeouts and error behaviour, so they're truly interchangeable. That's Liskov substitution in practice.
I added the Rebex provider and released it to production, moving vendors over one at a time by configuration. It's a good example of how a small abstraction made a risky change routine.

Situation: ComponentPro was our original SFTP library, but its updates had slowed. In 2024, a depot vendor hardened their server and disabled older algorithms, like ssh-rsa with SHA-1. Our connection to them broke, and shipment files stopped flowing. SSH.NET, which we also supported, is free and good, but for a regulated product we wanted a library with commercial support and guaranteed patching.
Task: I was asked to restore the connection quickly, and choose a sustainable long-term option.

Action: I compared all three libraries in an evaluation matrix: support for modern algorithms, like rsa-sha2-256 and 512 host keys, curve25519 key exchange and AES-GCM ciphers; the vendor's support and patch history; licence cost; and, most importantly, actual behaviour against each vendor's test server. Rebex came out best. Because we already had the ISftpClient abstraction, I could build a Rebex provider behind the same interface, without changing any caller code. We kept the other providers as fallbacks, and moved vendors over one at a time, purely through configuration.

Result: The broken vendor connection was restored, and other vendors were migrated safely without a single code change in the business logic. The matrix also made the decision objective and easy for others to review. The lesson for me was that the abstraction paid for itself.

Situation: After choosing Rebex, I had to release the new provider to production. SFTP transfers carry shipment data for clinical trials, so a broken transfer could delay drug supply to sites. The release had to be very safe.
Task: Get Rebex into production with a clear way to prove it worked, and to roll back instantly if it didn't.

Action: I built the provider behind the existing ISftpClient interface, with unit tests, and integration tests in CI against a containerised OpenSSH server. Those covered key exchange, host key verification, a 500 MB file, timeouts and reconnects. It went through our formal FV, TechOps and UAT environments with documented evidence. In production, I used the per-vendor provider setting as a canary. I deployed the code dark, then switched it on for one low-volume vendor only, for two weeks. During that time, I watched transfer success rates and durations per provider, with alerts on failures. The rollback plan was simple: flip the configuration back, with no redeployment. Once it was stable, we moved the remaining vendors in small groups.
Result: The switch caused no failed transfers, and all vendors moved over without incident. It's the same idea as a feature flag: deploy dark, enable gradually, measure, and keep rollback instant.

Situation: When a new clinical study is set up, its sites have to be created in IRT. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. Study setup teams were typing 300+ site records by hand, which took two to three days per large study and caused typos that were found later.
Task: I designed and built a CSV bulk import, working with our BA and QA, with the requirement that bad data must never get in, and users must see every problem before anything is saved.

Action: Files up to 5 MB, about 10,000 rows are read as a stream with CsvHelper, so memory stays flat. Validation runs in stages: first headers and structure, which fails fast, then types and mandatory fields, then duplicates, both within the file and against the database, using one set-based query instead of a lookup per row, and finally business rules, like the site's country being allowed for the study. The user sees a preview with every error, row, column and reason, and can download it as CSV. When they confirm, everything is saved all-or-nothing, in batches inside one transaction, with an audit entry per record. A file hash blocks re-importing the same file, and there's a limit of 2 concurrent imports per user. I covered each rule with unit tests, and the flow with Playwright.
Result: It's live in production, and a 300-site setup now takes under an hour, with no data-entry errors.

Situation: In 2024, a manual pre-check caught a study transfer, moving study configuration between environments, that was about to overwrite a target study that already had randomised subjects. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. It was caught by a person following a checklist. If it hadn't been, it could have affected live trial data.
Task: I proposed and built a guard in the backend, so this kind of mistake becomes impossible, rather than relying on someone remembering a checklist.

Action: Before any transfer runs, the guard performs five checks. One, the target study's status: block if it's live with subjects or dispensed kits. Two, version compatibility between source and target. Three, the transfer direction is allowed, for example never from a lower environment into production data. Four, no other transfer is already in progress for that study, enforced with a database lock, so two transfers can't race. And five, the user has the right role and has supplied a change request reference. It fails closed: if any check can't be evaluated, the transfer is blocked. Each failure returns a specific reason, so users can fix it themselves, and every attempt, allowed or blocked, is audited.
Result: It was released in 2025, and in its first months it blocked a handful of unsafe attempts that would previously have depended on a manual check.
My role in releases is integration and verification. I make sure what we release is exactly what was tested, and that it works on every node.

It starts with integration. For each release, I merge the features committed for it from about 5 scrum teams, resolve conflicts, and tag the version consistently across the application, APIs, database scripts and UI. I keep a release checklist per item: its status, validation evidence, configuration changes, and database scripts. Then we build once, producing versioned artifacts. Deployment to each environment uses automated multi-node installs, with Ansible, Python and Shell scripts, and we promote the same artifact through FV, TechOps, UAT and production. We never rebuild between environments.

Verification happens at every step: a version endpoint checked on every node, so no node is left on an old version, health checks, and key business smoke tests. Configuration and database changes are reviewed separately, because they're the most common cause of release issues. All evidence and approvals are recorded for the regulated process.
Since 2025, the CIRT MCP server runs most of these steps. Humans still approve and make decisions when something fails, but the manual effort dropped from 6 people to 1.

Situation: In mid-2024, one RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark while processing a large vendor shipment-status file. RabbitMQ blocked publishers and dropped connections. Because our services published without confirms, for about 40 minutes shipment status updates silently never reached the shipment service. There were no errors in our logs. Study teams noticed shipments stuck in the wrong status.
Task: I was on support duty, so I owned restoring the data and finding the root cause.

Action: I confirmed what happened using CloudWatch, Grafana and the RabbitMQ management UI: the memory alarm, blocked connections, and a gap in delivered messages. I drained the backlog, then replayed the missed window from the vendor files. That was safe because our consumers upsert, so reprocessing couldn't create duplicates. Then I separated the trigger from the root cause. The big file was the trigger, but publishing without confirms was the real problem. So I enabled publisher confirms with async tracking and retries, tuned memory, added consumer scaling on queue depth, and added alarms on memory, blocked connections, and the incoming rate dropping to zero during business hours. I shared a blameless post-mortem with the team.
Result: All about 1,200 updates were recovered that evening. Confirms cost about 5 percent throughput, and since then there's been no silent message loss.
In 2024, I delivered three security fixes, each from a real finding, and each with a guard so it couldn't come back.

The first was token-based logout. A security review found that tokens in one module kept working for up to 60 minutes after logout. I shortened access tokens to 15 minutes, revoked refresh tokens on the server at logout, and added a denylist of token ids in ElastiCache, checked on every request in about 1 ms. A Playwright test replays an old token and expects a 401. The second was the SSO "request header too long" error. Users in many studies had huge SSO cookies, over the server's header limit. I moved the authentication ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, so the cookie went from about 13 KB to under 1 KB, and about 30 support tickets stopped. The third was reverse tabnabbing. A scan flagged links opening new tabs without rel noopener. I fixed about 40 links, created a shared link component with safe defaults, and added an ESLint rule.
These map to OWASP risks: broken authentication and session management, security misconfiguration, and client-side risks.
My pattern is always the same: fix the root cause, add a test or rule, and release it through the regulated process.

Task: Build those services in the right language, while keeping them as operable and consistent as our .NET services.

Action: For I/O-heavy glue, like a build-log summariser for the MCP platform, which fetches and parses large logs, I used Node.js with TypeScript, because its async I/O suits that work well. For a vendor file pre-validation service, I used Python with FastAPI, because Pydantic schemas gave us field-level validation, returning clear 422 errors automatically, with very little code.
