Result: Support and on-call can operate these services exactly like the .NET ones, and a single log query by correlation id works across all of them. I was also careful to avoid polyglot sprawl: a new language only where it's a clear fit.
Although I'm mainly a backend developer, I do a fair amount of front-end work in IRT, which helps me understand the full request path, from the button click to the database.

Our UI uses both frameworks and is component-based: it started on Angular, and we are moving to React with TypeScript module by module, so older screens are Angular and new modules are React, all calling the same .NET Web APIs. I build responsive, reusable React components with TypeScript, and I also work on the Angular modules. Examples are the CSV import preview and error grid, which shows every validation error with its row and column, and a shipment status timeline. My practices are typed props, hooks, accessibility with proper labels and keyboard support, clear loading, error and empty states, and memoisation only where the profiler shows it's needed. API errors come back as ProblemDetails, and the UI maps them to friendly messages, including field-level validation errors.

On security, I fixed reverse tabnabbing across about 40 links, with a shared link component and a lint rule. On testing, I write Playwright and Cucumber end-to-end tests for user flows, with stable selectors like roles and data-testid.
Because I build the APIs behind these screens too, I can design both sides together, like shaping a DTO for exactly what a screen needs, which avoids extra calls and over-fetching.
When an API suddenly gets slow in production, I work in a fixed order: understand the scope, find the slow step, restore service, and then fix the root cause properly.

First, scope and timing. On the dashboards I check whether it's one endpoint or all of them, since when, and whether anything changed, like a release, a configuration change or a jump in traffic. Then I look at latency by dependency, database, downstream APIs and queues, and use traces and logs filtered by correlation id to find exactly which step got slow. I also rule out the usual .NET suspects: thread pool starvation from sync-over-async code, connection pool exhaustion, and garbage collection pressure.

A real example: in March 2025, our shipments API p95 jumped from about 200 milliseconds to about 3 seconds, with no release at all. The traces pointed to one SQL query. Query Store showed its execution plan had changed after a statistics update. It was parameter sniffing: the new plan was built for a small study and was terrible for big ones. To restore service quickly, I forced the previous good plan in Query Store. Then I fixed it permanently by improving the index and the query shape, so it no longer depended on a lucky plan.
Afterwards, I added a p95 latency alert per endpoint and a Query Store regression review to our routine, so the next time we'd know within minutes, not from users.

When memory keeps growing in a .NET service until it restarts, it's almost always something holding references to objects so the garbage collector can't free them. So I measure first, then find what's holding the memory.

I start with dotnet-counters to watch the GC heap size and gen 2 collections, to confirm it's managed memory growing steadily, not just a spike. Then I take two heap snapshots with dotnet-gcdump a few hours apart and compare them, to see which object types keep growing. If needed, dotnet-dump with the SOS gcroot command shows exactly what's keeping those objects alive. The usual suspects are unbounded static caches, event handlers that are never unsubscribed, timers, closures capturing large objects, singletons holding scoped services, and creating a new HttpClient per call.

I had exactly this case. One of our ECS worker services grew by about 150 MB a day and was killed for running out of memory every about 3 days. The heap comparison showed a static ConcurrentDictionary caching study configuration per version, with no eviction at all, so it just kept growing. I replaced it with a size-limited IMemoryCache with a 30-minute sliding expiry, and ran an overnight load test to prove it.
Memory now stays flat. I also added an alert on the memory trend, not just on hitting the limit, so slow leaks are caught early.

If 500 errors spike right after a release, my first priority is the users, not the investigation. So I decide quickly: if the impact is high, I roll back to the previous tagged release first, and investigate second. Because we build once and keep every release artifact, rolling back is fast and safe.

Then I find the cause, using the logs filtered for errors, the exception details, and the list of changes in that release, code, configuration and database scripts. Once I understand it, I fix forward with a proper change.

A real example: after a UAT release, 5xx errors rose to about 8 percent. The logs showed a null configuration value. The release had added a new required setting, but it had been missed in the UAT parameter store. I rolled back within 15 minutes, added the setting, and redeployed. But the more important fix was preventing it from happening again. I switched those options to use ValidateDataAnnotations with ValidateOnStart. Now if a required setting is missing, the service fails at startup, the readiness check fails, and the deployment stops, instead of the service starting happily and failing live requests.

I also added a configuration item to our release checklist, so every new setting is checked in each environment before deployment. That turned a runtime failure into a deploy-time failure, which is exactly where you want it.

When messages seem to go missing between two services, I trace one specific message, by its message id, through every hop: was it published, did the broker confirm it, did it land in the queue, was it delivered to the consumer, was it acknowledged, and was it actually processed. Somewhere in that chain, the evidence stops, and that's where the bug is.
I use the publisher's logs, the RabbitMQ management UI for queue and delivery rates, the consumer's logs by correlation id, and the dead-letter queue.

A real example: in our validation environment, kit-assignment notifications occasionally vanished. Tracing showed they were published and delivered to the consumer, but never processed. The consumer was using autoAck set to true. That means RabbitMQ deletes the message as soon as it's delivered. So when processing hit a transient database timeout, the message was already gone, and nothing retried it. I switched the consumer to manual acknowledgement, sending the ack only after the database transaction commits. I added 3 retries with exponential backoff, and then a dead-letter queue with an alert for messages that still fail. Because redelivery can now happen, I made sure the handler was idempotent.
The rule I took from it: acknowledge only after the side effect is safely committed, never before. Since that change, we haven't lost a notification.

When a multi-node deployment fails on only one node, the first thing I do is stop the rollout, so the nodes don't drift onto different versions. Then I compare the failing node with a healthy one: the deployment logs, disk space, file permissions, the service account, the service state and configuration. Usually the difference jumps out.

Once I find it, I fix the node, rerun the deployment step for just that node, and then verify that every node reports the same version and passes health checks. Because our deployment steps are idempotent, rerunning them is safe.

A real example: a UAT deployment failed on node 3 of 5. The logs showed a write failure, and checking the node, the disk was 98 percent full, filled with old release folders and logs that were never cleaned up. I cleaned up, keeping the last 2 releases for rollback, reran the step, and verified all five nodes were on the same version.

Then I prevented it from recurring in two ways. I added log rotation and release retention to the deployment playbook. And I added a prerequisite check tool to our CIRT MCP server that runs before every deployment, checking disk space, the service account and required ports on every node. So now this kind of problem is caught before any node is changed, not halfway through a deployment.

When deadlocks suddenly increase, I first get evidence of exactly which queries are involved. SQL Server captures deadlock graphs automatically in the system_health Extended Events session, and each graph shows the two transactions, the statements, and the resources each one held and wanted. A deadlock is just a cycle of locks, and SQL Server picks one victim and kills it with error 1205.

The usual fixes are: access tables in a consistent order, add indexes so queries lock fewer rows, keep transactions short, consider read committed snapshot so readers don't block writers, and retry the victim safely.

A real example: after one release, deadlocks jumped to about 20 a day. The graphs showed two code paths. Kit assignment updated the Inventory table and then Shipment, while the resupply job updated Shipment and then Inventory, the opposite order. On top of that, a missing index on Inventory by SiteId and Status meant the update scanned and locked far more rows than it needed. I aligned both paths to the same order, added the index, shortened the transactions by moving non-database work out of them, and enabled retry for deadlock errors through EF Core's retrying execution strategy.
Deadlocks fell from about 20 a day to about one a week or fewer, and the retry handles those rare ones without users noticing.

When a vendor says they didn't receive a file, I start with evidence rather than assumptions. I check our job logs for that transfer, then verify on the SFTP server itself: the file name, size, path, timestamps and permissions. Then I re-send safely, and confirm with the vendor that it's arrived.

A real example: one Monday, a depot vendor told us our order file hadn't arrived. Our logs clearly showed a successful upload, with the file name and size, so the transfer itself had worked. When I listed the remote server, the file was sitting in the old folder. It turned out the vendor had moved their pickup folder to /inbound/irt, and they had announced it to a different team, so it never reached us. Having the logs meant we could resolve it quickly without any blame either way.

I re-sent the file to the new path with the same file name. That was safe, because the vendor deduplicates files by name, so there was no risk of processing an order twice. Then I fixed the gaps. I added a check after every upload that lists the remote folder to confirm the file is really there, alerts on failed transfers, and a shared integration contact list so vendor changes reach the right people.
The communication fix was just as important as the technical one, and we haven't had a missed file like that since.
CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps starting and exiting, and Kubernetes waits longer and longer before each restart, up to five minutes. So I need to find out why it's exiting.

First, kubectl describe pod, which shows the events: image pull errors, OOMKilled, or failing probes. Then kubectl logs with the previous flag, which shows the logs from the crashed container, not the new one. The exit code helps too: 137 means it was killed, often out of memory, and 1 usually means the application itself failed, like missing configuration. Then I check the configuration, secrets, resource limits and probe settings.

A real example: a new Node.js tooling service in our dev cluster kept crash-looping, but the logs showed no error at all. The events showed liveness probe failures. The service needed about 40 seconds to warm up, loading data at startup, but the liveness probe started checking after 10 seconds. So Kubernetes decided it was stuck and killed it, over and over, before it could ever finish starting.

I added a startup probe allowing 60 seconds, which pauses liveness checks until the app has started, and I made part of the warm-up lazy, so it starts faster anyway. Then I updated our service template so every new service gets a startup probe by default. The lesson is that a crash loop isn't always a crash; sometimes the platform is killing a healthy but slow app.

When a Lambda function times out, I first check the pattern: does it time out on every call, only on cold starts, or only under load? Then I find the slow step, using logs, timings, and traces in X-Ray.

A real example: we had a Lambda triggered by a DynamoDB stream that sent shipment notifications. As volume grew, it started hitting its 30-second timeout. I found two problems. First, it created a new HttpClient on every invocation, which is slow and wastes connections. Second, it called a downstream API that was sometimes slow, with no timeout at all, so one slow call used up the whole Lambda budget. And because it processed batches of 100 records, one failure meant retrying the entire batch.

The fixes: I moved the HttpClient outside the handler, so it's reused across invocations. I set a 5-second timeout on the downstream call, with a retry. I reduced the batch size from 100 to 25. I enabled ReportBatchItemFailures, so only the failed records are retried, not the whole batch. And I increased memory from 512 MB to 1 GB, which in Lambda also gives more CPU. I also made sure failed records eventually go to an on-failure destination, so the stream can never get stuck.
The timeouts stopped. And as a general rule, if work genuinely needs a long time, it belongs in a queue with a worker on ECS, not in a single Lambda call.

When users say they're logged out randomly, or SSO fails for some of them, the word "random" usually hides a common factor. So I look for the pattern first: which users, which browsers, which applications, and what time. Then I inspect the technical suspects: cookie sizes and header sizes, token expiry, clock skew between servers, cookie domain conflicts, and whether data protection keys are shared across instances, because if they aren't, a cookie created on one instance can't be read by another.

A real example: in 2024, we got about 30 tickets in two weeks from users getting a 400 error after logging in through SSO. The pattern was that they were mostly study managers assigned to many studies. A test user with many groups reproduced it. Our authentication cookie stored every role and group claim, so for these users it was split into several chunked cookies totalling about 13 KB. Together with other cookies on the domain, that went over the server's 16 KB header limit, and the server rejected the request.

Raising the limit would only postpone it. So I moved the authentication ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, backed by Redis, so the cookie only holds a small key, and loaded study permissions per request through a cached claims transformation. The cookie dropped to under 1 KB, and the tickets stopped, with no visible change for users.

If the SonarQube quality gate fails just before a release, I look at exactly what failed, fix the real issues, add any missing tests, and tell the release owner early. What I never do is mark genuine issues as false positives just to get a green build. The gate is there because it protects a regulated product.

A real example: two days before code freeze, our gate failed for two reasons. Coverage on new code was 68 percent against our 80 percent threshold, and SonarQube flagged a hard-coded connection string in a test project. The connection string was easy and important: I moved it to .NET user secrets for local runs and a secret pipeline variable for CI, so nothing sensitive was in the repository. For coverage, I looked at which new code wasn't tested, and it was mostly the new validators. I wrote the missing validator tests, covering both valid and invalid cases, in about half a day.
I also told the release owner that same morning what had failed and my plan, so there were no surprises. The gate was green the next day, and the release date didn't slip.

SonarQube's idea is "clean as you code", focusing on new code, so the codebase gets better with every change. And when something truly is a false positive, we document the reason and get it reviewed, rather than silently suppressing it.

When a test passes on my machine but fails in CI, I assume an environment difference until proven otherwise. The usual suspects are culture and time zone, file paths and case sensitivity, the operating system, environment variables, test execution order and shared static state, and timing assumptions.

A real example: a date-formatting test passed on my Windows laptop but failed on our Linux build agent. The code formatted a date using the current culture implicitly. On my machine, the culture produced one format, and on the Linux agent, running with a different culture and invariant globalisation settings, it produced another. So the test was really testing my machine's settings, not the code.

I fixed the code to format with an explicit culture, set the culture explicitly in the test, and then verified it by running the tests inside the same .NET SDK container image the agent uses. That last step is very useful: reproducing CI locally usually finds the cause in minutes.

Other common causes I check: Linux paths are case-sensitive, so use Path.Combine and correct casing. xUnit runs test classes in parallel, so shared static state makes tests flaky. And code that calls DateTime.Now directly depends on time, so injecting TimeProvider makes it deterministic. The goal is tests that give the same result on every machine, every time.

When an AI tool suggests code that looks right but I'm not sure, I treat it like a pull request from a new teammate. I read it critically, check any APIs against the official documentation, build it, run it, add tests, and run our scans. And I never merge code I can't explain myself.

A real example: while building our deployment tooling, Copilot suggested an HTTP retry policy. It looked clean and professional, but it retried every failure, on every request. One of those requests was the POST that creates a release in Azure DevOps. If that POST times out, it may actually have succeeded on the server, so retrying it could create duplicate releases. That's a subtle bug, and it would only appear under real network problems.

I changed the policy to retry only idempotent requests, like GETs, and only transient failures, like 408, 429 and 5xx responses, with exponential backoff. In .NET 8 the standard resilience handler even has an option to disable retries for unsafe HTTP methods. Then I added a unit test proving that POSTs are never retried, so the rule can't be lost later.
I shared the example with the team as a reminder for reviews. AI tools make me much faster, but responsibility for correctness and security stays with me.
For behavioural questions, I use the STAR structure: Situation, Task, Action and Result.

The Situation is one or two sentences of context, just enough to understand the problem. The Task is what I was specifically responsible for. The Action is the longest part, about sixty percent of the answer, and I describe it in the first person, with real technical detail, so it's clear what I personally did, while giving the team credit where it's due. The Result is the outcome with real numbers wherever possible, like time saved, errors reduced, tickets stopped or latency improved, and then what I learned or what changed afterwards.
I keep each story to about two minutes, because longer stories lose the interviewer.

I also prepare a small bank of stories that I can adapt to different questions. For example, building the CIRT MCP server, which cut deployments from 6 hours to 2 and from 6 people to 1, works for initiative or innovation questions. The RabbitMQ outage works for production issues and ownership. The CSV bulk import works for delivering a feature end to end. The security fixes work for quality, and mentoring two graduates works for leadership. Having those ready means I can answer clearly instead of searching my memory under pressure.

Situation: In our team, every release deployment ran across 4 to 6 nodes on our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, and it was mostly manual. Each one needed about 6 people on a call for about 6 hours, following steps, checking each node, and copying logs around. Everyone accepted it as just how releases worked.

Task: Nobody asked me to fix it. But I had been following the Model Context Protocol, and I saw that AI agents could run these steps if they had the right tools. I wanted to prove it could work, without neglecting my sprint work.

Action: Before spending time on it, I agreed part of two sprints with my lead for a prototype, so it was initiative with alignment, not going off on my own. I started with 10 read-only tools, like build status, release status and logs, because they were safe and built trust. I demoed it to the team, collected feedback, and then added write tools, like queuing builds and deploying release stages, with confirmations before risky steps and our existing approval gates unchanged. Each increment had a demo. Over time, it grew into the CIRT MCP server, with about 77 tools, written in C# and packaged so anyone could install it with one command.

Result: Measured on comparable deployments, deployment time went from 6 hours to 2, and the people needed from 6 to 1. What I learned is that starting small, getting buy-in early, and showing results is what turns an idea into something a whole team uses.

Situation: In mid-2024, shipment status updates from a vendor suddenly stopped reaching our shipment service. There were no errors in our application logs, which made it confusing. Study teams noticed shipments stuck in the wrong status, and that matters because sites depend on it for drug supply.
Task: I was on support duty, so I owned finding the cause, recovering the data, and making sure it couldn't happen silently again.

Action: I started from the symptom. In CloudWatch and Grafana, our services appeared to be publishing normally, but the queue had received nothing for about 40 minutes. In the RabbitMQ management UI, I found that one node had hit its memory high watermark while processing a large vendor file. RabbitMQ had blocked publishers and dropped connections. And then the real cause: our services published without publisher confirms, so they never knew their messages had been lost. To recover, I drained the backlog and replayed the missed window from the vendor files, which was safe because our consumers upsert, so nothing could be duplicated. Then I fixed the root cause: I enabled publisher confirms with retries, tuned memory, added consumer scaling on queue depth, and alerts on memory, blocked connections and the incoming rate dropping to zero.

Result: All about 1,200 updates were recovered that same evening, and in the 12 months since, there's been no silent message loss. I also shared a blameless post-mortem so the whole team learned from it.

Situation: A quarterly release in 2024 carried changes from 5 scrum teams, and the production date was fixed, because a study go-live depended on it. Two days before formal verification, two problems appeared: a shared database script from two teams conflicted, and an integration test was failing.
Task: I was the release integrator, so it was my job to get a complete, validated release ready on time, without cutting corners on quality, which isn't an option in a GxP product.

Action: I tracked every release item daily, so I knew exactly where each one stood. Instead of long email threads, I got the owners of both conflicting scripts into a one-hour session, and we resolved the conflict together. I worked with the team that owned the failing test to get it fixed the same day. Then I ran the formal verification install overnight, so we didn't lose a day. One lower-priority feature wasn't fully validated yet, so rather than rush it, I went to the product owner with the facts, and we agreed to move it to the next release. The principle was to protect the date by cutting scope, not quality.

Result: We hit the go-live date, with full FV and UAT evidence for everything we shipped. The lesson I took was that early, honest communication and getting the right people in one room solves deadline problems far faster than anything else.

Situation: In 2023, I changed the date filter on a shipment report. I tested it carefully, but only in Indian Standard Time, which is where I work. During formal verification, the testers found that shipments created near midnight UTC appeared on the wrong day for US sites.
Task: It was my change, so it was my bug to own and fix, and I wanted to make sure that kind of mistake couldn't easily happen again.

Action: I raised it myself in the next stand-up, explained the cause, and gave a time for the fix. The root cause was that I compared local DateTime values, which only works if everyone is in the same time zone. I changed the logic to store and compare everything in UTC, using DateTimeOffset, and convert to each site's time zone only when displaying it, using TimeZoneInfo. Then I added unit tests for several time zones, with times right around midnight and daylight saving changes, using a fake TimeProvider so the tests are deterministic. I also added a time-zone item to my personal pull request checklist.

Result: It was fixed within a day and caught before UAT, so no users were affected. What I learned was to test outside my own context, and to think about edge cases like time zones up front. Since then, I always ask "where in the world will this run" when I touch dates.

Situation: While designing the CSV bulk import, a senior colleague and I disagreed. He wanted partial imports: save the valid rows and report the invalid ones. I preferred all-or-nothing: if any row fails, save nothing.
Task: We needed to agree on a design both of us could stand behind, and I wanted the decision to be made on the merits, not on seniority.

Action: First, I tried to understand his real concern. It was user frustration: if one bad row out of three hundred blocks everything, users get annoyed. That's valid. Then I wrote down the trade-offs. Partial import is friendlier, but in a GxP system it leaves a study half-configured, makes the audit trail messy, and makes rollback complicated. Then I proposed a third option: a validate-only preview that shows every error in the file, with row, column and reason, before anything is saved, followed by an all-or-nothing save. That way, users fix everything in one go, and the data is always consistent. We took both views to the BA and the QA lead, who understand the users and the validation requirements.

Result: The team chose the preview plus all-or-nothing approach, and my colleague agreed, because the preview solved his concern about frustration. The feature is in production and works well. What I learned is to disagree about ideas, not people, and that finding the concern behind someone's position often leads to a better solution than either original idea.
Situation: In 2024, two graduate developers joined our team. Our IRT system is large and regulated, and they were overwhelmed by the number of services, the domain terms and our release process.
Task: I volunteered to mentor them, with the goal of getting them contributing safely and then working independently as quickly as possible.

Action: I started with a one-hour architecture walkthrough, drawing how the services, the database and the messaging fit together, using one real flow end to end. Then I picked small but real stories for them, so their work mattered from the start. For the first two sprints, we paired: first I drove while explaining, then they drove while I guided. After that, I moved to code reviews, but I explained the reason behind each comment, so they learned principles, not just fixes. I showed them how to use Copilot and Cursor safely for writing tests, and how to check the output. And I held a 30-minute weekly check-in where any question was welcome, because feeling safe to ask is half of learning.

Result: Their first pull requests were merged in week two, they were working independently within about two months, and one of them later joined our release verification rotation. For me, it was very rewarding, and it taught me that good mentoring is a gradual handover: I do, we do, you do.

Situation: In 2024, a security review and a group of support tickets surfaced three issues in our IRT application. Tokens kept working after logout. Some users with many studies got "request header too long" errors after SSO login. And external links were open to reverse tabnabbing.
Task: I took ownership of all three, with the goal of fixing each root cause and adding a guardrail so it stayed fixed.

Action: I prioritised by risk, so logout came first. I shortened access tokens to 15 minutes, revoked refresh tokens on the server at logout, and added a denylist of token ids in ElastiCache that every API checks, which costs only about 1 ms per request. For the header problem, the SSO cookie held every claim and was about 13 KB, so I moved the authentication ticket to the server side with ITicketStore, and the cookie dropped to under 1 KB. For tabnabbing, I fixed about 40 links with rel noopener noreferrer, built a shared link component with safe defaults, and added an ESLint rule. Each fix had tests, including a Playwright test that replays an old token after logout and expects a 401, and each went through code review, the SonarQube quality gate and our regulated release process.
Result: All three passed security retest with no regressions, and the SSO tickets stopped. What I took from it is that a fix isn't complete until there's a test or rule that stops it coming back.

Situation: When a new clinical study was set up, the study setup team had to type site records into IRT one by one. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. For a 300-site study, that took two to three days, and typos were often found much later.
Task: I was responsible for delivering a CSV bulk import end to end: requirements, design, backend, UI, tests, validation support and release.

Action: Over three sprints, I first agreed the validation rules with our BA, so we knew exactly what "valid" meant. On the backend, I built an API that streams the file, so memory stays flat even for about 10,000 rows, validates in stages, first structure, then types and mandatory fields, then duplicates, then business rules, and saves all-or-nothing in one transaction, with an audit entry for every record. A file hash blocks importing the same file twice. On the front end, I built a preview screen that shows every error with its row, column and reason, with a downloadable error report. I wrote unit tests for every rule and Playwright tests for the upload, preview and confirm flow. Then I supported QA through FV and UAT, and wrote a short support runbook for the hand-over.

Result: It's live in production. A 300-site setup now takes under an hour instead of days, and errors are caught before anything is saved. Owning it end to end taught me a lot about working closely with the BA, QA and the release team.

Situation: In 2024, during a study transfer, which copies study configuration between environments, a person following a manual checklist noticed that the transfer was about to overwrite a target study that already had randomised subjects. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. It was caught, but only because someone remembered to check. If it had gone through, it could have affected live trial data.
Task: I wanted to make that mistake impossible, so safety didn't depend on someone's memory.

Action: I proposed and built a guard in the backend that runs five checks before any transfer is allowed. First, the target study's status: it blocks the transfer if the study is live with subjects or dispensed kits. Second, version compatibility between source and target. Third, the transfer direction must be allowed. Fourth, no other transfer can be in progress for that study, enforced with a database lock so two transfers can't race. And fifth, the user must have the right role and provide a change request reference. It fails closed: if any check can't be evaluated, the transfer is blocked. Every failure returns a clear reason, so users know what to fix, and every attempt, allowed or blocked, is audited for GxP.

Result: It was released in 2025, and in its first months it blocked a handful of unsafe attempts. The lesson for me is to turn important checklists into code, so the system prevents the risk, rather than just hoping people catch it.

Situation: In early 2025, the Model Context Protocol was very new, and nobody on my team had built an MCP server. I wanted to build one to automate our deployments, so I had to learn it quickly, alongside my normal work.
Task: Get from zero to a working, useful prototype fast, and make sure the design was sound before building a lot on top of it.

Action: I followed a simple learning approach. First, the official source: I read the MCP specification and the C# SDK samples over about a week, so I understood the concepts properly: hosts, clients, servers, tools and transports. Then a tiny but real use case. In two days, I built a prototype with three tools, list builds, get build status and get logs, against a test Azure DevOps project. Then I validated it with real usage: I tried it from both Cursor and Claude Code, which showed me how the model actually chooses tools. I asked a colleague to review the tool design, and iterated on names and descriptions based on what I saw.

Result: That three-tool prototype became the CIRT MCP server, with about 77 tools, which cut deployments from 6 hours to 2 and from 6 people to 1. I used the same approach later for the .NET 10 upgrade in early 2026: official documentation first, then a small real example, then early feedback.

Situation: When I started on the deployment automation that became the CIRT MCP server, there was no specification at all. There was just a slow, manual process that everyone disliked, and different people did it slightly differently.
Task: Turn that vague problem into a clear plan, so I'd build the right thing, not just something.

Action: First, I turned the ambiguity into data. I interviewed the 5 people who usually ran deployments, and wrote down every manual step they did, which came to about 30 steps. Then I ranked those steps by how much time they took and how risky they were, meaning how often mistakes happened. That gave an obvious order. I planned three increments. First, read-only tools for status and logs, which were safe and immediately useful. Second, build and release creation. Third, multi-node deployments, with confirmations before risky steps. After each increment, I demoed it to the team and collected feedback, and I wrote down my assumptions and confirmed them with the people doing the work, rather than guessing.

Result: The ambiguity became a clear roadmap that everyone understood, and the tool grew to about 77 tools that the team actually uses. Deployments went from 6 hours to 2. What I learned is that ambiguity becomes manageable when you collect facts, rank them, and deliver in small steps with feedback.

Situation: After I built the CIRT MCP server, the team mostly kept using the old manual deployment process. I had no authority to make anyone use my tool, and in a regulated environment, people are rightly cautious about changing how deployments work.
Task: Win adoption on merit, by making the tool clearly easier, safer and more valuable than the old way.

Action: First, I addressed concerns directly. The server acts with each person's own permissions, risky steps ask for confirmation, the existing approval gates are unchanged, and every action is logged. Then I removed friction. I ran a 30-minute live demo on a real UAT deployment, so people saw it work on something that mattered. I packaged it as a one-command install, and wrote a README with 10 example prompts, so nobody had to work out how to start. I paired with the first 4 engineers on their first real runs, and I added the tools they asked for, which showed I was listening. Those early users then helped others, which spread it much faster than I could alone.

Result: Within about two months, most release deployments used it, with 1 person instead of 6, and in about 2 hours instead of 6. What I learned is that influence without authority comes from making the right thing easy, safe and visibly valuable, and from letting early adopters become advocates.
I take feedback as information to improve, not as criticism, and I try to act on it visibly.

Situation: In 2023, my lead told me my pull requests were too big, often 1,500 lines or more, and that they were slow and hard to review. At first I felt I was being efficient by doing everything at once, but I realised reviewers were the ones paying the cost.
Task: Change how I worked so my changes were easy to review, without slowing down delivery.

Action: I asked my lead for specific examples, so I understood exactly what made them hard. Then I changed my approach. I split work into smaller pull requests, under 400 lines, each doing one logical thing, with a clear description of what changed, why, and how to test it. Where a feature wasn't ready to be visible, I used feature flags, so I could merge small pieces safely. After a few weeks, I checked back with the reviewers to see if it was actually better.

Result: Review turnaround dropped from two to three days to usually the same day, fewer bugs slipped through because reviews were more thorough, and my lead mentioned the improvement in my appraisal. The lesson for me was to ask for specifics, act quickly, and then close the loop by checking that the change worked.
We follow SAFe, the Scaled Agile Framework, because our engineering organisation is about 100 people across several teams, and the ceremonies work at two levels.

PI planning is the big-picture event. A program increment is several sprints, usually around ten weeks. All the teams plan it together: we look at the features coming up, agree each team's objectives, and map dependencies between teams, like one team needing an API from another before it can finish its feature. Risks are raised openly and someone owns each one. The output is a plan everyone has agreed, not one handed down.

Grooming, or backlog refinement, happens during the sprints. We take upcoming stories, clarify what they really mean with the product owner and BA, write clear acceptance criteria, split stories that are too big, and estimate them. In a GxP product, we also agree early what validation evidence each story needs.

Then each sprint has the usual ceremonies. Sprint planning, where we commit to stories based on our capacity. A daily stand-up to share progress and blockers. A sprint review or demo, where we show working software to the product owner and stakeholders and get feedback. And a retrospective, where we discuss what to improve in how we work.

I take part in all of these. Because I also coordinate release integration across about 5 teams, PI planning is especially useful for me, as that's where I spot cross-team dependencies that could affect a release.
I estimate in story points, relative to similar work we've already done, because relative estimates are more reliable than guessing hours.

First, I make sure I understand the story and its acceptance criteria. Then I break it into tasks, which shows the real size and often reveals hidden work. The key is to estimate everything that "done" really needs, not just the coding: unit and integration tests, code review, database scripts, documentation, validation evidence, and release work. In a GxP product, testing and evidence can be as big as the coding itself, and leaving them out is the most common reason estimates are wrong.

Then I compare with similar stories from the past: is this bigger or smaller than that one? The team estimates together, for example with planning poker, and big differences are useful, because they usually mean someone knows something the others don't.

If there's real uncertainty, like a new library or an unclear integration, I say so openly and suggest a short time-boxed spike to investigate first, instead of pretending to know. For example, before adding the Rebex SFTP provider, a short spike against the vendor's test server made the actual estimate much more accurate.
Finally, we check the total sprint commitment against our past velocity, so we commit to what we can actually finish, rather than what we hope to finish.
When everything seems urgent, my first step is to find out what's actually urgent, because often not everything is.

I clarify the real impact and the real deadlines with the product owner or my lead. Who is affected, how badly, and what happens if this waits a day? Then I prioritise in a clear order. Production issues, and anything that could affect patient safety or trial data, come first, because in a clinical system that's non-negotiable. Next come our committed sprint goals, because other teams and the release depend on them. Then improvements and nice-to-haves.

When something new and urgent comes in, I don't silently try to do everything. I explain the trade-off openly and early: "if I take this on, this other item will slip by two days. Which do you prefer?" That way the decision is made by the right person, with full information, and nobody gets surprised at the end of the sprint.

I also look at why things keep becoming urgent. If the same kind of urgent work keeps coming back, I automate it, so it stops being urgent. Our deployments are a good example. They used to take about 6 people and 6 hours every release, constantly pulling people off their work. By building the CIRT MCP server, they now take 1 person and about 2 hours, which removed a recurring fire drill for the whole team.
I see QA and validation as partners, not as a gate at the end, and in a GxP product, their sign-off is genuinely part of being done.

I involve them early. In refinement, we agree on clear, testable acceptance criteria together, so there's no argument later about what the story was supposed to do. For bigger features, I walk them through the design, so they can plan tests in parallel with development instead of waiting for the code.

Then I make their work easier. I provide realistic test data, and I write automated tests where I can, unit and integration tests, plus Playwright and Cucumber end-to-end tests for key flows, which speed up regression. I write clear release notes saying exactly what changed, what to test, and any configuration or database changes.
When they find a defect, I fix it quickly and explain the root cause, not just the fix, so they can judge what else might be affected and what to retest. I never treat a bug report as criticism.

For me, a story is done only when it's genuinely ready to release, not just when the code works on my machine.

That means several things. The code is reviewed by at least one colleague and merged through a pull request. Unit tests and integration tests are written and passing, and the build pipeline is green, including the SonarQube quality gate, so coverage on new code, bugs and vulnerabilities all meet the standard. Any database changes have reviewed migration scripts, and any new configuration has been added for every environment. Documentation and release notes are updated, so QA, support and the release team know what changed. The four main OOP principles are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.

Encapsulation means an object keeps its data private and changes it only through its own methods, so it protects its rules. Abstraction means exposing what something does and hiding how it does it, usually through an interface. Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the behaviour of a base class. And polymorphism means one interface, many implementations, where the right method is chosen at runtime.

They work best together. In my SFTP integration component, business code depends on an ISftpClient interface, which is abstraction. Three providers, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, implement it, which is polymorphism, since the caller just calls UploadAsync and configuration decides which one runs. They inherit shared retry and logging logic from a base class, which is inheritance. And each provider keeps its connection details private, which is encapsulation.
In practice I prefer composition over deep inheritance trees.
Encapsulation means bundling an object's data with the methods that change it, and hiding the internal state, so the object can protect its own rules.

In C# that means private fields, properties with private setters where needed, and public methods that enforce business rules. The outside world can only ask the object to do something; it can't put it into an invalid state directly. The benefit is that the rules live in one place, so the data stays valid and the code is safer to change later, because callers don't depend on the internals.

A real example is a shipment in our system. Instead of a public Status property anyone can set, the Shipment class has methods like MarkDispatched and MarkDelivered. MarkDelivered checks that the shipment was actually dispatched first, and records the time. If someone tries to deliver a cancelled shipment, it throws a clear domain exception. In a GxP system that's important, because every state change must be valid and auditable.
Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the behaviour of another class, called the base class. It models an "is-a" relationship; for example, a Rebex SFTP client is an SFTP client.

In C#, a class can inherit from only one base class, but it can implement many interfaces. The derived class gets the base members, can add its own, and can override virtual methods to change behaviour. It's powerful for sharing real code, but it creates tight coupling, because changes in the base class ripple into every child. Deep hierarchies also become hard to understand.

So I use it carefully. In our SFTP component, an abstract SftpClientBase class holds the common retry, timeout and logging logic, and each provider class inherits it and only implements the library-specific connect, upload and download. That removed a lot of duplication.
But when the relationship is really "has-a", or behaviour varies a lot, I prefer composition, injecting a collaborator instead of inheriting.
Polymorphism means "one interface, many forms". The same method call behaves differently depending on the actual object behind it.

In C# there are two kinds. Runtime polymorphism happens through virtual and override methods, or through interfaces: the method that runs is decided at runtime based on the real type of the object. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading, where the compiler picks a method by its parameters. Runtime polymorphism is the important one for design, because it lets code depend on an abstraction and lets new behaviour plug in without changing the caller.

My real example is the SFTP integration. The business code calls UploadAsync on an ISftpClient. Depending on the vendor's configuration, the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro implementation runs, and the calling code has no idea which one. When we added Rebex, nothing in the callers changed.
It also makes testing easy, because in unit tests I just pass a mock that implements the same interface.
Abstraction means showing only what the user of a class needs to know, and hiding the complex details of how it works.

In C#, we usually express abstraction with interfaces and abstract classes. They describe the essential contract, the operations and their meaning, while the implementation details stay inside. It's slightly different from encapsulation: encapsulation is about protecting an object's data, while abstraction is about modelling a simple concept that hides complexity. Good abstractions make code easier to use, easier to test and easier to change.

For example, our ISftpClient interface only exposes a few things: connect, upload, download and list files. Behind it, each library deals with its own complexity, like different authentication APIs, key formats, timeouts and error types. Business code just thinks "send this file to the vendor", and doesn't care about any of that.

The trap is creating abstractions too early, or leaking details, like exposing library-specific exceptions through the interface. I mapped all provider errors to our own exception types to avoid that.
A class is the blueprint, and an object is an actual instance created from that blueprint.

The class defines the type: what data it holds through fields and properties, and what it can do through methods. It's written once in code. An object is created at runtime with new, it has its own copy of the data in memory, and you can create as many objects from one class as you need. Changing one object's data doesn't affect the others, unless they share static members, which belong to the class itself rather than to any one object.

For example, Shipment is a class in our code. It defines properties like ShipmentId, Status and Destination, and methods like MarkDispatched. When EF Core loads ten shipments from the database, it creates ten Shipment objects, each with its own id and status.
A simple analogy is the plan of a house versus actual houses built from that plan.
Both let one method name have multiple versions, but they work at different times.

Overloading means having several methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class, for example a Log method that takes a string, and another that takes a string and an exception. The compiler picks the right one at compile time based on the arguments, so it's compile-time polymorphism. The return type alone isn't enough to overload.

Overriding means a derived class provides its own version of a virtual or abstract method from the base class, with the same signature. The decision is made at runtime, based on the actual object, even if you call it through a base-class reference. That's runtime polymorphism.

A real example: in our SFTP providers, the base class has a virtual method for building connection settings, and the Rebex provider overrides it to add its own key handling. Separately, we have overloaded upload methods, one taking a file path and one taking a stream.
The virtual keyword is used on a base-class method to say derived classes are allowed to replace it. The override keyword is used in the derived class to actually replace it.

When you call a virtual method, the runtime looks at the actual type of the object, not the type of the variable. So even if I hold the object through a base-class reference, the derived override runs. Without virtual, a method can't be overridden at all; C# methods are non-virtual by default, which is a deliberate design choice for performance and safety. An override can call the base version with base dot method name, and it can be marked sealed to stop further overriding.

In our SFTP component, the base class has a virtual method that builds connection options with sensible defaults. The Rebex provider overrides it, calls the base version first, and then adds its specific settings. That way the shared defaults live in one place.
Abstract methods are similar but have no body, so derived classes must override them.
Override and new both put a method with the same name in a derived class, but they behave very differently.

Override replaces a virtual method. Whichever reference you use, base type or derived type, the derived version runs, because it's decided at runtime by the actual object. That's normal polymorphism. The new keyword hides the base method instead, which is called method hiding. Then the version that runs depends on the declared type of the variable: through a base-class reference the base version runs, and through a derived reference the new version runs. So the same object can behave differently depending on how you hold it.
That's confusing and a common source of bugs, so I avoid it. If you forget both keywords, the compiler warns you that you're hiding a member, and in our projects we treat warnings as errors in CI.
The only legitimate use I've seen is when a base class you don't control adds a member with the same name as yours.
A sealed class is a class that can't be inherited from. A sealed method is an override that can't be overridden again by classes further down the hierarchy.

Sealing communicates design intent: this class wasn't designed for extension, so nobody should depend on its internals by subclassing it. It also prevents subtle bugs where a subclass breaks the class's assumptions. There's a small performance benefit too, because the JIT can devirtualise calls on sealed types. The string class is a well-known example of a sealed class. A sealed method is useful when you've overridden something carefully and want to lock that behaviour down.

In our code, we seal classes by default when they aren't meant to be inherited, which is most service classes, handlers and DTOs, and some analyzers even suggest it. If later we really need extension, we usually add an interface rather than unsealing.
For example, our concrete SFTP providers are sealed, while the shared base class is abstract, so the hierarchy is exactly one level deep.
The stack and the heap are two areas of memory that .NET uses in different ways.

The stack is per thread. It stores method call frames: parameters, local variables and return addresses. It works last-in, first-out, so it's extremely fast, and the memory is freed automatically when a method returns. The heap is shared memory where objects created with new live, mostly reference types. Objects on the heap stay until the garbage collector finds nothing references them.

A common misconception is that value types always live on the stack. Actually, a value type lives where it's declared. A local int is on the stack, but an int field inside a class object is on the heap, as part of that object. And boxing moves a value type onto the heap.

In practice this matters for performance. Fewer heap allocations means less GC work. For example, when tuning CSV parsing, using Span of T to slice strings without allocating new ones reduced GC pressure noticeably.
Boxing is when a value type, like an int or a struct, is wrapped inside an object on the heap. Unboxing is extracting the value back out with an explicit cast.

Boxing happens implicitly, for example when you assign an int to an object variable, put it in an old non-generic collection like ArrayList, or call an interface method on a struct through the interface. Each box is a new heap allocation, and it creates extra work for the garbage collector. Unboxing needs a cast to the exact type, or you get an InvalidCastException.

In normal business code it rarely matters, but in hot paths, like processing thousands of CSV rows or logging in a tight loop, it adds up. The fix is generics: List of int instead of ArrayList, generic methods instead of object parameters, and structured logging templates, which avoid boxing in newer .NET versions.
So my rule is simply: use generic collections and APIs, and watch allocations in a profiler when performance matters.

IDisposable is the interface for objects that hold resources the garbage collector doesn't manage, like file handles, database connections, network streams or SFTP sessions. Its Dispose method releases them deterministically, right away, instead of waiting for the GC.

The using statement is the safe way to call Dispose. You write using, create the object, and put the code in a block; Dispose is called automatically at the end of the block, even if an exception is thrown, because it compiles into try-finally. The newer using declaration, from C# 8, is just using var x equals something, without braces, and it disposes at the end of the current scope, which means less nesting. For async cleanup there's IAsyncDisposable with await using.

In our SFTP component, every connection is wrapped in a using, so sessions are always closed, even when a transfer fails halfway. With dependency injection, the container disposes scoped and transient services at the end of the request, so I don't dispose injected services myself.
All three make a value unchangeable, but at different times and in different ways.

A const is a compile-time constant. It's implicitly static, and its value is copied into every assembly that uses it. So it must be a simple literal, like a number or string, and if you change it, every calling assembly needs recompiling, otherwise they keep the old value. A readonly field can be set only in its declaration or in the constructor, so each object can have a different value, decided at runtime. A static readonly field is set once for the whole type at runtime, and it can hold any object, like a TimeSpan, a Regex or a list.

My rule is: const only for values that are truly fixed forever, like a header name. Static readonly for shared defaults and objects, like a compiled Regex for validating study codes. Readonly for injected dependencies in constructors, which is the most common use in our services.
And for configuration that can change between environments, I use the Options pattern, not constants at all.
ref, out and in are all ways to pass an argument by reference, instead of passing a copy.

With ref, the variable must be initialised before the call, and the method can read and change it, and the caller sees the change. With out, the method must assign a value before it returns, and the caller doesn't need to initialise it. The classic example is int.TryParse, which returns a bool for success and gives the parsed number through an out parameter. With in, you pass a read-only reference: the method can't change it, and the point is to avoid copying a large struct.

In everyday code I use out mostly for Try-pattern methods. For example, our CSV validator has a TryParseRow method that returns true or false and gives the parsed row as an out parameter, so we avoid exceptions for normal validation failures.
I use ref and in rarely, mostly in performance-sensitive code. Usually returning a result object or a tuple is clearer.
Nullable reference types are a C# 8 feature that makes null-safety part of the type system.

Once you enable it in the project, a normal reference type like string means "should never be null", and you mark something that can be null with a question mark, like string question mark. The compiler then does flow analysis and warns you if you might dereference something that could be null without checking, or if you assign null to a non-nullable reference. It doesn't change runtime behaviour, but it moves a whole class of NullReferenceException bugs to compile time.

All our newer IRT projects have it enabled, and we treat the warnings seriously in code review. It also makes APIs self-documenting: if a method returns Shipment question mark, callers know they must handle the not-found case.
When enabling it on an older project, I do it file by file, so the team isn't hit with hundreds of warnings at once.
Pattern matching lets me test the shape or type of a value and extract data from it in a single, readable step.

In C# there are several forms. The is keyword with type patterns, like if x is Shipment s. Switch expressions, which return a value. Property patterns, which check properties, like a status equal to Dispatched. Relational patterns like greater than 10, logical patterns with and, or and not, and list patterns. It replaces long if-else chains and casting code, and the compiler can warn you if a switch doesn't cover every case.

In our code, for example, I use a switch expression on shipment status to decide the next allowed status, and a property pattern to calculate shipping priority, like express shipments first, then heavy ones, then the rest. It also helps when handling messages: a switch on the message type routes each event to the right handler.
It makes business rules much easier to read and review.
An extension method is a static method that you can call as if it were an instance method on an existing type, without modifying that type.

You write it in a static class, and you put the this keyword before the first parameter, which is the type you're extending. Then it appears in IntelliSense on that type. It's resolved at compile time, so it can't access private members, and a real instance method with the same signature always wins. All of LINQ, like Where and Select, is built as extension methods on IEnumerable and IQueryable.

I use them for small, focused helpers. For example, a ToPagedResultAsync method on IQueryable, so every list API pages in the same way. And for clean dependency injection registration, like services.AddSftpProviders and app.UseCorrelationId, so Program.cs reads like a story instead of fifty lines of setup.
The rule I follow is not to overuse them for business logic, because it hides where behaviour lives.
An enum is a set of named constants backed by an integer type. For example, ShipmentStatus with Created, Dispatched, Delivered and Cancelled.

It makes code readable and type-safe compared with magic numbers or strings. The compiler stops you passing a random int where a ShipmentStatus is expected, and switch expressions can warn about missing cases. With the Flags attribute, values can be combined bitwise, like permissions. One thing to remember is that any integer can be cast to an enum, even if it isn't defined, so values coming from APIs or files must be validated, for example with Enum.IsDefined.

We also decide deliberately how to store them. EF Core stores enums as int by default, but for audit-friendly tables we sometimes store them as strings, so the data is readable, and so reordering the enum can't silently change meaning. In APIs we serialise them as strings with JsonStringEnumConverter.

And when an enum starts needing behaviour, like each status having its own rules about which next status is allowed, I replace it with a small class or a state machine, so the rules live in one place instead of being spread across switch statements.
An async deadlock happens when code blocks on async work, for example by calling .Result or .Wait() on a task, in an environment that has a synchronization context.

In classic ASP.NET or desktop UI apps, the synchronization context means the continuation after an await must resume on the original thread. If that same thread is blocked waiting on .Result, the task can never finish, because it needs the thread that's waiting for it. So both wait forever. ASP.NET Core doesn't have that synchronization context, so you don't get this exact deadlock, but blocking still causes thread-pool starvation under load, where requests pile up and the API slows to a crawl.
The fix is async all the way: await instead of blocking, and make callers async too. In library code we use ConfigureAwait(false) so it's safe in any environment.
I've seen the starvation version in practice: an old helper that called .Result on an HTTP call caused timeouts under load, and making it async fixed it.

ConfigureAwait controls where the code after an await continues running. ConfigureAwait(false) says "I don't need to come back to the original synchronization context; any thread-pool thread is fine."

This matters in environments that have a synchronization context, like WinForms, WPF or classic ASP.NET. There, by default, the continuation is posted back to the original UI or request thread. That costs a context switch, and if someone blocks on the task with .Result, it can deadlock, because the thread the continuation needs is the one that's blocked. With ConfigureAwait(false), the continuation runs on the pool, so it's a bit faster and avoids that deadlock.

ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so in application code like controllers and services it makes no practical difference, and we don't clutter our code with it. But in reusable libraries, which might be used from any kind of app, I still add ConfigureAwait(false) to every await. For example, our shared SFTP library does that.
The real fix for deadlocks is still async all the way.
LINQ stands for Language Integrated Query. It's a set of query operators built into C#, like Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, Join, Any and Sum, that work the same way on many data sources.

Over in-memory collections, which are IEnumerable, LINQ runs as normal C# code using delegates. Over IQueryable, like an EF Core DbSet, it builds an expression tree that the provider translates into SQL, so the work happens in the database. You can write it with method syntax, which is most common, or query syntax that looks like SQL. Most operators use deferred execution, so the query only runs when you enumerate it or call ToList.

I use LINQ every day. The important skill is knowing where each part runs. For example, on our shipment search I make sure the filters and paging are translated to SQL, and I check the generated SQL in logs, so we don't accidentally pull thousands of rows into memory or trigger client-side evaluation.
LINQ makes data code short and readable.
These three collection interfaces build on each other, each one adding more abilities.

IEnumerable is the simplest. It only lets you loop over items, forward only, and it supports deferred execution. ICollection adds Count, Add, Remove, Contains and Clear, so you know the size and can change the contents. IList adds access by index, like getting item number five, plus Insert and RemoveAt. There are also read-only versions, IReadOnlyCollection and IReadOnlyList, which give Count and indexing without allowing changes.

My rule for API design is: accept the smallest interface you need, and return the most useful read-only type. If a method only loops over items, it takes IEnumerable, so callers can pass a list, an array or a query. If it needs the count up front, it takes IReadOnlyCollection. And methods usually return IReadOnlyList, so callers can index but can't modify our internal list.
One caution: accepting IEnumerable and enumerating it twice can run an expensive query twice.
These four LINQ methods all return one element, but they behave differently when there are zero or multiple matches.

First returns the first matching element and throws if there's none. FirstOrDefault returns the first match, or the default value, which is null for reference types, if there's none. Single expects exactly one match: it throws if there are none, and also throws if there's more than one. SingleOrDefault allows zero, returning default, but still throws if there's more than one. In SQL terms, Single fetches up to two rows to check for duplicates, while First fetches one.

So the choice expresses intent. I use Single or SingleOrDefault when looking up by something that must be unique, like a study code or a kit number, because if duplicates exist, that's a data bug and I want to know about it immediately rather than silently picking one. I use FirstOrDefault when "not found" is normal, usually with an OrderBy so "first" is well-defined.
Using First without an order is a subtle bug, because the database can return rows in any order.
Any and Count can both tell you whether there are items, but Any is the right tool for checking existence.

Any stops as soon as it finds one matching item, so it's cheap no matter how big the data is. Count has to go through every item to count them, unless the collection already knows its size. In EF Core, Any translates into an EXISTS query, which SQL Server can stop at the first row, while Count translates to SELECT COUNT, which has to count every matching row. On a big table that difference is huge.
Note that the Count property on a List or an array is different, it's already stored, so reading it is free. The issue is the Count method on queries and lazy sequences.
So in our code, a check like "does this study already have an active import" is written with AnyAsync, never CountAsync greater than zero. Code analyzers even flag that pattern now.
A closure is a lambda or local function that captures variables from the code around it, and keeps using them even after that outer method has finished.

Under the hood, the C# compiler moves captured variables into a hidden class, and both the outer method and the lambda share that object. That's why the lambda sees the latest value of the variable, not a copy from when it was created. This is very useful, for example in LINQ filters that use a method parameter, or in callbacks.

There are two classic pitfalls. First, capturing a loop variable: in old C# a foreach loop shared one variable, so all the lambdas saw the last value. Modern C# fixed foreach, but a for loop index can still surprise you. Second, a closure can keep a large object alive longer than expected, for example an event handler lambda that captures a big service, which becomes a memory leak if it's never unsubscribed.
In performance-sensitive code, I also watch for closures allocating on every call, and use static lambdas where possible.

The Liskov Substitution Principle says that objects of a derived type must work anywhere the base type is expected, without the caller getting surprises. A subtype can add behaviour, but it must keep the base type's promises.

The textbook violation is Square inheriting from Rectangle. If code sets the width of a rectangle and expects the height to stay the same, a Square breaks that expectation. A more realistic violation is a read-only repository that inherits a Save method and throws NotSupportedException. The fix there is to split the interface, not to throw.

In my SFTP component, Liskov was a real design goal. All three providers implement ISftpClient, and they must behave the same way for the caller: same behaviour when a file already exists, same timeout handling, and every failure surfaces as our own SftpTransferException, never a silent failure or a library-specific exception. I enforced that with a shared set of contract tests that every provider must pass.
That's why we could switch a vendor from ComponentPro to Rebex with only a configuration change.
The Interface Segregation Principle says clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use. So it's better to have several small, focused interfaces than one big "fat" interface.

When an interface is too large, every implementer must implement methods it doesn't need, often by throwing, and every consumer gets access to more than it should. Changes to unrelated methods also force recompiles and test changes everywhere. Microsoft follows this principle with IReadOnlyList being separate from IList.

A practical example from our code: instead of one big IShipmentRepository with read, update and delete, we can split it into an IShipmentReader for queries and an IShipmentWriter for commands. A reporting service only takes the reader, so it physically can't modify shipments, which is nice in a GxP system, and its unit tests only need to mock two or three methods. Similarly, in the MCP server, tools are grouped by capability, so read-only tools don't get access to deployment operations.
The balance is not to go too far, with one-method interfaces everywhere.

The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level business code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level classes. Both sides depend on the interface, so the dependency direction is inverted.

Without it, a business service creates its infrastructure directly, like new-ing up a specific SFTP library. Then the business logic is tied to that library, changing it means editing business code, and you can't unit test the service without a real server.

In our vendor file exchange, the VendorExchangeService depends only on ISftpClient, which is defined alongside the business logic. The infrastructure layer contains the Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro implementations, and Program.cs registers them in the ASP.NET Core DI container. So the business code never references Rebex at all. When a vendor needed a different library, it was a configuration change, and in unit tests I simply inject a mock ISftpClient with Moq.
Dependency injection is the mechanism, and dependency inversion is the design principle behind it.
I chose an interface for our SFTP integration for three concrete reasons.

First, I needed several interchangeable implementations behind one contract. We had three libraries, Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro, and different vendors needed different ones. An interface let business code depend on ISftpClient and stay completely unaware of which library ran. Second, testability. With an interface I can inject a mock with Moq in unit tests, so testing the file-exchange logic doesn't need a real SFTP server. Third, extensibility. Interfaces let me add decorators, like retry and logging wrappers, around any provider without touching the providers, and adding a new library is just a new class.

I also used an abstract base class, because the providers shared real code like retry policies, timeouts and logging. So the interface is the contract, and the base class is shared implementation. Callers only see the interface.
The result was that switching a vendor to Rebex was a configuration change with no business code edits.
I avoid inheritance in a few situations.

First, when the relationship isn't truly "is-a". If I just want to reuse a few methods, inheritance is the wrong tool, and composition, having a collaborator, is better. Second, when behaviour varies in several independent ways. For example, transfer method and retry policy are separate concerns, and subclasses for every combination explode, so strategies or decorators work better. Third, when hierarchies get deep. A change in a base class ripples to every child, which is called the fragile base class problem. And fourth, across module or team boundaries, where others would inherit from my class and depend on its internals.

A real example: we needed retry and logging around SFTP clients. Instead of creating a RetryingRebexClient, a RetryingSshNetClient and so on, I wrote one retry decorator that wraps any ISftpClient. That's one class instead of three.
I still use inheritance where it's natural and shallow, like one abstract base class for shared provider code.
Garbage collection affects performance because, while the GC runs, it has to pause or slow down application threads to find and free unused objects.

Gen 0 collections are very quick, but if the app allocates a lot of objects, they happen very often. The expensive ones are gen 2 and Large Object Heap collections, which can cause noticeable pauses and push up tail latency, like p99. So the main lever is allocation rate: the less garbage you create, the less the GC has to do. ASP.NET Core uses server GC by default, tuned for throughput, with background collection to reduce pauses.

In hot paths I reduce allocations with a few techniques: Span of T and Memory of T to slice data without copying, ArrayPool to reuse buffers, avoiding boxing, avoiding big temporary strings and LINQ chains in tight loops, and streaming large data instead of loading it whole. I measure with dotnet-counters and a profiler before and after.
For example, for our CSV import I streamed the file row by row instead of loading it all, which kept memory flat even for large files.
When an exception happens inside an async method, it doesn't crash straight away. It's captured and stored inside the Task that the method returns.

When you await that task, the exception is rethrown at the await, with its original stack trace, so a normal try-catch around the await works exactly as you'd expect. But if nobody awaits the task, for example a fire-and-forget call, the exception is unobserved and effectively lost, which hides bugs. With async void methods it's worse: there's no task to hold the exception, so it's raised on the synchronization context or thread pool and can crash the whole process. That's why I only use async void for event handlers.
With Task.WhenAll, await throws the first exception, but the task's Exception property holds all of them, so I check that when I need every failure.
In our services, every async call is awaited, background work runs in a BackgroundService with its own try-catch and logging, and unhandled request exceptions go to our global exception handler.
Dependency injection means a class receives the objects it needs, its dependencies, from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself with new.

In ASP.NET Core there's a built-in DI container. In Program.cs I register services with a lifetime, singleton, scoped or transient, and when a controller or service is created, the container builds it and passes in everything it needs, then disposes things at the right time.

We use it for four reasons. Loose coupling, because classes depend on interfaces, not concrete types. Testability, because in unit tests I can pass mocks instead of real databases or servers. Flexibility, because I can swap implementations through configuration. And central lifetime management, so things like DbContext are created per request and disposed automatically.

A real example: our VendorExchangeService gets an SFTP client factory, a logger and its options injected. In production the factory returns the right library for each vendor, and in unit tests I inject a mock, so I can test the retry and error logic without a real SFTP server.
A dependency is anything a class needs in order to do its job.

Typical dependencies are a repository or DbContext for data, an HttpClient for calling another service, a logger, configuration options, a message publisher, or an SFTP client. Less obvious ones are the current time and random numbers, because code that calls DateTime.Now directly is hard to test. If a class creates its dependencies itself, with new or static calls, it's tightly coupled to them: you can't swap them, and you can't test the class in isolation.
With dependency injection, those dependencies are passed in through the constructor, so the class just declares what it needs and the container provides it.

For example, our study-transfer safety guard depends on a repository to read study state, a logger, and TimeProvider for the current time. Because time is injected, in unit tests I use a fake time provider to test rules like "block transfers after the cut-off date" without waiting for real time to pass.
A good sign of too many dependencies is a long constructor, which usually means the class does too much.

Inversion of Control is a design idea where the framework controls the flow of the program and calls your code, rather than your code controlling everything. It's often summed up as "don't call us, we'll call you".

In ASP.NET Core, I don't write a main loop that reads requests. The framework receives the request, runs the middleware pipeline, creates my controller and calls the action. Object creation is also inverted: instead of my classes creating their dependencies, something else creates and supplies them. Dependency injection is the most common form of IoC.
