An IoC container is the component that does that work. You register types and their lifetimes, and it builds the whole object graph, injects constructor parameters, manages singleton, scoped and transient lifetimes, and disposes objects at the right time. In .NET the built-in one is IServiceCollection for registration and IServiceProvider for resolution. Third-party ones like Autofac add features like property injection or modules.
In our services the built-in container is enough.
Both are ways of giving a class its dependencies, but constructor injection is the one I use almost always.

With constructor injection, dependencies are parameters of the constructor. That makes required dependencies explicit; you can't create the object without them, so it's always fully ready. The fields can be readonly, so they can't be swapped later, and it's easy to see in tests what to mock. With property injection, dependencies are set through public properties after the object is created. That hides what's required, allows half-initialised objects, and makes the dependency mutable. It's only reasonable for truly optional dependencies.
The built-in .NET container supports only constructor injection; property injection needs something like Autofac. With C# 12 primary constructors, constructor injection is also very concise.

One useful side effect: if a constructor grows to seven or eight parameters, it's a clear signal the class has too many responsibilities. I've split services for exactly that reason, for example separating CSV parsing from validation.
IServiceProvider is the interface of the built-in .NET DI container. It's the object that actually resolves services, through GetService or GetRequiredService.

You register services on an IServiceCollection in Program.cs, and when the host is built, that becomes the root IServiceProvider, which holds the singletons. For each HTTP request, ASP.NET Core creates a scope, a child provider, which holds that request's scoped services like DbContext, and HttpContext.RequestServices points to it. When the request ends, the scope is disposed, along with its scoped and transient disposables.

In normal code I don't use IServiceProvider directly. I use constructor injection, because calling the provider all over the code is the service locator anti-pattern and hides dependencies. I use it in a few specific places: inside factories that pick an implementation at runtime, and in singletons or background services where I create a scope with IServiceScopeFactory to get scoped services. For example, our background message consumer creates a scope per message to get a fresh DbContext.
The rule is that a service should only depend on services that live at least as long as it does.

A singleton lives for the whole application, so it should depend only on other singletons. A scoped service lives for one request, so it can depend on scoped and singleton services. A transient is created every time, so it can depend on anything, as long as it's resolved inside a scope when it needs scoped services. A singleton can technically take a transient, but that transient then effectively becomes a singleton, which can surprise you.

The dangerous case is a singleton depending on a scoped service, like DbContext. That's called a captive dependency: the singleton holds the first request's DbContext forever, which isn't thread-safe and serves stale data. ASP.NET Core catches this in development with scope validation, which throws at startup.
When a singleton genuinely needs scoped work, like our background consumer, it injects IServiceScopeFactory and creates a scope per unit of work.
Both resolve a service from the DI container, but they behave differently when the service isn't registered.

GetService returns null if the service isn't registered. So it's meant for optional services, where the caller handles the null case. GetRequiredService throws an InvalidOperationException with a clear message naming the missing type. So it's for services that must exist. GetRequiredService is an extension method on IServiceProvider, and there's a generic version of each.

I prefer GetRequiredService, because failing fast with a clear message is much easier to diagnose than a NullReferenceException somewhere later. With GetService, a forgotten registration can turn into a confusing null error in a completely different place. ASP.NET Core also validates the whole container at startup in development, which catches missing registrations early.

But honestly, I rarely call either one. In normal code I use constructor injection. I only call GetRequiredService in factories or after creating a scope in a background service, for example to get a fresh DbContext for each message in our consumer.
In ASP.NET Core, a controller simply declares what it needs as constructor parameters, and the framework supplies them for every request.

When a request arrives, ASP.NET Core creates a DI scope for it, available as HttpContext.RequestServices. The controller activator then creates the controller from that scope. The container looks at the constructor, chooses the one with the most parameters it can satisfy, and resolves each dependency, and their dependencies, recursively, building the whole object graph. Scoped services, like DbContext, are shared by everything in that one request. When the request ends, the scope is disposed, along with the scoped and transient disposables.
Minimal APIs work the same way but inject straight into the handler's parameters, and in controllers I can use the FromServices attribute to inject into a single action.
For example, our shipments controller takes an IShipmentService and a logger. The service takes the DbContext and a publisher. One request, one DbContext, shared by both, and disposed at the end.
The DI container lets you register several implementations of the same interface, and there are three main ways to resolve them.

First, if I inject IEnumerable of the interface, I get all registrations in the order they were added. That's perfect for a pipeline of validators or notifiers, where every one should run. Second, if I inject the interface on its own, I get the last one registered, which is how you override a default. Third, when I need one specific implementation, .NET 8 added keyed services: I register with AddKeyedScoped and a key, and inject with the FromKeyedServices attribute or resolve with GetRequiredKeyedService. Before .NET 8, I used a small factory that picks by configuration.

In our vendor exchange, each vendor's configuration names its SFTP library. Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro are registered as keyed services, and the factory resolves the right one by key. For our CSV import, a list of validators is injected as IEnumerable and each one checks a different rule.

Yes. You inject IServiceScopeFactory, call CreateScope, resolve the services you need from scope.ServiceProvider, and dispose the scope when the unit of work is done, usually with a using statement. There's also CreateAsyncScope for services that need async disposal.

You need this wherever there's no request scope but you need scoped services. The classic case is a BackgroundService or hosted service, which is a singleton. If it injected DbContext directly, that would be a captive dependency, one DbContext forever, which isn't thread-safe and fills up its change tracker. So instead it creates a new scope per unit of work.

In our system, the SFTP poller is a BackgroundService. On each polling run, it creates a scope, resolves the vendor exchange service and a fresh DbContext, processes the files, and disposes the scope. Our RabbitMQ consumer does the same per message. That keeps every run isolated, with clean change tracking and connections returned to the pool.

The service locator anti-pattern is when a class pulls its dependencies from the container itself, typically by injecting IServiceProvider and calling GetService inside its methods, instead of declaring them in the constructor.

It's called an anti-pattern because it hides the real dependencies. Looking at the constructor, you can't tell what the class needs, so the API lies. Missing registrations only fail at runtime when that line runs, not at startup. And tests get harder, because you have to build or mock a whole service provider instead of just passing two mocks. It also makes it easy to resolve the wrong lifetime by accident.

There are legitimate places for it: the composition root in Program.cs, factories that pick an implementation at runtime, middleware, and background services creating scopes. Those are infrastructure code.
In business classes, I always use constructor injection. In code reviews, if I see IServiceProvider injected into a service, I ask what it needs and move that to the constructor.
Because a DI-based service receives everything through its constructor, unit testing it is straightforward. I don't use the container at all in unit tests.

I create the class directly with new, passing mocks or fakes for its interfaces, usually with Moq, plus simple fakes like FakeTimeProvider for time or NullLogger for logging. Then I call the method and assert the outcome, like the return value or the state change, and verify only the key interactions, like "upload was called once with this file name". I avoid verifying every call, because that makes tests brittle.

For example, for the vendor exchange service, I mock ISftpClient to throw a timeout on the first call and succeed on the second, then assert that the retry worked and the transfer was logged as successful. No real SFTP server is needed.

Separately, I test the wiring. Integration tests with WebApplicationFactory replace only external services, and building the provider with ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes catches missing registrations and captive dependencies.
A good real example is our vendor file exchange service.

The VendorExchangeService takes three things through its constructor: an ISftpClientFactory, an IOptions of SftpOptions with vendor settings, and an ILogger. It has no idea which SFTP library is actually used. The factory reads each vendor's configuration and returns the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro implementation. In Program.cs, the factory is registered as a singleton because it's stateless, the exchange service is scoped, and each SFTP client is created per transfer and disposed afterwards, so connections are never shared across threads.

Across the system we use all three lifetimes deliberately. DbContext is scoped, one per request. The RabbitMQ connection is a singleton, because connections are expensive and thread-safe, while channels are per consumer. Validators are transient, because they're light and stateless.
The benefit was real: when a vendor needed a different library, it was a configuration change, and every piece is unit tested with mocks.
Choosing lifetimes is a trade-off, and both extremes cause problems.

Not everything can be a singleton, because one instance is shared by every thread and every request. So it must be thread-safe, and it must never hold per-request data, or one user could see another user's data. A singleton also can't safely hold scoped things like DbContext, which leads to captive dependency bugs, stale data and concurrency exceptions.

Not everything should be transient either. Creating new objects for every injection wastes allocations, expensive objects get rebuilt constantly, and you lose per-request sharing. For example, if two services in one request need the same unit of work, they need the same DbContext, which scoped gives you. Disposable transients resolved from the root also pile up until shutdown.

So my rule: singleton for stateless or thread-safe shared things, like configuration, caches, HttpClient factories and the RabbitMQ connection. Scoped for per-request state, like DbContext and the current user. Transient for light, stateless helpers, like validators.
When a request finishes, several things happen in a clean order.

First, the endpoint returns, and the response flows back out through the middleware pipeline in reverse order, so middleware can add headers or log the result. Then the response is completed and flushed to the client. After that, ASP.NET Core disposes the request's DI scope. That disposes every scoped service and every transient disposable created in that scope. For example, the DbContext is disposed, which returns its database connection to the pool. Finally, the HttpContext is released, and its objects can be reused for the next request.

There's also the early-end case. If the client disconnects before we finish, HttpContext.RequestAborted, the request's cancellation token, is triggered. Code that passes that token down to EF Core and HttpClient stops working instead of finishing a response nobody will read.
That's why I never keep references to scoped services, like DbContext, beyond the request, for example in a fire-and-forget task. That would use an already disposed object.
The rule is simple: the container disposes what it creates.

Scoped services, and transient services resolved inside a scope, are disposed when that scope ends. For web requests, that's at the end of the request. Singletons the container created are disposed when the root provider is disposed, which happens at application shutdown. The container calls Dispose, or DisposeAsync for IAsyncDisposable, in reverse order of creation.

There are two gotchas. First, if I create an instance myself and register it, like AddSingleton with new MyService, the container did not create it, so it won't dispose it. I'm responsible for that. Second, if a disposable transient is resolved from the root provider, not a scope, the container keeps a reference so it can dispose it at shutdown. That means every resolution stays in memory, which is a slow memory leak.
In our background services, that's exactly why we create a scope per unit of work, so disposables like DbContext are cleaned up each time.

ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's modern, open-source and cross-platform framework for building web applications, mainly web APIs, but also MVC sites, Razor Pages, real-time apps with SignalR, and gRPC services.

It's built around a few core pieces. A middleware pipeline that every request passes through. Built-in dependency injection. A flexible configuration system, from appsettings files, environment variables and secret stores. Built-in logging, and the Kestrel web server. It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, and in containers, and it's consistently one of the fastest mainstream web frameworks in benchmarks.
Compared with the old .NET Framework ASP.NET, it's modular, you only add what you need, it isn't tied to IIS, and it gets a new version every year.

In my work, all our IRT APIs are ASP.NET Core Web APIs, running in Docker containers on AWS ECS behind an Application Load Balancer. We recently upgraded them to .NET 10 in early 2026, which gave a 10 to 15 percent improvement in p95 latency on 3 services.
Kestrel is the web server built into ASP.NET Core. It's cross-platform, fully asynchronous, and very fast, and it supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, as well as HTTPS and WebSockets.

When an ASP.NET Core app starts, Kestrel listens on the configured ports, accepts connections, parses the HTTP request, and hands it to the middleware pipeline. It can be exposed directly to the internet, but in most production setups it sits behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, like IIS, Nginx or an AWS Application Load Balancer. The proxy handles TLS termination, routing, and protection, and Kestrel focuses on running the app. In that setup, you need the forwarded headers middleware so the app knows the original scheme and client IP.

In our case, each service runs Kestrel inside a Docker container on ECS. The ALB terminates TLS with an ACM certificate and forwards to Kestrel on port 8080. We configure request limits, like maximum body size, on Kestrel for endpoints like the CSV import.
Middleware runs in exactly the order it's registered, so a wrong order doesn't usually crash the app. It quietly breaks behaviour, which is worse.

Some common examples. If UseAuthorization comes before UseAuthentication, the user isn't identified yet when authorization runs, so every protected endpoint returns 401 or 403. If UseCors is placed after the endpoints, or after authentication, preflight requests don't get CORS headers and the browser blocks the call, even though Postman works fine. If the exception handler is added late, exceptions thrown by earlier middleware aren't caught, and the client gets a raw 500. And if static files come after authentication, even public files need a login.
A typical correct order is: exception handling and HSTS, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, then the endpoints.
I actually hit one of these. When adding our correlation-id middleware in 2024, we placed it after the exception handler, so error logs had no correlation id. Moving it earlier fixed that.
Use, Run and Map are the three basic ways to build the middleware pipeline.

Use adds middleware that receives the context and a next delegate. It can do work before calling next, call next to pass the request on, and then do more work as the response comes back. It can also choose not to call next and short-circuit. Run adds terminal middleware: it doesn't get a next delegate, so it always ends the pipeline, and anything registered after it never runs. Map branches the pipeline by path. For example, Map of "/health" creates a separate mini-pipeline for that path. MapWhen branches on any condition, and UseWhen branches but rejoins the main pipeline.

In practice, for normal application routes I use endpoint routing, MapControllers, MapGet and so on, not raw Map. Use is what I use for custom middleware, like our correlation-id middleware, which sets the id, calls next, and adds the id to the response.
A common mistake is putting Run in the middle and wondering why later middleware never executes.
Endpoint routing is the routing system in ASP.NET Core that separates matching a route from executing it.

UseRouting runs early in the pipeline. It matches the request to an endpoint, like a controller action or a minimal API handler, and stores that endpoint on the HttpContext. The endpoint carries metadata, such as the Authorize attribute, a CORS policy, a rate limiting policy or AllowAnonymous. So middleware that runs between routing and the endpoint, like CORS, authentication, authorization and rate limiting, can read that metadata and make decisions. Finally, the endpoint itself executes at the end of the pipeline.

The big benefit is one consistent routing system for controllers, minimal APIs, gRPC, SignalR and health checks, and policy-aware middleware. Before it, in old MVC, routing happened inside MVC, so middleware couldn't know which action would run.
I've used it directly. Our correlation-id and audit middleware calls GetEndpoint to read a custom attribute, so certain endpoints, like health checks, skip auditing.
Since .NET 6, Startup.cs is no longer part of the default template. Microsoft introduced the minimal hosting model, which merges Program.cs and Startup.cs into one file.

Previously, Program.cs built the host, and the Startup class had two methods: ConfigureServices for registering services, and Configure for building the middleware pipeline. Now, you create a WebApplicationBuilder. The service registrations that were in ConfigureServices go on builder.Services. Then you call builder.Build to get the app, and the pipeline that was in Configure goes on the app object, with app.Use and app.Map calls. Top-level statements remove the boilerplate.
Nothing is lost. Startup still works if you prefer it, and large apps often keep things organised with extension methods, like AddPersistence or AddMessaging, so Program.cs stays readable.

When we upgraded our services from older versions, we moved to the minimal hosting model step by step. We grouped registrations into extension methods per area, which made Program.cs much shorter and easier to review.
CORS does not protect your API. It's a browser rule, not a server security feature.

Browsers follow the same-origin policy, which stops a script on one site from reading responses from another origin. CORS, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, is a way for the server to relax that rule, by telling the browser which other origins are allowed to read its responses. For non-simple requests, the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request first and checks the headers.

But only browsers enforce it. Postman, curl, a script or another server can call the API regardless of the CORS settings. So CORS protects users in the browser from malicious sites reading data with their cookies. It doesn't stop anyone from calling your API directly.

Real API security comes from authentication, authorization, input validation and rate limiting. In our services, CORS only allows our own front-end origins explicitly, never a wildcard with credentials, and every endpoint still requires a valid token with the right roles.
HTTPS has two parts: where TLS is terminated, and how the app enforces it.

In development, ASP.NET Core uses a local dev certificate, trusted with dotnet dev-certs. In production you can configure a certificate on Kestrel directly, but more commonly TLS is terminated at a load balancer or API gateway. In the app, I add UseHttpsRedirection, so plain HTTP requests are redirected, and UseHsts in production, which tells browsers to always use HTTPS for that domain. When behind a proxy, I configure the forwarded headers middleware, so the app knows the original request was HTTPS and redirects and links are correct.

In our AWS setup, the Application Load Balancer terminates TLS using a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager, which renews automatically. HTTP on port 80 is redirected to 443 at the ALB. Traffic between components is also encrypted where our policy requires it, and the database connections use TLS.
For a regulated system, we also enforce modern TLS versions with a TLS security policy on the ALB.
Health checks are endpoints that report whether the app and its dependencies are healthy, so infrastructure can make routing and restart decisions automatically.

In ASP.NET Core, I call AddHealthChecks and add checks for important dependencies, like the database, RabbitMQ or Redis, either from community packages or custom IHealthCheck classes. Then I map them with MapHealthChecks. I usually expose two. A liveness endpoint that only says the process is running, and a readiness endpoint that checks dependencies, so the instance only receives traffic when it can actually serve it. Each check returns Healthy, Degraded or Unhealthy.

In our setup, the Application Load Balancer target group calls the health endpoint, and only healthy containers get traffic. ECS replaces tasks that keep failing. We keep liveness cheap, because if it checked the database, a database blip would make ECS restart every container at once, which makes things worse.
The health endpoints are excluded from authentication and audit logging.
Graceful shutdown means that when an instance is stopped, it finishes or safely hands back its current work, instead of dropping requests or messages halfway.

When a container is stopped, for example during a deployment, it receives a SIGTERM signal. The ASP.NET Core host then stops accepting new requests, lets in-flight requests finish within the shutdown timeout, which is 30 seconds by default, fires the ApplicationStopping event, and cancels the stopping token for every BackgroundService. After that, it disposes services and exits.

My job is to make the code cooperate. Background loops check the stopping token. Our RabbitMQ consumers stop taking new messages, finish and acknowledge the current message, and then close the channel. Anything not acknowledged goes back to the queue for another instance, so nothing is lost. On AWS, the ALB deregistration delay drains connections first, and the ECS stop timeout gives the container time before it's killed.
This is a big reason we use manual acks.
A CancellationToken is how .NET tells asynchronous work to stop early, and I treat it as a normal part of every async method signature.

In an API action, I accept a CancellationToken parameter. ASP.NET Core binds it to HttpContext.RequestAborted, which is cancelled if the client disconnects. I pass that token all the way down, to EF Core queries, HttpClient calls and Task.Delay, so an abandoned request stops using the database. For timeouts, I create a linked CancellationTokenSource with CancelAfter. In background services I use the stopping token.

When cancellation happens, an OperationCanceledException is thrown. I treat that as normal, not as an error, so it isn't logged as a failure or returned as a 500. And I'm careful where I stop: I don't cancel halfway through a database transaction without rolling back.
A concrete benefit: on a heavy shipment report endpoint, users often navigated away. Passing the token to the EF Core query meant SQL Server stopped running those abandoned queries.
PUT and PATCH both update a resource, but PUT replaces it completely, while PATCH changes only part of it.

With PUT, the client sends the full representation of the resource, and the server replaces what it has. Any field the client leaves out is cleared or set to its default. PUT is idempotent, so sending the same request twice gives the same final state, which makes it safe to retry. PATCH sends only the changes. There are two common formats: JSON Merge Patch, where you send just the fields to change, and JSON Patch, a list of operations like replace or remove. PATCH isn't guaranteed to be idempotent, for example an "add item" operation.
The risk with PUT is a client that sends an old or partial object and accidentally wipes fields. That's why, for small updates, PATCH is safer.

In our APIs, we use PATCH for things like updating only a shipment's status or a site's contact details, combined with a row version, so if someone else changed the record in the meantime, we return 409 instead of silently overwriting it.
Both are success codes, but they mean different things to the client.

200 OK is the general success response. The request worked and the result is in the body, for example a GET returning a shipment, or a PUT returning the updated resource. 201 Created specifically means the request created a new resource. By convention, a 201 response includes a Location header with the URL of the new resource, and usually the created resource in the body, including server-generated values like its id. There's also 202 Accepted, when work has been queued but not finished yet, and 204 No Content, when it succeeded with nothing to return, like a DELETE.
Using the right code helps clients and tools behave correctly without reading the body, and it makes the API self-documenting in OpenAPI.

In ASP.NET Core, I return CreatedAtAction or TypedResults.Created. For example, when a POST creates a shipment, we return 201 with a Location pointing to the GET endpoint for that shipment. And our CSV import returns 202 Accepted with a link to check the import status, because processing runs in the background.
These three are the most commonly confused client errors.

400 Bad Request means the request itself is wrong: invalid JSON, a missing required field, or a failed validation rule. The client needs to fix the request. 401 Unauthorized, despite its name, actually means unauthenticated. We don't know who you are, because the token is missing, invalid or expired, so the client should log in or refresh its token. 403 Forbidden means we know exactly who you are, but you're not allowed to do this. Logging in again won't help.

The distinction matters for the client's behaviour. On 401, our front end tries a token refresh once and then redirects to login. On 403, it shows an "access denied" message. If we returned 401 for permission problems, users would get stuck in a login loop.

A real example: in our IRT system, a user logged in with valid access to one study who tries to open another study's shipments gets a 403 from our resource-based authorization check. Some teams return 404 there to avoid revealing that the record exists.
Both mean the request couldn't be matched, but at different levels.

404 Not Found means the thing doesn't exist. Either there's no route for that URL at all, or the route exists but the specific resource doesn't, like GET on a shipment id that isn't in the database. 405 Method Not Allowed means the URL does exist, but not for that HTTP method. For example, sending DELETE to an endpoint that only supports GET and POST. The response should include an Allow header listing the supported methods, and ASP.NET Core endpoint routing returns 405 for you automatically.

This distinction really helps debugging. A 404 makes me check the URL, the route template or the data. A 405 tells me the URL is right, but the client is using the wrong verb, often a typo in the front end or a missing HttpPut attribute.
A small but important point: some teams intentionally return 404 instead of 403 for records the user isn't allowed to see, so we don't leak that the record exists.
409 and 422 are both about valid-looking requests that we still can't accept, but for different reasons.

409 Conflict means the request clashes with the current state of the resource. Typical cases are creating something that already exists, like a duplicate site number, or an optimistic concurrency conflict, where the client is updating an old version of a record that someone else has already changed. The client usually needs to reload and try again. 422 Unprocessable Entity means the request is well-formed, the JSON is valid and the fields are the right types, but it breaks a business rule. For example, requesting more kits than the depot has, or a ship date in the past.
Some teams use 400 for all validation errors, which is also fine, as long as it's consistent and the ProblemDetails body explains the problem.

In our APIs, the EF Core row-version check maps DbUpdateConcurrencyException to 409, and our business rule validation returns 422 with a ProblemDetails listing each failed rule. That gives the front end a clear way to react.
These are server-side errors, and each one points to a different layer, which is very useful when troubleshooting.

500 Internal Server Error means something failed inside our own service, usually an unhandled exception. The fix is in our code or data, so I go to the logs with the correlation id. 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or load balancer, like our ALB or API gateway, got an invalid response from the service behind it. Often the container crashed, closed the connection, or isn't listening on the right port. 503 Service Unavailable means the service is temporarily unable to handle requests, for example overloaded, in maintenance, or the load balancer has no healthy targets. Ideally it includes a Retry-After header. And 504 Gateway Timeout means the upstream took too long.
So when I see these, I know where to look. 500, our application logs. 502 or 503, the ALB target health and ECS task events. 504, slow queries or downstream calls.
During a deployment issue, a spike of 503s told us that new tasks were failing health checks, not that the code was throwing.

A DTO, or Data Transfer Object, is a simple class or record that defines exactly what data crosses a boundary, like what an API accepts in a request or returns in a response. It holds data only, with no business behaviour.

The main reason to use DTOs is to separate the API contract from the internal model. Database entities change for internal reasons, and if they were the contract, every schema change could break clients. DTOs also let us hide internal or sensitive fields, prevent over-posting, because input DTOs only contain fields the client may set, put validation attributes on inputs, and shape data per use case, like a short list item versus a full detail view.

In our services, DTOs are C# records, which are concise and immutable. For reads, we project directly into DTOs with a Select in EF Core, so SQL only fetches the needed columns. For writes, we map request DTOs to entities in the service layer.
In a clinical system this separation is important, because we must never accidentally expose something like treatment assignment data.
Exposing EF entities directly from an API looks quick, but it causes several real problems.

First, coupling. The database schema becomes the public contract, so renaming a column or splitting a table breaks clients. Second, data leakage. Entities often have internal or sensitive fields, and adding a new column could silently expose it. Third, over-posting. If you bind input directly to an entity, a client can set fields it shouldn't, like a status or an approval flag. Fourth, serialization problems. Navigation properties cause circular references, and with lazy loading, serializing can trigger many extra queries. And fifth, performance: you usually load full entities, and their relationships, instead of only the columns needed.
In a clinical trial system, the leakage risk is serious. Accidentally exposing a blinding-related field would be a major compliance issue, not just a bug.

So in our services, every endpoint uses DTOs. Reads use Select projections into DTOs, and writes map request DTOs to entities in the service layer, with tests that check responses contain only expected fields.
A DTO and a ViewModel are both simple data classes, but they serve different purposes.

A DTO, Data Transfer Object, carries data across a boundary, like between an API and its clients, or between services. It's a transport contract, shaped for the use case and kept stable, with no behaviour. A ViewModel is shaped for one specific screen, usually in server-rendered MVC or Razor Pages. It contains exactly what that view needs, and can include display-only data, like formatted dates, dropdown lists or flags that control what's shown.
In an API-first architecture with a separate front end, like React, the server mostly deals with DTOs. The front end builds its own view state from them, so the ViewModel concept moves to the client.

In our system, the APIs return DTOs, for example a ShipmentSummaryDto for lists and a ShipmentDetailDto for one shipment. The React front end then combines them into what each screen needs. In older MVC parts of the system, we had ViewModels with select lists for forms.
ApiController is an attribute I put on API controllers, and it switches on a set of behaviours that make building Web APIs simpler and more consistent.

First, automatic validation responses. If the model is invalid, it returns a 400 with a ValidationProblemDetails body before the action runs, so I don't need "if not ModelState IsValid" in every action. Second, binding source inference. Complex types come from the body, route values from the route, and simple types from the query string, so fewer FromBody attributes. Third, attribute routing is required, so routes are explicit. Fourth, error status codes are returned as ProblemDetails, the standard error format.
It's usually applied on a base controller, or at assembly level, so every API controller gets it.

In our services, we put it on a shared base controller and customised InvalidModelStateResponseFactory, so validation errors also include our correlation id. That way, every 400 from every service has the same shape, and support can trace it in the logs.
Routing is how ASP.NET Core maps an incoming URL and HTTP method to the code that handles it, like a controller action or a minimal API handler.

There are two styles. Attribute routing puts the route template directly on the controller and actions, for example Route "api/studies/{studyId}/shipments" on the controller, and HttpGet "{id}" on an action. It's explicit, supports route constraints like int, and matches REST resource design well, so it's the standard for APIs and is required with ApiController. Conventional routing defines one central pattern in Program.cs, like "controller/action/id", and all controllers follow it. It's common in traditional MVC websites, where URLs follow a predictable pattern.
Minimal APIs use their own MapGet and MapPost calls, which are essentially attribute routing in code, and route groups help share prefixes and policies.

In our services, we use attribute routing with versioned, resource-based routes, like api/v1/studies/{studyId}/shipments. That makes the URL design visible right in the code and in the OpenAPI document.
Filtering and sorting in an API is about giving clients flexibility while keeping the queries safe and fast.

I accept parameters in the query string, like status equals Shipped, siteId equals 12, sortBy equals shipDate and descending equals true, usually bound to a query object. Then I build the query step by step on IQueryable. For each filter that's present, I add a Where clause. For sorting, I map the sortBy value to a known expression from an allow-list, never to a raw column name or SQL string, which prevents injection and stops clients from sorting by unindexed columns. Then I apply paging with Skip and Take, or keyset paging for large tables, and return the total count or a next link.
Because everything stays on IQueryable until the end, EF Core translates it all into one SQL query, so the database does the work.

On our shipment search, I made sure the most common filter combinations, study, status and ship date, were covered by an index, and checked the execution plans. That kept the search fast as the data grew.

OpenAPI is a standard, machine-readable way to describe a REST API, in JSON or YAML. It lists every endpoint, its parameters, request and response models, status codes and security requirements. Swagger is the original name and now the name of the tooling around it, like Swagger UI, which renders the document as an interactive page where you can try the calls.

In .NET, the document is generated from the code. Historically we used Swashbuckle, and since .NET 9, there's built-in support with Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi. To make it genuinely useful, I add XML comments, ProducesResponseType for every status code, examples, and the authentication scheme so you can test with a token.

The real value is that the contract is shared. Front-end and vendor teams read it, and they can generate typed clients from it, so they don't hand-code requests. We also publish it per version, and in our pipeline, a check compares the new document with the previous one to catch breaking changes.
For security, Swagger UI is enabled only in non-production environments.
I secure an API in layers, so that if one control fails, the others still protect it.

First, transport: HTTPS only, with HSTS. Second, authentication: every request needs a valid JWT from our identity provider, and we validate the issuer, audience, signature and expiry. Third, authorization: role and policy checks, plus resource-level checks, like "does this user have access to this specific study", which is critical in multi-tenant clinical data. Fourth, input: DTOs, validation, parameterised queries through EF Core, and size limits. Fifth, abuse protection: rate limiting and restricted CORS. And sixth, operations: secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, no sensitive data in logs, least-privilege IAM and database roles, dependency scanning in the pipeline, and audit logs for every change.
Security also covers logout and token lifetime. We use short 15-minute access tokens, and for immediate logout, we added a token-id denylist in ElastiCache that the API checks in about 1 ms.
Every new endpoint goes through a security checklist in code review.
An access token and a refresh token work together, but they have very different jobs and lifetimes.

The access token is short-lived, in our case 15 minutes. It's sent with every API call, usually as a bearer JWT, and the API validates it to know who the user is and what they can do. Because it's short-lived, if it leaks, the damage window is small. The refresh token lives much longer, hours or days. It's never sent to the APIs, only to the identity provider's token endpoint, to get a new access token when the old one expires, so the user doesn't have to log in again. It must be stored securely, and it can be revoked on the server, and with rotation, each use issues a new one.

We used this in a real fix. Users reported that after logging out, their old token still worked until it expired. We revoked the refresh token on logout, and added a denylist of token ids in ElastiCache, which every API checks in about 1 ms. So logout became immediate.
Both control what an authenticated user can do, but policies are more flexible.

Role-based authorization checks whether the user is in a role, like Authorize with Roles equals StudyManager. It's simple, but coarse. You end up with many roles and checks scattered across code. Policy-based authorization defines a named policy, made of one or more requirements. A requirement can check a claim, a role, or run custom logic in an authorization handler. I register policies in AddAuthorization in Program.cs, then use Authorize with Policy, or RequireAuthorization on minimal API endpoints. Roles are really just one kind of policy underneath.
For checks that depend on the actual data, there's resource-based authorization. I inject IAuthorizationService, and call AuthorizeAsync with the user, the resource and a requirement.

That's essential in our clinical system. Being a study manager isn't enough, you must be assigned to that specific study. So we have a StudyAccess requirement and handler that checks the user's study assignments, and returns 403 if they're not on the study.
Over-posting, also called mass assignment, is when a client sends extra fields that the server didn't intend to accept, and they get saved because the API binds directly to an entity.

For example, a user updates their profile, but adds "isAdmin: true" or "status: Approved" to the JSON. If the action takes the EF entity as its parameter and saves it, those fields are written to the database. It's a well-known security issue in the OWASP API Top 10.

The main prevention is input DTOs. Each endpoint has a request DTO containing only the fields that the client is allowed to set. Then the service layer loads the entity and maps only those fields onto it. Server-controlled values, like status, created-by and approval flags, are set by the server logic, never by the client. The Bind attribute is an older alternative, but DTOs are cleaner.

We also have tests that send extra fields, like a different study id or an approval flag, and assert they're ignored. In a GxP system, an unauthorised status change would be an audit finding, so we take it seriously.
Large payloads can exhaust memory and threads, so I handle them in several ways.

First, limits. Kestrel has a default maximum body size of about 30 MB, and I set tighter limits per endpoint with the RequestSizeLimit attribute, so oversized requests are rejected early, before we read them. Second, streaming. Instead of buffering the whole body into memory, or into a big model object, I read the request stream directly and process it incrementally. Third, for really large files, I don't send them through the API at all. The client uploads directly to S3 using a presigned URL, and the API only gets the object key. Fourth, for heavy processing, the API accepts the request, returns 202 Accepted, and a background worker does the work. And on the response side, pagination and response compression.

Our CSV import follows this. Files are limited to 5 MB, roughly 10,000 rows, the parser streams rows instead of loading everything, and processing runs in the background with a status endpoint. Each user can have at most 2 imports running at once.
For file uploads, I think about three things: size, safety and where the file ends up.

For small files, I accept an IFormFile with a request size limit. For larger ones, I stream the multipart body with MultipartReader, so the file isn't buffered in memory, or I use presigned S3 uploads, where the client uploads straight to S3. Then validation. I check the size, the extension against an allow-list, and the actual content, like magic bytes, because the extension and content type can be faked. I never trust the original file name, I generate a random one. Files are stored outside the web root, usually in S3 with encryption, and scanned for malware when required. Processing happens asynchronously.

Our CSV import is a good example. The upload is limited to 5 MB. We check it's really a CSV, then a streaming parser validates the header and each row, collecting all row errors with their line numbers, before anything is saved. Users get a clear error report instead of a partial import.
For me, production-ready means the API is not only correct, but also safe, observable and easy to operate at 2 a.m.

I think in six areas. Contract: DTOs, OpenAPI documentation, versioning, which matters for us because the same APIs serve both our Angular screens and our newer React modules, validation, and consistent ProblemDetails errors. Security: HTTPS, JWT authentication, policy and resource-level authorization, rate limiting, restricted CORS, and secrets in a secret store. Resilience: timeouts and retries with Polly for downstream calls, idempotency keys for creates, health checks and graceful shutdown. Observability: structured logs with correlation ids, metrics, tracing and CloudWatch alarms. Performance: async all the way, paging, caching and efficient queries. And quality: automated tests, and a CI/CD pipeline with quality gates and security scans.
A detail people often skip is validating configuration at startup, with ValidateOnStart, so a missing setting fails the deployment instead of the first request.
When I joined new work, I turned this into a checklist that every new service in our team follows. That's how our correlation-id middleware ended up in 4 services.
Validation should happen at every boundary, but each layer validates for a different purpose.

At the API layer, I validate the shape and format of the request: required fields, lengths, ranges, formats, using data annotations or FluentValidation. ApiController returns a 400 automatically when that fails, so bad input is stopped as early and cheaply as possible. In the service or domain layer, I validate business rules, which need context or data, like "a site must belong to an active depot", or "you can't ship more kits than are available". Those return a 422 with a clear message. And in the database, constraints are the final safety net: primary and foreign keys, unique indexes and check constraints. They catch anything that slips through, including race conditions between two concurrent requests.
UI validation is useful for user experience, but it's never trusted, because anyone can call the API directly.
In our system, for example, the unique site number is checked in the service for a friendly message, and enforced by a unique index for correctness.
Duplicate requests happen all the time: users double-click, clients retry after a timeout, and message brokers redeliver. So I design for it on purpose.

The main technique for creates is an idempotency key. The client sends a unique key, often in an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the key with the result of the first request. If the same key comes again, it returns the stored result instead of executing again. I back that with database protection: natural keys with unique constraints, so even a race between two requests can't create two rows, and optimistic concurrency for updates. On the client side, disabling the button after submit helps, but it's never enough.
For messaging, consumers are idempotent too. We store processed message ids, so redelivered messages are skipped.
A real example is our CSV import. We store a hash of each uploaded file per study. If the same file is uploaded again, we reject it with a clear message instead of importing the rows twice.

Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's open-source ORM, an object-relational mapper, for .NET. It lets me work with the database using C# classes and LINQ, instead of writing SQL and mapping rows by hand.

It maps entity classes to tables and properties to columns, using conventions plus configuration in OnModelCreating. When I write a LINQ query over a DbSet, EF Core translates it into SQL, runs it, and turns the rows back into objects. When I change objects and call SaveChanges, its change tracker works out the INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements and runs them in one transaction. Migrations keep the database schema in step with the model. It supports many databases through providers, like SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite and Cosmos DB.
The trade-off is a little overhead and the risk of inefficient queries if you don't watch the generated SQL. So I always check the SQL for important queries.

In our IRT services, EF Core with SQL Server is the main data access layer. We use AsNoTracking and projections for reads, ExecuteUpdate for bulk changes, and reviewed idempotent migration scripts for releases.
ADO.NET and EF Core both talk to the database, but at very different levels of abstraction.

ADO.NET is the low-level foundation: you open a connection, create a command with SQL text and parameters, execute it, and read rows with a data reader, mapping each column to your objects by hand. It's the fastest option and gives full control, but it's a lot of repetitive code and easy to get wrong. EF Core sits on top of ADO.NET. You write LINQ, and it generates the SQL, maps the results, tracks changes, handles relationships, and manages migrations. That's much more productive and safer for everyday work, with a small performance overhead that rarely matters.
There's also a middle ground, Dapper, a micro-ORM: you write the SQL yourself, and it maps the results to objects very quickly.

My rule: EF Core for most CRUD and business operations, and Dapper or raw ADO.NET for hot paths or complex reporting SQL that's been tuned by hand. In our services, almost everything is EF Core, with a few heavy reports using Dapper.
DbContext and DbSet are the two central types in EF Core.

DbContext represents a session with the database. It combines several responsibilities: it's a unit of work, because it collects changes and saves them together in one transaction; it holds the change tracker, which knows the state of every loaded entity; and it manages the database connection, opening it only when needed. The model, meaning table names, keys, relationships and indexes, is configured in OnModelCreating, usually with separate configuration classes per entity. In ASP.NET Core, a DbContext is registered as scoped, one per request, and it's not thread-safe.

A DbSet of T represents a table, or more precisely the collection of entities of that type. I use it to query, with LINQ, which starts as an IQueryable that's translated into SQL, and to add or remove entities, which are saved on SaveChanges.

In our IRT services, each bounded context has its own DbContext, for example inventory and shipments, with only the DbSets it needs, rather than one giant context for the whole database. That keeps the models smaller and clearer.
Both are used for eager loading related data, but at different levels of the object graph.

Include loads a navigation property of the root entity you're querying. ThenInclude continues from that navigation to load the next level down. For example, querying studies, Include sites, then ThenInclude shipments, loads each study with its sites, and each site with its shipments, all in one query. You can chain multiple Includes for different branches, and since EF Core 5 you can filter inside Include too, like only active sites.

The thing to watch is that deep or multiple collection includes can create a huge result set, because SQL joins multiply the rows, which is called cartesian explosion. If a study has 300 sites and each has 50 shipments, the parent data is repeated for every row. AsSplitQuery fixes this by running a separate query for each collection. Often the better option is a Select projection into a DTO with just the fields needed.
In our IRT services, I prefer projections for read endpoints and use Include mainly when loading an aggregate to update it.
EF Core migrations are how the database schema evolves in step with the C# model.

When I change the model, for example adding a property or an index, I run dotnet ef migrations add with a descriptive name, like AddShipmentStatusIndex. EF Core compares the current model with the last snapshot and generates a migration class with an Up method, to apply the change, and a Down method, to reverse it. I review that code like any other code, because generated migrations can do surprising things, like dropping and recreating a column on a rename, which loses data. If needed, I edit it, for example to add a data migration step.

For deployment, I don't run migrations automatically at application startup. I generate an idempotent SQL script with dotnet ef migrations script with the idempotent option. That script checks the migrations history table, so it can safely run against any environment. It's reviewed and applied by the release pipeline.
In our regulated environment, that script is part of the release evidence for FV, UAT and production.
These are two approaches to deciding what's the source of truth: the C# model or the database.

In Code First, the C# entity classes and their configuration are the source of truth. You design the model in code, and migrations create and evolve the database schema. It works well when the development team owns the database, because the schema is versioned with the code, reviewed in pull requests, and reproducible in every environment. In Database First, the database already exists, often designed and owned by DBAs, or it's a legacy schema. You use dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold to generate the entity classes and DbContext from the existing tables, and you re-scaffold when the schema changes. It's the practical choice when you can't control the schema.
EF Core removed the old EDMX designer, so both approaches now produce plain code. You can also mix them: scaffold once from an existing database, then continue with migrations.
In our IRT services, newer services are Code First with migrations, while some older shared databases were scaffolded Database First, because other systems depend on that schema.
LINQ-to-Entities means writing LINQ queries against EF Core's DbSet, which is an IQueryable, and having EF Core translate them into SQL that runs in the database.

When I write something like Shipments where status is Pending, order by date, take 20, nothing runs yet. EF Core builds an expression tree describing the query. When I enumerate it, for example with ToListAsync, the provider translates the whole expression tree into one SQL statement, sends it to SQL Server, and maps the rows back into objects. So filtering, sorting, paging and aggregates all happen in the database, which is efficient.

The key restriction is that only translatable operations can be used. Standard operators, comparisons, many string and date functions, work fine. But a custom C# method inside a Where can't be translated, and EF Core will throw an exception rather than silently loading everything.

That's different from LINQ-to-Objects, which runs on in-memory collections using delegates. Knowing which one you're in, IQueryable or IEnumerable, is one of the most important things in EF Core performance.
Client-side evaluation is when part of a query runs in .NET memory instead of in the database, which can mean loading far more data than needed.

It happens when the query uses something EF Core can't translate into SQL, like calling a custom C# method inside a Where clause, or certain complex string operations. In old EF Core 2, it silently switched to client evaluation: it pulled every row into memory and then filtered, which was a hidden performance disaster. Since EF Core 3, it throws an exception instead, except in the final Select projection, where running C# on the results is harmless.
The other cause is our own code: calling AsEnumerable, ToList or ToArray too early in the chain. Everything after that point runs in memory. So filtering after ToList loads the whole table first.

To avoid it, I keep the query on IQueryable until the end, rewrite custom logic into translatable expressions, and check the generated SQL with ToQueryString or logging. In a code review on our team, I once caught a ToList before a Where on a large shipment table. Moving it to the end cut the data loaded from the whole table to a few rows.
For EF Core performance, I start by looking at the generated SQL and the execution plan, because most problems are in the query, not in EF itself.

Then I apply a set of habits. For read-only queries, AsNoTracking, so no change-tracking overhead. Project with Select into DTOs, so SQL fetches only the needed columns. Filter and page in the database, keeping everything on IQueryable. Avoid N+1 queries by using projections or Include, and use AsSplitQuery when several collections are included. Make sure the right indexes exist for the filters and sort order. For bulk changes, use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, which run one SQL statement without loading entities. For very hot paths, compiled queries and DbContext pooling reduce overhead. And always pass cancellation tokens, so abandoned requests stop querying.
I log the generated SQL in development, and in production, Query Store and CloudWatch latency metrics show which queries need attention.
A concrete example: our shipment list screen went from about 9 seconds to under 300 ms mainly through a SARGable rewrite, a covering index, and server-side paging.
SaveChanges is the method that writes all pending changes tracked by the DbContext to the database.

When I call it, EF Core first runs change detection, comparing tracked entities with their original snapshots to find what's added, modified and deleted. Then it generates the INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements, batching them where possible, and runs them all inside one transaction. So either all of the changes are saved, or none are. After success, it updates the entities, for example with generated identity values and new concurrency tokens, and marks them as unchanged. It returns the number of rows affected.

SaveChangesAsync does exactly the same, but asynchronously. While the database is doing the work, the thread is released back to the thread pool, instead of sitting idle. In ASP.NET Core, that's what you want, because it lets the server handle more requests under load. So in web APIs and services, I always use SaveChangesAsync, passing the cancellation token.
One more point: I call it once per unit of work, at the end of the operation, not after every small change. That keeps the operation atomic and reduces round trips.
Bulk operations are where the default EF Core approach, loading entities, changing them, and saving, becomes too slow.

For updates and deletes, EF Core 7 added ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete. They translate directly into a single set-based UPDATE or DELETE statement, without loading any rows into memory or using the change tracker. For example, marking all expired kits at a depot as unusable becomes one SQL statement instead of thousands of tracked updates. For inserts, AddRange plus SaveChanges already batches statements, which is fine for hundreds or a few thousand rows. For very large loads, like tens or hundreds of thousands of rows, I use SqlBulkCopy, or a bulk extensions library, which uses SQL Server's bulk insert path and is much faster. I usually process in chunks, so transactions and memory stay manageable.
One caution: ExecuteUpdate bypasses the change tracker, so audit logic in SaveChanges interceptors doesn't run. In a GxP system, we make sure auditing still happens for those operations.
Our CSV import of about 10,000 rows uses batched inserts in chunks inside a transaction, after validation.
Compiled queries are a way to skip the cost of translating a LINQ query into SQL every time it runs.

Normally, when EF Core executes a LINQ query, it has to process the expression tree and produce SQL. It caches that work internally, keyed by the shape of the query, so repeated queries are already fairly cheap. But there's still some overhead in computing the cache key from the expression tree on every call. With EF.CompileAsyncQuery, or EF.CompileQuery, I define the query once, as a static delegate with parameters. EF Core translates it once, and every call reuses it directly, so the overhead disappears.

The gain is real but small, usually noticeable only on very hot paths with simple queries, executed thousands of times per second. Compiled queries are also less flexible, because the query shape is fixed.

So my rule is to use them only after measuring shows translation overhead matters. In our services, I've used a compiled query for a frequently called lookup, getting a kit by its number, which sits on a hot path during dispensing. For most queries, indexes and projections matter far more.
Seeing the SQL that EF Core generates is essential, because that's where most performance problems show up.

There are a few ways. The simplest in development is LogTo on the DbContext options, for example LogTo Console.WriteLine, filtered to Information level. In an ASP.NET Core app, I can enable the log category Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command at Information level in configuration, and the SQL appears in the normal logs, with execution times. For a single query, ToQueryString returns the SQL without executing it, which is handy in tests and debugging. And for parameter values, EnableSensitiveDataLogging shows them, but only in development, because in production it could log personal or clinical data.
Outside the application, SQL Server tools help too: Query Store shows the heaviest queries over time, and Extended Events can capture specific ones.

In our team, during code reviews of data-heavy changes, we look at the generated SQL for new queries. That's how we've caught N+1 queries and accidental client-side evaluation before they reached production.
EF Core supports all three relationship types, configured by convention or with the Fluent API.

One-to-many is the most common. A principal has a collection navigation, and the dependent has a reference navigation and a foreign key. For example, a Site has many Shipments, and each Shipment has a SiteId. In Fluent API, that's HasMany Shipments WithOne Site HasForeignKey SiteId, and I choose the delete behaviour explicitly. One-to-one uses reference navigations on both sides, and the dependent holds the foreign key, for example a Subject and their ConsentRecord, configured with HasOne WithOne. Many-to-many, since EF Core 5, can be configured with collections on both sides, and EF creates the join table automatically.
But when the link itself has data, like a role or an assigned date, I model an explicit join entity instead.

That's our case for users and studies. A user can be on many studies, and a study has many users, but each assignment has a role and an assigned date, which our authorization checks use. So we have an explicit StudyAssignment entity.
Shadow properties are properties that exist in the EF Core model and in the database table, but not in the C# entity class.

You configure them in OnModelCreating with Property of type and a name, and EF Core tracks them like normal properties. To read or filter by them in queries, you use EF.Property with the entity and the property name. To set them, you go through the change tracker, for example entry.Property of "LastModifiedBy" CurrentValue. EF Core also creates shadow properties automatically, for example a foreign key column when the class only has a navigation property.

They're useful when a column matters to the database but shouldn't clutter the domain model. The classic use is audit columns, like CreatedBy, CreatedAt, LastModifiedBy and LastModifiedAt. Instead of adding these to every entity class, I define them as shadow properties on all entities, and set them centrally in a SaveChanges interceptor, using the current user and TimeProvider.
In our services, that's how audit columns are populated consistently, so no developer can forget to set them, which matters for GxP audit trails.
Owned entities are how EF Core maps value objects, types that don't have their own identity and only exist as part of another entity.

You configure them with OwnsOne for a single value object, or OwnsMany for a collection. For example, a Site has an Address, with street, city, postcode and country. Address isn't an entity on its own, it has no id, and it only makes sense as part of a site. With OwnsOne, EF Core stores the address fields as columns in the Site table, like Address_City, and loads them automatically whenever the site is loaded. OwnsMany stores the collection in a separate table, but it's still owned and loaded with its owner. Since EF Core 8, complex types offer a similar option for value objects.

The benefit is a richer domain model. Instead of loose string properties on Site, I have a proper Address type, with its own validation, which can be reused in other entities like Depot, while the database stays simple.
In our IRT model, addresses and some quantity-with-unit values are owned types. That made validation consistent across sites and depots.
In EF Core, indexes are part of the model, so they're defined in code and created through migrations, which keeps them versioned and reviewed.

With the Fluent API, in the entity configuration, I call HasIndex with the columns. For example, HasIndex of StudyId and Status creates a composite index, and column order matters. I can add IsUnique for a unique index, like a kit number. HasFilter creates a filtered index, for example only active rows. And with SQL Server, IncludeProperties adds included columns, to make a covering index. HasDatabaseName gives it a clear name. Alternatively, the Index attribute on the entity class works for simple cases. Then I add a migration, and the index is created through our normal release scripts.
The important part is choosing indexes from real query patterns, using the execution plan, rather than adding them everywhere, because every index slows down writes.
The covering index from our shipment list fix, on StudyId, Status and ShipmentDate including the displayed columns, was added exactly this way, through a reviewed migration script.
Primary and foreign keys are the basic tools for identity and integrity in a relational database.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. It can't be null, and there's only one per table, though it can span multiple columns. In SQL Server, the primary key creates a clustered index by default, so it often also defines the physical order of the data. A good primary key is small, stable and never changes, like an integer identity or a GUID. A foreign key is a column, or columns, in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. It enforces referential integrity: you can't create a shipment for a site that doesn't exist, and you can't delete a site that still has shipments, unless you've defined cascade rules, like cascade delete or set null.
In practice, I always index foreign key columns, because SQL Server doesn't do it automatically, and joins and deletes depend on them.
In a clinical system, foreign keys are a cheap but very strong guarantee of data integrity, so we never skip them for convenience.
A unique constraint guarantees that no two rows have the same value in a column, or a combination of columns. SQL Server enforces it with a unique index behind the scenes.

A primary key is also unique, but there are differences. A table has only one primary key, but can have many unique constraints. A primary key can't contain nulls, while a unique constraint in SQL Server allows one null, or with a filtered unique index you can allow many. The primary key is the row's main identity, used by foreign keys, while unique constraints protect alternate keys, which are natural business identifiers. And by default, the primary key is clustered, while unique constraints are non-clustered.
A typical design is a surrogate primary key, like an integer Id, plus unique constraints on natural keys that must never duplicate.

In our IRT database, kits have an integer Id as the primary key, but KitNumber has a unique constraint, because two physical kits with the same number would be a serious problem in a trial. The database enforces it even if two requests race each other.
A composite index is an index on more than one column, for example StudyId, Status and ShipmentDate together.

The order of columns matters a lot. The index is sorted by the first column, then by the second within that, and so on, like a phone book sorted by surname then first name. So it can support seeks on the leading columns: StudyId alone, or StudyId and Status, or all three. But it can't efficiently seek on Status alone, because Status isn't the leading column. That's called the leftmost prefix rule.

My rule for column order is: put equality columns first, the ones compared with equals, and range columns last, like dates with greater than or less than, because once you hit a range, the following columns can't be used for seeking. Then add INCLUDE columns for anything the query selects, to avoid key lookups.

Our shipment list index followed exactly that: StudyId and Status for equality, then ShipmentDate for the range, with the displayed columns included. That's what let the query seek directly to a study's pending shipments in a date range.
A filtered index is a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause, so it only contains a subset of the table's rows.

For example, an index on ShipmentDate, WHERE Status equals Pending. If only a small percentage of shipments are pending at any time, this index is much smaller than a full one. That means less storage, faster seeks, cheaper maintenance on writes, and more accurate statistics for that subset. It's ideal for queries that always target a "hot" subset of the data. Another classic use is a filtered unique index, like enforcing that a kit number is unique only where it's not null, or only among active records.

The catch is that the query's predicate has to match the filter, so SQL Server knows the index covers it. Parameterised queries can make that tricky, because the optimizer can't always prove a parameter matches the filter. It works best with literal values, like Status equals Pending in the query text.

In our IRT system, dashboards repeatedly query pending and in-transit shipments, which are a small fraction of all shipments. A filtered index on those statuses made those dashboard queries much faster.
Indexes improve performance by letting SQL Server find rows without reading the whole table.

An index is a B-tree, sorted by its key. Instead of scanning millions of rows, SQL Server navigates the tree in a few page reads, which is logarithmic, and seeks straight to the matching rows. A covering index, with included columns, can answer the whole query without touching the table. Indexes also help with sorting and joins, because data is already ordered.

But they have costs. Every insert, update and delete must also update every relevant index, so write-heavy tables slow down with too many indexes. They use disk and memory. Random keys can cause page splits and fragmentation. And indexes on low-selectivity columns, like a true or false flag, or indexes no query uses, are pure cost with no benefit.

So I add indexes based on real queries and execution plans, and periodically check the index usage DMVs to find unused or duplicate indexes to remove. When we added the covering index for our shipment list, we also tested the write impact in validation, because shipments are updated frequently.
An execution plan is the optimizer's recipe for running a query: which indexes to use, in what order to access tables, which join algorithms to use, and where to sort or aggregate.

SQL Server's optimizer creates the plan based on statistics about the data, and then caches it for reuse. The plan is a tree of operators, like index seeks and scans, key lookups, nested loops, hash and merge joins, and sorts. Each shows estimated rows and cost, and in the actual plan, the actual rows too. There are two versions: the estimated plan, which doesn't run the query, and the actual plan, which runs it and shows what really happened.

When I read a plan, I look for a few red flags: scans on large tables where I expected a seek, expensive key lookups, sorts or hash operations spilling to tempdb, and big differences between estimated and actual rows, which point to stale statistics or parameter sniffing. I use SSMS for single queries, and Query Store to see plans over time and spot regressions.
In our shipment list fix, the plan showed a clustered index scan and key lookups, and that directly told me what to fix.
These are three ways SQL Server can read data, and they differ hugely in cost.

A table scan reads every row of a heap, which is a table without a clustered index. An index scan reads all, or a large range, of an index, either the clustered index, which is effectively the whole table, or a non-clustered one. Both scale with the size of the table, so they get slower as data grows. An index seek uses the B-tree structure to navigate directly to the matching rows, reading only a few pages to find them. That scales with the number of matching rows, not the table size.

Seeks aren't always better, though. If a query needs a large percentage of the table, a scan can genuinely be cheaper than thousands of seeks plus lookups, and the optimizer chooses that on purpose. The problem is an unexpected scan for a selective query, usually caused by a missing index, a non-SARGable predicate, or a data type mismatch.

In our slow shipment list, the plan showed a clustered index scan for a query that needed a few hundred rows. Fixing the predicate and adding the right index turned it into a seek, and reads dropped from about 400,000 to 2,000.
Cardinality is the number of rows the optimizer expects at each step of a query plan. Statistics are what it uses to make those estimates.

Statistics are objects that describe how values are distributed in a column or index, mainly through a histogram of up to 200 steps, plus density information. When the optimizer sees a filter like StudyId equals 42, it uses the histogram to estimate how many rows will match. That estimate drives every decision: which index to use, which join type, and how much memory to grant. If the estimate is badly wrong, the plan can be terrible, for example a nested loop over a million rows, or a sort that spills to tempdb.

Statistics go stale when data changes a lot, for example after a big data load. SQL Server updates them automatically after enough changes, but on large tables that threshold can be reached late. Then I update them manually, or schedule maintenance.

The symptom to look for is a big gap between estimated and actual rows in the actual plan. In our IRT system, after a large data import, one query became slow until we updated statistics, which is why we now update stats after big imports.
Both combine the results of two or more queries into one result set, with the same columns. The difference is how they treat duplicates.

UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result. To do that, SQL Server has to compare all rows, which means an extra sort or hash operation, and that costs CPU and memory, and can spill to tempdb on large results. UNION ALL simply appends the results and keeps every row, including duplicates. It's faster, because there's no deduplication step, and it can stream results without waiting for all of them.

So my default is UNION ALL. I only use UNION when I actually need distinct rows, and the inputs can genuinely overlap. Very often the two queries can't produce the same row anyway, for example combining "shipments from depot A" with "shipments from depot B", and then UNION is just wasted work.

It's one of those small things I look for in code reviews of SQL, because people often write UNION out of habit. On a large reporting query, switching to UNION ALL removed an expensive sort from the plan.
EXISTS and IN both check whether a value has a match in another set, and modern SQL Server often produces the same plan for both. But there are differences worth knowing.

EXISTS checks whether a subquery returns any row, and stops at the first match, so it's naturally efficient for existence checks. It's also correlated, meaning it can compare several columns. IN compares a value against a list of values, or the result of a subquery. For a short fixed list, like status IN Pending and Shipped, IN is the clearest. For subqueries, the optimizer usually converts both into the same semi-join.

The important difference is with negation and NULLs. NOT IN returns no rows at all if the subquery returns even one NULL, because comparing with NULL is unknown. That's a classic, silent bug. NOT EXISTS doesn't have that problem. So I always prefer NOT EXISTS for "find rows with no match".

For example, "sites with no shipments" in our system is written with NOT EXISTS against the shipments table, which is correct and uses the foreign key index efficiently. In EF Core, a negated Any translates to exactly that.
Both hold an intermediate result inside a larger query, but they behave very differently.

A CTE, defined with WITH, is a named query that exists only for the single statement that follows it. It's not stored anywhere; the optimizer simply expands it into the main query, like a view. So it's mainly about readability, breaking a complex query into named steps. It's also the only way to write recursive queries, like walking a depot hierarchy. But if you reference a CTE twice, it may be computed twice. A temporary table, with a hash prefix, is actually materialised in tempdb. It can have indexes, it gets its own statistics, and it can be reused across several statements in the same session or procedure.

So my rule: CTE for readability and recursion in a single query. Temp table when the intermediate result is large, reused multiple times, or when the optimizer is making bad estimates on a complex query, because materialising it with real statistics often gives a much better plan.
In our IRT reporting, a heavy monthly report became much faster when I moved a large intermediate step from a CTE into an indexed temp table. Table variables are another option, for small sets.
All three are window functions that number rows within a partition, based on an ORDER BY. The difference is how they handle ties, rows with the same ordering value.

ROW_NUMBER gives every row a unique sequential number, 1, 2, 3, 4, even if values tie. The order among tied rows is arbitrary, unless you add a tie-breaker column. RANK gives tied rows the same rank, and then leaves a gap. So if two rows tie for second place, you get 1, 2, 2, 4. DENSE_RANK also gives ties the same rank, but without gaps: 1, 2, 2, 3.

The use cases follow from that. ROW_NUMBER is for picking exactly one row per group, like the latest status per shipment, or for deduplication, or paging. RANK is for competition-style rankings, where gaps make sense.
