In that form, the application runs as process 1 in the container and receives signals directly. If you use the shell form, a plain string, it runs inside a shell, and the shell may not pass the SIGTERM signal on. Then the app can't shut down gracefully, and Docker eventually kills it after a timeout.
For our .NET services, we use ENTRYPOINT in exec form with dotnet and the DLL, so the app receives SIGTERM and finishes in-flight requests on shutdown.
Smaller images build, push and start faster, and they have fewer packages that could contain vulnerabilities, so I always try to reduce image size.

The biggest win is multi-stage builds. In a .NET Dockerfile, the first stage uses the full .NET SDK image to restore, build and publish. The final stage starts from the much smaller ASP.NET runtime image and only copies in the published output. So the SDK, the source code and the build tools never reach the production image.

Second, choose a small base image: Alpine-based images, or Microsoft's chiseled Ubuntu images, which are very minimal, have no shell or package manager, and run as non-root by default. Third, use a .dockerignore file so things like bin, obj, .git and test folders aren't sent into the build. Fourth, combine RUN commands and clean up package caches in the same layer, because deleting files in a later layer doesn't shrink the image. Fifth, only install what's needed, with no extra debugging tools. And for .NET, options like trimming or native AOT can make some apps much smaller, if they're compatible.
In our services, moving to multi-stage builds and a smaller runtime base image noticeably reduced image size and also cut the number of findings in our image scans.

Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container applications with one YAML file. Instead of starting each container with a long docker run command, you describe all the services, their images or build folders, ports, environment variables, volumes, networks and dependencies, in a compose.yaml file. Then docker compose up starts everything together, and docker compose down stops and removes it.

Compose automatically creates a network for the application, and each service can reach the others by its service name, so the API can connect to a host called sqlserver or rabbitmq, without knowing IP addresses.

Its main use is local development and testing. For example, for one of our .NET services, a compose file starts the API, SQL Server, RabbitMQ and Redis, so a new developer can run the whole environment with one command, instead of installing and configuring each dependency. It's also useful for integration tests in a pipeline. Health checks with depends_on make sure, for example, the API waits until the database is ready.

For production, Compose isn't usually used, because it runs on a single machine and doesn't provide scaling, self-healing or rolling deployments. That's the job of orchestrators like Amazon ECS or Kubernetes. We use Compose locally, and ECS in our real environments.
Containers are isolated by default, so networking and volumes are how they talk to each other and keep data.

For networking, Docker uses network drivers. The default bridge network connects containers on the same host. With a user-defined bridge network, which is what Docker Compose creates, containers can reach each other by name, using Docker's built-in DNS. So an API container can connect to a database called sqlserver. Ports are only reachable from outside the host if you publish them, like mapping port 8080 on the host to port 8080 in the container. There's also host networking, where the container uses the host's network directly, and overlay networks that connect containers across multiple hosts.

For volumes: a container's own filesystem is temporary. When the container is removed, its writable layer and any data written there are gone. So anything that must persist, like database files, goes in a volume. Named volumes are managed by Docker and are the recommended option for data. Bind mounts map a folder from the host into the container, which is useful in development, for example to mount source code. And tmpfs mounts are memory-only.
In production, our services on ECS are stateless and don't keep data in the container at all. Data lives in managed services like RDS and S3, which is simpler and more reliable.
I secure Docker images at three points: how they're built, how they're scanned, and how they run.

When building: start from small, trusted, official base images, like Microsoft's .NET images, pinned to specific versions, and rebuild regularly to get security patches. Use multi-stage builds so compilers and build tools don't reach the final image. Run as a non-root user; the newer .NET images include an app user for this. Never put secrets in the image, in the Dockerfile, in build arguments or in copied files, because anyone with the image can extract them from the layers.

For scanning, every image is scanned in the pipeline before it's pushed or deployed, using a tool like Trivy, or the registry's own scanning, like Amazon ECR. The pipeline fails on high or critical vulnerabilities, so they're fixed before release, usually by updating the base image or a package. Images in the registry are also rescanned, because new vulnerabilities are discovered after release.
At runtime: a read-only root filesystem where possible, dropped Linux capabilities, resource limits, and secrets injected at runtime from a secrets manager.
In my team, we added image scanning to our Azure DevOps pipelines during the .NET 10 upgrade in early 2026, which made our image security visible on every build.
When a container misbehaves, I troubleshoot step by step, from the most basic information to the most detailed.

First, the status. Is it running, restarting, or exited? docker ps with the all flag shows that, and docker inspect shows the exit code and the reason. The exit code tells a lot: 137 usually means it was killed, often because it ran out of memory, 139 is a crash, and 1 is usually an application error at startup. Second, the logs, with docker logs, or CloudWatch in our ECS setup. Most problems show up there: a missing environment variable, a failed database connection, or an unhandled exception at startup. Third, configuration: environment variables, ports, mounted volumes and the image tag. A wrong port mapping, or a service listening on localhost instead of all interfaces, is a classic. Fourth, resources, using docker stats, to check memory and CPU against the limits. Fifth, go inside: docker exec to open a shell, check files, and test connectivity to the database or other services. If the container crashes immediately, I override the entrypoint to start a shell, and investigate.

On ECS, I check the stopped task's reason, the logs, and whether health checks are failing. One real case, in our dev Kubernetes cluster, was a service killed by its liveness probe because it needed about 40 seconds to warm up; a startup probe fixed it.
When a container crashes, the main process inside it exits, and the container stops with an exit code. What happens next depends on how it's being run.

With plain Docker, the restart policy decides. With "no", it stays stopped. With "on-failure", Docker restarts it when the exit code isn't zero. With "always" or "unless-stopped", it restarts automatically. In orchestrators, it's self-healing. On Amazon ECS, which we use, the service notices the task has stopped and starts a new one to keep the desired count, and the load balancer stops sending traffic to the failed task. Kubernetes does the same by restarting the container, and if it keeps crashing, you see CrashLoopBackOff, with longer and longer delays between restarts.
Any data written inside the container's own filesystem is lost, which is why our services are stateless and keep data in databases and S3.

To find the cause, I check the exit code and the stopped reason. 137 often means out of memory, and 1 is usually an application error. Then I check the logs, in CloudWatch for us, around the time of the crash, and the memory and CPU metrics.
The important thing is not to rely on restarts as the fix. Restarts keep the service available, but the root cause, like a memory leak or a bad configuration, still needs fixing.

Configuration and secrets should be passed into a container at runtime, never baked into the image. That way, the same image runs in every environment, and secrets aren't exposed to anyone who can pull the image.

For normal configuration, environment variables are the standard way. In Docker, you pass them with the e flag or an env file; in Docker Compose, in the environment section; and on Amazon ECS, in the task definition. In .NET, environment variables override appsettings.json automatically, and nested settings use a double underscore, like ConnectionStrings double underscore Default.

For secrets, plain environment variables in a task definition or Compose file are visible to anyone who can read that definition. So secrets should come from a secrets manager. On ECS, the task definition references a secret in AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, and ECS injects the value when the task starts, using the task's IAM role. Kubernetes has Secrets, ideally synced from a vault, and Docker Swarm has secrets as files. Another option is for the application to read secrets directly at startup through a configuration provider.
Also, secrets must never be logged, and they shouldn't be passed as build arguments, because those can remain in the image history.
In our services, connection strings and API keys come from AWS Secrets Manager into the ECS tasks at startup.
Kubernetes is an open-source platform for running containers across a cluster of machines. It's often called a container orchestrator.

The core idea is desired state. I describe what I want in YAML, like "run three copies of this image, with this much memory, reachable on this port", and Kubernetes continuously works to keep reality matching that description. If a container crashes, it restarts it. If a whole node fails, it reschedules the pods onto healthy nodes. If I change the image version, it does a rolling update, replacing pods gradually with no downtime, and it can roll back.

It also handles the other things you need to run services at scale: scheduling containers onto nodes based on the resources they need, service discovery and load balancing, so services find each other by name, scaling, manually or automatically based on CPU or custom metrics, configuration and secrets through ConfigMaps and Secrets, and health checks with readiness and liveness probes.

The main building blocks are pods, the smallest unit, wrapping one or more containers; Deployments, which manage replicas and updates; Services, which give pods a stable address; and Ingress, for HTTP routing from outside.

Our production services run on Amazon ECS, which follows the same ideas, and we use Kubernetes in our dev cluster for internal tooling services. Understanding Kubernetes helped me there, for example to fix a crash loop caused by a liveness probe that checked too early.
These are three types of Kubernetes Service, and they differ in where the service can be reached from.
A Service gives a set of pods one stable address, because pods come and go and their IP addresses change. The Service finds its pods by labels and load-balances traffic across them.

ClusterIP is the default type. It gives the service an internal IP address that's only reachable from inside the cluster. It's used for internal communication, for example an API calling another service, or connecting to a database inside the cluster. Most services are ClusterIP.

NodePort exposes the service on a fixed port, from a range like 30000 to 32767, on every node in the cluster. So anyone who can reach a node's IP can reach the service on that port. It's simple, but you have to manage node addresses and the unusual port numbers yourself, so it's mainly used for testing, or behind your own load balancer.

LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider to create an external load balancer, like an AWS load balancer, which sends traffic to the service. It's the standard way to expose one service publicly, but each one creates a separate load balancer, which costs money.

Each type builds on the previous one. And for HTTP services, it's usually better to use an Ingress, or the Gateway API: one load balancer that routes many hostnames and paths to internal ClusterIP services.

A ReplicaSet is a Kubernetes object whose job is to make sure a specified number of identical pods are running at all times. You say "I want three replicas of this pod", and the ReplicaSet watches the cluster. If a pod crashes or a node fails, and there are only two, it creates a new one. If somehow there are four, it removes one. It finds the pods it owns using a label selector.

In practice, you almost never create ReplicaSets directly. You create a Deployment, and the Deployment creates and manages ReplicaSets for you. The reason is updates. A ReplicaSet can keep pods running, but it doesn't know how to update them from one version to another. A Deployment does. When you change the image version in a Deployment, it creates a new ReplicaSet for the new version, and gradually scales the new one up and the old one down. That's a rolling update. The old ReplicaSet is kept, scaled to zero, which is what makes a quick rollback possible: the Deployment just scales the old ReplicaSet back up.
So the relationship is: a Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and a ReplicaSet manages pods.
When I'm troubleshooting a deployment, kubectl get replicasets is useful, because it shows the old and new versions and how many pods each one has, which tells me whether a rollout is stuck.
A rolling deployment updates an application gradually, replacing old instances with new ones a few at a time, so the service stays available throughout, with no downtime.

In Kubernetes, when you change a Deployment's image, it creates new pods with the new version, waits for each one to pass its readiness probe, and only then removes old pods. Two settings control the pace. maxSurge says how many extra pods can be created above the desired count, and maxUnavailable says how many can be missing during the update. Readiness probes are critical here; without them, traffic could go to pods that aren't ready yet. Amazon ECS works the same way, using minimum and maximum healthy percentages, and the load balancer's health checks.

A rollback means returning to the previous version when the new one has problems. In Kubernetes, kubectl rollout undo switches back to the previous ReplicaSet, which is kept for exactly this reason. On ECS, you redeploy the previous task definition, and ECS also has a deployment circuit breaker that can roll back automatically if new tasks keep failing.

Two important points. During a rolling update, old and new versions run at the same time, so they must be compatible, including with the database schema. That's why we make database changes backward compatible. And rollback doesn't undo data changes, so those need their own plan.
When a pod's container crashes, Kubernetes handles it automatically, based on the pod's restart policy, which is Always for Deployments.

The kubelet on that node sees that the container's process has exited, and restarts the container inside the same pod. If it keeps crashing, Kubernetes waits longer between each restart, 10 seconds, 20, 40, up to five minutes. That's the CrashLoopBackOff status you see in kubectl get pods. While the container isn't ready, its readiness check fails, so the Service stops sending it traffic, and the other replicas keep serving users. If a whole pod is lost, for example because its node fails, the ReplicaSet notices there are fewer pods than desired, and creates a new pod on another healthy node.
Anything stored in the container's own filesystem is lost on restart, which is why apps should be stateless or use persistent volumes.

To find the cause, I use kubectl describe pod to see the events and the last state, including the exit code and reason, like OOMKilled for out of memory, and kubectl logs with the previous flag, to see the logs from the crashed container.

A real example from our dev cluster: a service kept crash-looping with no errors in its logs. The events showed it was being killed by its liveness probe, because it needed about 40 seconds to warm up. A startup probe fixed it.
Service discovery is how one service finds another, when pods are created and destroyed all the time, and their IP addresses keep changing.

Kubernetes solves this with Services and DNS. A Service selects a group of pods by their labels, and gets a stable virtual IP address and a stable DNS name. Kubernetes keeps track of the IPs of the healthy pods behind it, the endpoints, and updates them automatically as pods come and go. Only pods that pass their readiness probe are included.

The cluster runs a DNS server, CoreDNS. Every Service gets a DNS name like orders-api dot shop dot svc dot cluster dot local. Within the same namespace, a pod can simply call http colon slash slash orders-api, and from another namespace, orders-api dot shop. When a request is sent to the Service's IP, kube-proxy on each node routes it to one of the healthy pods, which also gives basic load balancing.
There's also a headless Service, with no virtual IP, where DNS returns the individual pod addresses. That's used for things like databases, where clients need to talk to specific pods.

The benefit is that application code doesn't need any discovery logic. In a .NET app, the other service's base URL is just its service name in configuration. Amazon ECS offers the same idea with Service Connect or Cloud Map.
I'd secure Kubernetes in layers: who can access the cluster, what workloads can do, how they talk to each other, and what goes into them.

First, access control. Use RBAC with least privilege, so people and service accounts only get the permissions they need, preferably limited to a namespace. Users sign in through the company's identity provider, and the API server isn't exposed publicly. Second, workload security. Pods run as non-root, with a read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation, and dropped Linux capabilities. Pod Security Admission can enforce the restricted standard for a namespace. Pods should only mount a service account token if they need one. Third, network policies. By default, every pod can talk to every other pod, so I'd add network policies that only allow the traffic each service needs. Fourth, secrets. Kubernetes Secrets are only base64 encoded, so enable encryption at rest, restrict who can read them, and preferably sync them from an external vault, like AWS Secrets Manager. Fifth, images. Use trusted, minimal base images, scan them in the pipeline with a tool like Trivy, and only allow images from our own registry. And sixth, keep Kubernetes and nodes updated, and enable audit logging and monitoring.
Resource limits on every container also matter, so one workload can't starve the others.
To deploy a .NET application to Kubernetes, I'd go through four steps: containerise it, publish the image, describe how it runs, and deploy it through a pipeline.

First, a multi-stage Dockerfile. The SDK image builds and publishes the app, and the final image uses the smaller ASP.NET runtime image, runs as a non-root user, and listens on port 8080. Second, the pipeline builds the image, runs tests, scans it, tags it with the build version, and pushes it to a registry, like Amazon ECR.

Third, the Kubernetes manifests, often as a Helm chart. A Deployment sets the image tag, the number of replicas, CPU and memory requests and limits, and environment variables, with normal settings from a ConfigMap and secrets from Kubernetes Secrets, ideally synced from a secrets manager. It also sets readiness and liveness probes, pointed at the app's health check endpoints, which I add in ASP.NET Core with AddHealthChecks and MapHealthChecks. For slow-starting apps, a startup probe too. A Service gives it a stable internal address, and an Ingress exposes it over HTTP. A horizontal pod autoscaler can scale it on CPU.
Fourth, the pipeline deploys with helm upgrade, or a GitOps tool like Argo CD, as a rolling update.
And the app itself must handle SIGTERM, so it finishes in-flight requests before shutting down. ASP.NET Core does this by default, within the shutdown timeout.
In CI, unit tests run automatically on every pull request and every merge, and if any test fails, the build fails, so broken code can't be merged.

In our Azure DevOps pipelines for .NET, the steps are: restore the NuGet packages, build the solution in Release mode, then run dotnet test, which finds and runs all the test projects. I use a logger that produces results in the TRX format, which the pipeline publishes, so the test results appear in the build summary, with each failing test, its error and its history. I also collect code coverage, using the XPlat Code Coverage collector with Coverlet, and publish a coverage report, which is also sent to SonarQube, where the quality gate checks the coverage of new code.
Branch policies in Azure DevOps require this build to pass before a pull request can be completed. So nothing reaches the main branch without passing tests.

A few practical points. Unit tests must be fast and independent of databases or networks, so they run quickly on every change. Slower integration tests can run in a separate stage. Flaky tests are fixed or quarantined quickly, because if people stop trusting the tests, they start ignoring failures.
I once had a quality gate fail at 68 percent coverage against an 80 percent requirement, and we fixed it in half a day by adding meaningful tests.

SonarQube is a static code analysis platform. It examines source code without running it, and reports problems in a few categories: bugs, which are code likely to behave wrongly; vulnerabilities and security hotspots, like possible SQL injection or hard-coded passwords; code smells, which are maintainability issues, like overly complex methods or duplication; plus code coverage from our test results, and duplicated code.

The key feature is the quality gate. It's a set of conditions that new code must meet, for example: coverage on new code at least 80 percent, no new bugs or vulnerabilities, all security hotspots reviewed, and duplication below a threshold. If the code fails the gate, the pipeline fails, so problems are caught before merging. Focusing on new code is important, because it lets a team improve gradually without having to fix all the old issues first.

In Azure DevOps, we run the SonarQube prepare step before the build, the analysis after build and tests, and then check the quality gate, with the result shown on the pull request. Developers can also use SonarLint in the IDE to see issues while coding.
One time our gate failed with 68 percent coverage against 80 percent. Instead of lowering the bar, we added meaningful tests for the missing paths and passed it in half a day.
I prevent bad code from reaching production with several layers of checks, so that if one misses something, another catches it.

First, before merging. Every change goes through a pull request with at least one reviewer, and branch policies stop anyone pushing directly to main. The CI build must pass: compile with warnings treated as errors for important rules, unit tests, and the SonarQube quality gate, which checks bugs, vulnerabilities and coverage on new code. Dependency and image scanning catch vulnerable packages. Second, before release. Integration and end-to-end tests run in the test environment. In our GxP setup, releases move through FV, TechOps and UAT, with approvals by named people before controlled environments. The same build artifact moves through every environment, so what we tested is what we release. Third, during release. Rolling deployments with health checks, feature flags to turn new features on gradually, monitoring, and a quick rollback plan.

And just as important is culture: small pull requests that are easy to review, tests written with the code, and blameless reviews after any escape, adding a check so the same problem can't happen twice.

One improvement I drove was smaller pull requests. Ours had grown to 1,500 lines or more, and we brought them down to under 400, which cut review time from 2 to 3 days to the same day, and reviews got much more careful.

An artifact is the output of a build that gets deployed, for example a zip of published .NET files, a NuGet package, or a Docker image. The key principle is "build once, deploy many": the pipeline builds the artifact once, and that exact same artifact is promoted through every environment, dev, test, UAT and production. We never rebuild for production, because a rebuild could produce something different from what was tested.

Versioning makes each artifact uniquely identifiable and traceable. I use semantic versioning for releases, major, minor and patch, plus the build number, for example 4.2.1 plus build 345. Many teams calculate this automatically from Git tags, with a tool like GitVersion. For Docker images, the tag is the version, or the commit hash, never just "latest", because latest is ambiguous and makes rollback hard. The artifact also records the Git commit it came from.

Artifacts are stored in a repository: Azure Artifacts or the pipeline's own artifacts for packages and build output, and Amazon ECR for images, with retention rules so old ones are cleaned up, but released versions are kept.

In our GxP environment, this traceability is essential. For any version in production, we can show exactly which commit, build, tests and approvals produced it. It also makes rollback simple: redeploy the previous artifact.
To build Docker images in a pipeline, I want the build to be repeatable, fast, secure and traceable.

In Azure DevOps, the steps are: build the image using the multi-stage Dockerfile from the repository, tag it with a unique version, like the build number or commit hash, never just latest, run the tests, scan the image, and only then push it to the registry, which is Amazon ECR for us.

The Dockerfile itself does the restore, build and publish in a build stage using the .NET SDK image, and the final stage uses the small runtime image. Tests can run in their own stage, so a failing test fails the image build.

Speed comes from layer caching: copying project files and restoring before copying the rest of the source, and using BuildKit with a cache from the registry, because pipeline agents are often fresh machines with no local cache.

Security: the pipeline authenticates to the registry using a service connection, with short-lived credentials where possible. No secrets are passed as build arguments, because they can end up in the image history. And the image scan, with a tool like Trivy, fails the pipeline on high or critical vulnerabilities.
The image digest and tag are saved with the build, so the release stages deploy exactly that image to every environment. That's the build-once, deploy-many principle applied to containers.

Our Azure DevOps Server is on-premise, a legacy from Cenduit's CIRT, but new services run on AWS, IQVIA's standard cloud. So we deploy to AWS from Azure DevOps by connecting the pipeline to AWS securely, pushing the image, and then telling ECS to run the new version.

First, the connection. Azure DevOps uses an AWS service connection. The best option is OpenID Connect, where the pipeline gets short-lived credentials by assuming an IAM role, so no long-lived access keys are stored anywhere. The role only has the permissions the deployment needs, like pushing to ECR and updating specific ECS services.
Second, the build stage builds the Docker image, tests and scans it, and pushes it to Amazon ECR with a unique version tag.

Third, the release stage, per environment. It registers a new revision of the ECS task definition with the new image tag, then updates the ECS service to use it. ECS performs a rolling deployment: it starts new tasks, waits for them to pass the load balancer health checks, then stops the old ones. The deployment circuit breaker can roll back automatically if the new tasks keep failing. Infrastructure changes, like new queues or alarms, go through Terraform steps in the same pipeline, with plan and apply.
Each environment is a stage with its own variables, and controlled environments have approvals by named people before the stage runs.
Rollback is simply redeploying the previous task definition revision, which is quick because the old image is still in ECR.
In CI/CD, my rule is that non-secret settings live with the pipeline or the application configuration, and secrets live in a secrets manager, never in code, YAML or logs.
For normal settings, like environment names, URLs or feature flags, I use variable groups or stage variables in Azure DevOps, per environment, or the application's appsettings files per environment.

For secrets, there are two kinds. Secrets the pipeline itself needs, like credentials to reach AWS or a registry, are stored as secret variables or service connections in Azure DevOps. Secret variables are encrypted, masked in logs, and not passed to forked pull request builds. Even better is OIDC to AWS, so there's no long-lived key at all. Secrets the application needs at runtime, like database passwords, shouldn't go through the pipeline. They live in AWS Secrets Manager, and the ECS task reads them at startup through its IAM role. The pipeline only deploys a reference to the secret, not the value. Azure Key Vault can also be linked to a variable group when it's needed during the pipeline.

On top of that: least privilege for service connections, approvals on who can use production connections, rotation of secrets, and never echoing secrets in scripts. And we scan the repository for accidentally committed secrets.
Deployment approvals make sure a human, with the right authority, checks a release before it goes into a controlled environment.

In Azure DevOps, there are two main ways. In classic release pipelines, which we use, each stage, like UAT or production, can have pre-deployment approvals: named people or groups who must approve before the stage runs, and post-deployment approvals to confirm it went well. You can require more than one approver, prevent the person who started the release from approving it, and set a timeout. In YAML pipelines, the same is done with environments: you add approvals and checks to an environment, like production, and any stage deploying to it waits. Checks can also include things like business hours, a required branch, or a query that there are no open critical bugs.
Every approval is recorded with who approved, when, and their comments, which gives an audit trail.

In our GxP environment, this is essential: releases to controlled environments need approvals from named approvers, linked to a change request. When I built the CIRT MCP server to automate deployments, I deliberately kept these approvals exactly as they were. The agent can show pending approvals, but it can't approve anything. So we cut deployments from 6 hours to 2, without weakening the approval process.

Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. It stores streams of events in an ordered, durable log, and lets many applications publish and read those events at high volume. Unlike a traditional queue, reading a message doesn't delete it; events are kept for a retention period, so several consumers can read the same data independently, and even replay it.

The main terms: a broker is a Kafka server, and several brokers form a cluster. A topic is a named stream of events, like shipment-status. Each topic is split into partitions, which are the unit of parallelism and scaling; each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on brokers. An offset is the position of a message inside a partition, a number that only increases, and consumers track their offset to know where they've got to. A producer is an application that writes events to a topic; it chooses the partition, usually by hashing the message key, so all events with the same key, like the same shipment id, go to the same partition and stay in order. A consumer reads events, and consumers with the same group id form a consumer group, where each partition is read by only one consumer in the group, so the group shares the work.
In our platform, we use Kafka for events like shipment status updates, which several services consume, each in its own consumer group, and which we sometimes need to replay.
Kafka achieves scalability mainly through partitioning, and fault tolerance mainly through replication.

For scalability: each topic is split into partitions, and the partitions are spread across the brokers in the cluster. Producers write to different partitions in parallel, and in a consumer group, each partition is read by one consumer, so adding consumers, up to the number of partitions, increases processing in parallel. Adding brokers spreads the load further. Kafka is also very efficient by design: it writes sequentially to an append-only log, batches and compresses messages, and relies on the operating system's page cache, so it handles very high throughput.

For fault tolerance: each partition is replicated to several brokers, usually three, set by the replication factor. One replica is the leader, which handles reads and writes, and the others are followers, which copy from the leader. The replicas that are fully caught up are the in-sync replicas. If the leader's broker fails, one of the in-sync followers automatically becomes the new leader, and clients carry on. With producer acks set to all, and a minimum of two in-sync replicas, a write is only confirmed once it's safely on more than one broker, so a single failure doesn't lose data. Consumers also store their offsets in Kafka, so after a consumer crashes, another one continues from the last committed position.

The replication factor is how many copies of each partition Kafka keeps, on different brokers. A replication factor of three, which is the common choice for production, means every partition exists on three brokers, so the cluster can lose a broker without losing data.

Among those copies, one is the leader and the others are followers. The leader handles all the writes for that partition, and usually the reads too. The followers continuously copy new messages from the leader. Followers that are fully caught up are called in-sync replicas, the ISR. If a follower falls too far behind, it's removed from the ISR until it catches up.

If the leader's broker fails, the cluster controller chooses one of the in-sync followers as the new leader, and producers and consumers automatically switch to it. Because it was in sync, nothing confirmed is lost. Leaders are spread across brokers, so the load is balanced.

Two settings work together for durability. On the producer, acks set to all means a write is only acknowledged when all in-sync replicas have it. On the topic, min.insync.replicas set to two means a write is rejected if fewer than two replicas are in sync. So with a replication factor of three and a minimum of two in-sync replicas, the cluster tolerates one broker failure with no data loss and no downtime.
Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition, but not across a whole topic.

Each partition is an append-only log. Messages are written in order and each gets an increasing offset, and a consumer reads them in that same order. But a topic has several partitions, processed in parallel by different consumers, so there's no global order between messages in different partitions.

In practice, you usually don't need global ordering; you need ordering per entity, like all the events for one shipment or one order. You get that by using a message key. The producer hashes the key to choose the partition, so every event with the same key, like the shipment id, always goes to the same partition, and stays in order. So "shipment created", "shipped" and "delivered" for one shipment are always processed in sequence.

There are some things that can break ordering. Retries on the producer can reorder messages, which the idempotent producer, now the default, prevents. Increasing the number of partitions changes which partition a key maps to, so existing keys can move. And on the consumer side, if you process messages from one partition in parallel threads, you lose the order, unless you parallelise per key.

If you really need a total order across everything, you'd use a single partition, but that limits throughput to one consumer. In our shipment events, we key by shipment id, which gives the ordering that matters.
Retention and log compaction are the two ways Kafka decides when to remove old messages from a topic.

Retention removes messages based on time or size. By default, messages are kept for seven days, set by retention.ms, or until the partition reaches a size limit. After that, old segments of the log are deleted, whether or not anyone has read them. Consumers just need to read within the retention window. Because consumption doesn't delete data, many consumers can read independently, and you can replay events within that window, for example after fixing a bug in a consumer.

Log compaction works differently. Instead of deleting by age, Kafka keeps at least the latest message for each key, and removes older messages with the same key. So the topic becomes a snapshot of the current state of every key. For example, a topic of customer addresses keyed by customer id would keep the latest address for each customer forever. To delete a key completely, you send a message with that key and a null value, called a tombstone. Compacted topics are great for rebuilding a cache or state store, and Kafka uses one internally to store consumer offsets.
The choice depends on the use: for event history, like shipment status events, time-based retention; for "latest value per key" data, compaction. A topic can also combine both.
When a Kafka consumer crashes, the consumer group recovers automatically, and the key question is just whether messages get processed twice.

Each consumer in a group sends heartbeats. When one crashes, it stops sending them, and after the session timeout, the group coordinator considers it dead. Then a rebalance happens: its partitions are reassigned to the remaining consumers in the group. The new owner of each partition starts reading from the last committed offset for that partition.

Here's the important part. If the crashed consumer had processed some messages but hadn't committed their offsets yet, those messages will be processed again by the new consumer. That's at-least-once delivery. So consumers must be idempotent, meaning processing the same message twice has the same effect as once, for example by recording processed message ids, or using upserts with a unique key. The opposite mistake is committing the offset before processing; then a crash would skip messages, so I commit after processing.

To make crashes less disruptive: tune the session timeout, use the cooperative rebalancing strategy, so only the affected partitions move, and handle shutdown gracefully, committing offsets before leaving the group.
And while a consumer is down and before the rebalance, lag grows on its partitions, which is why we alert on consumer lag.

Consumer lag is the difference between the latest offset written to a partition and the offset the consumer group has committed. In simple words, it's how many messages are waiting to be processed. Some lag is normal, but lag that keeps growing means consumers can't keep up, and data is getting more and more delayed. And if lag grows beyond the retention period, messages are deleted before they're processed.
I monitor it per partition, with tools like Burrow, Kafka exporters for Grafana, or the cloud provider's metrics, and alert when it keeps growing.

To troubleshoot, I ask a few questions. Is the lag on all partitions or just one? If one, it might be a hot key, where one key gets most of the traffic, or a poison message that keeps failing. Did the incoming volume increase? Then I may need more consumers, up to the number of partitions. Did processing get slower? Then I check what each message does: often a slow database call, an external API, or processing one message at a time where batching would help. Are consumers rebalancing a lot? Frequent rebalances, often because processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, stop consumption repeatedly. And are the consumers healthy, with enough CPU and memory?
The fix follows the cause: scale out, add partitions, optimise processing, batch, tune poll settings, or move poison messages to a dead-letter topic.

Kafka consumers scale through consumer groups. All consumers with the same group id share the work: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, and one consumer can handle several partitions. So with six partitions and two consumers, each gets three. Adding consumers spreads the partitions out, and the group rebalances automatically.

That means the number of partitions is the maximum parallelism for a consumer group. If you have more consumers than partitions, the extra consumers sit idle, with no partitions assigned. They do act as hot standbys, taking over if another consumer fails, but they don't add throughput.

So to scale beyond the number of partitions, you have a few options. Add partitions to the topic, keeping in mind that this changes which partition each key maps to, which can affect ordering for existing keys, so it's best to plan enough partitions from the start. Or increase parallelism inside each consumer, processing messages concurrently with a worker pool, while keeping order per key if it matters. Or make processing itself faster, with batching and efficient database writes.
Separate applications that need the same events use different consumer groups; each group gets every message independently.
For autoscaling, I'd scale consumers on consumer lag rather than CPU, for example with KEDA in Kubernetes, up to the partition count.
When I design Kafka topics, I think about what the events represent, who consumes them, how they need to be ordered, and how they'll change over time.

First, one topic per type of business event or entity, like shipment-status or order-events, named with a clear convention, for example domain, entity and version. Not one giant topic for everything, and not one topic per customer. Second, the key. I choose the message key based on ordering needs. If events for one shipment must be in order, the key is the shipment id. A good key also spreads load evenly, so one key doesn't overload a partition. Third, the number of partitions: enough for the consumer parallelism I need now and in the near future, because increasing it later changes key placement. Fourth, retention: time-based for event streams, or compaction for "latest value per key" topics. Fifth, the replication factor, three for production, with a minimum of two in-sync replicas.

Sixth, the schema. Events have a defined schema, with Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema, preferably in a schema registry, with backward-compatible changes. Events include an event id, a timestamp, a type, a version and a correlation id. And seventh, a plan for failures: a retry topic and a dead-letter topic.
Our shipment status topic follows this: keyed by shipment id, with versioned events and correlation ids.

A poison message is a message that a consumer can never process successfully, for example because it's malformed, has invalid data, or triggers a bug. Without handling, the consumer keeps retrying it forever. In Kafka, that's especially bad, because it blocks every message behind it in that partition.

My approach separates two kinds of failure. Transient failures, like a database timeout or an unavailable service, are worth retrying. Permanent failures, like a message that can't be deserialised or fails validation, will never succeed, so retrying is pointless.

For transient errors, I retry a few times in the consumer with exponential backoff. If it still fails, or for longer delays, I publish the message to a retry topic, sometimes several with increasing delays, like one minute, then ten, so the main partition isn't blocked while waiting. For permanent errors, or after the maximum attempts, the message goes to a dead-letter topic, with headers saying the original topic, partition, offset, the error, and the number of attempts. Then the consumer commits the offset and moves on.

The dead-letter topic is monitored, with an alert, and after investigating and fixing the cause, messages can be replayed to the main topic. Consumers are idempotent, so retries never cause duplicates.
We use exactly this pattern with RabbitMQ too: limited retries with backoff, then a dead-letter queue, with alerts.
To secure Kafka, I cover four things: encryption, authentication, authorisation and network access.

Encryption in transit with TLS, between clients and brokers and between the brokers themselves, so messages can't be read on the network. Encryption at rest on the broker disks, which managed services like Amazon MSK provide. Authentication with SASL, for example SCRAM, or mutual TLS, or IAM authentication on MSK, so only known applications can connect. Authorisation with ACLs, applying least privilege: each service can only write to the topics it produces, and read from the topics it consumes, with its own consumer group. And network access: brokers in private subnets, reachable only from our services, never from the internet. Also, sensitive data in messages should be minimised or encrypted, and schemas validated.

For monitoring, the key metrics are: consumer lag per group and partition, which is usually the first sign of trouble; under-replicated partitions, which mean data is at risk; offline partitions and controller status; broker CPU, disk usage and network; and request latency, errors and throughput for producers and consumers. I'd collect these with Prometheus exporters or CloudWatch for MSK, show them in Grafana, and alert on growing lag, under-replicated partitions and disk space.
Consumers also log and trace with correlation ids from message headers, so one event can be followed across services.

RabbitMQ is a message broker. Applications send messages to it, and it routes them to queues, where consumers pick them up and process them. It decouples services: the sender doesn't wait for the receiver, and if the receiver is slow or down, messages wait safely in the queue.

The main concepts come from the AMQP protocol. Producers don't publish directly to queues. They publish to an exchange, with a routing key. A queue is where messages wait until a consumer receives and acknowledges them. A binding is the rule that connects an exchange to a queue, saying which messages should go there.

There are four main exchange types. Direct sends a message to queues whose binding key exactly matches the routing key, which is great for commands like "process this file". Fanout sends every message to all bound queues, like a broadcast. Topic matches routing keys with patterns, like shipment dot star, so different queues can subscribe to different groups of messages. And headers routes based on message headers.

Unlike Kafka, once a message is acknowledged, it's removed from the queue. So RabbitMQ is ideal for tasks and work queues, where each message should be processed once by one consumer, with retries and dead-lettering.
In our platform, we use RabbitMQ for work like processing vendor updates and sending notifications.
Acknowledgements are how RabbitMQ makes sure messages aren't lost, and there are two separate kinds, one on each side.

Publisher confirms are about the producer. When a publisher sends a message, it can't assume the broker received and stored it. With confirms enabled on the channel, the broker sends back an acknowledgement once it has taken responsibility for the message, for a persistent message, that means written to disk. If something goes wrong, it sends a negative acknowledgement, and the publisher can retry. Without confirms, a message can be lost silently, for example if the connection drops at the wrong moment.

Consumer acknowledgements are about the consumer. When RabbitMQ delivers a message, it waits for the consumer to acknowledge it before deleting it. With manual acknowledgement, the consumer acks only after it has finished processing. If the consumer crashes before acking, RabbitMQ redelivers the message to another consumer. A consumer can also reject a message, and send it to a dead-letter queue. With automatic acknowledgement, the message is deleted as soon as it's delivered, so if processing fails, it's gone.

I learned this the hard way in mid-2024. Our publisher had no confirms, and during a 40-minute problem, about 1,200 updates were lost silently. We recovered them by replaying the vendor files that evening, then added publisher confirms, at about 5 percent throughput cost. There's been no silent loss in the 12 months since.
Durability in RabbitMQ means messages survive a broker restart, and it needs several settings to work together.

First, the queue must be durable. A durable queue's definition survives a restart; a non-durable one disappears. Second, the message itself must be persistent, by setting the delivery mode to persistent when publishing. A persistent message in a durable queue is written to disk. If either part is missing, the message is lost on restart: a persistent message in a non-durable queue disappears with the queue. The exchange should also be durable, so the routing still exists after a restart.

But durability alone isn't enough. A message can still be lost before it's written, for example if the connection fails right after publishing. That's why publishers should use publisher confirms, which tell the publisher the broker has really stored the message. And consumers should use manual acknowledgements, so messages aren't removed until they're processed.

For surviving the loss of a whole node, not just a restart, you need replication. Modern RabbitMQ uses quorum queues, which replicate each queue across several nodes using the Raft consensus algorithm, and are the recommended choice for important data.

Persistence does cost some throughput, because of disk writes, but for business messages, it's worth it. After we lost about 1,200 updates in mid-2024 without confirms, we made sure all of these were in place.
If RabbitMQ goes down, what happens depends on how it's set up, and on how well producers and consumers handle it.

On the broker side: with a single node, everything stops until it's back. Durable queues with persistent messages are recovered from disk after a restart, but non-durable queues and transient messages are lost. In a cluster with quorum queues, losing one node isn't a problem: the queue's leader moves to another node, and clients reconnect, with no data loss.

On the producer side: while the broker is unavailable, publishing fails. Without publisher confirms, a producer might think a message was sent when it wasn't. So producers should use confirms, retry with backoff, and, for critical messages, use the outbox pattern, saving the message in the database with the business change, and publishing it later, when the broker is back. That way nothing is lost during an outage.

On the consumer side: consumers lose their connection. Unacknowledged messages go back to the queue and are redelivered when consumers reconnect, so consumers must be idempotent. Client libraries support automatic connection recovery, and our services also have health checks and alerts on connection failures.

In mid-2024, we had a 40-minute problem where our publisher had no confirms, and about 1,200 updates were lost silently. We recovered them by replaying vendor files, and adding confirms has prevented silent loss since.
RabbitMQ doesn't have a single built-in retry feature, so I build retries from a few pieces, separating transient failures from permanent ones.
For quick transient failures, like a brief database timeout, the consumer retries in memory a few times with exponential backoff, for example using Polly, before giving up on the message.

For longer delays, I use a retry queue. When processing fails, the consumer rejects the message, or publishes it to a retry queue that has a message time-to-live, like 30 seconds, and a dead-letter exchange pointing back to the main queue. So the message waits in the retry queue, expires, and returns to the main queue to be processed again. Several retry queues with increasing delays give backoff. I track the number of attempts in a message header. Another option is the delayed message exchange plugin.

After the maximum attempts, or immediately for permanent errors like invalid data, the message goes to a final dead-letter queue, with the error details, and an alert, so someone can investigate and replay it after fixing the cause.
What I avoid is simply requeueing a failed message straight away, because it goes back to the front and can loop forever, blocking the queue.

A real case: some kit-assignment notifications vanished because the consumer used autoAck. I switched to manual acknowledgement, added 3 retries with exponential backoff, and then a dead-letter queue.
To prevent message loss in RabbitMQ, I protect every step of the message's journey: publishing, storing, and consuming.

First, publishing. Use publisher confirms, so the publisher knows the broker actually stored each message, and retry when a confirm doesn't arrive. Use the mandatory flag, or an alternate exchange, so messages that can't be routed to any queue aren't silently dropped. For critical business messages, use the outbox pattern: save the message in the database in the same transaction as the business change, and a background process publishes it, so even a broker outage doesn't lose it.
Second, storing. Durable exchanges and queues, persistent messages, and quorum queues, which replicate across nodes, so a node failure doesn't lose data.

Third, consuming. Manual acknowledgements, only after processing has completed, for example after the database transaction commits. Never auto-ack for important messages. Failed messages are retried, and then go to a dead-letter queue, not discarded.
And finally, monitoring: alerts on dead-letter queues, unroutable messages and connection failures, plus idempotent consumers, because these measures can cause duplicates.

I learned this from a real incident in mid-2024: without publisher confirms, about 1,200 updates were lost silently in 40 minutes. We recovered them by replaying the vendor files, added confirms at about 5 percent throughput cost, and there's been no silent loss since.
To scale RabbitMQ, I first scale the consumers, and only then think about the broker.

Scaling consumers: several consumers on the same queue share the work, with RabbitMQ distributing messages between them. The prefetch count controls how many unacknowledged messages each consumer gets at once; a sensible value, like 10 to 50, balances throughput and fairness. Consumers can be autoscaled on queue depth. Scaling the broker: run a cluster of three nodes, with quorum queues for important data, replicated for availability. A single queue is handled by one node, so for very high throughput, you can spread load across several queues, for example with the consistent hash exchange, or use RabbitMQ streams. Keep messages small and queues short, because RabbitMQ performs best when queues are near empty. Use long-lived connections with several channels, instead of opening a connection per message.

For monitoring, the key metrics are: queue depth and how it's changing, publish and acknowledge rates, unacknowledged messages, consumer count per queue, dead-letter queue size, connections and channels, memory and disk alarms, which block publishers, and node health. We use the management UI and Prometheus with Grafana dashboards, with alerts on growing queues, dead letters, zero consumers and resource alarms.
A queue with growing depth and no consumers is the classic warning sign I always alert on.
To work out whether an issue is in the application, the database or the infrastructure, I start with the scope and timing of the problem, then follow the evidence layer by layer.

First, scope. Is it every endpoint or one? Every user or some? One service instance or all of them? Did it start suddenly, and did it line up with a deployment, a configuration change or a traffic spike? A deployment at that time points to the application.

Then I check each layer's signals. Infrastructure: CPU, memory, disk, network, container restarts, and the health of hosts and load balancers. If one node is out of disk or memory, or tasks are being killed, it's infrastructure. Database: database CPU, active connections, blocking, deadlocks, and slow queries, using Query Store or the monitoring tools. If the database is slow and the app is just waiting, it's the database. Application: error logs and exceptions, response times broken down by dependency in traces, and thread pool or connection pool exhaustion.
Distributed tracing is the most useful tool here, because a trace shows exactly where the time goes: in our code, in a database call, or in a call to another service.

A real example: an API suddenly became slow, around 200 milliseconds to 3 seconds. The application and servers looked healthy, but the trace showed one query taking all the time. It was parameter sniffing in SQL Server, a database issue, fixed with a better plan.
To trace a request across microservices, I use two things together: a correlation id in every log, and distributed tracing.

Distributed tracing, with OpenTelemetry, is the standard approach. When a request enters the system, it gets a trace id. Every operation along the way, like the API handling it, a database query, an HTTP call to another service, or publishing a message, is recorded as a span, with its duration and its parent. The trace context is passed between services in the W3C traceparent header for HTTP calls, and in message headers for RabbitMQ or Kafka. The result is a timeline of the whole request, across every service, which shows exactly where time is spent and where it failed. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient support this with very little code.

Logs are the other half. Every log line includes the trace id, or a correlation id, using structured logging with Serilog. So when I find an error, I search for that id and see all the related logs from every service, in order. The id is also returned in error responses, so a user or support person can give it to us.

I implemented correlation id middleware in 2024 across 4 services. It reads the id from the incoming header or creates one, adds it to the logging scope, and passes it on to downstream calls. Triage time went from about an hour to a few minutes.
Which logs I check first depends on the symptom, but I always start closest to where the problem is visible, and use a correlation id to follow it inward.

First, the application logs of the service that's failing, filtered by the time window and by errors and warnings. If the user or the error response gave me a correlation id or trace id, I search for that, which shows the whole path of that request across services. I look for the first error, not the loudest, because later errors are often just consequences.

Second, the edge: the load balancer or API gateway logs. They show whether requests reached our service at all, the status codes, and the response times. If the load balancer shows 502 or 503 errors, the service might be down or failing health checks.

Third, the platform: container or task events, like ECS stopped-task reasons or Kubernetes events, which show crashes, out-of-memory kills or failed health checks. Then deployment history, to see if something changed.
Fourth, dependencies: database logs and slow query data, message broker logs, and logs of downstream services.
Along with logs, I check the dashboards, like error rate, latency and resource usage, because they show the pattern and the start time quickly.
With our correlation id middleware, this usually takes a few minutes, instead of about an hour of searching through separate logs.
A symptom is what you see; the root cause is why it happened. Distinguishing them means not stopping at the first explanation that makes the alarm go away.

My main technique is to keep asking "why" until I reach something that, if fixed, would stop the problem from ever happening again. For example: the API is slow, that's the symptom. Why? The database CPU is high. Why? One query is doing a full scan. Why? It got a bad execution plan. Why? Parameter sniffing, where the plan was compiled for an unusual parameter value. That's the root cause. Restarting the server, or adding more CPU, would only treat the symptom.

A few other habits help. I look for the first error in the timeline, not the most frequent one, because later errors are often side effects. I check what changed around the time it started: a deployment, configuration, data volume or traffic. And I confirm the cause with evidence, ideally by reproducing it, and by checking that the fix actually removes it.
Often there are two fixes: an immediate mitigation to restore service, and the real fix for the root cause. Both are fine, as long as the second one happens.
For example, a service leaking about 150 MB a day was being restarted every 3 days. The restarts were the mitigation. The root cause was a cache with no expiry, so I added a 30-minute expiry.
I handle production incidents in two phases: restore service first, then understand and prevent it.

During the incident: first, assess the impact. Who's affected, how badly, and is it getting worse? I raise the incident through our process, so the right people know, and one person coordinates, while others investigate. Second, mitigate quickly. The fastest safe way to restore service often isn't the real fix. It might be rolling back a recent deployment, turning off a feature flag, scaling up, or failing over. Third, communicate regularly with stakeholders, even if the update is "still investigating". Fourth, keep a timeline of what happened and what we did.

After the incident: a blameless post-incident review. We look at what happened, the root cause, why we didn't detect it earlier, and what made recovery slower. The focus is on systems and processes, not on blaming people. Then concrete actions with owners and dates, like a fix, a test, an alert, a runbook, or a pipeline check, so the same class of problem can't happen again, or is caught early.

A real example: a release caused about 8 percent 5xx errors in UAT. We rolled back within 15 minutes, which restored service. Then we found the cause, a missing configuration value, and added a startup check so the service fails fast and visibly when configuration is missing.

Situation: in 2024, a security review of our web applications found a reverse-tabnabbing issue. Many external links in our UI opened in a new tab using target blank, without rel noopener. When a link opens that way, the new page gets a reference back to our original tab, through window.opener. A malicious or compromised external site could use that to quietly redirect our tab to a fake login page, and users might enter their credentials there.
Task: I was asked to fix it across our applications and make sure it couldn't come back.

Action: first, I searched the React and Angular codebases for every link and window.open call that opened a new tab, and found about 40 of them. I added rel noopener noreferrer to each link. Noopener removes the reference back to our page, and noreferrer also stops sending our URL to the external site. For window.open calls, I passed the noopener option as well. Then, to prevent it from coming back, I turned on an ESLint rule that fails the build if anyone adds a target blank link without noopener. And I created a small shared external-link component, so developers don't need to remember the attributes.

Result: the issue passed the security retest, with no regressions, and since then, the lint rule has caught a couple of new cases before they were merged. It was a small fix, but a good example of fixing a class of problem, not just individual instances.

Mocking means replacing a real dependency, like a database, an email service or an external API, with a controlled stand-in during a unit test. That way, I test only my own code, the test is fast and reliable, and I can easily simulate situations like errors or timeouts.
The general term for any stand-in is a test double, and there are a few kinds.
A stub provides fixed answers to calls. For example, a repository stub that always returns a specific customer. It's used to set up the situation for the test, and I don't check how it was called.

A mock is set up with expectations about how it should be used, and the test verifies those interactions. For example, verifying that the email service's Send method was called exactly once with the right address. It's used when the interaction itself is the behaviour I care about.

A fake is a working, lightweight implementation, but not suitable for production. For example, an in-memory repository that stores items in a list, or an in-memory message bus. It behaves realistically, which is useful for more complex scenarios.
In .NET, I use Moq or NSubstitute, and in practice the same object often acts as a stub and a mock.

One guideline I follow is not to over-mock. If a test checks every internal call, it breaks whenever the code is refactored. I prefer checking results and state, and only verify interactions that really matter, like sending an email or publishing a message.
To test a service that has dependencies, I make sure the dependencies can be replaced, then I test at two levels.

First, the design. The service gets its dependencies through constructor injection, using interfaces, like a repository, a message publisher, or an HTTP client for another API. Time is also a dependency, so I inject TimeProvider instead of using DateTime.Now directly. That makes everything controllable in tests.

Second, unit tests. I create the service with test doubles, using Moq or NSubstitute: stubs that return the data I need for the scenario, and mocks where I need to verify an important interaction, like a message being published. Then I test the business logic, including the important edge cases and error paths, like the repository returning nothing, or the other service timing out. These tests are fast and don't need any infrastructure.

Third, integration tests, because mocks can hide real problems, like a wrong SQL query or a serialisation issue. For these, I use real dependencies in containers with Testcontainers, like a real SQL Server or RabbitMQ, and WebApplicationFactory to run the API in memory. External third-party APIs are replaced with a fake HTTP server, like WireMock.
For example, for our shipment service, unit tests cover the status rules, and integration tests check the real database queries and message publishing end to end.
I test ASP.NET Core controllers in two ways, and I prefer the second for most cases.

The first is a unit test of the controller class. I create the controller directly, passing mocked dependencies, like the service it calls, then call the action method and check the result. For example, if the service returns null, the action should return NotFound; if it returns an order, the result should be Ok with that order. This is quick, but it doesn't test the important parts of the framework around the controller: routing, model binding, validation, filters, authentication, serialisation and status codes. And controllers should be thin anyway, with the logic in services, which have their own unit tests.

The second, which I prefer, is an integration test with WebApplicationFactory. It starts the whole API in memory, and I send real HTTP requests with its HttpClient. So I test the endpoint exactly as a client uses it: the URL, the JSON, the status code, the validation errors, and authorisation. I can replace dependencies, like the database with a Testcontainers SQL Server, or fake external services, by overriding service registrations. For authentication, I add a test authentication handler that creates a user with specific roles, so I can test both allowed and forbidden cases.
For example, I'd check that posting an invalid shipment returns 400 with a problem details response, and a user without the right role gets 403.
For EF Core code, I choose the test approach based on what I'm actually testing.

If I'm testing business logic that just happens to use data, I keep it in a service that depends on a repository interface, or I keep queries simple, and unit test the logic with test doubles. That's fast and focused.

If I'm testing the data access itself, meaning the queries, mappings, relationships and constraints, I use a real database. The best option is Testcontainers, which starts a real SQL Server in a Docker container for the tests. I apply the migrations, seed test data, run the code, and check the results. This catches the things that matter: whether the LINQ query translates correctly to SQL, unique constraints, cascade deletes, transactions and concurrency tokens. To keep tests independent, I reset the data between tests, for example with Respawn, or run each test in a transaction that's rolled back.

What I avoid for this is the EF Core in-memory provider. It's not a relational database: it doesn't enforce constraints, it doesn't support transactions properly, and some queries that work in memory fail on SQL Server. Microsoft itself discourages it for testing. SQLite in-memory is closer, but still differs from SQL Server.
In our services, repository and query tests run against SQL Server in Testcontainers in the pipeline, which gives real confidence that the queries work in production.
Playwright and Cucumber solve different problems, so they're often used together rather than as alternatives.

Playwright is a browser automation and end-to-end testing tool from Microsoft. It drives real browsers, Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, to click, type, navigate and check what's on the page, just like a user. Its strengths are reliability and speed: it automatically waits for elements to be ready, which reduces flaky tests, it can run tests in parallel, it can intercept network calls, and it records traces with screenshots and videos for debugging failures. It works with TypeScript, .NET, Java and Python.

Cucumber is a behaviour-driven development framework. Tests are written as scenarios in plain language using Gherkin, with Given, When and Then steps. For example: Given a study with two sites, When I create a shipment, Then the shipment status is Pending. Each step is linked to code that performs it. The benefit is that business analysts, testers and developers can all read and agree on the scenarios, and they act as living documentation of the requirements.
So Cucumber describes what should happen in business language, and Playwright does the actual work in the browser. In .NET, Reqnroll, the successor to SpecFlow, plays the Cucumber role.
I'd use Playwright alone for technical UI tests, and add Cucumber when business stakeholders need to read and own the scenarios.

A flaky test is a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails, without any change to the code. It's harmful because it destroys trust in the test suite. When tests fail randomly, people start rerunning builds and ignoring failures, and then they miss real bugs.

The usual causes are: timing issues in asynchronous code, like fixed sleeps, or not waiting for something to finish; shared state between tests, where the order they run in matters; dependence on the real time, time zones or random values; reliance on external services or the network; and in UI tests, not waiting for elements properly.

To handle them, first, I identify them: CI test history shows which tests fail intermittently. Then I don't ignore them. If I can't fix one immediately, I quarantine it, so it doesn't block the build, but I create a ticket to fix it quickly, so it doesn't stay hidden forever. Then I fix the root cause: replace sleeps with proper waiting, like awaiting the task or polling for a condition with a timeout; make each test create and clean up its own data; inject TimeProvider instead of using the real clock; use fixed seeds for random values; and replace external calls with fakes or containers. Automatic retries can hide flakiness, so I use them very carefully.
I once fixed a test that failed only around midnight, because it used the real clock. That was part of our time-zone bug in 2023.

Test coverage measures how much of the code is executed when the tests run, usually as the percentage of lines or branches. Branch coverage is more useful, because it shows whether both sides of each if statement were tested.

Coverage is useful for one thing in particular: finding code that has no tests at all. If an important class has zero coverage, that's a clear risk. Teams often set a minimum for new code, for example 80 percent in a SonarQube quality gate, so coverage doesn't drop over time.

But high coverage doesn't mean good tests. A test can execute every line and check nothing, with no meaningful assertions, and still count as 100 percent. Coverage shows what code ran, not whether the behaviour was verified.

So is 100 percent desirable? Usually not as a goal. Getting from about 80 to 100 percent often means testing trivial code, like simple properties, generated code or framework configuration, which costs time and produces fragile tests that break on every refactoring. That effort is better spent on testing important business logic and edge cases well, and on integration tests. For critical logic, like calculations or security rules, I do aim for very thorough coverage.
When our quality gate failed at 68 percent against 80 percent, we didn't just add tests to hit the number. We added meaningful tests for the real missing paths, and fixed it in half a day.
A good unit test is fast, independent, repeatable, and tests one behaviour, so that when it fails, you immediately know what broke.

I structure every test with Arrange, Act, Assert. Arrange sets up the situation: create the object under test, its test doubles, and the input data. Act performs the one action being tested, usually a single method call. Assert checks the outcome: the return value, the changed state, or an important interaction, like a message being published. Keeping these three parts clearly separated makes tests easy to read.

Some principles I follow. Name tests by behaviour, for example CalculateDeliveryDate_WhenSiteIsClosedOnWeekend_ReturnsNextMonday, so the name explains what broke. Test one behaviour per test. Test behaviour, not implementation, so refactoring doesn't break tests needlessly. Don't share state between tests, so they can run in any order. Avoid logic like loops and if statements inside tests. Use realistic, meaningful test data. Cover the edge cases and error paths, not only the happy path. And make tests deterministic: control time with TimeProvider and avoid real network calls.
For similar cases with different inputs, I use parameterised tests, like xUnit's Theory with InlineData, instead of copying the same test.
In my team, I review test quality as carefully as production code, because tests are what let us change code with confidence.

For asynchronous code, the main rule is to make the test itself async and await the code under test. In xUnit or NUnit, the test method returns Task, and I await the call. I never use .Result or .Wait, because they can deadlock and hide the real exception inside an AggregateException. To set up async dependencies with Moq, I use ReturnsAsync, or ThrowsAsync to simulate failures.

For exceptions, I assert both that the right exception is thrown and that it has the right details. In xUnit, that's await Assert.ThrowsAsync of the exception type, passing the call, and then I check the message or properties. With FluentAssertions, it's await act.Should().ThrowAsync, with the type and message. I also test what happens around the exception: for example, that a failed save doesn't publish a message, or that a retry policy tries the right number of times before giving up.

Some async-specific cases are worth testing. Cancellation: pass a cancelled CancellationToken and check that the method stops with OperationCanceledException. Timeouts and delays: use the injected TimeProvider, with FakeTimeProvider in tests, so I can move time forward instantly instead of waiting. And background work: instead of sleeping, wait for a condition with a timeout.
These keep async tests fast, reliable and free of flakiness.
I test Kafka and RabbitMQ integrations at three levels, because each one catches different problems.

First, unit tests of the message handling logic. I keep the business logic separate from the messaging library, so a handler receives a deserialised message and does its work. I can test it with test doubles, including edge cases like duplicate messages, which should be idempotent, and invalid messages, which should go to the dead-letter path. I also test serialisation, so the message format matches the contract.

Second, integration tests with a real broker. With Testcontainers, the tests start real RabbitMQ or Kafka containers. Then I publish a message, and check that the consumer processes it and that the expected result happens, for example a row in the database or a message published to the next queue. For waiting, I poll for the result with a timeout, never a fixed sleep. These tests catch real problems: wrong exchange or queue names, bindings, acknowledgements, retries, dead-lettering, and serialisation settings.
Third, contract tests between producers and consumers, using a schema registry or a tool like Pact, so a producer can't change a message in a way that breaks consumers.
After the kit-assignment notification problem caused by autoAck, I added an integration test that makes processing fail once, and checks that the message is retried, not lost.

React is a JavaScript library, created by Meta, for building user interfaces out of components. It focuses only on the view layer, and leaves things like routing and data fetching to other libraries you choose.

There are a few core ideas. First, components: the UI is split into small, reusable pieces, like a button, a form or a shipment table, and each component is a function that returns what should be shown, written in JSX, which looks like HTML inside JavaScript. Second, it's declarative: I describe what the UI should look like for the current data, and React takes care of updating the page when that data changes. I don't manipulate the DOM by hand. Third, state and props: props are inputs passed from a parent, and state is data a component owns and can change. When state changes, React re-renders the component. Fourth, efficient updates: React compares the new output with the previous one, a process called reconciliation, and only changes the parts of the real DOM that actually changed. And data flows one way, from parent to child, which makes behaviour easier to follow.
Hooks, like useState and useEffect, let function components manage state and side effects.
