In our applications, we use React with TypeScript for newer screens, like the CSV import screen I built, where users upload a file and see a clear row-by-row error report.
A component and an element are related, but they're different things.

A component is a function, or in older code a class, that describes a piece of UI. It accepts inputs, called props, and returns what should be displayed. For example, a ShipmentRow component that takes a shipment and returns a table row. It's like a blueprint, or a template, that can be reused many times.

An element is the result of using a component. It's a plain, lightweight JavaScript object that describes what should appear on the screen: its type, like a div, or the ShipmentRow component, and its props. When I write JSX, like angle bracket ShipmentRow with a shipment, that creates an element. Elements are immutable; once created, you don't change them. When data changes, React creates new elements, compares them with the previous ones, and updates the real DOM only where something changed.

So a simple way to say it: a component is the recipe, and an element is a description of one dish made from that recipe, at one moment in time. Elements are not the actual DOM nodes either; they're descriptions that React uses to create and update the DOM.
This distinction also explains why we never call components directly as functions in JSX code; we create elements, and React decides when to call the component.
In React, components can be written as classes or as functions, and today functional components with hooks are the standard.

Class components extend React.Component. They have a render method that returns the UI, state stored in this.state and updated with this.setState, and lifecycle methods for side effects, like componentDidMount when the component first appears, componentDidUpdate after updates, and componentWillUnmount for cleanup. The downsides were more boilerplate, confusion around the this keyword and binding, and related logic being split across different lifecycle methods.

Functional components are plain functions that take props and return JSX. Since hooks were introduced in React 16.8, they can do everything classes can. useState manages state, useEffect handles side effects, with the cleanup function replacing componentWillUnmount, and other hooks like useContext, useMemo and useRef cover the rest. They're shorter and easier to read and test. Most importantly, custom hooks let you reuse stateful logic between components, like a useShipments hook that fetches data with loading and error states, which was hard to do with classes.
The only thing that still needs a class is an error boundary, though libraries provide function-friendly wrappers.
In our code, all new components are functional with hooks, and we convert older class components when we work on them.
Props and state are the two kinds of data that control what a React component shows.

Props, short for properties, are inputs passed into a component from its parent, like arguments to a function. For example, a ShipmentRow receives a shipment object as a prop. Props are read-only inside the component: the component must never change them. If the parent passes new props, the component re-renders with them.

State is data that a component owns and manages itself, and which can change over time, usually because of user actions or data loading. For example, whether a dropdown is open, the text in a search box, or the list of shipments after an API call. In a functional component, I create state with useState, which gives me the current value and a setter function. Calling the setter tells React the state changed, and React re-renders the component.

So the difference is: props come from outside and are read-only; state lives inside and is changed by the component itself. Props flow down from parent to child. When a child needs to change something, the parent passes down a callback function as a prop, and the child calls it. That's how data flows one way, which keeps behaviour predictable.
A practical rule is to keep state in the closest common parent of the components that need it, which is called lifting state up.

The dependency array is the second argument to hooks like useEffect, useMemo and useCallback. It tells React when to rerun the effect, or recalculate the value: only when one of the listed values has changed since the last render.

For useEffect, there are three cases. With no array at all, the effect runs after every render, which is rarely what you want. With an array of values, like userId, the effect runs after the first render and then again whenever userId changes. That's the normal case, for example fetching a user's data whenever the selected user changes. With an empty array, the effect runs only once, after the component first mounts, because there's nothing that can change. That's used for one-time setup, like subscribing to an event. If the effect returns a cleanup function, React runs it before the effect runs again, and when the component unmounts. That's where you unsubscribe, or cancel a request.

The important rule is that the array must include every value from the component that the effect uses, like props, state, and functions. If you leave one out, the effect keeps using an old value, which is called a stale closure, and causes subtle bugs. The ESLint rule for exhaustive dependencies catches this, and we keep it switched on.
Also, in development with Strict Mode, React runs effects twice on purpose, to help find missing cleanups.
useMemo and useCallback are both React hooks for avoiding unnecessary work between renders, by remembering something until its dependencies change.

useMemo remembers the result of a calculation. You give it a function and a dependency array, and it only recalculates when a dependency changes. For example, filtering and sorting a large list of shipments: useMemo makes sure that work only happens when the list or the filter changes, not on every render.

useCallback remembers a function itself. Normally, every render creates a new function object, even if the code is the same. That matters when the function is passed as a prop to a child component wrapped in React.memo, or used in another hook's dependency array: a new function each time would make the child re-render, or the effect rerun, every time. useCallback returns the same function instance until its dependencies change.
So the difference is: useMemo caches a value, useCallback caches a function. In fact, useCallback of a function is the same as useMemo returning that function.

I don't use them everywhere, because they have their own cost and make code harder to read. I use them when there's a real reason: an expensive calculation, a memoised child component, or a value used as a dependency. And the new React Compiler can apply this memoisation automatically, which reduces the need to write them by hand.

useRef is a React hook that gives you a mutable object with a current property, which stays the same for the whole life of the component. The key difference from state is that changing ref.current does not cause a re-render.

It has two main uses. The first is accessing a DOM element directly. You create a ref, attach it to an element with the ref attribute, and then ref.current points to that DOM node. That's useful for things React doesn't handle declaratively, like focusing an input when a dialog opens, scrolling to an element, measuring its size, or integrating with a non-React library, like a chart.

The second is keeping a value between renders without displaying it. For example, storing a timer id so you can clear it later, an AbortController for cancelling a request, the previous value of a prop for comparison, or a flag saying whether a request is still current. If that value were in state, every change would re-render the component unnecessarily.
So my rule is: if changing a value should update what's on screen, use state; if it's just something the component needs to remember behind the scenes, use a ref.
One caution: you shouldn't read or write ref.current during rendering, only in effects and event handlers, because rendering should stay predictable.
The Context API is React's built-in way to share data with many components without passing props down through every level, which is called prop drilling.

You create a context, wrap part of the component tree in its Provider with a value, and any component inside can read that value with the useContext hook. It's ideal for data that many components need and that changes rarely: the current user, the theme, the language, or feature flags. One thing to know is that when the provider's value changes, every component that uses that context re-renders, so it's not great for data that changes very often.

Redux is a separate library for managing global application state. All the shared state lives in one store, and it's changed only by dispatching actions, which reducers handle in a predictable way. Modern Redux Toolkit removes most of the old boilerplate, and RTK Query handles API data and caching. Redux gives you very good dev tools, like seeing every action and the state at each step, middleware for side effects, and fine-grained subscriptions, so components only re-render when the part they use changes.

So I'd use Context for simple, low-frequency shared values, and Redux, or a lighter library like Zustand, for complex, frequently changing shared state. And for server data, like API results, I prefer a dedicated tool like React Query or RTK Query rather than putting it in global state myself.
For API calls in React, I want three things handled consistently: loading, errors, and avoiding race conditions or outdated data.

My preferred approach is a server-state library like TanStack Query, also called React Query, or RTK Query. You give it a key and a fetch function, and it returns the data along with isLoading and error states. It also handles caching, so the same data isn't fetched twice, retries, refreshing stale data, and cancelling outdated requests. For changes, it has mutations, which can refresh related data afterwards.

Without a library, I'd write a custom hook, like useShipments, using useEffect and useState for data, loading and error. It's important to cancel the request with an AbortController in the effect's cleanup, so if the user changes the filter quickly, an old response doesn't overwrite a newer one.

The API calls themselves go through one shared API client, using fetch or axios, which adds the auth token, handles common errors like 401 by redirecting to login, and reads our problem details responses.
On screen, I show a loading skeleton or spinner, a clear error message with a retry button, and an empty state when there's no data. An error boundary catches unexpected rendering errors.
In our CSV import screen, that meant clear progress while the file was being validated, and a helpful row-by-row error report when it failed.
Controlled and uncontrolled components are two ways to handle form inputs in React.

In a controlled component, React state is the single source of truth for the input's value. The input's value attribute is set from state, and an onChange handler updates the state on every keystroke. So React always knows the current value. That makes it easy to validate as the user types, disable a submit button until the form is valid, format input automatically, or change the value from code, like resetting the form. The downside is more code, and re-rendering on every keystroke, which can matter in very large forms.

In an uncontrolled component, the DOM itself keeps the value, like in a plain HTML form. React doesn't track each change. When I need the value, usually on submit, I read it, either through a ref, or from the form data. You can set a starting value with defaultValue. It's simpler and faster for basic forms, and it's required for file inputs, because their value can only be set by the user.

In practice, for most real forms, I use React Hook Form. It uses uncontrolled inputs internally for performance, but still gives full validation, often with a Zod schema, error messages and form state. So I get the convenience of controlled behaviour without the re-render cost.
Unnecessary re-rendering happens when components render again even though what they show hasn't changed. A little is normal and fine, but in large screens it can make the UI slow.

The common causes are these. First, a parent re-renders, and by default, all its children re-render too, even if their props are the same. Second, new object, array or function props created on every render, like an inline style object, or an inline arrow function as onClick. Even with React.memo on the child, those are new references each time, so the child still re-renders. Third, Context: when a provider's value changes, every consumer re-renders, and if the value is a new object on every render, they re-render every time. Fourth, state kept too high in the tree, so a small change, like typing in a search box, re-renders a whole page. Fifth, derived data stored in state and synced with effects, causing extra render cycles. And sixth, unstable list keys, like using the array index, which can make React recreate items.

To fix them: measure first with the React DevTools Profiler. Then move state down to where it's used, memoise expensive children with React.memo, use useMemo and useCallback for stable props, split contexts, use stable ids as keys, and virtualise long lists, so only visible rows render.
The new React Compiler handles much of the memoisation automatically.
In React, authentication is mostly handled by the identity provider and the backend; the React app's job is to sign the user in, call APIs with the token, and show only the right screens.

For sign-in, I use OpenID Connect with the authorization code flow and PKCE, through a library like MSAL or oidc-client, with our corporate single sign-on. Even better, for security, is the backend-for-frontend pattern: the server handles the tokens and the browser only gets a secure, HttpOnly session cookie, so no tokens are exposed to JavaScript. If tokens are in the browser, I keep them in memory rather than local storage, to reduce the risk from cross-site scripting.
The auth state, like the current user and their roles, is provided through a context, so any component can check it.

To protect routes, I wrap private routes with a component, often called ProtectedRoute or RequireAuth. With React Router, it checks the auth state: if the user isn't signed in, it redirects to login and remembers where they were going; if they don't have the required role, it shows a forbidden page. Menus and buttons are also hidden based on permissions.

But the most important point: hiding things in the UI is only for user experience. Real security is enforced on the server, where every API validates the token and checks permissions. A user can always bypass front-end checks.
For forms in React, I want three things: good performance, clear validation, and simple code. For anything beyond a couple of fields, I use React Hook Form.

React Hook Form registers inputs and keeps their values mostly uncontrolled, so typing doesn't re-render the whole form, which keeps large forms fast. It tracks the form state, like which fields are touched, dirty or invalid, and whether it's submitting. On submit, it gives me all the values, already validated.

For validation, I define a schema with Zod, and connect it with a resolver. The schema describes each field, like required, a maximum length, a valid date, or a rule across fields, like the end date being after the start date. With TypeScript, the same schema also gives me the form's type, so there's one source of truth. Error messages appear next to each field, and the first invalid field is focused, which helps accessibility.

On submit, I disable the button while the request is in progress, to avoid double submissions. If the API returns validation errors, as a problem details response, I map them back onto the matching fields, because the server always validates too.
For very simple forms, controlled inputs with useState are fine.
In the CSV import screen I built, the upload form used this approach, with clear client-side checks for file type and size, and server-side validation for the content.
For a large React application, I structure it by feature rather than by type of file, so the code for one business area lives together.

At the top, there's an app folder for application setup: routing, providers, like the auth and query client providers, and the main layout. Then a features folder, with one folder per business area, like shipments, studies or imports. Each feature contains its own components, hooks, API calls, types and tests, and exposes a small public interface through an index file. Other features use only that interface. Then shared folders for things used across features: UI components like buttons and tables, often from a design system, utility functions, and the shared API client.

A few principles go with it. Keep components small and focused, with logic in custom hooks. Keep server data in a library like React Query, and only truly global client state in Context or a store. Use TypeScript in strict mode. Use lazy loading for routes, so users only download the code for the pages they open. Enforce rules with ESLint, Prettier and import restrictions. And test with Vitest or Jest and React Testing Library, plus Playwright for end-to-end tests.
When an app becomes very large, with separate teams, it can be split further into packages in a monorepo, or micro-frontends, but I'd only do that when the team structure really needs it.
React and Angular are both excellent choices, so it depends on the team and the project. Here are the trade-offs, and why we use React.

Angular is a complete, opinionated framework from Google. It includes routing, forms, an HTTP client, dependency injection and testing tools, and it uses TypeScript by default. Everything has an official way to do it, which gives consistency across large teams. It has a steeper learning curve, though, with concepts like modules, decorators and RxJS.

React is a library focused on the UI. You choose your own libraries for routing, state and data fetching, which gives a lot of flexibility. It's mostly just JavaScript or TypeScript with JSX, so it's quick to learn, and it has a huge ecosystem and community, with plenty of developers available.

For our team, we chose React for new screens for a few reasons: the team's experience, the flexibility to pick lightweight libraries like React Query and React Hook Form, the ecosystem, and how easy it is to build small, reusable components. We didn't rewrite everything at once, because it's a GxP-regulated product. Older screens stay in Angular, new modules are built in React with TypeScript, module by module, and both call the same .NET Web APIs with types from one OpenAPI contract, so I work with both. For example, when I fixed the reverse-tabnabbing issue, I fixed about 40 links across both React and Angular code.
If I joined a team that uses Angular, I'd be happy with it. The fundamentals, components, state, and calling APIs safely, are the same.
var, let and const are the three ways to declare variables in JavaScript, and they differ in scope, hoisting and reassignment.

var is the old way. It's function-scoped, meaning it's visible throughout the whole function, ignoring blocks like if statements and loops. It's hoisted and initialised as undefined, so you can use it before its declaration line without an error, which hides bugs. And it can be declared again in the same scope. A classic problem is var in a loop with callbacks: all the callbacks share one variable and see the final value.

let and const were introduced in ES2015 and are block-scoped: they only exist inside the nearest curly braces. They're also hoisted, but not initialised, so using them before the declaration throws an error. That period is called the temporal dead zone. They can't be redeclared in the same scope.

The difference between let and const is reassignment. let can be reassigned. const can't be reassigned after it's created. But const doesn't make the value immutable. A const object or array can still have its contents changed; you just can't point the variable to a different object.
My rule is: use const by default, let only when the value must change, like a counter, and never var. ESLint rules enforce this in our projects.

Hoisting is JavaScript's behaviour of processing declarations before running the code in a scope. It feels as if declarations are moved to the top of their scope, though really the engine registers them during a setup phase.

How it behaves depends on what's declared. Function declarations are hoisted completely, both the name and the body, so you can call a function before the line where it's written. var declarations are hoisted and initialised to undefined. So if you use a var variable before its declaration, you don't get an error, you get undefined, which can hide bugs. let and const are hoisted too, but not initialised. Using them before the declaration throws a ReferenceError. The time between the start of the scope and the declaration is called the temporal dead zone. Classes behave like let. And function expressions or arrow functions assigned to a variable follow the variable's rules. So with var, the variable exists but is undefined, and calling it fails with "is not a function"; with const, you get a ReferenceError.

In practice, hoisting is mostly something to understand, not rely on. I declare variables before using them, use const and let instead of var, and let ESLint flag anything used before it's defined. That avoids the confusing bugs hoisting can cause.
A closure in JavaScript is a function that remembers the variables from the place where it was created, and can keep using them even after that outer function has finished running.

Every function in JavaScript keeps a reference to its surrounding scope. So if an outer function creates a local variable and returns an inner function that uses it, the inner function keeps access to that variable, and the variable stays alive as long as the inner function exists.

A simple example: a function makeCounter creates a variable count set to zero, and returns a function that adds one to count and returns it. Each time I call makeCounter, I get a new counter with its own private count. Nothing outside can change count directly, so closures are also a way to create private state.

Closures are everywhere in real code: event handlers and callbacks that use variables from the component, functions like debounce and memoise, and React hooks, where every render's functions capture that render's props and state. That's also where a common bug comes from: a stale closure, when a callback or effect keeps using an old value of state. That's why the dependency array in useEffect matters.
The classic loop issue is a closure issue too: callbacks created in a loop with var all share one variable, while let creates a new variable for each iteration.

A Promise is an object that represents the future result of an asynchronous operation, like an API call. It's in one of three states: pending, while waiting; fulfilled, with a value; or rejected, with an error. Once it's settled, it doesn't change.

With Promises directly, you handle the result by chaining then for success, catch for errors, and finally for cleanup. Each then returns a new Promise, so steps can be chained one after another. There are also helpers for running several at once: Promise.all waits for all of them and fails if any fails, Promise.allSettled waits for all and reports each result, Promise.race takes the first to settle, and Promise.any takes the first success.

async and await is newer syntax built on top of Promises. It doesn't replace them; it makes them easier to read. An async function always returns a Promise, and inside it, await pauses that function until the Promise settles, without blocking the main thread. Errors are handled with a normal try, catch and finally. So the code reads top to bottom like synchronous code.

I use async and await almost everywhere for clarity. But I still use Promise.all to run independent calls in parallel, because awaiting them one after another would make them run in sequence and be slower.

Callback hell is what happens when asynchronous code is written with nested callbacks, where each step is passed a function to call when it finishes, and the next step goes inside that function. With several steps in a row, the code keeps moving to the right, forming a pyramid shape, which is why it's also called the pyramid of doom.

For example: read a file, and in its callback, parse it, and in that callback, call an API, and in that callback, save the result. Each level also needs its own error check, usually the "if error, return" pattern in Node.js. The problems are that it's hard to read, hard to follow the flow, easy to forget error handling at one level, and difficult to do things like run steps in parallel or retry.

The solutions came in stages. First, naming the functions and keeping them flat helps a little. Then Promises allowed chaining with then, and one catch for all errors. And today, async and await lets you write the same sequence as straight, top-to-bottom code, with normal try and catch. In Node.js, most built-in modules now have Promise versions, like fs/promises, and util.promisify converts older callback functions.
So in modern code, callback hell is mostly avoided simply by using async and await consistently.
Optional chaining and nullish coalescing are two JavaScript and TypeScript operators that make it much safer and cleaner to work with values that might be null or undefined.

Optional chaining, the question mark dot operator, lets you access a property deeply without checking each level. For example, user question-mark-dot address question-mark-dot city. If user or address is null or undefined, the whole expression simply returns undefined, instead of throwing a "cannot read property of undefined" error. It also works for calling functions that might not exist, and for array access.
Nullish coalescing, the double question mark operator, provides a default value, but only when the left side is null or undefined. For example, settings dot pageSize double question mark 20.

The important difference is from the older OR operator. OR returns the right side for any falsy value: zero, an empty string, false, and NaN, as well as null and undefined. So if pageSize was deliberately set to zero, OR would wrongly replace it with 20. Double question mark keeps zero, empty strings and false, and only replaces null or undefined.

They're often used together, like user question-mark-dot name double question mark "Guest". There's also the nullish assignment operator, which sets a value only if it's currently null or undefined. I use these all the time, especially with API data that may have missing fields.
any and unknown are both TypeScript types that can hold any value, but they're opposites in terms of safety.

any switches off type checking. You can assign anything to it, and you can do anything with it: call methods, access properties, pass it anywhere, and TypeScript won't complain. So errors only appear at runtime. It's also contagious: values derived from an any are any too, so type safety silently disappears from parts of the code.

unknown is the safe version. You can assign anything to it, but you can't use it until you prove what it is. Before calling a method or reading a property, you must narrow the type, using checks like typeof, instanceof, the in operator, or a type guard function, or validate it with a schema library like Zod. So TypeScript forces you to handle the uncertainty.

In practice, I use unknown for values whose type I genuinely don't know: JSON from an API, data parsed from storage, or the error in a catch block, which TypeScript now types as unknown by default in strict mode. Then I validate it, for example with Zod, which also gives me the correct type.

I avoid any, and our ESLint rules flag explicit any. The only acceptable uses are temporary migrations from JavaScript, or rare cases with badly typed libraries, and even then, I keep it as small and isolated as possible.

Generics in TypeScript let you write functions, classes and types that work with many types, while still keeping full type safety. Instead of fixing a type, you use a type parameter, usually called T, which is filled in when the code is used.

A simple example is a function that returns the first item of an array. Without generics, you'd either write it for each type, or use any and lose type information. With a generic, function first of T, taking an array of T and returning T, if you pass an array of shipments, TypeScript knows the result is a shipment.

Generics are used everywhere in real code. For example, a generic API helper, like get of T taking a URL, which returns a Promise of T, so each call is typed. Or a generic ApiResponse of T type that wraps any data. React's useState is generic, so useState of Shipment array gives you typed state. Generic components, like a Table of T that receives rows of T and column definitions for T.

You can also constrain generics with extends, for example T extends an object with an id property, so the function can safely use id. You can give defaults for type parameters, and the built-in utility types, like Partial, Pick, Omit and Record, are all generics.
The benefit is reusable code without losing type checking. It's the same idea as generics in C#, which I use every day.
Union types, intersection types and narrowing are how TypeScript models values that can take different shapes.

A union type, written with a vertical bar, means a value can be one of several types. For example, string or number, or a status that's one of the literal strings Pending, Shipped or Delivered. That's a very common way to model fixed sets of values.

An intersection type, written with an ampersand, combines several types into one that has all their properties. For example, a Shipment type and an Auditable type combined give an object with the shipment fields and the audit fields.

Type narrowing is how TypeScript works out the more specific type inside a union, based on checks in your code. If a value is string or number and I check typeof value equals string, inside that if block TypeScript knows it's a string. Other ways to narrow are instanceof, the in operator, equality checks, and custom type guard functions that return "value is Type".

The most useful pattern is a discriminated union. Each type in the union has a common literal property, like kind or status. For example, an API result that's either success with data, or error with a message. A switch on that property narrows it fully. And with a never check in the default case, TypeScript gives an error if I add a new case and forget to handle it.
Strict mode can mean two things, and both are worth knowing.

In TypeScript, strict mode is the strict option in tsconfig. It turns on a group of stronger type checks. The most important is strictNullChecks, where null and undefined are no longer allowed everywhere, so TypeScript forces you to handle missing values, which prevents the most common runtime errors. Others include noImplicitAny, which reports values whose types TypeScript can't infer instead of quietly using any; strict function types; strictPropertyInitialization, which checks class properties are initialised; and treating catch errors as unknown. For new projects, I always turn strict mode on, and many teams add extra options too, like noUncheckedIndexedAccess. For older code, it can be enabled gradually.

In JavaScript, strict mode is enabled with the "use strict" directive at the top of a file or function. It makes JavaScript less forgiving. For example, assigning to an undeclared variable throws an error instead of creating a global variable by accident, this is undefined in plain function calls instead of the global object, and some unsafe features, like the with statement, aren't allowed. ES modules and classes are in strict mode automatically.
And in React, there's also StrictMode, a component that runs extra checks in development, like rendering components twice to find side effects.
All three exist to catch mistakes early, which is why I keep them on.
Node.js runs JavaScript on a single main thread, using an event loop. Understanding synchronous versus asynchronous code is critical because of that.

Synchronous code runs line by line and blocks the thread until it finishes. In Node, that's dangerous, because while the main thread is busy, nothing else can happen: no other request is handled, no timer fires, and no response is sent. For example, using readFileSync on a large file inside a request handler, or doing a heavy calculation like hashing a big file, freezes the whole server for every user.

Asynchronous code starts an operation, like reading a file, querying a database or calling an API, and lets the main thread continue with other work. Node hands the I/O to the operating system, or to its internal thread pool from libuv, and when the result is ready, a callback is queued, and the event loop runs it. With Promises and async and await, the code still reads top to bottom, but the thread is free while waiting. That's why Node can handle thousands of concurrent connections with one thread, as long as the work is mostly I/O.

So my rules in Node are: always use the asynchronous versions of I/O functions, never synchronous ones in request handling. For CPU-heavy work, use worker threads, or move it to a separate service or queue. And monitor event loop delay, because it shows when something is blocking.
It's the same principle as async and await in ASP.NET Core: don't block threads while waiting for I/O.

Express is the most popular web framework for Node.js. It's minimal and flexible: it gives you routing, middleware and helpers for requests and responses, and you add whatever else you need through packages.

Middleware is the core concept of Express. A middleware is a function that receives three things: the request, the response, and a next function. Middleware functions run in the order they're registered, forming a pipeline that every request passes through. Each one can do something with the request, like reading headers or adding data, modify the response, end the request by sending a response, or call next to pass control to the next middleware. If it neither responds nor calls next, the request just hangs.

Typical middleware includes parsing JSON bodies with express.json, logging, CORS, security headers with Helmet, authentication that validates a token and attaches the user to the request, and rate limiting. Middleware can be applied globally with app.use, to a path, or to a single route, and routers group related routes with their own middleware.

Error-handling middleware is special: it has four parameters, starting with the error. When any middleware or route calls next with an error, or, in Express 5, an async handler throws, Express skips to the error middleware, which can log it and send a consistent error response.
It's the same idea as the middleware pipeline in ASP.NET Core, which I use every day.
In Node.js, I handle errors at three levels: where they happen, in one central place, and as a last safety net for the whole process.

Where they happen: for asynchronous code with async and await, I use try and catch around operations that can fail and that I can do something about, like retrying a call or returning a specific message. For Promises without await, every chain needs a catch. I never leave a Promise rejection unhandled.

Central handling: in Express, I add error-handling middleware with four parameters at the end of the pipeline. All errors are passed there, either by calling next with the error, or automatically in Express 5 when an async handler throws. It logs the error with the request details and correlation id, and sends a consistent response, like a problem details JSON with the right status code, without exposing stack traces in production. I use custom error classes, like a NotFoundError or ValidationError, with a status code, so the handler can map them correctly.

The safety net: process-level handlers for unhandledRejection and uncaughtException. They log the error and then shut down gracefully, letting the container or process manager restart the service, because after an uncaught exception, the process may be in a broken state.
And I validate input early with a schema library like Zod, which turns bad input into clear 400 errors instead of crashes later.
I secure Node.js APIs in the same layers as any API, using the tools from the Node ecosystem.

First, authentication and authorisation. Every protected route validates a JWT from our identity provider, checking the signature, issuer, audience and expiry, with a library like jose or passport, and then checks the user's roles or permissions, including whether they own the resource they're asking for. Second, input validation. Every request body, parameter and query is validated with a schema library like Zod, rejecting anything unexpected, with a limit on body size. Third, injection. Use parameterised queries or a safe ORM, never build SQL from strings, and avoid passing user input to shell commands. Fourth, security headers and CORS: Helmet adds headers like content security policy, and CORS allows only known origins. Fifth, rate limiting against brute force and abuse. Sixth, secrets in a secrets manager or environment variables, never in code. Seventh, safe errors, with no stack traces in responses. Eighth, dependencies: npm audit or Snyk in the pipeline, keeping packages updated, and committing the lock file. And finally, HTTPS everywhere, running as a non-root user in the container, and logging security events.
These are the same principles I apply to our .NET APIs; only the libraries differ.
Node.js and .NET are both strong backend choices, and I choose between them based on the workload and the team.

Node.js is excellent for I/O-heavy services, like APIs that mostly call other services or databases, real-time features with WebSockets, and lightweight tools. It starts quickly, it has a huge package ecosystem, and teams can use one language, JavaScript or TypeScript, on both front end and back end. The trade-offs are that it runs JavaScript on one main thread, so CPU-heavy work needs care, and the ecosystem is fragmented, with lots of choices and varied package quality.

.NET, with ASP.NET Core, has very high performance, including for CPU-heavy work, because it's compiled and truly multi-threaded. C# has strong static typing, and there's a complete, consistent platform built in: dependency injection, configuration, logging, Entity Framework Core and great tooling. It's very well suited to large, long-lived business systems with complex domain logic, and it's long-term supported by Microsoft.

In our case, our core domain services, like shipments and supply, are in .NET, because of the complex business rules, the team's skills, and long-term maintainability in a regulated environment. We use Node for small tooling services where it fits better, and Python for some validation and automation work.
So I don't see it as one being better. I'd pick the right tool for the job, with a strong reason to add a new language to a team.
We used Python where it was clearly the right tool, not to replace .NET, which remains our main platform for core services.

The main example is a vendor file pre-validation service that I built with FastAPI. Vendors send us files in various formats, and errors in those files used to be found only when our .NET import failed, which was slow to diagnose. With Python and Pydantic, I could describe each file format as a model, with types and validation rules, in very readable code. The service checks a file and returns exact, row-by-row errors, like "row 52, ship date is in the future", before our .NET import runs. That made problems much faster to find and explain to vendors, and the models were easy for others to read and update.

Python is also part of our release automation, together with Shell and Ansible, for the install scripts that run across our environment nodes. Python is well suited to that kind of scripting and automation work, with excellent libraries for files, APIs and configuration.

So my view is: our core domain services stay in .NET, for consistency and maintainability, and we use Python where its strengths, like data validation and automation, give a real benefit. I'm comfortable in both.
I structure a FastAPI application by separating the web layer, the business logic and the data access, much like I would in ASP.NET Core.

The entry point, main.py, creates the FastAPI app, includes the routers, adds middleware, like CORS and logging, and sets up startup and shutdown with a lifespan function. Then there's a routers folder, with one router per feature, like files or shipments, each defining its endpoints. Those endpoints stay thin: they receive validated input, call a service, and return a response. A schemas folder contains Pydantic models for requests and responses, which give automatic validation and appear in the generated OpenAPI documentation. A services folder holds the business logic, independent of FastAPI, so it's easy to test. And a data or repositories folder handles the database, for example with SQLAlchemy.

Dependencies, like the database session, the settings or the current user, are provided with FastAPI's Depends, which works like dependency injection and makes them easy to replace in tests. Settings come from environment variables through pydantic-settings, so there's no configuration in code.
For quality: async endpoints where we do I/O, tests with pytest and FastAPI's TestClient, overriding dependencies, linting with Ruff, type checks with mypy, and the app runs in Docker.
That's the structure of the vendor file pre-validation service I built.
In FastAPI, authentication is built with its dependency system, so each endpoint simply declares that it needs a signed-in user.

In our setup, users sign in through our corporate identity provider using OpenID Connect, so the API doesn't handle passwords at all. Clients send an access token in the Authorization header as a Bearer token. I create a dependency, like get_current_user, that reads the token using FastAPI's security helpers, such as HTTPBearer or OAuth2PasswordBearer, and validates the JWT with a library like PyJWT: it checks the signature against the identity provider's public keys, which are fetched and cached, plus the issuer, the audience and the expiry. If it's invalid, it raises a 401 HTTPException. If it's valid, it returns a user object with the claims.

Endpoints add that dependency as a parameter, with Depends, and get the user. For authorisation, I add another dependency, like require_role of admin, which checks the user's roles or scopes and raises 403 if they're missing. It can be applied to one endpoint, or a whole router.
Because these are dependencies, tests can easily override them with a fake user. And FastAPI automatically shows the security scheme in the OpenAPI docs page.
It's the same idea as JWT bearer authentication with authorisation policies in ASP.NET Core.

SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol. It transfers files over an SSH connection, usually on port 22, so both the login and the data are encrypted. It's widely used for exchanging files between companies, like the order and status files we exchange with depot vendors.

FTP is the original File Transfer Protocol. It sends everything, including the username and password, in plain text, so anyone on the network could read it. It also uses two connections, a control channel and a separate data channel, which makes firewalls harder to configure. It shouldn't be used for anything sensitive.

FTPS is FTP with TLS encryption added, the same encryption used by HTTPS. It's secure, but it's still FTP underneath, with separate control and data connections and ranges of ports, so it's more difficult with firewalls and proxies. It also uses certificates, like HTTPS.

SFTP, despite the similar name, isn't FTP at all; it's a completely different protocol built on SSH. It uses a single connection and a single port, which is simple for firewalls, and it supports authentication with SSH keys as well as passwords, plus host key verification.

That's why SFTP is the standard choice for secure business file transfers, and it's what our IRT system uses with external vendors. I own the SFTP integration component, which works with three different SFTP libraries behind one interface.
SFTP authentication happens in two directions: first the client checks the server, then the server checks the client.

First, host key verification. When the client connects, the server presents its host key. The client compares the key's fingerprint with the one it expects. If they don't match, it could be a man-in-the-middle attack, so the connection must be refused. That's why we pin the expected fingerprint for each vendor in configuration, instead of accepting any key.
Then the client authenticates, usually with a password or a private key.

With password authentication, the client sends a username and password over the encrypted SSH connection. It's simple, but passwords can be guessed, reused or leaked, and they have to be shared with the other party.

With private key authentication, the client has a key pair. The public key is given to the vendor and added to their server, and the private key never leaves our side. When connecting, the server sends a challenge, and the client proves it has the private key by signing it. Nothing secret is sent over the network, it can't be brute-forced in practice, and keys can be revoked individually.

So private keys are much more secure, and they're what we prefer with vendors. Some vendors still require passwords, so our component supports both. In either case, the keys and passwords are stored in AWS Secrets Manager, never in code or configuration files.

Our SFTP integration supports three libraries, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, because different vendors' servers work best with different ones. The key to switching between them was one abstraction.

I defined an ISftpClient interface with the operations we need: connect, upload, download, list and delete. Each library has its own implementation of that interface, an adapter that translates our calls into that library's API and its errors into our own exception types. The rest of the code, like the jobs that send order files or collect status files, only uses the interface, and has no idea which library is underneath.

A factory decides which implementation to use for each vendor, based on configuration. For example, the configuration for DepotA says Rebex, and another vendor says SSH.NET. When a job runs for a vendor, it asks the factory for a client, and gets the right one. So moving a vendor to a different library is just a configuration change, which still goes through our change control, but needs no code change or deployment.
Every implementation passes the same set of contract tests, for things like overwriting files, timeouts and errors, so they really are interchangeable.
This design made it safe to introduce Rebex in 2024: we moved vendors over one at a time, starting with one low-volume vendor for two weeks, and could switch back instantly.

SFTP connections to external vendors fail for many reasons, like network problems, vendor server restarts, or timeouts on slow links, so I built retries and failure handling into the shared base of our SFTP component, so every vendor and library gets the same behaviour.

Every operation, like connect, upload or download, is wrapped in a Polly policy, with 3 retries, exponential backoff and jitter. So it waits a little longer before each attempt, with some randomness, to avoid hammering the vendor's server. Each retry uses a fresh connection, because a broken SSH session can't be trusted.

Importantly, not every error is retried. Temporary errors, like timeouts, dropped connections or "server busy", are retried. Permanent errors, like a failed login, or a host key that doesn't match, are not retried, because they won't fix themselves, and repeated failed logins could even get our account locked by the vendor. Those fail immediately with a clear message.
There are also sensible timeouts on connecting and on each operation, so nothing hangs forever.

If all retries fail, the job is marked as failed, the error is logged with the vendor, the file and a correlation id, and an alert goes to our support team. The next scheduled run tries again automatically, and because processing is idempotent, a retried upload or download never causes duplicates.
This turned what used to be manual follow-ups into mostly self-healing transfers.

File integrity matters a lot for us, because these files contain shipment orders and status updates for clinical trial medication. I protect against corrupted and partial files on both upload and download.

For uploads, the biggest risk is the vendor picking up a file while we're still writing it. So I upload with a temporary name, like a .tmp extension, and only rename it to the final name when the upload is complete. The rename is a quick, atomic operation on the server, so the vendor only ever sees complete files. After uploading, I compare the remote file size with the local size, and where the vendor supports it, we also exchange a SHA-256 checksum, so we can confirm the content is identical.

For downloads, I only pick up files that are complete, following the vendor's convention, for example a final name, a matching checksum file, or a marker file. After downloading, I check the size and checksum, and validate the content, like the header, the expected format and the record count in the trailer, before processing anything. If a file fails validation, it's moved to an error folder and an alert is raised, instead of importing bad data.
For large files on slow connections, I use longer timeouts and resumable transfers where the library supports it.
These checks mean a network problem can delay a file, but never silently corrupt our data.

Duplicate files happen for normal reasons: a vendor resends a file, a retry after a timeout uploads it again, or a file stays on the server and gets picked up twice. Processing the same shipment update twice could cause wrong data, so I made the processing idempotent.
First, predictable names. Files follow a naming convention with the vendor, the file type, a timestamp and a sequence number, so each file has a unique, meaningful name.

Second, a processed-files table in the database. Before processing a file, we check whether we've already seen it, using the file name and a SHA-256 hash of its content. The hash matters, because the same content might arrive with a different name, or a corrected file might come with the same name. If it's already been processed, we skip it, log it, and move it aside, without importing it again. The record is saved in the same transaction as the import, so a crash can't leave the file half-recorded.
Third, after successful processing, the file is moved to an archive folder on the server, so it isn't picked up again in the next run.

And finally, the records inside the files are handled idempotently too, using business keys like the shipment id and status, so even if two different files contain the same update, it's only applied once.
Together, these mean that resends and retries are completely safe.
SFTP credentials give access to our vendors' systems, so I treat them like any other production secret.

First, storage. Private keys and passwords are stored in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypted with KMS. They're never in the code, the repository, configuration files or build pipelines. The service reads them at runtime, using its IAM role, which only has permission to read the specific secrets it needs.

Second, key-based authentication wherever the vendor supports it, because private keys are much stronger than passwords and are never sent over the network. Each vendor gets its own key, so one can be revoked without affecting the others.
Third, host key pinning. Each vendor's expected host key fingerprint is stored in configuration, and the connection is refused if it doesn't match, which protects against man-in-the-middle attacks.

Fourth, rotation. Keys and passwords are rotated on a schedule, and immediately if there's any suspicion of exposure. The rotation is coordinated with the vendor and goes through our change control process, like any production change.
Fifth, no leaks in logs. Credentials are never logged, and error messages don't include them.
And finally, access to the secrets is limited to a few people, and every access is recorded in CloudTrail, which helps with auditing in our regulated environment.
SFTP looks simple, but vendors' servers all behave slightly differently, so I've faced a few real problems.

The biggest one was in 2024. A depot vendor hardened their server and disabled older algorithms, like ssh-rsa with SHA-1. Our original library, ComponentPro, couldn't connect anymore, and shipment files stopped flowing to that vendor. We used SSH.NET for some vendors, but it had its own limitations there, so I evaluated options and introduced Rebex, which supported the modern algorithms. Because of our ISftpClient abstraction, I added Rebex behind the same interface, tested it, including with a 500 MB file, and moved that vendor over by configuration.

A second problem: one Monday, a vendor told us our order file hadn't arrived, though our logs showed a successful upload. The vendor had moved their pickup folder to /inbound/irt, and announced it to a distribution list we weren't on. The file was sitting in the old folder. We fixed the configuration, and I added a post-upload check that confirms the file is visible in the expected folder, plus an alert if the vendor hasn't picked it up in time.
A third: large files timing out on slow vendor links. I increased the operation timeouts and used resumable transfers where supported.
The common lesson is to verify outcomes, not just assume success, and to design for change.
I test an SFTP integration at several levels, because the most painful bugs only show up against real servers.

First, unit tests. The business logic, like naming files, deciding which files to process, detecting duplicates and handling errors, depends only on our ISftpClient interface, so I test it with a mocked client. I can easily simulate failures, like a timeout on the second attempt, to check that retries and alerts behave correctly.

Second, contract tests for each library implementation. All three implementations, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, run the same test suite against a real SFTP server, to prove they behave the same way: uploading, downloading, listing, overwriting existing files, handling a missing folder, and the errors they raise.

Third, integration tests against a real SFTP server in a container, an OpenSSH server started with Testcontainers in our CI pipeline. These cover key exchange, host key verification, password and key authentication, large files, like a 500 MB file, timeouts and reconnects. I also configure the server to reject old algorithms, to mimic hardened vendor servers.
Fourth, in the test environments, connectivity tests against the vendors' test servers, if they provide them, before any change reaches production.
Finally, in our regulated process, changes go through FV, TechOps and UAT with recorded evidence, and a new library is rolled out to one low-volume vendor first.
WCF and Web API are two Microsoft technologies for building services, from different eras and with different goals.

WCF, Windows Communication Foundation, came with .NET Framework 3.0. It's a general communication framework, designed mainly for SOAP services. It supports many transports, like HTTP, TCP, named pipes and message queues, and the WS-star standards, for things like message-level security, reliable messaging and transactions. It's very powerful, but complex, with a lot of configuration in XML, of endpoints, bindings and behaviours, and it's tied to the Windows-based .NET Framework.

Web API, now part of ASP.NET Core, is designed specifically for HTTP services, usually REST with JSON. It uses HTTP the way it was intended: resources in URLs, methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, and status codes. It's lightweight, simple to configure, easy to call from any client, including browsers and mobile apps, easy to test, and runs cross-platform in containers.

The important practical point is that WCF server isn't supported in modern .NET. There's a community project, CoreWCF, that helps migrate existing services, and modern .NET still has a WCF client for calling SOAP services. But new services are built with ASP.NET Core Web API for REST, or gRPC when you need high-performance, strongly typed service-to-service communication, which covers many of the cases WCF was used for.
Our IRT platform has some older WCF services, and new work is in ASP.NET Core Web API.
SOAP, the Simple Object Access Protocol, is a messaging protocol for web services, where every message is an XML document.

A SOAP message is an envelope with two parts: an optional header, for things like security tokens, routing or transaction information, and a body, which contains the actual request or response. Errors are returned in a standard structure called a SOAP fault. Messages are usually sent over HTTP POST, but SOAP can use other transports too.

A SOAP service is described by a WSDL document, the Web Services Description Language. It's a formal, machine-readable contract that defines every operation, its inputs and outputs, and the data types, using XML Schema. Tools read the WSDL and generate a strongly typed client proxy automatically, so the client code calls methods as if they were local. In .NET, that's Add Service Reference, or the dotnet-svcutil tool.

SOAP also has a family of WS-star standards, like WS-Security for signing and encrypting messages, and others for reliable messaging and transactions. That's why it was popular in enterprise environments.
The downsides are that it's verbose, heavier to process, and harder to use from browsers and mobile apps than REST with JSON.

It's still common in older enterprise and healthcare systems. Our platform has some older WCF SOAP services, and some external systems still expose SOAP interfaces, so I work with it when integrating.
In WCF, contracts define what a service offers, and there are three main kinds, each marked with an attribute.

A service contract defines the service itself. It's an interface marked with the ServiceContract attribute, and it describes the set of operations the service exposes, like IShipmentService. Clients see this as the service's public API.

An operation contract marks each method of that interface that should be exposed, using the OperationContract attribute. Only methods with this attribute are part of the service. It can also control details, like whether the operation is one-way, meaning the client doesn't wait for a reply, and the action names used in SOAP messages.

A data contract describes the data that's passed in and out. A class is marked with the DataContract attribute, and each property that should be serialised is marked with DataMember. It controls exactly which fields are included, their names, their order and whether they're required, and it supports versioning, so new optional members can be added without breaking old clients. The DataContractSerializer uses these to convert objects to and from XML.
There are also fault contracts, which define the typed errors an operation can return as SOAP faults, and message contracts, for full control of the SOAP message.
Together, these generate the WSDL that clients use. When we migrate a WCF service to ASP.NET Core, these contracts map naturally to controllers, endpoints and DTOs.
In .NET Framework, there was no built-in dependency injection container, unlike modern .NET, where it's part of the platform. So teams added it themselves.

The common approach was a third-party container, like Unity, Autofac, Ninject, Castle Windsor or Simple Injector. You registered your interfaces and their implementations with the container at application startup, usually in Global.asax, with their lifetimes, like transient, per request or singleton. Then you connected the container to the framework. For ASP.NET MVC, you set a custom dependency resolver; for ASP.NET Web API, you set the configuration's DependencyResolver, and the framework would ask the container to create controllers with their dependencies through constructor injection.

WCF was harder, because WCF creates the service instances itself. To use constructor injection, you needed a custom instance provider and a service behaviour, or a custom service host factory, and the containers often provided integration packages for that, like Autofac's WCF integration.
Without a container, some older code used the service locator pattern, or created dependencies with new directly, which made it hard to test.

In modern .NET, dependency injection is built in, through IServiceCollection, and used consistently by ASP.NET Core, background services and libraries. That's one of the advantages when we migrate older WCF and Framework code: it becomes easier to test, because dependencies can be replaced.

We migrate away from WCF because WCF server isn't supported in modern .NET. Staying on it means staying on the .NET Framework, which is Windows-only, receives only security fixes, and can't use modern features, performance improvements, or container hosting on Linux, like the ECS setup the rest of our services use. REST APIs, or gRPC, are also much easier to build, test, monitor and integrate with modern clients and tools.

There are several challenges. First, existing clients. Some external or internal clients still expect SOAP, and we can't always change them at the same time, so we may need to keep a SOAP endpoint, for example using CoreWCF, or a facade that translates, during a transition period. Second, WCF-specific features, like WS-Security message signing, duplex callbacks, or transactions, which have no direct REST equivalent and need a redesign. Third, behaviour must stay exactly the same, including data formats, edge cases and errors, which is especially important in a validated GxP system. Fourth, configuration and hosting, moving from XML configuration and IIS to code-based configuration and containers.

So the approach is to migrate one service at a time, not big bang, using the strangler fig pattern. We write characterisation tests against the existing service first, to capture its current behaviour, run old and new side by side, compare results, and switch clients over gradually, with a rollback path, through FV and UAT validation.

IRT stands for Interactive Response Technology. It's the system that clinical trials use to manage patients and the trial medication, and it's the domain I work in. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles.

An IRT system does a few key things. Randomisation: when a patient is enrolled at a site, IRT assigns them to a treatment group, following the study's randomisation rules, so the trial is scientifically fair. Blinding: it keeps the treatment assignment hidden from the people who mustn't know, like the patient and the site staff, in a blinded study, while still letting authorised people see what they need. Drug supply management: it decides which kit to give each patient at each visit, tracks stock at every site and depot, and triggers resupply shipments automatically, so sites don't run out but medication isn't wasted. And shipment tracking: it creates shipment orders for depots and couriers, and tracks them until delivery, including expiry dates and temperature excursions.
In the past, these were called IVRS and IWRS, for interactive voice and web response systems, because sites used to phone in. It's also called RTSM, randomisation and trial supply management.
Because it directly affects patients and the integrity of the trial, IRT is a GxP-regulated system, with strict validation, audit trails and change control.
My work covers integrations with depot and courier vendors, data import features, security, and deployment automation for this platform.

GxP is a general term for good practice quality guidelines and regulations in life sciences. The x stands for the specific area, like GMP for good manufacturing practice, GCP for good clinical practice, and GLP for good laboratory practice. They're enforced by regulators, like the FDA in the US and the EMA in Europe.
The purpose is to make sure that products like medicines are safe and effective, and that the data used to make decisions about them is reliable and trustworthy.

For software, the key regulations are FDA 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11, which cover computerised systems and electronic records. The core idea is data integrity, often summarised as ALCOA plus: data must be attributable, meaning we know who did it, legible, contemporaneous, meaning recorded at the time, original, and accurate, plus complete, consistent, enduring and available.

Why does it matter? Because in clinical trials, software mistakes can affect real patients. If our IRT system gave a patient the wrong kit, or lost a record of what they received, it could harm the patient, or make the trial's results unreliable, which could invalidate years of research. Regulators can reject trial data, or take action against a company, if its systems aren't compliant.
So in our work, GxP means validated systems, complete audit trails, strict change control and documented evidence for everything. It shapes how we develop, test and release software every day.
GxP affects almost every part of how we build and release software, because we must be able to prove that the system does what it should, and that every change is controlled.

First, requirements and traceability. Every requirement is documented, and traced to its design, its tests and the test results, so we can show that every requirement was tested. Second, validation. Before release, the system is formally validated: the FV team runs scripted tests against the requirements and records evidence, like screenshots and signatures. Third, change control. Every change to a validated system needs an approved change request, an impact and risk assessment, and the right approvals before it reaches production. Fourth, environments. Releases move through controlled environments, like FV, TechOps and UAT, using the same validated build artifact, and production access is very restricted. Fifth, data integrity and audit trails. The system records who changed what, when and why, and those records can't be edited. Electronic signatures must meet regulations, like 21 CFR Part 11. Sixth, documentation and training. Procedures are written down, and people are trained on them.
For developers, that means more discipline: thorough testing, clear documentation, careful code reviews and no shortcuts in production.
It also shaped my CIRT MCP server. It speeds up deployments from 6 hours to 2, but keeps every approval and audit trail exactly as the process requires.
These three ideas are at the heart of working in a regulated environment.

Validation means proving, with documented evidence, that a system consistently does what it's intended to do, and meets its requirements. It's not just testing; it's planned and documented. There's a validation plan, requirements, risk assessment, test scripts with expected results, executed tests with recorded evidence, and a summary report signed off before the system is used. It's often described as installation, operational and performance qualification. In our process, the FV team does the formal validation testing.

Traceability means being able to follow the links between things. Each requirement is linked to its design, to the code changes, to the tests that verify it, and to their results, usually in a traceability matrix. So we can answer: was this requirement tested? Which requirement does this change affect? In Azure DevOps, we link work items, commits, builds and test results to make this possible.

Auditability means anyone reviewing the system, like an auditor or regulator, can reconstruct what happened. Every change to data is recorded in an audit trail: who did it, when, what the old and new values were, and why. Audit trails can't be changed or deleted. The same applies to changes to the system itself, through change records and approvals.
Together, they let us prove that the system is correct and that its data can be trusted.

Change control is a formal process for managing any change to a validated system, so every change is justified, assessed, approved, tested and documented before it reaches production, and the system stays in a validated state.

The steps usually are these. First, a change request describing what's changing and why, whether it's a new feature, a bug fix, a configuration change or an infrastructure update. Second, an impact and risk assessment: what parts of the system are affected, the risk to patients and data, and how much testing and validation are needed. Third, approval, by the right people, like the system owner and quality assurance, before work goes into controlled environments. Fourth, implementation and testing, with the release moving through our environments, FV, TechOps and UAT, with documented evidence. Fifth, approval to release, then deployment to production, following the documented plan, including a rollback plan. And sixth, closure, with verification that it worked and all documentation complete.
Emergency changes are possible, for urgent production fixes, but they still need approval and must be documented, often with some testing completed afterwards, within a defined time.

In practice, our releases are linked to change requests, and the Azure DevOps approvals for controlled environments are part of that process. That's why, when I automated deployments with the CIRT MCP server, I deliberately kept every approval and change control step exactly as it was.

FV, TechOps and UAT are three of the controlled stages a release goes through before production in our regulated process. Each has a different purpose, and the same build artifact moves through all of them, so what's tested is exactly what's released.

FV stands for formal validation. In this stage, the validation team executes scripted test cases against the documented requirements, records the actual results, captures evidence like screenshots, and signs them. It produces the documented proof that the system meets its requirements, which is what regulators expect to see.

TechOps is the technical operations team, and also the environment they manage. They install releases in the controlled environments following the documented installation steps, verify the installation, like checking that every node is on the right version and services are healthy, and confirm the environment is ready. This also proves the installation process itself is reliable before it's used in production.

UAT is user acceptance testing. Business users, like study managers or clinical supply teams, confirm that the release meets their real business needs, using realistic scenarios, and sign off before it goes to production.

Each environment has several nodes, 4 to 6, and deploying to all of them used to need about 6 people for about 6 hours. My CIRT MCP server automates those deployments and checks, cutting it to 1 person and about 2 hours, while all the validation and approvals stay the same.
Production changes in a regulated system must be controlled, traceable and reversible. I make sure of that through process, pipelines and access control together.

First, every production change has an approved change request, with an impact and risk assessment, linked to the work items and the release. Second, the release goes through gated pipelines in Azure DevOps. The same validated build artifact is promoted through FV, TechOps and UAT, with evidence recorded, and we never rebuild for production. Third, production deployment requires pre-deployment approval from named approvers, and the person who prepared the release can't approve it alone. Fourth, access is restricted. Only a small number of people have production access, nobody changes production by hand, and all access and actions are logged. Fifth, every deployment has a documented plan, including verification steps and a rollback plan, which is usually redeploying the previous release. Database changes are written to be backward compatible, so rollback is safe. Sixth, configuration changes follow the same process as code changes.
Emergency fixes follow an expedited version of the same process, with approval and documentation, not a bypass.

Even our automation respects this. My CIRT MCP server makes deployments faster, but it uses each engineer's own permissions, can't approve releases, and logs every action, so the control and audit trail are exactly what the process requires.
In a regulated environment, quality isn't just a team value; we have to prove it. I maintain quality through prevention, verification and evidence.

Prevention starts with clear requirements and risk assessment, so the riskiest parts of the system get the most attention. Then good engineering practices: small pull requests, careful code reviews by a colleague, coding standards, and static analysis with SonarQube, where the quality gate checks new code for bugs, vulnerabilities and coverage, at least 80 percent for new code. Dependency and image scanning catch known vulnerabilities.

Verification means testing at several levels: unit tests, integration tests with real databases and message brokers in containers, end-to-end tests, and then formal validation by the FV team, and user acceptance testing. Every pipeline runs the automated tests, and nothing merges if they fail.
Evidence means traceability from requirements to tests and results, recorded approvals, change requests, and audit trails, so we can show an auditor exactly what was done and why.
And continuous improvement: blameless reviews after incidents or escaped defects, adding a test or check so the same issue can't happen again.

Some improvements I drove were smaller pull requests, from 1,500 lines or more down to under 400, which made reviews faster and more thorough, and mentoring two graduates in 2024 on testing and review practices.

Security in clinical-trial software protects two things: patients' personal and health data, and the integrity of the trial itself. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles.

First, access control. Role-based access means people only see the studies, sites and functions they need. A site user sees only their site; a study manager sees their study. Second, blinding. In blinded studies, information about which treatment a patient receives must only be visible to specifically authorised, unblinded roles. Exposing it accidentally could ruin the trial's scientific value, so we test those permissions carefully. Third, authentication: single sign-on with multi-factor authentication through our identity provider, short-lived tokens, and immediate revocation on logout. Fourth, data protection: encryption in transit with TLS, and at rest, minimal personal data, and secrets in a secrets manager. Fifth, audit trails for every change, as required by GxP. Sixth, secure development: code reviews, SonarQube, dependency and image scanning, and regular security testing for OWASP issues, like injection, broken access control and cross-site scripting. And finally, secure vendor integrations, with key-based SFTP and pinned host keys.

Several of my contributions came from this work. I fixed a reverse-tabnabbing issue on about 40 links, made logout take effect immediately with a token denylist, and shrank an SSO cookie from about 13 KB to under 1 KB to stop random logouts.
Shipment tracking connects our IRT system with external depots and couriers, so we always know where trial medication is.

When IRT decides a site needs medication, it creates a shipment order. That order is sent to the depot vendor, either as a file over SFTP, using our SFTP integration component, or through an API, depending on the vendor. The depot picks and packs the kits, and the courier transports them. As the shipment moves, the vendor sends status updates back, like dispatched, in transit, delivered, or a temperature excursion, again as files or API calls.

On our side, integration services collect those updates and handle them carefully. They validate the format and content, check for duplicates, using the file name and content hash, and the shipment id and status, so a resent update isn't applied twice, and then update the shipment. They publish events, through RabbitMQ and Kafka, so other parts of the system can react, like updating site inventory, and notifying site staff that medication is on its way or has arrived.

Failures are expected, so there are retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, alerts to support, and a reconciliation report that compares what we sent with what the vendor has acknowledged, to catch anything missed.
I learned the importance of this the hard way in mid-2024, when about 1,200 updates were lost silently. We recovered them by replaying the vendor files, and added publisher confirms.
Our IRT system has several kinds of external integrations, and each one is built with monitoring and recovery in mind.

The main ones are depots and couriers. We send shipment orders and receive status updates, either through files over SFTP, using the SFTP integration component I own, which supports three libraries behind one interface, or through APIs. Then clinical data systems, like EDC, electronic data capture, which share patient and visit information with IRT, so randomisation and dispensing data stay consistent with the clinical records. Then identity: our corporate identity provider, for single sign-on and multi-factor authentication. Then notifications: email services that inform site staff and study teams about shipments, low stock, and other events. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. And bulk data import, like the CSV import feature I built, which lets users upload site and study data that previously took 2 to 3 days of manual work.
Internally, our services exchange data through RabbitMQ for work queues and Kafka for events.

For every integration, I make sure there are a few things: validation of incoming data, idempotent processing so duplicates are harmless, retries with backoff for temporary failures, dead-letter handling, alerts to support, correlation ids for tracing, and reconciliation reports to confirm that nothing was lost between systems.
