For immediate revocation, like logout, a small denylist of token ids in Redis can be checked very quickly.
Passwords, if stored at all, are hashed with a strong algorithm like bcrypt or Argon2. Add rate limiting and lockout against brute force, and log every sign-in for audit.
I've implemented exactly that denylist pattern after finding that tokens worked for 60 minutes after logout. The check in ElastiCache takes about 1 ms.
A distributed cache stores frequently read data in memory across several nodes, so applications get fast reads and the database gets less load.

I'd use something like Redis, or a managed version like ElastiCache, rather than building one. The data is split across nodes, using consistent hashing or Redis cluster hash slots, so adding nodes only moves a small part of the keys. Each primary node has replicas in other availability zones for failover.

For how the application uses it, the usual pattern is cache-aside: read from the cache first, and on a miss, read from the database, then store the result with a time-to-live. When data changes, the application updates the database and removes the cache key, so the next read gets fresh data.

There are a few problems to design for. Cache stampede, when a popular key expires and many requests hit the database at once; I'd use locking, so only one request reloads it, or refresh it early. Randomised expiry times, so many keys don't expire together. Eviction policies, like least recently used, with memory limits. And treating the cache as optional: if Redis is down, the application should fall back to the database, maybe more slowly, but still working.
At work, we cache reference data and study configuration in Redis, and we also use ElastiCache for the token denylist, which needs very fast lookups.

Our platform supports clinical trials: setting up studies, randomising patients, and managing the supply of trial medication to sites around the world. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. At a high level, I'd describe it like this.

Users and vendors come in through an API gateway, with single sign-on for users and secure APIs and SFTP for vendors. Behind that, there are services for each business area: study setup behind our internal Admin console, screening and subjects, randomisation and re-randomisation, eConsent, supply planning and shipments, and DARM for drug accountability. The UI is component-based, with older screens in Angular and newer modules in React with TypeScript. Each service owns its own SQL Server database, with audit tables that record every change, because in a GxP regulated environment, every change must be traceable.

Services communicate through APIs for things that need an immediate answer, like randomising a patient, and through messaging for everything else. Kafka carries events like shipment status updates that several services consume. RabbitMQ handles work queues, like processing vendor files and sending notifications. Vendor integrations with depots use SFTP and APIs, with validation and retries. Redis caches reference data.

Everything runs in containers on AWS ECS across availability zones, with CloudWatch and Grafana for monitoring. Releases go through Azure DevOps pipelines with FV, TechOps and UAT environments, approvals and change control, and I built the CIRT MCP server to automate those deployments, which cut them from 6 hours to 2.
The key design themes are reliability, auditability and compliance, because real patients depend on the medication arriving.
To scale the architecture, I'd first find the real bottleneck using metrics, rather than guessing. Then I'd scale each layer appropriately.

The application layer is the easy part if services are stateless. No session data in memory, so I can run more instances behind the load balancer, with autoscaling on CPU, request count, or queue length for workers. Slow work moves to background workers through queues, so the API stays fast.

The database is usually the harder part. Step one is optimising: the right indexes, efficient queries, avoiding N plus one problems, and short transactions. That often gives the biggest win. I once took a query from 8 to 12 seconds to under 300 milliseconds just by fixing the query and the index. Step two is caching hot data in Redis. Step three is read replicas, sending read-only queries to replicas while writes go to the primary, accepting slight replication delay. Step four is scaling up the database server, which is simple but has limits. Step five, only if really needed, is partitioning data, for example archiving old data, or sharding by a key like study or tenant, which adds a lot of complexity.
I'd also split data by service, so each service owns its own database and they scale independently. And I'd load test before going live, to know the limits before users find them.
I choose between these based on what each interaction needs: an immediate answer, a task to be done, or an event that others care about.

Synchronous APIs are for when the user or caller needs an answer right now. For example, viewing a study, or randomising a patient, where the site staff wait for the result. They're simple, but they couple services together in time, so I keep synchronous chains short and use timeouts and circuit breakers.

Caching, with Redis, is for data that's read often and changes rarely, like reference data, countries, depots, study configuration and permissions. Also for very fast lookups, like a token denylist. It cuts latency and database load, with expiry and clear invalidation.

RabbitMQ is for tasks and commands, work that one consumer should do once, like sending an email, processing a vendor file, or generating a report. It offers flexible routing, acknowledgements for each message, retries and dead-letter queues.

Kafka is for event streams: high-volume facts that several services consume independently, and might need to replay, like shipment status updates or audit events. It keeps events in an ordered log, so new consumers can read history.
In our platform, we use all four in exactly those ways. And whichever messaging tool, I make sure publishing is reliable and consumers are idempotent.
I handle failures by assuming they will happen, and designing so the system degrades gracefully and recovers on its own, instead of failing completely.

For calls between services: every call has a timeout, so nothing waits forever. Transient errors are retried with exponential backoff and jitter, but only for idempotent operations. A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing, giving it time to recover, and a fallback, like cached data or a friendly message, keeps the user experience reasonable. In .NET, I use Polly, or the standard resilience handler, for this.

For messaging: consumers acknowledge only after processing, so messages aren't lost when a consumer crashes. Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue. Consumers are idempotent, and publishers use confirms and the outbox pattern, so events aren't lost on the way.
For infrastructure: multiple instances across availability zones, health checks so the load balancer removes unhealthy instances, and database failover with backups.
For deployments: rolling or blue-green releases, quick rollback, and backward-compatible database changes.
And finally, monitoring and alerts, so we know before users tell us, plus a blameless review after incidents.
I learned a lot from a real incident: about 1,200 RabbitMQ updates were lost silently because publishing had no confirms. We added publisher confirms, and there's been no silent loss since.
For monitoring, I use the three pillars of observability, plus alerts that matter.

Logs are structured, with Serilog, and every log line carries a correlation id, so one request can be followed across all services. Metrics cover the basics for every service: request rate, error rate and latency, especially p95, plus resource usage, queue depth and consumer lag. Traces, using OpenTelemetry, show where time goes in a request across services and databases. We use CloudWatch and Grafana for dashboards, and alerts on symptoms users feel, like rising errors or slow responses, with runbooks so whoever is on call knows what to do. Health checks feed the load balancer and the orchestrator.

For security, I use defence in depth. Single sign-on with OpenID Connect for users, and validated JWTs on every API, with authorisation policies including ownership checks. Services in private subnets, with security groups allowing only needed traffic, and TLS everywhere. Least-privilege IAM roles, secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, and encryption at rest. In the pipeline, static analysis with SonarQube, dependency and image scanning, and approvals for controlled environments. And full audit trails, which are essential under GxP.
The correlation id middleware I added in 2024 across 4 services was a big win: triage time went from about an hour to a few minutes.

The CSV import lets users upload site and study data in bulk, which used to take 2 to 3 days of manual entry. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. I processed the validation synchronously, within the request, and that was a deliberate decision based on the size of the work.

Files are limited to 5 MB, about 10,000 rows. I read the file as a stream, so it's never fully loaded into memory, and validation finishes in a few seconds. So users upload the file and immediately see a preview: how many rows are valid, and a clear row-by-row list of errors. Then they confirm, and the valid data is saved in one transaction. That immediate feedback was a big part of why users liked it. A background job would have added complexity, like job tables, polling and notifications, without a real benefit at this size.

Synchronous didn't mean blocking, though. All the file reading and database work is asynchronous, using async and await, so no server threads are blocked while waiting for I/O, and the server can handle other requests.
I also limited it to 2 imports per user at a time, to protect the server.

If the files grew much larger, I'd change the design: upload directly to S3 with a pre-signed URL, process the file in a background worker, return 202 Accepted with a status endpoint, and show progress in the UI.
The result was that processing that used to take 2 to 3 days now takes under an hour, including review.
Uploaded files are untrusted input, so I secured the CSV import at every step: who can upload, what can be uploaded, how it's handled, and how it's recorded.

First, authorisation. Only signed-in users with the right role for that specific study can upload data to it. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. That's checked on the server, not just by hiding the button. Second, validation of the file itself. There's a size limit of 5 MB, checked by the server before reading everything. I check the extension, but I don't trust it; I also check that the content really is text in the expected CSV format, with the expected headers. Third, safe handling. The file is processed as a stream, in memory or temporary storage. It's never executed, never saved in a public location, and never served back to anyone as it is. Values are validated, and saved using parameterised queries, so there's no injection risk. Fourth, safe output. When users download the error report, I protect against CSV injection, where a cell starting with an equals sign, plus, minus or at sign could run as a formula in Excel. I prefix those values so they're treated as text. And fifth, auditing. Every upload is recorded, with who uploaded which file, when, for which study, and the result.
These controls passed our security review, and they're especially important in a GxP system, where data integrity has to be proven.
Even with files of about 10,000 rows, performance mattered, because users wait for the preview. I optimised in a few ways.
First, streaming. I read the file with CsvHelper as a stream, row by row, instead of loading the whole file into memory. That keeps memory low and starts work immediately.

Second, validation in stages, failing fast. First the headers: if the columns are wrong, we stop straight away with one clear message, instead of producing 10,000 errors. Then each row's format, like required fields, types and dates. Then the business rules.

Third, no database call per row. That was the biggest win. The rules need to check things like whether a site already exists, or whether a country or depot is valid. Doing a query for every row would mean thousands of round trips. Instead, I load the reference data once, at the start, into dictionaries and hash sets, so each check is an in-memory lookup. Duplicates within the file are found with a hash set as well.
Fourth, efficient saving. Valid rows are inserted in batches, inside one transaction, rather than one insert per row, with EF Core change tracking kept minimal.
The result was that a full 5 MB file validates in a few seconds, and the whole process, which used to take 2 to 3 days manually, now takes under an hour.
I tested the CSV import at several levels, because it touches data that matters, in a regulated system.

First, unit tests for every validation rule, both passing and failing: missing required fields, wrong data types, invalid dates, values that are too long, duplicates within the file, duplicates against existing data in the database, and invalid references, like an unknown country or depot. Each rule had its own clear test, so a failure pointed straight at the problem. I also tested the error report format, including the protection against CSV injection.

Second, integration tests against a real SQL Server database. They imported a valid file and checked the data was saved correctly. And importantly, they forced a failure in the middle and checked that everything was rolled back, so a study is never left half set up. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. They also checked the concurrency rule, where only one import per study can run at once.
Third, end-to-end tests with Playwright: uploading a file, seeing the preview, downloading the error report, and confirming the import, from the user's point of view.
Fourth, edge cases: an empty file, a file with only headers, a file at the maximum size, different encodings and line endings, and a file with the wrong headers.
Finally, the feature went through FV with scripted test cases and evidence, then UAT, where users tested it with real-looking files. It's been running across 300+ sites without data issues.

Concurrent imports could cause real problems: two people importing data into the same study at the same time could create duplicates or inconsistent data. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. So I added a few protections.

First, only one import per study can run at a time. I enforced this with a lock row in the database, which is checked and taken inside the same transaction as the import. If a second user tries to import into the same study while one is running, they get a clear message saying an import is already in progress, and who started it, instead of a confusing error. Because the lock is in the database, it works correctly even with several instances of the API running on ECS, where an in-memory lock wouldn't help. The lock is released when the transaction ends, so a crash can't leave it stuck.

Second, duplicate files. I store a hash of each imported file's content, so if the same file is uploaded again, maybe by mistake, by another user, it's detected and the user is warned before anything is imported.
Third, a limit of 2 imports per user at a time, which protects the server from one user starting many large imports at once.
And finally, the database itself has unique constraints on the key fields, as a last line of defence, so even if something slipped through, duplicates couldn't be saved.
Together, these made concurrent use safe across 300+ sites.
If the import fails halfway through, nothing is saved. The import is all or nothing.

All the rows are written inside a single database transaction. If anything fails during saving, like a database error, a timeout, a constraint violation or the application crashing, the transaction is rolled back, and the database is exactly as it was before. So a study is never left half set up, with some sites created and others missing, which in a clinical trial system could cause real problems. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles.

Validation happens before saving, so most problems are found in the preview, and the user fixes the file first. A failure during saving is rare, but it's handled clearly. The user sees a clear message that nothing was imported and they can safely try again. The study lock is released automatically when the transaction ends, so they're not blocked. And the failed attempt is recorded in the audit log, with the user, the file, the time and the error, which matters in our GxP environment.
Because nothing was saved, retrying is simple and safe. The file hash check also recognises it's the same file, but since the previous attempt didn't complete, it's allowed.

I tested this specifically: an integration test forces a failure in the middle of saving, and checks that no rows exist afterwards. That gave us, and the validation team, confidence that the import is safe.
For millions of records, the current design, synchronous validation within the request and one transaction, wouldn't work, so I'd redesign it as a background, staged process.

First, the upload. The client uploads the file directly to S3, using a pre-signed URL, so the API never handles the large file. The API creates an import job record, with an id and status, and returns 202 Accepted, with a link to check the status.

Second, background processing. An S3 event, or a message on a queue, starts a worker, for example an ECS task. It streams the file in chunks and loads the raw rows into a staging table using SqlBulkCopy, which is extremely fast for bulk inserts.

Third, set-based validation. Instead of checking row by row in code, I'd validate with SQL across the whole staging table: joins to find invalid references, grouping to find duplicates, and so on. Errors are written to an error table, and exported as an error file.
Fourth, merging. Valid rows are merged into the live tables in controlled batches, to avoid long locks, and the import can resume from the last completed batch if it fails.
Fifth, the user sees progress in the UI, and gets a notification when it's done.
The file hash and job id keep it idempotent, so a retry never imports twice. It's the same principles as the current design, just built for scale.

The study transfer safety guard stops study data from being transferred between environments when it isn't safe, for example into a live production study that already has randomised patients. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles. Because a mistake there could affect a real trial, I tested it very thoroughly.

The guard runs five checks before a transfer is allowed, such as: is the target study live with randomised patients, is there an approved change request, are the source and target environments a permitted combination, and does the user have the right role.

First, unit tests for each of the five checks, with both passing and failing cases, plus combinations, so each rule is proven on its own. For example, a live study with randomised patients must be blocked, and a missing change request must be blocked, with the right reason.

Second, integration tests against a real database, covering the transaction and the lock. That included two transfers started at the same time, to prove that only one can proceed, and that no partial data is left if something fails.
Third, audit tests, confirming that every attempt, allowed or blocked, writes an audit record with the right details, even when the transfer itself is rejected.
Fourth, formal validation. The FV team's scripts cover each blocking scenario, with recorded evidence, and UAT users confirmed the messages made sense.
The guard was released in 2025, and it has blocked unsafe transfers without stopping legitimate ones.

For the study transfer safety guard, auditing was just as important as blocking, because in a GxP system we must be able to show who tried to do what, and why it was or wasn't allowed. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our IRT system, with its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and user roles.

Every transfer attempt writes an audit record, whether it was allowed or blocked. The record contains the user, the time, the source and target study, the source and target environment, the change request reference if one was given, the result, and, for a blocked attempt, which check failed and the reason, in plain language.

One important design detail: the audit record is written separately from the transfer's own transaction. If the transfer is blocked, or fails and rolls back, the audit record is still saved. Otherwise, the most important records, the blocked attempts, would disappear with the rollback.
The audit records can't be edited or deleted by users, in line with our audit trail requirements.

Validators and support staff can report on them, for example all blocked attempts in the last month, or all attempts for a particular study. That's useful in audits, and also for spotting patterns, like a team repeatedly trying a transfer without a change request, which tells us they need guidance or a process change.

I tested this specifically, confirming that a blocked attempt always produces a complete audit record. Since release in 2025, the audit has given clear answers whenever anyone asked what happened with a transfer.
Release integration means bringing together all the changes from every team for one release, and turning them into one consistent, tested set of artifacts that can be installed and validated.

In practice, it involves several things. Collecting what's in the release: the application changes, API changes, database scripts and UI changes from each team, and confirming they're complete and approved. Merging everything into the release branch and resolving conflicts, especially in shared areas like database scripts. Making sure the changes work together, through builds and integration tests on the combined code. Tagging one release version, so everyone refers to the same thing, and producing the artifacts: the builds, the database scripts and the release notes. Then planning the deployment order, like database first, then APIs, then services, then the UI. And coordinating the installation and validation through FV, TechOps and UAT.

I'm the release integrator for our team, which means I coordinate with about 5 teams for each release. I run the status checks in the days before a release, chase anything incomplete, and make the call, with the leads, to move an unfinished feature to the next release rather than risk the whole release.
That experience is also what led me to build the CIRT MCP server, which automated the deployment part, cutting it from 6 hours and 6 people to 2 hours and 1 person.
We validate a release in layers, and promote to production only the exact artifacts that passed every layer.

Validation starts with automated tests in the pipeline: unit and integration tests, and the SonarQube quality gate. After each installation into a controlled environment, we run smoke tests of key flows, like logging in, randomising a patient in a test study, and viewing the shipment list, and we verify that every node is running the expected version and is healthy. Then the FV team executes the formal validation scripts against the requirements, recording evidence. TechOps verifies the installation in their environment. And in UAT, business users test the release with realistic scenarios and sign off.

To promote to production, we take the exact same tagged artifacts that passed UAT, never a rebuild, so what was validated is exactly what's released. The release is linked to an approved change request. The production stage in Azure DevOps requires approval from named approvers. Then it's deployed through the controlled pipeline, following the documented plan, with a rollback plan ready.
After deployment, we verify again: versions on every node, health endpoints, smoke tests, and logs and dashboards for any new errors. Then the release is signed off in the release record.
My CIRT MCP server automates the deployment and verification steps, but all the approvals and sign-offs stay with people.
Coordinating a release across the application, APIs, database and UI is mainly about compatibility and order, plus clear communication.
First, one release version and one checklist. Everything that's in the release has the same version tag, and a shared checklist lists every component, its owner, its status, and the deployment steps.

Second, the deployment order. Database scripts go first, and they must be backward compatible, meaning they only add things, like new columns or tables, so the current version of the application still works with the new schema. Then the APIs, which must also stay compatible with older clients, for example by adding new fields instead of changing existing ones. Then the application services that use those APIs. And finally, the UI, which depends on everything else. Removing old columns or endpoints happens in a later release, once nothing uses them. That's called expand and contract.
Third, feature flags. If a feature isn't fully ready across all layers, its code can still be released, but switched off, so it doesn't block the release or force a rushed finish.
Fourth, communication. As release integrator, I do a short daily status check with each team in the days before the release, and flag risks early, like a feature that should move to the next release.
This order also makes rollback safer, because each layer stays compatible with the one before it.
We use Python and Shell for deployment automation because they fit the work our environment needs.

Our environment nodes run Linux-based install steps: stopping and starting services, copying files, setting permissions, and checking disk space and ports. Shell is the natural tool for that. It's available on every machine, and it's the simplest way to run system commands.

But Shell gets hard to maintain when there's real logic. So Python handles the logic: reading release manifests, comparing installed versions with the expected ones, parsing configuration, calling APIs, and producing clear reports. Python is readable, well tested, and has good libraries for files, JSON, YAML and HTTP.

Ansible ties it together. It runs the same steps on all the nodes, in the right order, and stops when something fails. Ansible playbooks are mostly idempotent, meaning running them again is safe, which is important when a step fails on one node and we need to rerun it.

Before this automation, many of these steps were done by hand, on each node, following documents, which was slow and error-prone, with small differences between nodes. Now installs are repeatable and identical on every node, and every step is logged.
That automation is also the foundation the CIRT MCP server builds on. The MCP tools trigger and monitor these proven scripts through Azure DevOps, rather than replacing them.

Each environment of our core CIRT application has 4 to 6 server nodes, still on-premise for the validated environments, and the most important thing is that they all end up running exactly the same release, because a mismatch can cause subtle, serious problems.

For the deployment itself, an Azure DevOps release stage runs Ansible playbooks, which call our Python and Shell install scripts on each node. The steps run in a defined order, for example stopping services, installing the new version, running configuration, and starting services. If a step fails on any node, the playbook stops, so we don't end up with a half-updated environment without knowing. Steps are idempotent, so after fixing the cause, we can safely rerun just the failed node.
Before deploying, pre-checks verify each node: disk space, service accounts and ports. We added the disk check after a node once failed because its disk was 98 percent full.

To prove every node has the same version, each node reports its installed version in two ways: a version file written by the installer, and a version and health endpoint exposed by the running services. A verification step compares every node's version with the release tag. Any mismatch fails the verification, and the deployment isn't signed off.

My CIRT MCP server automates all of this: it starts the deployment, shows a per-node status table, retries a single node when needed, and runs the version check across every node. That's how one person can now do what took 6.
I verify a deployment in four steps, from the most basic check to the business level, and only then sign it off.

First, versions. I check that every node in the environment is running the expected release version, using each node's version file and version endpoint, and comparing them with the release tag. A single node on the wrong version fails the verification.

Second, health. Every service's health endpoint must be green, which confirms the service is running and can reach its critical dependencies, like the database and message broker. I also check that the load balancer sees all targets as healthy, and that no containers or services are restarting.
Third, smoke tests of key business flows, like logging in, randomising a patient in a test study, viewing the shipment list, and checking that messages are flowing through the queues.
Fourth, monitoring. I watch the logs and dashboards for a while after the deployment, looking for new errors, rising latency, or growing queues, and compare them with the period before the release.
If everything passes, I sign off in the release record, which is part of our audit trail. If not, we investigate, retry a node, or roll back to the previous release.
The CIRT MCP server automates most of this. It runs the version check across every node and summarises the health and status, so verification takes minutes instead of a long manual checklist.

Agile is an approach to software development that delivers working software in small increments, gets feedback often, and adapts to change, instead of planning everything up front and delivering once at the end. Scrum and Kanban are two common ways to work in an Agile way.

Scrum works in fixed-length iterations called sprints, usually two weeks. It has defined roles: a product owner, who owns and prioritises the backlog, a scrum master, who helps the team follow the process and removes blockers, and the developers. It has regular events: sprint planning, a short daily stand-up, a sprint review to show the work to stakeholders, and a retrospective to improve how we work. The team commits to a sprint goal, and changes are usually saved for the next sprint.

Kanban is a continuous flow. There are no sprints. Work items move across a board with columns, like to do, in progress, review and done, and the key rule is limiting work in progress, so the team finishes things before starting new ones. It's measured by flow, like cycle time. It suits work that arrives unpredictably, like support, operations or maintenance.
Our team uses Scrum with two-week sprints. For release and support work, which is more unpredictable, Kanban-style practices, like limiting work in progress, work well alongside it.
Either way, what matters is the Agile mindset: small batches, feedback and continuous improvement.

Sprint planning happens at the start of each sprint. The product owner brings the highest-priority items from the backlog, which have already been refined, meaning they're clear, have acceptance criteria, and are estimated. The team discusses each one, asks questions, and pulls in what fits our capacity, considering holidays, release work and support. We agree a sprint goal, a short statement of what we want to achieve, and break the stories into tasks. In our GxP environment, we also make sure validation and documentation work is included in the estimates. That's something I learned after once underestimating a story because I forgot it.

The retrospective happens at the end of the sprint, after the review. It's the team's time to improve how we work, not what we build. We discuss what went well, what didn't, and what we want to change. The important part is to agree one or two concrete actions, with an owner, and actually check them in the next retrospective. Too many actions usually means nothing changes. It only works if it's a safe space where people can be honest, without blame.

One real example: in a retrospective, we agreed our pull requests were too large and slow to review. We set a guideline to keep them small, and over a few sprints, they went from 1,500 lines or more to under 400, with review time dropping from 2 to 3 days to the same day.
Requirements change, especially in long projects, so I try to handle changes in a structured way, without either refusing them or letting them silently break the sprint.

First, I understand the change and the reason behind it, by talking with the product owner and the business analyst. Sometimes the underlying need can be met in a simpler way, or the change is less urgent than it first sounds.
Second, I assess the impact: how much work it is, what it affects, like other features, data, or tests, and what risks it adds. Then I share that clearly with the product owner.

Third, we decide together. If the change is urgent and goes into the current sprint, something of similar size comes out, so the team isn't overloaded. Otherwise, it goes into the backlog to be prioritised for a future sprint.

Fourth, in our GxP environment, we update the requirements, the acceptance criteria and the traceability, so the documentation, tests and validation scripts match what we actually build. That's essential for validation.
And over the long term, I write code that's easy to change: clear boundaries between components, good automated tests, and feature flags, so changes are cheaper and safer when they come.
For example, the CSV import's validation rules changed several times during development, and because each rule was separate and tested, those changes were quick and low risk.
I see code reviews as a way to improve the code and share knowledge, not to judge the person.

When I review, I look at correctness first: does it do what the story needs, including edge cases and error handling. Then security, like input validation, authorisation and secrets. Then tests: are there meaningful tests for the change. Then readability and design: will the next person understand this, and does it fit our patterns. I keep my comments about the code, I explain why, not just what, and I mark clearly what's a must-fix and what's just a suggestion. I also point out things that are done well. Small pull requests make all of this much better, so I encourage them.

When there's a disagreement, I first make sure I understand the other person's reasoning, because often they've considered something I haven't. Then I try to base the discussion on facts: documentation, measurements, our team standards, or a quick test. If comments keep going back and forth, I suggest a short call, which is usually faster and friendlier than long threads. If we still disagree and it's a matter of preference, I'm happy to accept their approach. If it's a bigger question, we agree a team rule with the lead, so it's settled for the future.
The goal is the best result for the codebase and a good working relationship, not winning the argument.

Situation: our release deployments needed about 6 people on a call for about 6 hours. Each person handled one area, like the release, the database, the application nodes or monitoring, and most of that time was spent waiting and checking by hand.
Task: nobody had been asked to fix it, but I believed AI agents with the right tools could automate most of it safely, and I wanted to convince the team.

Action: instead of just proposing an idea, I built a small proof first. I spent about a week reading the MCP specification and the Azure DevOps APIs, then built a prototype with three read-only tools in two days, so it couldn't change anything. I demoed it to my lead and the release manager in a 30-minute session, using real release data. They raised concerns about safety, like whether the AI could deploy to the wrong environment or bypass approvals. I addressed each one in the design: each person uses their own token, write actions need confirmation, and Azure DevOps approvals stay exactly as they are. Then I built it out to about 77 tools over about two months, trained the team, and measured the results on 8 vs 8 comparable deployments.

Result: the team adopted the CIRT MCP server. Deployments went from 6 hours to about 2, and from 6 people to 1, without weakening our approvals. What I learned is that a working prototype and taking concerns seriously are far more persuasive than slides.
Under production pressure, my priority is to stay calm and structured, because panicking leads to risky decisions.

First, reduce the impact. Before searching for the root cause, I look for the fastest safe way to restore service, like rolling back a recent release, switching off a feature flag, restarting a stuck component, or scaling up. The real fix can come later.

Second, communicate. I tell the right people what's happening, who's affected, and when the next update will come, and then I give updates regularly, even if there's no news. That stops people interrupting the team for status.
Third, organise. If several people are helping, I make sure the work is clearly split, so two people aren't doing the same thing, and one person coordinates.
Fourth, avoid risky changes. Under pressure, it's tempting to try quick, untested fixes in production. I prefer small, reversible steps, and a second pair of eyes before any change.
Fifth, use what's prepared: runbooks, checklists and dashboards. They're what keep things calm in the moment.
And afterwards, a blameless review, and actions to prevent it from happening again.

A real example: a release caused about 8 percent 5xx errors in UAT. We rolled back within 15 minutes, restoring service. Then, calmly, we found the cause, a missing configuration value, fixed it, and added a startup check so it couldn't happen silently again.
When I explain technical problems to non-technical stakeholders, I focus on what they need to know and decide, not on the technical details.

First, I start with the impact, in business terms: who is affected, what they can or can't do, and how serious it is. For example, "Sites can't see shipment updates since 9 a.m., but no data has been lost."
Second, what we're doing about it, and when they'll hear from me next, so they're not left wondering.

Third, plain language. I avoid jargon and acronyms, and use simple comparisons when they help. For example, explaining a message queue as a post office that holds letters until the recipient is ready.
Fourth, if they need to make a decision, I give two or three clear options, with the trade-offs for each, like time, cost and risk, and my recommendation, so they can decide quickly.
Fifth, I'm honest about uncertainty. If I don't know yet, I say so, and when I'll know more, rather than guessing.
And afterwards, a short written summary of what happened, why, and what we've done to prevent it.

A real example: when about 1,200 shipment updates were lost in mid-2024, I explained to the business that some status updates hadn't reached the system, that we'd recover them that evening by replaying the vendor files, and that we were adding a safeguard so it couldn't happen silently again. That clear message kept everyone calm and confident.
Spring Boot is a framework built on top of the Spring framework, for building Java applications and services quickly, with very little setup. It's the Java world's equivalent of ASP.NET Core.

The Spring framework itself provides the core features, like dependency injection, web support with Spring MVC, data access and security. But on its own, it needed a lot of configuration. Spring Boot removes most of that with a few key ideas.

First, auto-configuration. Spring Boot looks at the libraries on the classpath and configures sensible defaults automatically. For example, if a database driver and Spring Data JPA are present, it sets up a data source and repositories. You only configure what's different.
Second, starters. These are dependency bundles, like spring-boot-starter-web, which bring in everything needed for a feature with compatible versions.
Third, an embedded web server, like Tomcat, so the application runs as a single executable JAR, with java -jar, which is ideal for containers.
Fourth, production-ready features with Actuator: health checks, metrics and other operational endpoints.
And externalised configuration, with application.yml files, environment variables and profiles for each environment.

My main platform is .NET, but the concepts map almost one to one: auto-configuration and starters are like ASP.NET Core's defaults and NuGet packages, the embedded server is like Kestrel, and Actuator is like health checks and metrics. So I can work comfortably in a Spring Boot codebase.
Dependency injection in Spring works the same way as in .NET. Instead of a class creating its own dependencies, they're provided from outside, which makes the code loosely coupled and easy to test.

Spring's IoC container, Inversion of Control, is called the ApplicationContext. It creates and manages objects called beans, and wires their dependencies together. Classes become beans in two main ways: through component scanning, where classes marked with annotations like Component, Service, Repository or Controller are discovered automatically, or through Bean methods in a Configuration class, which is useful for third-party classes. Beans have scopes: singleton by default, which means one instance for the whole application, prototype, which means a new instance each time, and web scopes like request.

Autowired is the annotation that tells Spring where to inject a dependency. It can be used on constructors, setters or fields. The recommended approach is constructor injection, with final fields, because the dependencies are explicit, required, and easy to provide in tests. And if a class has only one constructor, Autowired isn't even needed; Spring uses it automatically. Field injection, with Autowired on a private field, is discouraged, because it hides dependencies and makes testing harder.
When there are several implementations of an interface, Qualifier or Primary chooses one.
Coming from .NET, the ApplicationContext is like the service provider, and constructor injection works exactly as I use it every day.

Component, Service and Repository are Spring annotations that all register a class as a Spring bean, through component scanning. Technically, Service and Repository are specialisations of Component. The difference is mostly about meaning, with one important extra feature for Repository.
Component is the generic annotation. It means "this class is a Spring-managed component". I use it for classes that don't fit a specific layer, like a helper or a mapper.

Service marks a class in the business logic layer, like a ShipmentService that applies business rules. It doesn't add special behaviour today, but it makes the code's structure clear, and tools or aspects can target it, for example applying transactions or logging to all services.

Repository marks a data access class. It has one real extra feature: exception translation. Spring automatically converts database-specific exceptions, like those from JDBC or Hibernate, into Spring's own consistent DataAccessException hierarchy, so the rest of the application doesn't depend on a particular database technology. With Spring Data JPA, you often just declare a repository interface, and Spring creates the implementation.
There's also Controller and RestController, for the web layer.

So the reason to use the specific ones is clarity and layering: anyone reading the code knows each class's role straight away. It's similar to how I organise .NET code into controllers, services and repositories.

To build a REST controller in Spring Boot, I create a class with the RestController annotation. That combines Controller with ResponseBody, so the return values are written straight into the response as JSON, using Jackson. A RequestMapping annotation on the class sets the base path, like api slash shipments.

Each endpoint is a method with an annotation for the HTTP method and path: GetMapping, PostMapping, PutMapping, PatchMapping or DeleteMapping. Parameters are bound from the request with annotations: PathVariable for parts of the URL, like the shipment id, RequestParam for query string values, like page and size, RequestBody for the JSON body, and RequestHeader for headers. Adding Valid to the request body triggers Bean Validation, with annotations like NotNull and Size on the request class, and invalid input returns a 400 error.

The controller stays thin. The service is injected through the constructor, and each method just calls the service. For the response, I return ResponseEntity to control the status code and headers, for example 201 Created with a Location header for a new shipment, or 404 when it doesn't exist. Request and response DTOs, often Java records, keep the API separate from the database entities.
Errors are handled centrally with a RestControllerAdvice class.
It's the same structure as an ASP.NET Core controller, with attributes like HttpGet, FromRoute and FromBody, and returning results like Ok or CreatedAtAction.
Spring Boot reads configuration from several sources, in a defined order of priority, so the same application can run in every environment without code changes.

The main source is application.properties or application.yml in the project. Values can be overridden by environment variables, command-line arguments, and external configuration services, with higher-priority sources winning. Environment variables are mapped automatically, for example SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL overrides spring.datasource.url, which is ideal for containers.

In code, configuration can be read with the Value annotation for single values, but the better approach is a ConfigurationProperties class: a typed class, or record, bound to a section of the configuration, with validation. That's very similar to the options pattern in .NET.

Profiles let you have different configuration for different environments. You create files like application-dev.yml, application-uat.yml and application-prod.yml, and activate a profile with the spring.profiles.active setting, usually from an environment variable. Spring loads the common file first, then the profile's file on top. Profiles can also turn beans on or off, using the Profile annotation, for example a fake email sender in dev.
Secrets don't go in these files. They come from environment variables or a secrets manager, like AWS Secrets Manager, through Spring Cloud integrations.
It's the same idea as ASP.NET Core's appsettings files with environment-specific overrides, like appsettings.Production.json, plus environment variables.
JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA are three layers that together handle database access in Java.

JPA, now called Jakarta Persistence, is the standard specification. It defines how Java classes are mapped to database tables, using annotations like Entity, Id, Column, and relationships like OneToMany, plus the EntityManager API and the JPQL query language. It's just a specification, not an implementation.
Hibernate is the most popular implementation of JPA. It does the actual work: generating SQL, tracking changes to entities, caching, and loading related data, lazily or eagerly.

Spring Data JPA sits on top. You declare a repository interface, like ShipmentRepository extends JpaRepository, and Spring creates the implementation at runtime, with methods for saving, finding and deleting. You can even declare methods like findByStatusAndSiteId, and Spring generates the query from the method name. For complex queries, you use the Query annotation with JPQL or native SQL.

Compared with EF Core, the concepts are very similar: entities, a unit of work, change tracking, lazy loading, and the N plus one problem to watch out for. The main differences are: EF Core uses LINQ, which is type-checked and composable in C#, while JPA uses JPQL strings or the more verbose Criteria API. EF Core has migrations built in, while Java projects usually use Flyway or Liquibase. And EF Core's DbContext plays the role of the EntityManager.
My experience is mainly EF Core, and those concepts transfer directly.
For exception handling in Spring Boot, I use a central handler, so every error returns a consistent response, and controllers stay clean.

I create a class annotated with RestControllerAdvice, containing methods annotated with ExceptionHandler for specific exception types. For example, a ShipmentNotFoundException returns 404, a validation exception, like MethodArgumentNotValidException, returns 400 with the field errors, and a general handler for unexpected exceptions logs the full error and returns 500 without exposing internal details. Spring supports the standard ProblemDetail format, RFC 9457, the same format ASP.NET Core uses, so responses are consistent across services. That's very similar to exception-handling middleware with problem details in .NET.

For security, I use Spring Security. Every request passes through a security filter chain, which is configured as a SecurityFilterChain bean. For an API, I configure it as an OAuth2 resource server: it validates JWT access tokens from our identity provider, checking the signature, issuer, audience and expiry, and the API stays stateless. Then I set authorisation rules for URL patterns, like requiring a role for admin endpoints, and use method security, with the PreAuthorize annotation, for fine-grained checks on service methods. CORS and security headers are configured there too.
This maps directly to ASP.NET Core's JWT bearer authentication and authorisation policies, which I use every day.

Java and C# are very similar languages. Both are statically typed, object-oriented, run on a managed runtime with garbage collection, the JVM and the .NET runtime, and have large ecosystems. Someone who knows one well can learn the other quickly.

The main differences are these. C# often added language features earlier: properties, LINQ, async and await, which arrived in 2012, records, pattern matching, nullable reference types, and extension methods. Java has caught up in many areas, with lambdas, streams, records and pattern matching, but often later. Generics work differently: C# keeps generic type information at runtime, called reified generics, and supports generics over value types, like List of int, without boxing. Java uses type erasure, so generic types disappear at runtime. C# also has custom value types, structs, and features like Span for high-performance code. For concurrency, C# uses async and await, while Java introduced virtual threads in Java 21, which make blocking code scale well, with a different approach. For ecosystems, Java has many JVM vendors and other JVM languages, like Kotlin, and a huge open-source ecosystem, while .NET is led by Microsoft, with a very consistent set of official libraries and tooling.
In practice, both are excellent for backend systems. My strength is C# and .NET, and the concepts I use daily transfer directly to Java.
Spring Boot and .NET are both excellent, mature platforms for backend services, so I'd choose based on the organisation and the team, not on personal preference.

I'd choose Spring Boot when the organisation's platform is already Java: the existing services, shared libraries, deployment tooling, monitoring and, most importantly, the people's skills. Then adding .NET would mean extra maintenance, hiring and support costs. Spring Boot also has a huge ecosystem, with Spring Cloud for distributed systems, and very wide community support.

I'd choose .NET when the team and codebase are already .NET, or for a new team that values productivity and performance. ASP.NET Core is one of the fastest mainstream web frameworks. C# has features like LINQ, async and await, and records, which make code concise. EF Core is very productive. The platform is very consistent, with dependency injection, configuration, logging and health checks built in, and the tooling, like Visual Studio and Rider, is excellent. It's cross-platform and runs well in containers.
Technically, they're very close. Both run well on AWS, in containers, with the same architecture patterns.

So my answer is that team skills and existing systems should decide. In our case, .NET was the right choice, because our team and our core IRT services are .NET. If I joined a Java team, I'd happily work in Spring Boot, because the concepts are the same.
This role matches both what I do best and what I want to grow in.

What I do best is building backend services in .NET, running them on AWS, and making distributed, event-driven systems reliable. In my current role, I build and support .NET services on ECS, work with Kafka and RabbitMQ, own our SFTP vendor integrations, and act as release integrator across about 5 teams. Those are exactly the skills this role needs, so I can contribute quickly.

What I want to grow in is owning design and delivery end to end, and bringing better engineering practices to a team. This role has that ownership. I've already shown I enjoy it: I built the CIRT MCP server on my own initiative, which cut our deployments from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1, and I led changes like smaller pull requests that cut review time from 2 to 3 days to the same day.
I'm also very interested in using AI tools safely in engineering, which I've been doing with MCP and agent tooling, and I can see that fits well with where your team is heading.
And from what I've learned about your team and products, I like that the work has real users and real scale, and that the team values quality. That's the kind of environment where I do my best work.
So overall, it's a role where I can add value from the start, and keep growing toward technical leadership.

In the short term, over the next two to three years, I want to grow into a strong senior engineer who owns services end to end, from design and development, to deployment, monitoring and support in production. I also want to raise the engineering standards of the team around me, through good code reviews, testing, automation and mentoring. I've already started on that: I mentored two graduates in 2024, and I've introduced improvements like smaller pull requests and the CIRT MCP server for deployments.

In the longer term, I'd like to become a technical lead or architect for distributed systems. That means designing systems that are reliable, secure and scalable, making good technical decisions with the team, and helping other engineers grow. But I want to stay hands-on, because I believe good technical leaders still understand the code and build things themselves.

I'm also very interested in AI-assisted engineering, and I'd like to be someone who helps teams adopt AI tools safely and effectively, with the right controls, as I did with our deployment automation, which went from 6 hours to 2 without weakening our approval process.
To get there, I keep learning: system design, cloud architecture, and new .NET versions. For example, I led the upgrade of our services to .NET 10 in early 2026.
This role fits that path well, because it combines strong backend ownership with room to lead.

Situation: in 2023, I worked with a project lead who asked for very frequent status updates, sometimes several times a day, and changed priorities in the middle of sprints. The team was constantly interrupted, and people were getting frustrated.
Task: I didn't want to just complain, or ignore his requests. I wanted to understand what he needed, and find a way that worked for both him and the team.

Action: I asked him for a short one-to-one conversation, and asked what the updates were for. It turned out he had to report to the client regularly, and he felt he didn't have enough visibility, so he kept asking. Once I understood that, I offered a solution. I'd send him a short written update every morning, covering progress, risks and blockers, and we'd keep a shared board that he could check at any time. For priority changes, I suggested that new requests go through the product owner, who could decide what came out of the sprint, so the team wasn't pulled in different directions. I kept the tone positive and focused on helping him do his job.
Result: he agreed. The interruptions dropped significantly, the team could focus, and our relationship improved. He even said the morning updates made his client reporting easier.
What I learned is that difficult behaviour often comes from an unmet need. If you understand that need, you can usually find a solution that works for everyone.
Situation: in 2023, I was asked to estimate a new shipment reporting API. I estimated it at one sprint, based on the development work.
Task: I was responsible for delivering it within that sprint.

Action: about halfway through, I realised my estimate was wrong. I had focused on the code, and missed the validation documentation and FV preparation that every change needs in our GxP environment. That work was significant. Instead of hoping to catch up, or staying quiet until the last day, I told the product owner mid-sprint, as soon as I saw the problem. I explained what I'd missed, and proposed a way forward. We split the work, so the main reporting endpoint, which the client needed first, was completed and validated on time, and the export feature moved to the next sprint.
Result: the client's plan wasn't affected, because the most important part arrived on time. But it was still my mistake, and I took responsibility for it.

What I learned changed how I work. Now, I always include validation, documentation and testing effort in my estimates, not just the coding, and I check estimates against similar past work. I also raise risks early, because a problem raised in the middle of a sprint has options, while a problem raised on the last day only has excuses.
In general, I deal with failure by owning it quickly, fixing the impact, and changing something so it doesn't happen again.

Situation: in 2023, I estimated a new shipment reporting API at one sprint. Partway through, I realised it would take two, because I had missed the GxP validation documentation and FV preparation that the change needed. In our regulated environment, that work is a significant part of any delivery.
Task: I was responsible for the delivery, and the client was expecting it at the end of the sprint, so I needed to deal with the risk honestly and limit the impact.

Action: I raised it mid-sprint, as soon as I saw it, not on the last day. I went to the product owner with the facts: what I had missed, how much extra work it was, and an option to reduce the impact. Together we split the scope. The main reporting endpoint, which the client needed most, would be finished and validated in the current sprint. The export feature, which was less urgent, would follow in the next sprint. I focused on delivering the main part properly, including all the documentation.
Result: the main endpoint went out on time, the export came the next sprint, and the client's plan wasn't affected. The product owner appreciated the early warning, because it gave us options.

What I learned is to include validation and documentation effort in every estimate, and to communicate risks as early as possible. Since then, my estimates have been much more accurate, and I haven't had a surprise like that again.

Situation: during the quarterly release in 2024, just two days before the FV installation, we hit two problems at once. There was a merge conflict in a shared database script between two teams' changes, and an integration test was failing on the release branch. FV had a fixed start date, and many people depended on it.
Task: as the release integrator, it was my responsibility to get the release ready on time, without compromising quality.

Action: first, I stayed calm and prioritised. The database conflict was the most critical, because everything depended on it. I got the two script owners together, and we resolved the conflict in one hour, making sure both changes were preserved and the script stayed backward compatible. In parallel, I worked with the owner of the failing test to find the cause, which was a test data issue, and get it fixed. Then I reran the full build and tests. I also checked every feature's status, and found one feature that wasn't fully complete. Rather than rushing it, I flagged it early to the leads, and we agreed to move it to the next release behind a feature flag. Finally, I ran the FV installation overnight, so it was ready in the morning.
Result: FV started on time, and production went live as planned.
What I learned is that under pressure, clear priorities, calm communication, and being willing to cut scope are better than trying to do everything at once.

Situation: our release deployments needed about 6 people on a call for about 6 hours. Each person handled one area, and most of the time was spent waiting and checking manually. Everyone found it painful, but nobody owned improving it.
Task: I decided to take ownership of fixing it, even though it wasn't assigned to me.

Action: I studied the Model Context Protocol and the Azure DevOps APIs, and built a prototype of an MCP server in my own time, starting with read-only tools, so it was safe. I demoed it to my lead, and with their support, it became part of my work. I built it out into the CIRT MCP server, with about 77 tools for builds, releases, multi-node deployments and verification. I took safety seriously: each engineer uses their own token, write actions need confirmation, and Azure DevOps approvals stay exactly as they are. I didn't stop at the code. I packaged it as a .NET global tool so installation was simple, wrote documentation, and trained the team. Setup went from about an hour to about 10 minutes.

Result: deployments went from about 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1, measured across 8 vs 8 comparable deployments. And I still own it: I maintain it, fix issues, and add tools based on the team's feedback.
For me, ownership means seeing a problem through, from idea, to adoption, to long-term support, not just writing the first version.

I think my manager would say I'm reliable and that I take ownership. When I take something on, they don't need to follow up, and things like releases and production issues are in safe hands. They'd probably also mention that I bring improvements without being asked, like building the CIRT MCP server, which cut our deployments from 6 hours to 2, and that I raise risks early instead of surprising people at the last minute.

If they mentioned something to improve, it would probably be that I sometimes take on too much myself. I've been working on that by delegating more, and by involving others earlier, which also helps them grow.

My teammates would say I'm helpful and approachable. I'm happy to explain things, whether it's a tricky bug, a design decision, or how our deployment process works, and I explain without making people feel bad for asking. I think they'd also say I give careful, constructive code reviews. I'm the person people come to for questions about deployments, our SFTP integrations, and AI tools.

The graduates I mentored in 2024 would probably say I gave them a lot of support at the start, with pairing and architecture walkthroughs, and then gave them space and trust to do things on their own.
Overall, I'd like people to see me as someone who makes the team stronger, not just someone who delivers their own work.

I like working in a collaborative team where people are honest and respectful with each other, where code reviews are about improving the work, and where each person has clear ownership. I value teams that care about quality, share knowledge, and are always looking for ways to improve how they work, through things like retrospectives that lead to real changes.

What motivates me is solving real problems that have a visible impact on people. For example, the CIRT MCP server took our deployments from 6 hours and 6 people to 2 hours and 1 person, and seeing the team's evenings freed up was very rewarding. Similarly, the CSV import turned 2 to 3 days of manual work into under an hour. I'm also motivated by learning new things, like MCP and AI tooling, and by helping others grow, like the graduates I mentored.

What frustrates me is repeated manual work that could be automated, and unclear requirements that lead to rework. But I try to turn frustration into action. When I see repetitive work, I automate it, as I did with deployments. When requirements are unclear, I ask questions early, and write down the agreed understanding, so we build the right thing the first time.
So in short, I like collaborative teams, I'm motivated by impact, and I deal with frustrations by fixing their causes.
Let me take our Shipment service as a real example, because it shows the main design choices.

Its responsibility is clear: it owns shipments of trial medication, from creation to delivery. It exposes a REST API, built with ASP.NET Core, to create a shipment, get one, and list shipments with filters and paging. It owns its own SQL Server database, which no other service reads directly, with audit tables recording every change, because we're in a GxP environment.

For communication, when a shipment changes status, the service publishes a shipment status event to Kafka. It uses the outbox pattern: the status change and the event are saved in the same database transaction, and a background publisher sends the event, so events are never lost. Other services, like supply, notifications and reporting, consume those events independently. Status updates from depot vendors arrive through our SFTP integration, and are processed by idempotent handlers, so duplicate files never cause duplicate updates.

For scalability, it's stateless, packaged as a Docker image, and runs on ECS across two availability zones behind a load balancer, with autoscaling on CPU and request count. Redis caches reference data, like depots and countries.
For resilience, calls to vendors use Polly, with timeouts, retries and circuit breakers. And for observability, it has structured logs with correlation ids, metrics and traces, plus health checks.
That combination makes it independent, scalable and reliable.
I've worked with .NET 6, 8 and 10, which are all long-term support releases, each supported for three years.

.NET 6, released in 2021, was the release that brought .NET Core and the old .NET Framework world together into one platform. It introduced minimal APIs, and the simpler hosting model, where all the startup code lives in one short Program.cs file. It also brought C# 10, with global usings and file-scoped namespaces, and hot reload.

.NET 8, released in 2023, brought large performance improvements, Native AOT for more types of apps, so they start fast with low memory, and the TimeProvider abstraction, which makes time-dependent code testable. It added keyed services in dependency injection, frozen collections, and built-in resilience with Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience. C# 12 added primary constructors for classes and collection expressions.

.NET 10, released in November 2025, brings C# 14, with features like extension members and the field keyword, plus more performance work in the runtime and JIT, built-in validation for minimal APIs, and improvements in ASP.NET Core and EF Core.

I led the upgrade of our services to .NET 10 in early 2026. We started with 3 of 6 services, over about six weeks. We saw about 10 to 15 percent better p95 latency, and at the same time, we added Trivy image scanning to the pipeline. The key to a smooth upgrade was good test coverage and upgrading service by service.
Each of our .NET services runs on Amazon ECS, and the architecture is the same for all of them, which makes them easy to operate.

Each service is built as a Docker image in our Azure DevOps pipeline, scanned, and pushed to Amazon ECR with a version tag. In ECS, each service has a task definition, which describes how to run it: the image, CPU and memory, the port, environment variables, secrets injected from AWS Secrets Manager, the logging configuration, and an IAM task role, which gives the service only the AWS permissions it needs, like reading a specific S3 bucket or secret.

The ECS service keeps the desired number of tasks running, spread across two availability zones, in private subnets, so they're not reachable from the internet. An Application Load Balancer in the public subnets receives traffic and routes it to the healthy tasks, using health check endpoints in each service. Security groups only allow traffic from the load balancer to the service, and from the service to the database. Autoscaling adjusts the number of tasks based on CPU and request count.
Logs go to CloudWatch, with alarms, and we use Grafana dashboards. The services connect to RDS SQL Server, ElastiCache Redis, and our messaging systems.
Deployments are rolling updates triggered from Azure DevOps: a new task definition revision, new tasks start and pass health checks, then old ones stop. Rollback is redeploying the previous revision.
We use both Terraform and CloudFormation because of history and ownership, not because we planned to use two tools.

Our core platform stacks were already in CloudFormation, owned by the platform team. Things like the main networking and shared infrastructure were built that way years ago. Rewriting them in Terraform would have been a big, risky project with no direct benefit, so when we needed changes there, we extended the existing CloudFormation templates, following the platform team's process.

Newer, smaller pieces and tooling used Terraform modules. For new components, the team chose Terraform, because of its reusable modules, its readable plan output before every change, and the fact that it can manage things beyond AWS, through other providers. So new service infrastructure, like queues, alarms and service-specific resources, was written in Terraform.

I can read and change both. The concepts are similar: infrastructure as code, reviewed in pull requests, previewed before applying, with change sets in CloudFormation and plan in Terraform, and applied through pipelines.

Honestly, if I were designing it from scratch, I'd standardise on one tool, to avoid duplication, two sets of skills, and confusion about where things are defined. And I'd make sure each resource is managed by only one tool, never both, because that leads to conflicts.

To be honest and precise: our production IRT services run on Amazon ECS, not Kubernetes. My Kubernetes experience is with some internal workloads, like the Node.js build-log summariser and the FastAPI vendor file validator, in a shared non-production cluster.

For those, I wrote the Kubernetes manifests myself: Deployments with the image, replicas, resource requests and limits, and environment variables; Services to give them stable internal addresses; ConfigMaps for configuration, and Secrets for sensitive values; and readiness, liveness and startup probes connected to each app's health endpoints. I deployed them through our pipeline and troubleshot them with kubectl: describe, logs and events.

One real problem taught me a lot. One of these services kept crash-looping, but its logs showed no errors. The events showed that the liveness probe was killing it, because it needed about 40 seconds to warm up, but liveness checks started after 10 seconds. I added a startup probe allowing 60 seconds, made part of the warm-up lazy, and updated our template so every new service gets a startup probe by default.

So my production container experience is mainly ECS, and my Kubernetes experience is practical but smaller scale. The core concepts, like desired state, health checks, rolling updates, configuration and secrets, are the same on both, so I'm confident working with Kubernetes in production.
We use both, because they're good at different things.

Kafka is for events that several services need to know about. Our main use case is shipment status events. When a shipment changes status, like dispatched, in transit or delivered, the Shipment service publishes an event to a Kafka topic, keyed by shipment id. Several services consume it independently, in their own consumer groups: supply, which updates site inventory, notifications, which informs site staff, and reporting. Kafka fits because the events must stay in order for each shipment, which the key guarantees, several consumers read the same events, and we can replay events, for example to rebuild a report or recover a consumer after a bug, because Kafka keeps them for the retention period.

RabbitMQ is for tasks: work that one consumer should do once. Our use cases are things like sending notifications, processing vendor status updates, and generating reports. RabbitMQ fits because of acknowledgements for each message, flexible routing to different queues, retries, and dead-letter queues for failures.

RabbitMQ is also where I learned an important lesson. In mid-2024, our publisher had no publisher confirms, and during a 40-minute problem, about 1,200 updates were lost silently. We recovered them by replaying the vendor files that evening. I root-caused it and added publisher confirms, at about 5 percent throughput cost, and there's been no silent loss in the 12 months since.
What I orchestrated was release deployments, using an AI agent and my CIRT MCP server.

The agent runs in Cursor or Claude Code, and the CIRT MCP server gives it about 77 tools for our on-premise Azure DevOps Server and our deployment process. When an engineer asks something like "deploy release 4.2 to UAT and verify it", the agent works in a loop. It queues the build and polls its status. It creates the release from the build artifacts. It starts the deployment to the chosen environment. It polls each of the 4 to 6 nodes and shows a per-node status table. If a node fails, it summarises the failing step and the key log lines, and with the user's confirmation, retries just that node. Finally, it verifies that every node is running the right version.

Humans stay in control at the important points. Every write action needs the user's confirmation, the agent uses each engineer's own permissions, and production approvals stay in Azure DevOps with named approvers, which the agent can't bypass.
The result was that deployments went from about 6 hours with 6 people to about 2 hours with 1 person.

Separately, I ran an AutoGen experiment with two agents, a coder that drafted unit tests and a reviewer that checked them against our conventions, with me approving the final output. That taught me when multi-agent setups help, and when one agent with good tools is enough.

The RAG workflow I built is an internal assistant over our release runbooks, deployment guides and past incident notes. Engineers ask questions like "what do we check if a node fails the version verification?", and get an answer grounded in our own documents, with links to the sources.

The architecture has two parts. First, ingestion. The documents are collected, cleaned, and split into chunks of a sensible size, with some overlap, so each chunk has enough context. Each chunk is turned into an embedding, a vector representing its meaning, and stored in a vector index, along with metadata like the document title, section and link.

Second, answering. When someone asks a question, the question is embedded the same way, and the most similar chunks are retrieved from the index. Those are re-ranked to put the most relevant first. Then the top chunks are sent, together with the question, to Azure OpenAI, with instructions to answer only from the provided content, to cite the source documents, and to say "I don't know" if the answer isn't there. That reduces made-up answers.

For quality, we tested it with 30 real questions from the team, checking whether the answers were correct and cited the right documents, and adjusted the chunk size and retrieval based on the results.
For safety, it only contains internal engineering documents. No patient or study data is included, and it runs on our enterprise Azure OpenAI, where data isn't used for training.
A good example is a configurable data table component that I built and that's used across many of our IRT screens.
Before it, different screens had their own tables, each built slightly differently. Sorting, paging and filtering behaved inconsistently, and every new screen meant writing the same code again.

So I built one reusable table component in React with TypeScript. It's generic over the row type, so it's fully typed: a screen passes its rows and a list of column definitions, and TypeScript checks that each column matches a real property of the row. Each column can define its header, how to display the value, and whether it's sortable or filterable. The component handles sorting, paging and filtering, either on the client, or on the server for large data, by calling back to the screen. It shows consistent loading, empty and error states. Row actions, like edit or cancel, are passed in, and they respect the user's roles, so actions a user isn't allowed to perform aren't shown. And it's accessible, with keyboard navigation and proper table semantics for screen readers.
I documented it with examples, and covered it with tests using React Testing Library.
The result is that every screen's tables now look and behave the same, new screens are much faster to build, and when we improve the component, every screen benefits.
I used FastAPI for the vendor file pre-validation service, and it was the right fit for a few reasons.

The service checks vendor files before our .NET import runs, and returns exact errors, so problems are found early and are easy to explain to vendors. The heart of that is describing each file format precisely. FastAPI is built on Pydantic, where each format is a Python model with types and validation rules, like required fields, date formats and allowed values.
