Those models are very readable, so the integration team can easily understand and update them when a vendor changes its format.

FastAPI also gave us a lot for free. When a request doesn't match a model, it automatically returns a 422 response with the exact field and reason, which was exactly the kind of error report we wanted. It automatically generates OpenAPI documentation, with an interactive docs page, which made it easy for others to try the service. It supports async, so it handles I/O efficiently, and its performance is very good for a Python framework. Dependency injection, through Depends, kept it clean and testable.
And practically, the integration team already knew Python, so they could maintain it without depending on me.
It follows our standards, like logging, health checks, Docker and the pipeline, while our core business services stay in .NET.
I used Node.js for small, I/O-heavy tools, where it was a better fit than .NET, while our core business services stay in .NET.

The main example is a build-log summariser. Build and deployment logs can be huge, and when something fails, engineers used to scroll through thousands of lines to find the problem. The summariser fetches the logs for a failed build or deployment step from Azure DevOps, parses the text to find the errors and the most relevant lines around them, and returns a short JSON summary. It's also used by our MCP tooling, so the agent gets a concise summary instead of a huge log.

Node fitted well for a few reasons. The work is mostly I/O and text processing, which Node handles very efficiently with its asynchronous model. TypeScript gave us type safety, and the TypeScript libraries for MCP and HTTP made it quick to build. And it's small and fast to start, which suits a lightweight tool.

Even though it's a different language, it follows the same standards as our .NET services: structured logging, health checks, Docker, the same Azure DevOps pipeline with tests, and the same security practices.

My general view is that every new language adds maintenance cost, so there should be a clear reason for it. Here there was, but our core business logic stays in .NET, for consistency and long-term maintainability.
Technically, GxP means the system must be able to prove that it works correctly and that its data can be trusted. That turns into concrete technical features and practices.

First, audit trails. Every change to important data records who made it, when, the old and new values, and the reason. Users can't edit or delete audit records. Second, access control and electronic signatures. Role-based access ensures people only do what they're authorised to do, and electronic signatures follow 21 CFR Part 11 rules, like re-entering credentials to sign, linking the signature to the record, and recording its meaning. Third, validated releases. Requirements are traced to their tests and results. Every release goes through formal validation, FV, and UAT, with documented evidence. Fourth, change control. Every change has an approved change request with a risk assessment. Fifth, controlled deployments. The same validated artifact is promoted through environments, production deployments need named approvers, and production access is limited and logged. Sixth, data integrity, following the ALCOA plus principles: data is attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate, plus complete, consistent, enduring and available. That means constraints, transactions, validation, idempotent processing and reconciliation. And seventh, backups with tested restores, and disaster recovery.

In my day-to-day work, this shows up everywhere: in how we design data changes, write tests, document releases, and even in how I built the CIRT MCP server, which kept every approval and logged every action.
Directly, I mentored two graduate developers who joined our team in 2024.

I started by giving them a walkthrough of our architecture: the main services, how data flows through the system, our messaging, and how releases and validation work in our GxP environment, because that context makes everything else make sense. Then I paired with them for two sprints on real stories. At first I drove and explained my thinking, and gradually they took over while I guided. They shipped their first pull requests in week two, which was a great confidence boost for them.

After that, I moved to a lighter approach: detailed, friendly code reviews, where I explained why, not just what, and pointed to good examples in our codebase, plus a weekly check-in, where they could ask anything, and we discussed what they wanted to learn next. I gradually gave them more ownership, like owning a small feature end to end. By the end of the year, they were working independently and reviewing others' code.
More broadly, I've helped 3 to 4 teammates in other ways: through code reviews, onboarding them onto the CIRT MCP server, and running sessions on using AI tools safely and effectively.
What I've learned is that good mentoring means giving a lot of support at the start, and then trust and space, so people grow their own judgement.
I want to be precise about this, because it matters for credibility.

The 100 figure refers to the IRT engineering organisation, which is about 100 people across several scrum teams, working on the same platform. That's the environment I work in, and as release integrator, I work with many of those teams.

My own scrum team is about 8 people: 5 developers, 2 QA engineers and a business analyst, with a shared scrum master. That's the team I work with every day, where I build features, review code, and mentored two graduate developers in 2024.

For each release, I coordinate with about 5 teams, collecting their changes, resolving conflicts, planning the deployment order and running status checks before the release. So my influence goes beyond my own team in that role.
Similarly, the CIRT MCP server is used beyond my own team for deployments, and that's where the result of 6 hours to 2, and 6 people to 1, comes from.

So the accurate picture is: I'm an engineer in a team of about 8, inside an engineering organisation of about 100, with a cross-team role as release integrator. I'd rather be clear about that than let the number sound like something it isn't.

Middleware is a component that sits in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline. Every HTTP request passes through a chain of middleware, and each one gets the HttpContext and a reference to the next one in the chain.

Each middleware can do three things. It can do some work before the request goes further, like reading headers. It can call next, to pass the request to the next middleware. And after next returns, it can do work on the way back, like adding a response header or logging the duration. It can also decide not to call next and end the request early, which is called short-circuiting. The pipeline is built in Program.cs with app.Use calls, and it runs in exactly the order you register them, which is why the order matters so much.
A lot of the framework is just middleware: exception handling, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and finally the endpoints.
In my project, I wrote a correlation-id middleware, so every request carries one id across our 4 services, and one log search shows the whole journey.

First, what middleware is. In ASP.NET Core, every HTTP request passes through a pipeline of components called middleware. Each middleware gets the request, can do some work, then either passes it to the next middleware by calling next, or ends the request itself, for example returning an error. On the way back, the response passes through the same middleware in reverse order, so each one can also act on the response. The order is set in Program.cs, and it matters: exception handling first, then HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, and finally the endpoints. Built-in examples are UseAuthentication and UseExceptionHandler.

Custom middleware is simply my own component in that same pipeline. I write one when I need logic that should run for every request, or a group of requests, and that doesn't belong to one controller: things like correlation ids, request timing, audit logging, or adding security headers.

The usual way is a class whose constructor takes the next RequestDelegate, with a public InvokeAsync method that receives the HttpContext. Inside InvokeAsync, I do my work on the request, then await next with the context, then do any work on the response. I register it in Program.cs with app.UseMiddleware, at the right position. One rule: because this class is created once, scoped services like DbContext must be taken as parameters of InvokeAsync, not in the constructor.

My real example is our correlation-id middleware, built in 2024. It reads the X-Correlation-ID header, or creates a new id, adds it to the response headers and to the logging scope, and then calls next. Every log line for that request carries the id across our 4 services, and triage time went from about an hour to a few minutes.

Middleware is a component in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline: each one receives the HttpContext, does some work, calls next to pass the request on, and can act on the response on the way back. When I write my own middleware as a class, there are two ways to do it, and the difference is really about lifetime.

Convention-based middleware is a class with a constructor taking RequestDelegate next, and an InvokeAsync method. ASP.NET Core creates it once, when the pipeline is built, so it's effectively a singleton for the life of the app. Factory-based middleware implements the IMiddleware interface. I register it in the DI container, as scoped or transient, and the framework resolves a new instance from the request scope on every request.

That leads to the classic pitfall. If you inject a scoped service, like DbContext, into the constructor of convention-based middleware, it's captured once and reused for every request forever. That's a captive dependency: it's not thread-safe and it serves stale data. In development, scope validation throws an exception at startup to catch it.

There are two fixes. For convention-based middleware, take scoped services as extra parameters of InvokeAsync, which are resolved per request. Or use IMiddleware, where constructor injection of scoped services is fine. Our audit middleware needed the DbContext, so we made it IMiddleware and registered it as scoped.

Situation: In 2024, our IRT platform had 4 services involved in a single shipment update: the API, the inventory service, the notification service and a vendor integration worker, connected by HTTP calls and RabbitMQ. When something failed, support had to trace it by matching timestamps across CloudWatch log groups. A single investigation took about an hour, and sometimes we simply couldn't connect the logs.
Task: I took on making every request traceable end to end, without each team doing their own thing.

Action: I wrote a correlation-id middleware and placed it at the very top of the pipeline in our shared service template. It reads the X-Correlation-ID header, or creates a new id if there isn't one, returns it in the response header, and opens a logging scope, so every log line in that request automatically carries the id. To pass it on, I added an HttpClient DelegatingHandler that copies the id to outgoing calls, and our RabbitMQ publisher puts it in the message headers, so consumers continue the same scope. For the audit side, an IMiddleware component records who changed what with the same id. I rolled it out service by service, with a short wiki page and a saved Logs Insights query.

Result: One query by correlation id now shows the whole journey across all 4 services. Triage dropped from about an hour to a few minutes, and support could include the id in tickets. It became part of our standard for every new service.

Middleware runs in the ASP.NET Core pipeline for every request and only sees the HttpContext. Filters are similar, but they run inside MVC, around controller actions, so they know which action is running and can see its arguments and results.

They run in a fixed order. First authorization filters, which can block the request. Then resource filters, which run before model binding and can short-circuit, which is useful for caching. Then model binding happens. Then action filters, before and after the action itself. If anything throws, exception filters handle it. Then result filters run around the execution of the result, like serialising the response.

To write a custom action filter, I implement IAsyncActionFilter, or inherit ActionFilterAttribute. In OnActionExecutionAsync, I do work before, call await next, and then inspect the executed context afterwards. I can register it globally in AddControllers options, as an attribute on a controller or action, or with ServiceFilter or TypeFilter when it needs dependencies from DI.

The rule I follow: middleware for concerns that apply to every request, like correlation ids, and filters for MVC-aware concerns. For example, we have an audit action filter that records which study an action changed, reading the action arguments.
All three give your code access to strongly-typed configuration, but they differ in lifetime and in how they handle configuration changes.

IOptions is a singleton. The values are read once, the first time they're needed, and never change while the app runs. It's the simplest, and it's fine for settings that only change with a deployment. IOptionsSnapshot is scoped. The values are recomputed for each request, so if appsettings changes on disk, the next request sees the new values. It also supports named options. But because it's scoped, you can't inject it into a singleton. IOptionsMonitor is a singleton that always gives the latest values through CurrentValue, supports named options, and has an OnChange callback, so it works in singletons and background services.
I also add ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart, so bad configuration fails at startup, not on the first request.

In our vendor exchange, each vendor's SFTP settings are named options, and our background poller is a singleton, so it uses IOptionsMonitor, reading CurrentValue at the start of each run. That way, we can change a vendor's polling settings without a restart.
Hosted services are how you run background work inside an ASP.NET Core or worker app, managed by the same host as the web server.

The base interface is IHostedService, with StartAsync and StopAsync. The host calls StartAsync when the app starts, and StopAsync during graceful shutdown. BackgroundService is a helpful base class on top of it. You just override ExecuteAsync, which usually contains a loop that runs until the stopping token is cancelled. You register it with AddHostedService, and it's registered as a singleton.

Two things are important. First, because it's a singleton, it must not inject scoped services, like DbContext, directly. Instead, it injects IServiceScopeFactory and creates a scope per unit of work. Second, it must respect the stopping token, so shutdown is clean, and it should catch and log exceptions inside the loop, because since .NET 6, an unhandled exception in a BackgroundService stops the whole host by default.
In our system, the SFTP poller and the RabbitMQ consumers are BackgroundServices. Each poll or each message runs in its own scope with a fresh DbContext.

ILogger of T is the built-in logging abstraction in .NET. I inject it into a class, and T sets the log category, which is the class's full name. That category lets you filter logs in configuration, for example showing debug logs for one namespace only.

Structured logging means logging with message templates and named placeholders, instead of building strings. For example, "Shipment {ShipmentId} moved to {Status}". The values are captured as separate fields, not just text, so in the log system you can search and filter by ShipmentId, or count failures by Status. It's also more efficient, because the string isn't formatted if that log level is disabled. Providers decide where logs go, like the console, Serilog, or CloudWatch, and logging scopes add context, like a correlation id, to every log line inside them.
A common mistake is string interpolation in log calls, which loses the structure. For hot paths, the LoggerMessage source generator avoids allocations.
In our services, logs are written as JSON to CloudWatch. Because every line has a CorrelationId and fields like ShipmentId, one Logs Insights query finds everything about a failed shipment.

Rate limiting limits how many requests a client, or an endpoint, can make within a period. When the limit is exceeded, the API returns 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with a Retry-After header. It protects the service from abuse, accidental loops in a client, and one noisy consumer starving everyone else.

Since ASP.NET Core 7, there's built-in rate limiting middleware. In Program.cs I call AddRateLimiter and define policies. There are four algorithms: fixed window, like 100 requests per minute; sliding window, which smooths the edges between windows; token bucket, which allows short bursts; and a concurrency limiter, which limits how many requests run at the same time. Policies can be partitioned, so each user, IP address or API key gets its own limit. Then I add UseRateLimiter to the pipeline, and apply policies per endpoint with RequireRateLimiting or the EnableRateLimiting attribute.
In a multi-instance setup, these limits are per instance, so for global limits we also use API Gateway or WAF limits.
For our CSV import, we used a concurrency-style limit, so each user can run only 2 imports at a time.
A minimal API is a lightweight way to build HTTP APIs in ASP.NET Core without controllers. You map routes directly to handlers, using MapGet, MapPost and so on, with a lambda or method.

The handler's parameters are bound automatically: route values, query strings, the body, and services from DI, all just as parameters. You return results using TypedResults, like TypedResults.Ok or TypedResults.NotFound, which also documents the response types in OpenAPI. For structure, MapGroup creates route groups that share a prefix, authorization and filters, and endpoint filters give you filter-like logic. Since .NET 10, there's built-in validation, which used to be a gap compared with controllers.

The benefits are less ceremony, faster startup, and slightly better performance. It's also more friendly with native AOT. For larger APIs, I organise endpoints into extension methods per feature, so Program.cs stays small.
In our team, older services use controllers, and newer small services, like an internal lookup service, use minimal APIs. Both share the same middleware, DI and authentication.

Exception middleware is the safety net at the top of the pipeline that catches unhandled exceptions from everything after it, and turns them into a proper error response instead of a crash or a raw stack trace.

In ASP.NET Core, it's UseExceptionHandler. In .NET 8, Microsoft added the IExceptionHandler interface, which makes this much cleaner. I write a handler class with a TryHandleAsync method that maps exception types to status codes. For example, a validation exception becomes 400, a not-found exception becomes 404, and a concurrency exception becomes 409. I register it with AddExceptionHandler, and you can chain several handlers. With AddProblemDetails, every error is returned in the standard ProblemDetails format, with a type, title, status and a trace id.

The important rule is never leak internals. Stack traces and exception messages are only shown in development. In production, the client gets a generic message, plus a trace id, and the full details go to the logs.
In our services, the ProblemDetails response also includes our correlation id, so when a user reports an error, support searches the logs by that id and finds the exact exception.
IHttpClientFactory is the recommended way to create HttpClient instances in .NET, because using HttpClient naively causes two opposite problems.

If you create and dispose a new HttpClient for every request, each one opens new connections, and closed sockets stay in the TIME_WAIT state for a while. Under load, you can run out of sockets. But if you go the other way and keep one static HttpClient forever, it never picks up DNS changes, which is a problem in cloud environments where IPs change. IHttpClientFactory solves both. It pools the underlying message handlers and rotates them, by default every two minutes, so connections are reused but DNS is refreshed.

It also gives a central place for configuration. I use typed clients, where a class like VendorApiClient gets a preconfigured HttpClient injected, with its base address, timeout and headers. I can add DelegatingHandlers as outgoing middleware, and AddStandardResilienceHandler for retries and circuit breaking.
In our services, our correlation-id DelegatingHandler is attached to every typed client, so the id automatically flows to downstream calls.

Span of T is a type that gives you a view over a contiguous block of memory, like part of an array, a string, or stack memory, without copying it. Slicing a span is free, it just points to a different start and length.

That makes it perfect for high-performance parsing. For example, instead of calling Substring, which allocates a new string each time, I can slice a ReadOnlySpan of char and parse numbers directly from it. Span is a ref struct, so it can only live on the stack. That's what makes it safe and fast, but it also means it can't be a field in a class, can't be boxed, and can't be used across an await. Memory of T is the companion type that can live on the heap, so it works in async methods, and you get a span from it when you need to do the work.
Many .NET APIs now accept spans, like int.Parse, so you can avoid allocations entirely.
I used this when optimising our CSV parsing. Reading fields as spans instead of splitting strings reduced allocations a lot, which reduced garbage collection during large imports.

IAsyncEnumerable of T is an asynchronous sequence. It lets you produce and consume items one at a time, where getting each item may involve async work, like reading from a database, a file or a network stream.

To produce one, you write an async iterator: an async method returning IAsyncEnumerable that uses await and yield return. To consume it, you use await foreach. The big benefit is that items are processed as they arrive, instead of waiting for the whole list to be loaded into memory first. So memory stays flat, and the first results are available sooner. It supports cancellation through the EnumeratorCancellation attribute, or WithCancellation.

It's well integrated. EF Core can stream query results with AsAsyncEnumerable. ASP.NET Core can return IAsyncEnumerable from an action, and System.Text.Json serialises it without buffering everything.

We used it for a large data export endpoint. Instead of loading tens of thousands of rows into a list, we streamed them from EF Core straight into the response, so memory usage stayed constant regardless of the export size.
These four are all caching, but at different levels.

Response caching is based on HTTP headers. The server sets Cache-Control headers, and browsers and proxies can reuse the response. The response caching middleware can also cache on the server, but it strictly follows HTTP rules. Output caching, added in .NET 7, is a server-side cache of whole responses that the server controls. You define policies, vary by query or header, and evict by tags, for example evicting all "sites" responses when a site changes. IMemoryCache caches data in code, inside one process. It's fast, but each instance has its own copy. IDistributedCache, like Redis, shares it across instances. And HybridCache, in .NET 9, combines both: a fast local cache and a distributed cache, with stampede protection, so many concurrent misses trigger only one database call.
The hard part is always invalidation. I prefer short expiries and explicit eviction when data changes.
In our services, reference data like depots and country rules is cached in memory with expiry, and shared data is in ElastiCache Redis, which is also where our token denylist lives.
JWT bearer authentication in ASP.NET Core is split between two middleware: authentication, which works out who you are, and authorization, which decides what you can do.

When a request comes in, UseAuthentication runs the default scheme handler, which is JwtBearerHandler. It reads the Authorization header, "Bearer" followed by the token, and validates it. It checks the signature using the identity provider's public keys, which it downloads from the authority's JWKS endpoint and caches. Then it checks the issuer, the audience and the expiry. If it's valid, it builds a ClaimsPrincipal from the token's claims and sets HttpContext.User. Then UseAuthorization reads the endpoint's metadata, like Authorize with a policy, and evaluates it. If there's no valid user, it returns a 401 challenge. If the user is authenticated but fails the policy, it returns 403.
I configure it with AddAuthentication and AddJwtBearer, with the authority and audience, and keep clock skew small.
In our services, we added one extra step in the OnTokenValidated event: checking the token's id against our ElastiCache denylist, so logged-out tokens are rejected immediately.
Keyed services, added in .NET 8, let you register several implementations of the same interface under different keys, and then ask the container for a specific one by its key.

Before .NET 8, if you registered three implementations of an interface, injecting the interface gave you the last one, and to pick a specific one you had to write your own factory, or register a Func of string returning the interface. Now, you register with AddKeyedSingleton, AddKeyedScoped or AddKeyedTransient, giving a key, like "rebex". To consume it, you use the FromKeyedServices attribute on a constructor parameter, or call GetRequiredKeyedService with the key at runtime.
It's a clean fit for the strategy pattern, where configuration decides which implementation to use.

That's exactly our SFTP case. Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro clients are registered as keyed services, using the library name as the key. Each vendor's configuration names its library, and our factory simply resolves GetRequiredKeyedService with that name. That replaced a hand-written switch statement, and adding a new library is just a new registration.
System.Threading.Channels provides high-performance, thread-safe queues for the producer-consumer pattern inside one process.

You create a channel with Channel.CreateBounded or CreateUnbounded. Producers write items with WriteAsync, and consumers read them with ReadAllAsync in an await foreach loop. It's fully async, so no threads are blocked while waiting. A bounded channel has a maximum capacity, which gives you backpressure. When it's full, you choose whether the writer waits, or the channel drops the oldest or newest item. That stops a fast producer from exhausting memory. You can also have multiple readers to process items in parallel.

The typical pattern is pairing it with a BackgroundService. An HTTP request quickly writes a job into the channel and returns 202 Accepted, and the background service reads and processes jobs one by one. Of course, it's in-memory, so for work that must survive a restart, a durable queue like RabbitMQ or SQS is the right choice.
We used a bounded channel for sending non-critical notification emails, so slow email calls never delayed API responses.
TimeProvider is an abstraction over the clock and timers, added in .NET 8. Instead of calling DateTime.UtcNow directly, I inject TimeProvider and call GetUtcNow.

The problem it solves is testability. Code that reads the real clock directly is hard to test. If a rule says "a token expires after 15 minutes" or "retry after 30 seconds", tests either wait for real time to pass or become flaky. With TimeProvider, production uses TimeProvider.System, and tests use FakeTimeProvider from Microsoft's testing extensions, where I can set the time and call Advance to move it forward instantly. It also covers timers through CreateTimer, and many APIs accept it, like Task.Delay and CancellationTokenSource, so even timeouts can be tested deterministically.
Before .NET 8, every team wrote its own IClock or ISystemClock interface. Now there's one standard.

In our system, rules like "block shipments after the study cut-off date" and our token expiry logic use TimeProvider. The tests set the fake time to just before and just after the cut-off, and run in milliseconds.
Resilience means handling the temporary failures that always happen with network calls, like timeouts, brief outages or throttling, so they recover on their own instead of becoming errors for users.

Polly is the standard .NET library for this. In Polly version 8, you build a resilience pipeline from strategies: retry, circuit breaker, timeout, rate limiter, fallback and hedging. In .NET 8, Microsoft added the Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience package on top of Polly. With one line, AddStandardResilienceHandler on an HttpClient, you get sensible defaults: an overall timeout, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker, and a timeout for each attempt. You can customise each part, or build your own pipeline.

A few rules matter. Only retry transient errors, like 5xx, 408 and 429, never a 400. Make sure retried operations are idempotent. And use the circuit breaker so you stop hammering a service that's clearly down.

We use it for vendor API calls. Before, a short vendor outage meant failed shipments and manual retries. With the standard handler, most of those blips now recover automatically, and the circuit breaker protects the vendor.

Angular is a complete front-end framework from Google for building single-page applications, written in TypeScript. Unlike React, which is a UI library, Angular gives you everything in one box: components, dependency injection, a router, forms, an HTTP client, and RxJS for asynchronous work, plus a CLI that generates code and builds the app.

An Angular app is a tree of components. Each component has a TypeScript class with the logic, an HTML template, and its own styles. Business logic and API calls live in services, which Angular injects into components through its dependency injection system. Routes map URLs to components, and features are usually loaded lazily, so the browser only downloads what the user needs. Older apps group things into NgModules; newer apps use standalone components, which declare their own imports.
The main building blocks, then, are components for the UI, services for logic and data, directives and pipes to extend templates, the router for navigation, and RxJS or signals for reactive data.

In our IRT product, the older screens are built in Angular and the newer modules in React with TypeScript. Both are component-based: small reusable UI components that call the same .NET Web APIs. So I work in Angular when a feature touches those older screens, and in React for the new ones.
A component is the basic building block of an Angular user interface. It controls one part of the screen, like a header, a data table, or a whole page.

A component has three parts. A TypeScript class, decorated with @Component, that holds the data and the logic, like properties and event handlers. An HTML template that describes what to show, using Angular's binding syntax to display data and react to events. And styles, which are scoped to that component by default, so they don't leak into the rest of the app. The decorator also defines a selector, like app-shipment-table, which is the custom HTML tag used to place the component inside other templates.

Components receive data from their parent through inputs, and send events back up through outputs, so they stay reusable and loosely coupled. They usually delegate API calls and business rules to injected services, which keeps the component focused on presentation. Angular also gives components lifecycle hooks, like ngOnInit for setup and ngOnDestroy for cleanup.

The idea is the same as in React: the UI is built from small, reusable pieces. In our IRT UI, for example, the older Angular screens use shared components like a site selector and a status badge across many pages, and the newer React modules follow the same component-based approach.

NgModules were Angular's original way of organising an application. An NgModule is a class decorated with @NgModule that declares a set of components, directives and pipes, imports other modules it needs, provides services, and exports what other modules can use. A typical app had an AppModule, a SharedModule for common components, and feature modules for each area, often lazy-loaded.

The problem was extra boilerplate and indirection. To use a component, you had to know which module declared it and import that module, and it was a common source of confusing errors, like "is not a known element".

Standalone components, introduced in Angular 14 and the default since Angular 17, remove that layer. A standalone component lists its own imports directly in its @Component decorator, like CommonModule, other components or pipes. The application starts with bootstrapApplication, and routes can lazy-load a standalone component or a set of routes directly. Services are usually provided with providedIn root, or in route providers.

Both still work, and they can be mixed, which matters for real projects. In an older codebase like the Angular part of our IRT UI, most screens use NgModules. New Angular work can use standalone components, and migration can happen gradually, one feature at a time, using Angular's schematics. For new code, I'd choose standalone, because it's simpler, easier to understand, and makes lazy loading more direct.
Data binding is how Angular keeps the template and the component's data in sync, without manually changing the DOM. There are four kinds.

Interpolation, with double curly braces, displays a value as text, like the patient count or a study name. Property binding, with square brackets, sets a property of an element or a child component from the component's data, for example binding the disabled property of a button to whether the form is valid, or passing an input to a child component. Event binding, with round brackets, listens for an event, like a click or a keyup, and calls a method in the component. And two-way binding, with the banana-in-a-box syntax, square brackets around round brackets, combines both: it shows a value and updates it when the user changes it. The classic example is ngModel on a form input.
So data flows from the component to the view with interpolation and property binding, from the view to the component with event binding, and both ways with two-way binding.

In practice, I use one-way flows most of the time, because they're easier to reason about, and I use reactive forms instead of ngModel for anything non-trivial. It's a similar mindset to React, where data flows down through props and events flow up through callbacks.
A directive is a class that adds behaviour to elements in an Angular template. There are three kinds.

Components are technically directives with their own template. Structural directives change the structure of the DOM by adding or removing elements. The classic ones are ngIf, which shows an element only when a condition is true, ngFor, which repeats an element for each item in a list, and ngSwitch. They're written with an asterisk, like star ngIf. Attribute directives change the appearance or behaviour of an existing element, without adding or removing it. Built-in examples are ngClass and ngStyle, and you can write your own, for example a highlight directive, or a directive that disables a button when the user lacks a permission.

Since Angular 17, there's also built-in control flow syntax: @if, @for and @switch blocks in the template. It's easier to read, it doesn't need imports, and @for requires a track expression, which is like a key in React, so Angular can update lists efficiently.

A custom attribute directive is a good example of reuse. In an IRT-style app, a directive that hides or disables actions based on the user's role keeps permission checks out of every template, though the real authorisation is always enforced by the .NET API.

A pipe transforms a value for display in a template, without changing the underlying data. You use it with the vertical bar. Built-in examples are the date pipe for formatting dates, currency and decimal pipes for numbers, uppercase and lowercase, json for debugging, and the very important async pipe, which subscribes to an observable or promise and shows its latest value.

You can write a custom pipe by creating a class with the @Pipe decorator and a transform method. For example, a pipe that turns a shipment status code into a friendly label, or masks part of an identifier.

Pipes are pure by default. A pure pipe only runs again when its input reference changes, so Angular can skip it during change detection. That makes it efficient. But it also means that if you change an array in place, like pushing an item, a pure pipe won't notice; you need to create a new array. An impure pipe, marked with pure false, runs on every change detection cycle. That's needed for things that change internally, like the async pipe, but it can be expensive, so custom impure pipes should be rare and very cheap.
A practical rule I follow is to use pipes instead of calling methods in templates, because a method in a template runs on every change detection cycle, while a pure pipe is cached.

A service in Angular is a class that holds logic or data that doesn't belong to one component, like calling an API, sharing state between components, logging, or permission checks. It's marked with the @Injectable decorator.

Angular then provides it through dependency injection. Instead of creating the service with new, a component asks for it, either in its constructor or with the inject function, and Angular gives it an instance. That keeps components small, and makes testing easy, because a test can provide a fake service.

The scope depends on where it's provided. With providedIn root, there's one shared instance for the whole app, a singleton, and it's tree-shakable, so it's removed from the bundle if nobody uses it. You can also provide a service in a route, or in a component's providers, which creates a separate instance for that part of the tree. Angular's injectors are hierarchical: a component looks for a provider in its own injector, then its parents, then the root.

It's the same principle as dependency injection in ASP.NET Core, which I use every day: register once, ask for the abstraction, and let the container create it. In our IRT Angular screens, for example, a study service wraps the HTTP calls for study data and caches reference lists, and components just inject it.

RxJS is a library for reactive programming, and Angular uses it heavily. Its core type is the Observable: a stream of values over time that you can subscribe to. HttpClient calls, router events, and form value changes are all observables in Angular.

The differences from a Promise are important. A Promise represents one future value; it's eager, meaning the work starts immediately when it's created, and it can't be cancelled. An Observable can emit zero, one or many values over time, it's lazy, so nothing happens until someone subscribes, and it can be cancelled by unsubscribing. For an HTTP call, unsubscribing actually cancels the request.

Observables also come with operators, like map, filter, debounceTime, switchMap and catchError, which you chain with pipe to transform streams. That makes complex asynchronous flows, like a search box that waits for the user to stop typing, cancels the previous request, and handles errors, very concise.

For a single API call, a Promise or an Observable both work, but in Angular I stay with observables to use the async pipe and operators. In our IRT Angular screens, a typical example is a site search box: valueChanges, then debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged, and switchMap to the API, so only the latest search result is shown.

All four take each value from a source observable and map it to an inner observable, like an HTTP request. The difference is what happens when a new value arrives while an earlier inner observable is still running.

switchMap cancels the previous inner observable and switches to the new one. It's perfect for search-as-you-type or loading details for the currently selected item, because only the latest result matters, and stale responses can't overwrite newer ones. mergeMap runs them all in parallel and merges the results as they arrive, in any order. It's good for independent work, like saving several items at once, but you lose ordering. concatMap queues them and runs one at a time, in order, waiting for each to finish. That's right when order matters, like a sequence of updates to the same record. exhaustMap ignores new values while the current one is still running. That's ideal for a submit button, so double clicks don't send two requests.
Choosing the wrong one causes real bugs. For example, using mergeMap for a search box can show results for an old query if its response arrives last.

In practice: switchMap for searches and selections, concatMap for ordered saves, exhaustMap for submits and logins, and mergeMap for parallel independent calls. In our Angular screens, the save button on a form uses exhaustMap, so a double click can never create a duplicate record.

A Subject is both an observable and an observer: you can subscribe to it, and you can push values into it with next. It's used to multicast values to many subscribers, often inside a service to share state or events between components.

The difference between the types is what a new subscriber receives. A plain Subject has no memory: subscribers only get values emitted after they subscribe. That suits events, like "a file was uploaded". A BehaviorSubject requires an initial value and always holds the current value. A new subscriber immediately receives the latest value, and you can read it synchronously with getValue. That makes it ideal for state, like the currently selected study or the logged-in user. A ReplaySubject replays a number of previous values, or values within a time window, to new subscribers, which is useful for things like a recent activity log. There's also AsyncSubject, which only emits the last value when it completes.
A common pattern in Angular services is a private BehaviorSubject for state, exposed publicly as a read-only observable with asObservable, so components can read but only the service can change it.
In newer Angular, signals cover much of this state use case more simply, but BehaviorSubject is still everywhere in existing code, including our older IRT screens.

A memory leak happens when a component subscribes to a long-lived observable, like a service's state, a timer or router events, and never unsubscribes. When the component is destroyed, the subscription keeps it alive, and its callback keeps running, which wastes memory and can cause strange behaviour, like duplicated API calls.

There are several ways to prevent it. The best is the async pipe in the template. It subscribes when the view is created and unsubscribes automatically when it's destroyed, and it also works nicely with OnPush change detection. The modern option in code is takeUntilDestroyed, from Angular's rxjs-interop package, which completes the subscription when the component is destroyed. The older pattern is takeUntil with a destroy Subject that's completed in ngOnDestroy. And for signals, converting with toSignal handles cleanup automatically.
It's also worth knowing that HttpClient observables complete after one response, so they don't leak in the usual sense, but unsubscribing still cancels the request if the user leaves the page.

My rule is: prefer the async pipe, and if I must subscribe in code, always pair it with takeUntilDestroyed. In code reviews of our Angular screens, a bare subscribe without cleanup is something I always flag.

Change detection is how Angular keeps the screen in sync with the component's data. After something happens that might change data, like a click, an HTTP response or a timer, Angular checks the component tree from the top and updates any bindings whose values changed.

Traditionally, Angular knows when to run this through zone.js, which patches browser async APIs, so after any async event, Angular runs change detection. With the default strategy, every component is checked on every cycle. That's simple, but in large screens with big tables, it can become slow.

OnPush is an optimisation. A component with ChangeDetectionStrategy OnPush is only checked when one of its inputs changes by reference, when an event happens inside it, when an async pipe in its template receives a value, or when you call markForCheck. That means you must treat input data as immutable: create a new array or object instead of changing it in place, otherwise the component won't update.
Newer Angular adds signals, which tell Angular exactly which component needs updating, and supports zoneless change detection, removing zone.js entirely.

In practice, I use OnPush for presentational components, especially lists and tables, with immutable data and the async pipe. On a large grid screen in our Angular UI, switching row components to OnPush noticeably reduced lag when filtering.
Lifecycle hooks are methods Angular calls at specific moments in a component's life, so you can run code at the right time.

In order: ngOnChanges runs whenever an input property changes, and receives the previous and current values. ngOnInit runs once after the first inputs are set; it's the usual place for initial setup, like loading data. Constructors should only do simple dependency injection, not real work. ngDoCheck runs on every change detection cycle, for custom change checks, and should be used rarely. ngAfterContentInit and ngAfterContentChecked run after projected content, from ng-content, is initialised and checked. ngAfterViewInit and ngAfterViewChecked run after the component's own view and child components are ready; that's where you can safely access elements with ViewChild, for example to focus an input or initialise a chart. And ngOnDestroy runs just before the component is removed, which is where you clean up, like unsubscribing or stopping timers.
Newer Angular also offers the DestroyRef and takeUntilDestroyed for cleanup, and afterNextRender for DOM work, but the classic hooks are still used everywhere.

The React equivalent is useEffect: an effect with an empty dependency array is similar to ngOnInit, and its cleanup function is similar to ngOnDestroy. Since our IRT product uses both Angular and React, I often map between these two models.
There are three main ways components share data in Angular.

From parent to child, with inputs. The child declares a property with @Input, or the newer input function that creates a signal, and the parent binds a value to it in the template with square brackets. For example, a parent page passes a list of sites to a site table component.

From child to parent, with outputs. The child declares an @Output, an EventEmitter, or the newer output function, and emits an event, for example when a row is selected. The parent listens with round brackets and handles it in a method. This keeps the child reusable, because it doesn't know what the parent will do.

Between components that aren't directly related, through a shared service. The service holds the state, for example in a BehaviorSubject or a signal, and components inject it, read the state, and call methods to change it. For larger apps, a state management library like NgRx or a signal store plays this role.

There's also ViewChild, to call a method on a child directly, and the router, for passing ids through the URL. The design rule I follow is the same as in React: data down, events up, and shared state in one well-defined place. That's how our Angular and React screens in IRT stay consistent, even though they're built with different frameworks.

The Angular router maps URLs to components, so a single-page application can have different pages and deep links without full page reloads. You define a list of routes, each with a path and a component, or a lazily loaded component or set of child routes. A router-outlet in the template marks where the routed component appears, and routerLink creates navigation links. Route parameters, like a study id in the URL, are read through ActivatedRoute, or bound directly to component inputs in newer versions.

Guards decide whether navigation is allowed. canActivate runs before entering a route, typically to check that the user is logged in or has a role, and can redirect to login. canMatch decides whether a route definition should even match, which also prevents lazy code from loading for users who can't use it. canDeactivate runs before leaving, for example to warn about unsaved changes on a form. Resolvers can load data before the route activates. In modern Angular, guards are simple functions that use inject.
An important point is that guards are for user experience, not security. They hide screens, but the real protection is the .NET API checking the token and permissions on every request.
In our IRT UI, for example, guards check that the user has a role on the selected study before showing an admin screen, and a canDeactivate guard protects forms with unsaved changes.

Lazy loading means the browser only downloads the code for a feature when the user actually navigates to it, instead of downloading the whole application at the start. It makes the first load much faster, especially for large enterprise apps with many modules that most users never open.

In Angular, you configure it in the routes. For a whole feature, loadChildren points to a function that imports that feature's routes or module. For a single standalone component, loadComponent imports just that component. The Angular CLI then automatically splits the code into separate bundles, called chunks, and the router downloads a chunk the first time its route is visited.

There are some useful extras. Preloading strategies can download lazy modules in the background after the app has loaded, so navigation is still instant. A canMatch guard prevents loading a module for users who aren't allowed to use it. And the newer defer block can lazy load parts of a template, like a heavy chart, only when they become visible.

In a product like our IRT UI, with separate areas for different modules and roles, lazy loading is essential. Site users never download the admin screens, for example. The same idea exists in React with React.lazy and route-based code splitting, which we use in the newer React modules.
Angular has two ways to build forms.

Template-driven forms define the form mostly in the HTML template, using ngModel and validation attributes like required. Angular builds the form model behind the scenes. They're quick and simple for small forms, like a login or a search box, but harder to test and to manage when the logic grows.

Reactive forms define the form model explicitly in the component's TypeScript code, with FormGroup, FormControl and FormArray, usually created with FormBuilder. The template just binds to that model. Validation is done with validator functions, including custom and cross-field validators, like "end date must be after start date", and asynchronous validators, like checking on the server that a code is unique. Value and status changes are observables, so you can react to them, and since Angular 14 the forms are strongly typed.
For anything non-trivial, I prefer reactive forms. They're explicit, predictable, easy to unit test without a browser, and handle dynamic forms well, like adding rows to a FormArray.

In our IRT Angular screens, data entry forms, like the ones for site or study settings, use reactive forms with custom validators, and the server validates everything again, returning field-level ProblemDetails errors that we map back onto the form.

HttpClient is Angular's service for calling HTTP APIs. You inject it into a service and call methods like get and post, typed with the response model, and they return observables. In a well-structured app, components don't call HttpClient directly; they call a service, like a shipment API service, which keeps URLs and mapping in one place.

Interceptors sit in the middle of every request and response, like middleware in ASP.NET Core. They're perfect for cross-cutting concerns. An auth interceptor adds the access token to the Authorization header. A correlation interceptor adds a correlation id header, so a request can be traced through the backend logs. An error interceptor handles common errors in one place: on 401, it redirects to login or refreshes the token; on 403, it shows a permission message; and on validation errors, it passes the ProblemDetails through to the form. A loading interceptor can show a global spinner. Interceptors run in the order they're provided, and in modern Angular they're simple functions registered with provideHttpClient and withInterceptors.
For testing, HttpTestingController lets unit tests check the exact request and return a fake response.
In our IRT UI, the Angular interceptors and the React API client do the same jobs: token, correlation id and error mapping, so both parts of the UI behave identically against our .NET APIs.

Signals are Angular's newer reactive primitive, stable since Angular 17. A signal is a wrapper around a value that tells Angular when it changes. You create one with signal and an initial value, read it by calling it like a function, and update it with set or update. computed creates a derived signal that recalculates only when the signals it depends on change, and it's cached. effect runs side effects, like logging or saving to local storage, whenever the signals it reads change.

The big benefit is fine-grained change detection. Angular knows exactly which component uses which signal, so it can update just that component, and it enables zoneless applications without zone.js. Signals are also simpler to read and write than observables for plain state. Inputs and queries can now be signals too.

Signals don't replace RxJS. Signals are best for synchronous state: the current value of something, like the selected site or a filter. RxJS is still best for asynchronous streams and events: HTTP calls, debouncing, cancellation and combining streams. The interop functions toSignal and toObservable connect the two, for example turning an HTTP observable into a signal for the template.

For new Angular code, I'd use signals for component and service state, and keep RxJS for async flows. It's similar in spirit to useState and derived values in React, which helps when moving between our Angular and React screens.
I choose the simplest option that fits how widely the state is shared and how complex it is.

Local state stays in the component, as properties or signals, like whether a panel is open. Shared state for one feature lives in a service, using a BehaviorSubject or signals, exposed as read-only, with methods to change it. That covers most needs, like the currently selected study and site shared across a few screens. Server data, like lists from the API, can be cached in those services too, with care to refresh it.

For large applications with complex, widely shared state, NgRx is the standard library. It follows the Redux pattern: a single store, actions that describe events, reducers that produce new state, selectors to read it efficiently, and effects for side effects like API calls. It's very predictable and has great dev tools, but it adds a lot of boilerplate, so I only use it where it pays off. The newer NgRx Signal Store is lighter and based on signals.

Whatever the tool, the principles are the same: one source of truth, immutable updates, and keeping server state separate from UI state. That's the same thinking as Redux Toolkit and React Query in the React part of our IRT UI, which makes it easier for the team to work in both frameworks.
I start by measuring, with Angular DevTools' profiler and the browser's performance tools, so I fix real problems rather than guesses. Then the usual improvements fall into three groups.

Loading time. Lazy load feature routes, so users only download what they open. Use defer blocks for heavy parts of a page, like charts. Keep bundles small: check them with a bundle analyser, remove unused libraries, and rely on tree-shakable providedIn root services. Production builds with ahead-of-time compilation are the default.

Rendering. Use OnPush change detection with immutable data, or signals, so Angular checks only what changed. Always use track in @for, or trackBy in ngFor, so lists reuse DOM elements instead of recreating them. Avoid calling methods in templates; use pure pipes or computed signals instead. For very long lists, use virtual scrolling from the CDK, so only visible rows are rendered.

Data. Avoid duplicate HTTP calls by caching reference data in services, use switchMap to cancel stale requests, debounce search inputs, and ask the API for paged, filtered data instead of loading everything.
A real example from our Angular UI: a large grid felt slow when filtering. Adding trackBy, OnPush on the row component, and server-side paging made it responsive again.
I test Angular at three levels.

Unit tests for services, pipes and plain logic. These don't need the framework much: I create the service, provide fakes for its dependencies, and check the results. For services that use HttpClient, HttpTestingController lets me check that the right request was made, with the right URL and body, and return a fake response or an error.

Component tests with TestBed. TestBed configures a small testing module with the component, its imports, and fake versions of its services. I create the component, set inputs, trigger events like clicks, run change detection, and check what the template shows. Angular Testing Library makes these tests read more like what a user does, querying by role and label rather than CSS classes. The test runner has traditionally been Karma with Jasmine; many teams now use Jest, and newer Angular moves towards Vitest.
End-to-end tests with Playwright or Cypress, running the real app in a browser, for the key user flows. We use Playwright, with Cucumber scenarios for business-readable flows.

The principles are the same as for React: test behaviour, not implementation details, keep unit tests fast, and keep a small number of reliable end-to-end tests for the critical paths, like randomising a subject in a test study.
Angular templates aren't plain HTML; they have to be compiled into JavaScript instructions that create and update the DOM. There are two ways to do that.

Just-in-time, or JIT, compiles templates in the browser at runtime. It was used for development in older versions, but it means shipping the compiler to the browser and doing extra work at startup. Ahead-of-time, or AOT, compiles templates during the build. The browser receives ready-to-run code, so the app starts faster, the bundle is smaller because the compiler isn't shipped, and template errors, like binding to a property that doesn't exist, are caught at build time instead of by users. AOT has been the default for both development and production builds for several versions.

Ivy is Angular's rendering and compilation engine, the default since Angular 9, replacing the older View Engine. Ivy compiles each component independently into efficient instructions, which made bundles smaller through better tree-shaking, builds faster, debugging easier, and it made features like standalone components and signals possible.

In day-to-day work, you rarely think about Ivy directly, but understanding AOT helps explain build errors in templates, and why strict template type-checking is worth enabling. We keep strictTemplates switched on in our Angular projects, so template mistakes fail the build.

Content projection lets a parent pass a piece of markup into a child component, which places it inside its own template using ng-content. It's how you build flexible container components. For example, a card or dialog component provides the frame, title bar and buttons, and the parent decides what goes inside. With multi-slot projection, using select, a component can have several slots, like a header, a body and a footer. It's the Angular equivalent of passing children in React.

ViewChild and ContentChild are ways for a component to get a reference to something. ViewChild looks inside the component's own template, for elements, directives or child components it declares itself. For example, getting a reference to an input to focus it, or to a child component to call a method. ContentChild looks at the content that was projected into the component by its parent. For example, a tab group component finding the tab components placed inside it. The plural versions, ViewChildren and ContentChildren, return lists. They're available after the view or content is initialised, and newer Angular offers signal-based versions.

These features are what make good reusable component libraries possible. In our shared component set, dialogs and panels use content projection, so every screen gets consistent layout and behaviour, while each feature supplies its own content.
I handle errors at three levels, so users see helpful messages and we still get the details we need to investigate.

First, HTTP errors, in one place. An HTTP interceptor catches failed responses. A 401 sends the user to login or refreshes the token, a 403 shows a "no permission" message, a 404 shows a not-found message, and 5xx errors show a friendly "something went wrong" with the correlation id, so support can find the request in the backend logs. Validation errors, returned by our .NET APIs as ProblemDetails, are passed back to the form and shown next to the right fields.
Second, local handling where the screen needs it, using the catchError operator in RxJS to show an inline error state, fall back to empty data, or let the user retry. I don't swallow errors silently.

Third, a global ErrorHandler. Angular lets you replace its default ErrorHandler with your own class, which catches any unhandled error in the app, logs it, ideally to a monitoring service with the user's context, and shows a generic message instead of a broken screen.

It's the same structure as our backend: specific handling where it's needed, plus a global safety net. The React modules mirror it with error boundaries and a shared API client, so both parts of the IRT UI behave consistently.
In a React and TypeScript project, I type everything at the boundaries, so mistakes show up in the editor instead of in production.

For props, I define an interface or a type, like ShipmentTableProps, with each prop and its type, marking optional ones with a question mark, and I type the function's parameter with it. I usually don't use React.FC; a plain function with typed props is clearer. For children, I use React.ReactNode. For event handler props, I type the callback, like onSelect taking a site id and returning void. For variants, union types are great: a status prop typed as "active", "on hold" or "closed" means you can't pass anything else.

For hooks, useState usually infers the type from the initial value, but when it starts as null, I give it explicitly, like useState of Study or null. useRef gets the element type, like HTMLInputElement. Custom hooks return typed objects. For reusable components, like a data table, generics let one component work for any row type while keeping full type safety.
For API data, I use types generated from the backend's OpenAPI definition, so the front end and the .NET API share one contract.
When our team moved new modules from Angular to React, strict TypeScript was non-negotiable, because Angular had already given us typed code, and we didn't want to lose that safety.

A custom hook is a JavaScript function whose name starts with "use", and which calls other hooks, like useState, useEffect or useContext. It's React's way to reuse stateful logic between components, without copying code and without wrappers like higher-order components.

The important point is that a custom hook shares logic, not state. Each component that calls it gets its own independent state. And the rules of hooks apply: call hooks only at the top level of a component or another hook, never inside conditions or loops, so React can match them up on every render.

Some examples I've used. A useDebounce hook that takes a value and a delay, and returns the value only after the user stops typing, used for search boxes. A usePermission hook that reads the current user's roles from context and returns whether they can perform an action, so components just ask "can I edit this site?". And a useStudyContext hook that returns the currently selected study and site, and throws a clear error if it's used outside the provider.
For data fetching, I now mostly use React Query's useQuery inside small custom hooks, like useShipments with a study id, so components don't know about URLs or caching at all.

Custom hooks make components short and readable, and the logic is easy to unit test on its own. They're the React equivalent of injectable services in Angular, which is a comparison I often make, since our IRT UI uses both frameworks.
React Query, now called TanStack Query, is a library for managing server state in React: data that lives on the backend and that the UI fetches, caches and keeps up to date.

Without it, every component needs its own useEffect, loading flag, error flag and caching logic, which leads to duplicated requests and stale data. With React Query, you call useQuery with a query key, like shipments and a study id, and a function that calls the API. It returns the data, plus isLoading and error states. It caches the result by that key, so other components asking for the same data reuse it, deduplicates requests that happen at the same time, retries failures, and refetches in the background when data becomes stale or the window regains focus.

For changes, useMutation sends a POST or PUT, and on success I invalidate the related query keys, so lists refresh automatically. Optimistic updates are also possible, where the UI updates immediately and rolls back if the server fails.
My rule is to keep server state in React Query and only UI state, like open panels or selected filters, in useState, context or Redux Toolkit. That removes a lot of state management code.
In the newer React modules of our IRT UI, data fetching is wrapped in small typed hooks around React Query, calling the same .NET Web APIs as the older Angular screens.

An error boundary is a React component that catches JavaScript errors thrown while rendering its child components, logs them, and shows a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole application. Without one, an error in a single component unmounts the entire React tree, and the user sees a blank screen.

Error boundaries are still class components, because they rely on two lifecycle methods: getDerivedStateFromError, to switch to the fallback UI, and componentDidCatch, to log the error and component stack, for example to a monitoring service. In practice, most teams use the small react-error-boundary library, which gives a ready component with a fallback and a reset button, so you can write everything else as function components.

There are limits to know. Error boundaries don't catch errors in event handlers, in asynchronous code like promises and timeouts, or in server-side rendering. Those are handled with try-catch, or with the error states of React Query.

Placement matters. I put one boundary at the top of the app as a final safety net, and others around each major area or widget, like a dashboard panel, so one failing part doesn't take down the page. The fallback shows a friendly message and the correlation id, which helps support trace the failure in the backend logs.
It's the React counterpart to Angular's global ErrorHandler, and in our IRT UI both are set up to behave the same way.
I test React components the way a user uses them, with React Testing Library, running on Jest or Vitest.

The idea is to test behaviour, not implementation. I render the component, find elements the way a user would, by role, label or text, for example getByRole button with the name Save, interact with user-event, like typing and clicking, and assert what the user sees, like a validation message or a new row in the table. I don't test internal state or which hooks were called, so I can refactor the component without breaking tests. findBy queries wait for asynchronous updates, like data arriving from an API.

For API calls, I use Mock Service Worker, MSW, which intercepts requests at the network level and returns fake responses. That way, the real data fetching code, including React Query, runs in the test. For components that need context, like the current study or the user's permissions, I wrap them in a test render helper that provides those providers. Custom hooks can be tested on their own with renderHook.
Above that, Playwright end-to-end tests cover the key flows in a real browser, like randomising a subject in a test study.
In our IRT product, this matters even more because it's GxP-regulated: tests are part of the evidence that the software works as intended, and they run in every pipeline.

The virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript description of what the UI should look like. When state or props change, React calls your components again to produce a new description, compares it with the previous one, and then applies only the necessary changes to the real browser DOM. That comparison is called reconciliation. Updating the real DOM is the expensive part, so doing the minimum there keeps apps fast, while you write code as if the whole UI is redrawn each time.

React's diffing uses two simple assumptions to be fast. If an element's type changes, for example from a div to a span, or from one component to another, React throws away the old subtree and builds a new one. And for lists, it uses keys to know which item is which between renders.

That's why keys matter. A key should be a stable, unique id from the data, like a site id. If you use the array index, and items are inserted, removed or sorted, React matches the wrong items, which can cause wrong input values, lost focus, or unnecessary re-rendering. Keys also let you reset a component on purpose, by changing its key.
Modern React does this with its Fiber architecture, which can split rendering work and prioritise urgent updates, like typing.
Angular has the same concern with track in @for loops, so in both parts of our IRT UI, lists are always tracked by a real id.
Both hooks hold state inside a component, and the choice is about how complex the state and its updates are.

useState is the simple one. You get a value and a setter. It's ideal for independent, simple values, like whether a dialog is open, the text in a search box, or a selected tab. When the new value depends on the old one, I use the function form of the setter, so updates are never lost.

useReducer is better when the state has several related fields that change together, or when there are many different kinds of updates. You write a reducer function that takes the current state and an action, like "row added" or "file validated", and returns the new state, and components call dispatch with actions. All the update logic is in one pure function, which is easy to read and easy to unit test without rendering anything, and impossible states are easier to avoid. With TypeScript, I type the actions as a discriminated union, so each action's payload is checked.
A real example: a multi-step import screen, with steps, a selected file, validation results and errors, fits useReducer much better than five separate useState calls that must be kept in sync.
If that state needs to be shared across many components, I move the same reducer pattern into Redux Toolkit, which is on my resume and uses exactly this model.
The most reliable way is to make the API's OpenAPI definition the single source of truth, and generate TypeScript types from it, instead of writing them by hand.

On the .NET side, ASP.NET Core produces an OpenAPI document from the controllers and DTOs, using Swashbuckle or the built-in OpenAPI support, with nullable and required annotations so the generated types are precise. On the front end, a tool like openapi-typescript or NSwag generates TypeScript types, and optionally a typed client, from that document. We run the generator as part of the build, so when a backend developer renames a field or adds a required property, the front-end build fails right away, instead of a user finding a broken screen.

A few practices make it work well. The API is versioned, and breaking changes go into a new version, so older screens keep working. DTOs are designed for the API, not copied from database entities. Dates are sent as ISO strings, and enums as strings, so they're readable on both sides. And contract tests check the important responses.

This mattered a lot in our project, because the same .NET Web APIs serve both the older Angular screens and the newer React modules. Both front ends generate their types from the same OpenAPI documents, so they always agree with the backend and with each other.

Code splitting means breaking the JavaScript bundle into smaller pieces that load on demand, instead of making the user download the whole app before seeing anything. Lazy loading is loading those pieces only when they're needed.

In React, the built-in way is React.lazy with a dynamic import. You wrap a component, like the reports page, in React.lazy, and the bundler, like Vite or webpack, automatically puts it into its own chunk. You render it inside a Suspense boundary, which shows a fallback, like a spinner, while the chunk downloads.

The most effective place to split is by route: each major page or module loads separately, so a site user never downloads the admin screens. Inside pages, heavy components that aren't immediately visible, like charts, editors or large dialogs, are also good candidates. You can prefetch likely next routes on hover or when the browser is idle, so navigation still feels instant. And I check the result with a bundle analyser, because sometimes one large library is the real problem.
Errors while loading a chunk, for example after a new deployment, should be caught by an error boundary with a reload option.
It's the same idea as lazy-loaded routes in Angular. In our IRT UI, both the older Angular modules and the newer React modules load per feature, so users only download what their role needs.
Redux Toolkit is the official, modern way to use Redux, and it's on my resume. It removes most of the old boilerplate, and it works very well with TypeScript.

The setup is simple. configureStore creates the store with good defaults, like the dev tools and checks for accidental mutations. Each feature has a slice, made with createSlice, which defines its initial state and reducers in one place, and generates the action creators automatically. Inside reducers, you can write code that looks like it mutates state, because Immer turns it into immutable updates. createAsyncThunk handles async logic, like calling an API, with pending, fulfilled and rejected actions.

With TypeScript, I define a RootState type from the store, and an AppDispatch type, and then create typed hooks, useAppSelector and useAppDispatch, which every component uses. That way, selectors and dispatched actions are fully checked, and state shapes are defined once with interfaces.

RTK Query is the data-fetching part of Redux Toolkit. You define an API with endpoints, and it generates hooks, like useGetShipmentsQuery, with caching, deduplication and cache invalidation through tags, similar to React Query.

I keep Redux for truly global client state, like the selected study, user preferences or a multi-step workflow, and let a query library handle server data. That keeps the store small, which matters in a large app like our IRT UI.

Our project uses both. The IRT web UI started on Angular, and we're moving to React with TypeScript, so today the older screens are in Angular and the newer modules are built in React with TypeScript.

Both parts are component-based. The UI is built from small, reusable components, like a data table, a site selector, a status badge, form fields and dialogs, and both frameworks call the same .NET Web APIs on the backend. Users don't see a difference: both parts sit behind one login and one navigation shell, and they follow one shared design system, so the screens look and behave the same.

The way we move is module by module, not a big-bang rewrite. Existing Angular screens keep running and get fixes and small features. New modules, and old screens that need a major redesign anyway, are built in React. Because the APIs are shared, with types generated from the same OpenAPI contract, the backend doesn't care which framework calls it.

My own front-end work covers both. I build reusable React components with TypeScript, using hooks and Redux Toolkit where shared state is needed, and I maintain and extend Angular modules in the older parts of the UI. Since I also build the .NET APIs behind these screens, I can shape the API for what each screen needs, whichever framework it's in.
It wasn't because Angular is bad. Angular is a strong framework, and our existing Angular screens work well. It was a practical decision for our team and product.

First, people and skills. Most of the developers joining the team, and most of the existing team, were more experienced with React, and it's easier to hire for. Second, flexibility and ecosystem. With React we could choose lightweight, focused libraries, like React Query for server data, React Hook Form for forms, and Redux Toolkit only where shared state is needed, instead of one large framework. Third, our older Angular code was on an older Angular version with NgModules, and many screens needed a redesign anyway. Upgrading and redesigning them in Angular was a similar amount of work to building them fresh in React with TypeScript. And fourth, building small, reusable components with plain functions and hooks fitted the shared component library we wanted.

What we deliberately did not do was a big-bang rewrite. In a GxP-regulated product, every change must be validated, so rewriting working screens just to change the framework would add risk and validation effort with no benefit for users.

So the rule became: new modules in React with TypeScript, existing Angular screens maintained until they need major change, and both calling the same .NET Web APIs. If I join a team that uses Angular, I'm comfortable with it; the fundamentals are the same.
We run them side by side using an incremental, module-by-module approach, like the strangler fig pattern on the backend: new parts grow around the old ones until the old ones can retire.
