There are a few pieces. Routing: a thin web shell owns the login, the top navigation and the URL space, and each module, Angular or React, is mounted under its own route. So the user moves between an Angular screen and a React screen without noticing. Authentication: both use the same SSO session and token handling, so there's no second login. Shared context, like the currently selected study and site, is passed through the URL and the backend, not through framework-specific state, so either side can pick it up. Look and feel: a shared design system, with the same design tokens for colours, spacing and fonts, keeps them consistent. And the backend is the real contract: both call the same .NET Web APIs, with TypeScript types generated from the same OpenAPI documents.

There are trade-offs. Two frameworks mean two sets of dependencies, two build pipelines and two sets of skills. We limit this by not mixing frameworks inside a single screen, and by keeping each module owned by one framework.
The benefit is that we deliver new features in React without stopping to rewrite working, validated Angular screens, which is important in a GxP-regulated product.
The goal is that users can't tell whether a screen is Angular or React. Everything should look and behave the same.

The foundation is design tokens: colours, spacing, font sizes, shadows and breakpoints, defined once as CSS variables in a shared stylesheet package that both the Angular and React apps import. So if a colour changes, it changes everywhere. On top of that, we share the base styles and layout rules, like the grid, form layout and typography.

Components are the harder part, because an Angular component can't be used directly in React. We handle that with a shared specification rather than shared code: each common component, like a data table, a status badge, a site selector or a dialog, has one documented behaviour, including states like loading, empty and error, keyboard support and accessibility labels. The React version is built first for new work, and the Angular version follows the same specification. For truly framework-neutral pieces, web components are an option, but we've kept that limited.
We also share patterns, not just pixels: the same way of showing validation errors from ProblemDetails, the same confirmation dialogs for risky actions, and the same date formats.
My part was building several of the reusable React components, like the configurable data table, and making sure the matching Angular screens followed the same behaviour.

Situation: Our IRT web UI started on Angular. Over time, the Angular code was on an older version with NgModules, many screens needed a redesign, and most new developers were stronger in React. But it's a GxP-regulated product, so rewriting everything at once would mean huge risk and re-validation.
Task: The team decided to move to React with TypeScript gradually. My part was to help set up the React side so new modules could be built quickly and safely, while the Angular screens kept working.

Action: We chose a module-by-module approach. A thin web shell handles login and navigation, and each module is mounted under its own route, either Angular or React, so users see one product. I helped build the shared foundations on the React side: a typed API client generated from our .NET OpenAPI documents, which also adds the token and correlation id, and maps ProblemDetails errors, just like the Angular interceptors do. I built reusable components, like the configurable data table and the import error grid, following our shared design tokens, so React and Angular screens look the same. I also wrote short guidelines on typing, hooks and testing with React Testing Library and Playwright. Meanwhile, I kept maintaining Angular modules, including the tabnabbing fix across about 40 links in both frameworks.

Result: New modules have been delivered in React since then without any change to the backend APIs, both frameworks run side by side behind one login, and Angular screens are only rewritten when they need major change anyway. Users see one consistent, component-based UI.

A clinical trial, which we also call a clinical study, is a research study in people that tests whether a new medicine or treatment is safe and works. Before a medicine can be approved by regulators, like the FDA in the US or the EMA in Europe, it has to go through these trials.

There are a few key players. The sponsor is usually the pharmaceutical company that owns the drug and pays for the trial. A CRO, a contract research organisation like IQVIA, runs parts of the trial and provides technology like IRT. Sites are the hospitals and clinics where patients, called subjects, take part, run by investigators and site staff.

Every trial follows a protocol, a detailed plan that defines who can join, what treatments are compared, how patients are assigned to them, what happens at each visit, and what is measured. Trials usually run in phases. Phase one tests safety in a small group, phase two tests whether it works and the right dose, and phase three compares it with standard treatment in thousands of patients across many countries.
To keep results fair, most trials are randomised, meaning a computer decides by chance which treatment each patient gets, and blinded, meaning patients and doctors don't know which one it is.

In IRT, a study is that one trial set up in our system: its protocol rules, countries and sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and users. Our software makes sure the randomisation and the drug supply follow the protocol exactly.
In IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in our system. It contains everything the system needs to follow that trial's protocol, the plan that defines how the trial runs.

First, the basic details: the protocol number, the sponsor, phase, and settings like whether the study is blinded. Second, the countries and sites that take part, each with its staff, address and the depot that supplies it. Third, the treatment arms, the groups being compared, like the new drug versus placebo, with their ratio, such as one to one. Fourth, the randomisation setup: the randomisation lists, and stratification factors like age group or region, so the groups stay balanced. Fifth, the visit schedule: screening, randomisation, and treatment visits, with which visits dispense drug, and the allowed time windows. Sixth, the drug supply setup: the kit types, how many kits each arm gets at each visit, depots, expiry rules, and resupply levels for sites. Seventh, users and roles, like site coordinators, pharmacists, unblinded staff and study managers, each with permissions. And finally, settings for the modules used, like eConsent forms, re-randomisation rules and DARM return rules.
All of this is configured by internal study teams in our Admin console, validated, and then moved to production before the first patient is screened.

Our IRT product helps run clinical trials. A study here means one clinical trial set up in our system, with its protocol rules, sites, treatment arms, visit schedule, drug kits and users. The product has client-facing modules used by site staff and study teams, and an internal tool used to build the studies.

The client-facing modules follow a patient's journey. Screening registers a new patient at a site and checks whether they qualify for the trial. Randomisation assigns an eligible patient to a treatment group, fairly and secretly, and tells the site which numbered drug kit to give. Re-randomisation assigns a patient to a new group later in the trial, when the protocol has a second stage. eConsent lets patients review and sign consent forms electronically, with version tracking. And DARM, Drug Accountability and Return Management, tracks every kit after it's given out: what was used, what was returned, and what was destroyed, so every kit is accounted for. Behind these, drug supply management keeps sites stocked.
Internally, we have the Admin console. Study teams use it to create and configure a study: sites, arms, randomisation, visits, kits and roles, before it goes live for end users.

The UI is component-based, with older screens in Angular and newer modules in React with TypeScript, and all modules are backed by .NET Web APIs, SQL Server and messaging with Kafka and RabbitMQ. My work spans the APIs, integrations and screens behind several of these.

Screening is the first step of a patient's journey in a trial. In our IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in the system, with its protocol rules, sites, arms, visits and kits, and screening is how a patient enters that study.

End to end, it works like this. A site coordinator logs in, selects the study and site, and screens a new patient. They enter the basic details the protocol requires, like date of birth, gender and consent date, without names, because the patient's identity stays at the site. IRT checks the rules: the site must be active, enrolment must be open, the patient must have given consent, and caps, like the maximum number of patients per country, must not be reached. Then it creates a subject record with a unique subject number, records the visit, and writes an audit entry.

During the screening period, the site runs tests to confirm eligibility. Then one of two things happens. Either the patient passes and moves on to randomisation, or they're recorded as a screen failure, with a reason. Some protocols allow rescreening, which creates a new attempt linked to the same person.

On the technical side, it's an ASP.NET Core API with validation and role checks, SQL Server for the subject data, an audit trail for every change, and events published for notifications and reporting. The screen itself is component-based, in our case an older Angular screen.

Randomisation is the heart of IRT. A study is one clinical trial set up in our system, with treatment arms, like the new drug versus placebo, and randomisation decides, by chance, which arm each patient gets, so the comparison is fair.

End to end: a site user selects a screened patient and confirms they're eligible, answering the protocol's eligibility questions and entering stratification factors, like age group. The UI calls the randomisation API with an idempotency key, so a retry after a timeout can't randomise the patient twice. The .NET service checks the user's role at that site, that the subject is in the right state, and that the study and site are open. Then, inside one database transaction with locking, it takes the next available slot from the randomisation list for the patient's stratum, assigns a randomisation number, picks a kit of the right type from the site's stock, writes the audit record, and adds an outbox event.

The response gives the site the randomisation number and the kit number. The kit number hides the treatment, so blinded users never see the arm. After that, events trigger the rest: supply checks that may order resupply for the site, and notifications to the study team.
The key principle is strong consistency: exactly one correct assignment per patient, and two sites can never get the same slot.

messages.note: slot, kit, audit, outbox in one transaction

s: These are the rules that decide how patients are assigned to treatment groups in a study, which is one clinical trial set up in IRT.

A randomisation list is a pre-generated, ordered list of slots, each with a randomisation number and a treatment arm. It's usually generated by an unblinded statistician, uploaded securely, and never shown to blinded users. When a patient is randomised, IRT gives them the next free slot.

Block randomisation keeps the groups balanced over time. The list is made of small blocks, say blocks of four for a one-to-one ratio, where each block contains exactly two of each arm in a random order. So at any point, the groups can't drift far apart. Block sizes are often varied, so site staff can't guess the next assignment.

Stratification makes sure important factors are balanced too. If age or region could affect the result, the study defines strata, like "under sixty-five in Europe", and there's a separate list, or a separate sequence of blocks, for each stratum. The site enters the factors at randomisation, and IRT picks from that stratum's list.
Some studies use dynamic methods, like minimisation, which compute the assignment at that moment to minimise imbalance, instead of using a fixed list.
Technically, the critical part is allocating the next slot safely, in a transaction with locking, so two sites can never take the same one.

Re-randomisation means randomising a patient again, later in the same study, to assign them to a new treatment group. A study here is one clinical trial set up in our IRT, and its protocol decides whether re-randomisation exists.

It's used in trials with more than one stage. For example, after a first treatment period, patients who respond might be randomised again to either continue the drug or switch to placebo, to see if the benefit lasts. Or in a crossover design, or when patients move into an extension phase. The rules can depend on the first assignment or on the patient's response.

In IRT, it works much like the first randomisation, but with extra rules. Only patients in the right state can be re-randomised, for example randomised, still active, and at the right visit. The second assignment uses its own randomisation list or scheme, often stratified by the first arm or by response. The original assignment is never overwritten; the patient's history keeps both, with full audit. Blinding still applies, so site users only see kit numbers. And the kits dispensed from then on follow the new arm.

Technically, the same safeguards matter: an idempotency key, a database transaction with locking for the slot, and strict state checks. A double re-randomisation is exactly the kind of bug the design must make impossible.

eConsent is electronic informed consent. Before anyone joins a clinical study, which is one clinical trial with its own protocol and sites, they must give informed consent: they must understand the trial's purpose, procedures, risks and their rights, and agree in writing. eConsent replaces the paper forms with a digital process.

End to end: the study team sets up the consent documents for the study, often per country and language, and each document has a version, approved by an ethics committee. At the site, the patient reviews the document on a tablet or online. It can include multimedia and comprehension questions. The patient signs electronically, and the site staff and investigator sign too. The system records who signed, which version, and when, with an audit trail, and the signatures meet electronic signature rules, like 21 CFR Part 11.

A key feature is version control. When the protocol changes and a new consent version is approved, the system identifies patients who must re-consent, and the site is prompted at their next visit. And because consent must come before screening, IRT can check that a valid consent exists before a patient is screened.

Technically, the important parts are document versioning, secure electronic signatures, strict audit, and privacy, since consent contains personal data. In our product, the newer eConsent screens are built in React with TypeScript.

DARM stands for Drug Accountability and Return Management. In a clinical study, which is one clinical trial set up in IRT, every single drug kit must be accounted for, from the depot to the patient and back. Regulators require it, and sponsors need it to know the drug was used correctly.

The lifecycle looks like this. A kit is shipped to a site, and the site confirms it was received in good condition. At a visit, it's dispensed to a patient, which IRT records against the subject. At the next visit, the patient returns the kit, used or partly used, or reports it lost. The site records the return, often with the quantity, like the number of tablets left, which also shows whether the patient took the medication as prescribed, called compliance.

Then comes reconciliation: a monitor checks that the counts match, kits dispensed versus returned versus still in stock, including expired or damaged kits at the site. Once reconciled, kits are either destroyed at the site with a record, or sent back to a depot for destruction, and IRT tracks those return shipments too.

Technically, DARM is about accurate state transitions for each kit, with rules on which change is allowed when, a full audit trail, and reports that sponsors and monitors rely on. Our DARM screens are among the newer React modules.

Blinding means hiding which treatment a patient is getting, so it can't influence the results. In a double-blind study, which is a clinical trial where neither the patient nor the site staff know, everyone sees only kit numbers, and the kits look identical.

IRT protects blinding in a few ways. The treatment arm is never shown to blinded users or returned by APIs they call. Kit numbers are random, so they don't reveal the arm. Some roles must be unblinded to do their job, like an unblinded pharmacist or the supply team, and their access is separated and audited. Even reports and emails are designed so they don't leak the arm through things like counts by treatment.

Emergency unblinding, also called a code break, is for patient safety. If a patient has a serious medical event and the doctor must know what they're taking, an authorised investigator can unblind that one patient in IRT. The system asks for a reason, often requires confirmation, reveals the arm only for that patient, records exactly who did it, when and why in the audit trail, and notifies the sponsor's study team. Depending on the protocol, the patient may then have to stop treatment.
Technically, it's role-based access control plus field-level protection, with the unblinding action strongly audited, because protecting blinding is as important as protecting the data itself.
In a study, which is one clinical trial set up in IRT, drug supply makes sure every site has the right kits for its patients, without running out and without wasting expensive drug.

Dispensing happens at visits. When a patient is randomised, or comes for a dispensing visit, IRT looks at the patient's arm and the visit schedule to know which kit type and how many, then picks specific kits from that site's stock. It skips kits that are expired, or that would expire before the next visit, and kits that are damaged or quarantined. The site gets only kit numbers, so blinding is protected.

Resupply runs in the background. Each site has stock levels configured, like a trigger level and a maximum, often per kit type. When stock drops below the trigger, after dispensing or as expiry approaches, IRT creates a shipment order from the assigned depot, so the site is topped up. Initial shipments are sent when a site is activated. Shipments are then tracked through depot and courier systems, which in our case connect through SFTP file integrations and APIs, until the site confirms receipt.

Technically, dispensing must be transactional and consistent, while resupply is event-driven: dispensing publishes an event, and supply and shipment services react asynchronously. After that, DARM tracks the kits through return and destruction.

The Admin console is our internal tool for creating and configuring studies. A study is one clinical trial set up in IRT, and before any site can use it, someone has to build it to match the trial's protocol. End users at sites never see the Admin console; it's used by our internal study build and project teams.

Building a study follows a clear flow. First, create the study with its basic details: protocol number, sponsor, phase and settings like blinding. Then configure it: countries and sites, treatment arms and ratios, randomisation lists and strata, the visit schedule, kit types and dispensing rules, depots and resupply levels, user roles and permissions, and which modules are switched on, like eConsent, re-randomisation and DARM. Large data, like hundreds of sites, can be loaded with the CSV bulk import I built, instead of being typed by hand.

Then it's validated. The configuration is checked for gaps and conflicts, and tested in lower environments in user acceptance testing, because it's a GxP system. Once approved, the configuration is moved to production through a study transfer, protected by the study-transfer safety guard I built, which blocks unsafe transfers, for example over a live study that already has randomised subjects.
Finally the study goes live, and sites can start screening. Every configuration change is versioned and audited.
A study is one clinical trial set up in IRT, with its sites, arms, randomisation, visits, kits and roles. Going live, and changing it safely later, are two of the most sensitive moments.

Before go-live, the study is built in the Admin console in a lower environment. The configuration is reviewed against the protocol and the requirements, and tested in user acceptance testing, often by the sponsor too, with documented evidence, because it's GxP. After approval, it's moved to production through a study transfer, with the study-transfer safety guard checking things like the target study's status and the user's role. Then sites are activated, initial drug shipments go out, and the first patient can be screened.

A protocol amendment is a change to the trial's plan while it's running, like adding a country, a new arm, an extra visit, or a new consent version. In IRT, it's handled like a controlled release. The change is configured and tested in a lower environment first. It's applied as a new configuration version with an effective date, never by overwriting history, so patients already in the study keep a correct record of what applied when. Some changes trigger follow-up actions, like re-consent for eConsent, or adjusted resupply levels.
The guiding rule is that a live study's existing data must never be damaged by a configuration change, which is exactly why the transfer guard exists.

In IRT, access is always scoped to a study, which is one clinical trial set up in our system, and usually to specific sites within it. So the question is never just "who is this user", but "what can this user do, in this study, at this site".

There are typical roles. Site coordinators screen and randomise patients and record dispensing at their own sites. Investigators can also perform emergency unblinding. Site pharmacists manage kit receipt and returns, and in some studies they're unblinded. Monitors, also called CRAs, review data and reconcile drug accountability. Study managers on the sponsor side see reports across sites. Supply managers handle depots and shipments. And internal study build teams use the Admin console. Each role has a defined set of permissions, configured per study.

Technically, users authenticate through SSO, and the .NET APIs check every request: a valid token, a role on that study, and access to that site, using policy-based authorisation. Blinded and unblinded data are separated, so blinded roles can't see treatment information, even through APIs or reports. The front end, both the Angular and React parts, hides actions the user can't perform, but the real enforcement is always on the server.
Every access change, like granting a role, is audited, and access is reviewed regularly, because it's a GxP system.

The visit schedule defines the sequence of visits each patient makes during a study, and what IRT has to do at each one. A study here is one clinical trial set up in our IRT, with its protocol, sites, arms, kits and users, and the visit schedule comes straight from the protocol.

A typical schedule has a screening visit, a randomisation visit, which is often day one, and then treatment visits, like week two, week four and so on, until an end-of-treatment and a follow-up visit. For each visit, the configuration says whether drug is dispensed, which kit types and how many, whether returns are collected for DARM, and the allowed time window, like plus or minus three days around the target date.

IRT uses it in several ways. It guides the site through the right actions at each visit. It checks windows and warns, or blocks, if a visit is too early or too late. It calculates which kits will last until the next visit, so a kit doesn't expire in the patient's hands. It forecasts upcoming demand per site, which drives resupply. And unscheduled visits are supported, for example to replace a damaged kit.
Technically, it's configuration data in the Admin console, versioned, because protocol amendments can change visits mid-study, and patients must follow the version that applied to them.
Every IRT module works on a study, which is one clinical trial set up in our system, and the backend is what makes those modules correct, secure and auditable.

The front end, Angular for older screens and React with TypeScript for newer ones, calls ASP.NET Core Web APIs through an API Gateway, with SSO tokens. Behind it are .NET microservices for areas like screening and randomisation, supply and shipments, and the newer modules such as eConsent and DARM, running in containers on AWS. Each API validates the request, checks the user's role on that study and site, and applies the protocol's rules.

The core data lives in SQL Server, because strong consistency matters: randomisation and dispensing run inside transactions with locking, so a slot or a kit can never be used twice. Every change writes an audit record. The outbox pattern makes sure events are published reliably after the transaction commits. Kafka carries business events, like a subject randomised or a shipment created, to several consumers, and RabbitMQ handles work queues, with publisher confirms, which I added after an outage. Vendor integrations with depots and couriers run over SFTP files and APIs.
Across everything, there are correlation ids for tracing, CloudWatch and Grafana for monitoring, and Azure DevOps pipelines for validated releases. I work mainly on this backend side.
I'd design it around the study, which is one clinical trial set up in IRT, because almost every table belongs to one study.

There are three groups of tables. Configuration, which is built in the Admin console: study, country, site, arm, stratum, randomisation list and slots, visit, kit type, dispensing rules, depot, and resupply settings, plus user role assignments. Configuration is versioned, with effective dates, because protocol amendments change it during the trial. Then transactional data: subject, subject visit, randomisation assignment, which links a subject to exactly one slot, with a unique constraint so a slot can't be used twice, kit, with its current status and location, dispensing records, shipments, and returns for DARM. And audit and events: append-only audit tables with who, what, when, why, and old and new values, and an outbox table for reliable events.

Some design rules. Every row carries the study id, and it leads most indexes, because nearly every query filters by study. Status changes, like a kit going from available to dispensed to returned, are validated in code and recorded, not silently overwritten. Concurrency is handled with transactions, row locks for allocation, and rowversion for optimistic concurrency on edits. Blinded data, like the arm on a slot, is protected so it's only exposed to unblinded roles.
In practice, this sits in SQL Server, with EF Core for most access and tuned SQL where performance matters.

IRT is a GxP-regulated system, because it directly affects patient safety and the integrity of clinical studies, where a study is one clinical trial set up in our system. That shapes how every module is built.

The audit trail is central. Every create, update and delete, like screening a patient, randomising, dispensing a kit, signing a consent or recording a return, writes an audit record: who did it, when, what changed, from which value to which, and why. It's append-only and can't be edited, and it follows the ALCOA principles: data must be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate. Electronic signatures, like in eConsent, follow 21 CFR Part 11 rules.

Validation means proving the system does what it's supposed to. Every requirement is traced to a design, to tests, and to test evidence. Releases go through formal testing and approvals, through FV, UAT and production, and changes follow change control, so nothing reaches production unreviewed. Study configurations from the Admin console are also tested before go-live.

For developers, it means writing clear requirements traceability, automated tests that serve as evidence, never fixing data directly in production without a controlled process, and designing safety into the code, like the study-transfer guard and idempotent randomisation. I see GxP not as paperwork, but as building trust that the data is right.

Situation: In IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in our system, and randomisation assigns each patient to a treatment group. Every patient must get exactly one assignment. In 2024, while we were adding re-randomisation support for a study with a second treatment stage, we found in testing that if a site user double-clicked, or the network retried a slow request, the patient could, in rare cases, be re-randomised twice. In a live trial, that would be a serious data integrity issue.
Task: I owned the backend fix, and the goal was to make a duplicate assignment impossible, not just unlikely.

Action: I fixed it at three levels. First, idempotency: the UI sends an idempotency key with each request, and the API stores the key with the result, so a retry returns the original result instead of running again. Second, the database: I added a unique constraint, so a patient can have only one assignment per randomisation stage, and the slot allocation runs inside a transaction with row locking, so two concurrent requests can't both take a slot. Third, state checks: the service verifies the patient is in the right state for that stage before doing anything. On the front end, the button is disabled while the request runs. I added concurrency tests that fire parallel requests at the same patient.

Result: The concurrency tests that previously produced a duplicate now always produce exactly one assignment, it passed validation, and we've had no duplicate assignments since. The same pattern was then reused for the first randomisation and for kit dispensing.

Situation: In IRT, a study is one clinical trial, and our internal Admin console is where study teams build it: sites, arms, randomisation, visits, kits and roles. Configuration mistakes, like a visit that dispensed a kit type not assigned to any arm, or a site without a depot, were often only found late, in user acceptance testing, which meant rework and delayed go-lives.
Task: I was asked to help catch these problems earlier, inside the Admin console, before the study reached UAT.

Action: I designed a configuration validation service in .NET that checks a study's configuration as a whole. I worked with the study build team to collect the most common mistakes, and turned them into rules, like every dispensing visit having a valid kit type for each arm, every active site having a depot and resupply levels, strata matching the randomisation lists, and required roles being assigned. Each rule returns a clear message, with the exact item to fix. The Admin console shows the results as a checklist, and errors must be resolved before the study can be transferred. Rules are unit tested, and adding a new rule is simple, so the team kept adding them. This sits alongside the CSV bulk import for sites and the study-transfer safety guard I built, so the whole setup path is safer.
Result: Configuration defects found in UAT dropped noticeably, study teams fix issues themselves in minutes, and go-lives became more predictable.

Situation: In IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in our system, and DARM, Drug Accountability and Return Management, tracks every kit after it's dispensed: returned, lost, or destroyed. Monitors reconciling kits at large sites were exporting data to spreadsheets and comparing counts by hand, which took hours per site and caused mistakes.
Task: I worked on a reconciliation view and API, so monitors could see, per site, every kit's status and any mismatch, and confirm reconciliation in the system.

Action: On the backend, I built a .NET API that calculates, per site, kits received, dispensed, returned, expired and destroyed, and flags mismatches, like a kit dispensed but never returned, or returned quantities that don't add up. I used set-based SQL queries with the right indexes, filtered by study and site, so it stays fast even for large sites. Every reconciliation action, like confirming a return or marking a kit for destruction, is a validated state change with an audit record. Blinding was protected: the API never returns the treatment arm to blinded roles. On the front end, I built the screen in React with TypeScript, using our reusable data table component, with filters and a downloadable report.
Result: Reconciliation for a site went from hours of spreadsheet work to minutes in the system, with fewer errors, and the audit trail gave sponsors clear evidence for inspections.

Situation: In IRT, a study is one clinical trial set up in our system, and eConsent lets patients sign consent forms electronically. When a protocol amendment introduces a new consent version, patients already in the study must re-consent. Sites were tracking who needed to re-consent manually, and there was a risk of a patient having a visit without valid consent on the current version.
Task: I worked on the backend that tracks consent versions per patient and flags re-consent automatically.

Action: I modelled consent documents as versions with effective dates, per country and language, and stored each patient's signed versions with full audit, never overwriting earlier ones. When a new version becomes effective, an event triggers a job that finds every active patient whose latest signature is on an older version and marks them as needing re-consent. The visit API checks this, and warns the site, or blocks actions the protocol says require current consent. I made the job idempotent, so it can safely run again, and covered the rules with tests for edge cases, like patients who withdrew or moved site. The site-facing screens are in React with TypeScript.
Result: Sites now get a clear list of patients to re-consent at their next visit, there's no manual tracking, and the audit trail shows exactly which version every patient signed and when.

It comes from the history of our product. Our IRT platform started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT system. Cenduit was later acquired by IQVIA, and IQVIA standardises on AWS for its cloud. So we have two worlds that grew at different times.

The CIRT world was built on the Microsoft stack, on-premise: .NET, SQL Server, and Team Foundation Server for source control, builds and releases, which was later upgraded to Azure DevOps Server, still on-premise. The core application, its validated environments, and all its build and release pipelines, with variable groups, classic release stages and approval gates, live there.

The AWS world is where new services and migrated services go, following IQVIA's cloud standards: Docker containers on ECS, RDS SQL Server, Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, Terraform, and CloudWatch.

Why not move everything at once? Because it's a GxP-regulated product. Every validated environment and every release process has documented validation evidence. Moving a validated system means re-validating it, which takes real time and money and adds risk for live clinical trials. So the transition is gradual: new things go to AWS, and older pieces move when there's a good reason, like a major change that needs re-validation anyway.

Today we still use both. Our on-premise Azure DevOps Server builds and releases everything, including the AWS services, and the validated core is still deployed with multi-node installs. That's also why I built the CIRT MCP server, to automate those on-premise deployments, which cut them from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.

Our product began as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT platform. After IQVIA acquired Cenduit, the direction was to align with IQVIA's standards, and IQVIA's cloud is AWS. The transition has been gradual, in phases, because it's a GxP-regulated system running live clinical trials.

The first phase was about tooling, before I joined. Team Foundation Server was upgraded to Azure DevOps Server, still on-premise, and source code moved from TFVC to Git, with YAML build pipelines. That gave us modern pull requests and branching without touching the validated runtime.

The second phase, from around 2022, when I joined, was building new services on AWS. New .NET microservices run in Docker containers on ECS, with RDS, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and Terraform. We kept the same on-premise Azure DevOps Server, so teams didn't have to learn a new release process, and the pipelines push images to ECR and deploy to ECS through an AWS service connection that assumes an IAM role.

The third phase is moving older workloads, lowest risk first: the lower environments, like FV and TechOps, before UAT and production, each with validation evidence. Some validated production pieces are still on-premise, because moving them means re-validation, and we time that with major releases.

My part has been on both sides: building and deploying the AWS services, running release integration on the on-premise Azure DevOps Server, and automating those deployments with the CIRT MCP server, which took them from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.

s: Our IRT platform started as CIRT, Cenduit's system, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new work moved to AWS, which is IQVIA's cloud standard. But a few important things are still on-premise today.

First, our build and release tooling: the Azure DevOps Server, which grew out of Team Foundation Server. All our repositories, build pipelines, release pipelines, variable groups and approval history are there. That history is part of our validation and audit evidence, so moving it isn't just a technical copy; the evidence must stay intact and traceable. Its build agents also run on-premise, with some agents for AWS work running in our AWS account.

Second, parts of the validated core CIRT application environments, which are deployed with multi-node installs: Azure DevOps release stages running Ansible, Python and Shell scripts on 4 to 6 nodes per environment.
Third, some legacy integrations, like older WCF services, that still serve partners and are being replaced over time.

The reason is the same for all of them: in a GxP product, moving a validated system means re-validating it, with test evidence and approvals, and that has a real cost and risk for live clinical trials. So we move pieces when there's a good business reason, or when a major change needs re-validation anyway, not just to change hosting.

Meanwhile, I make the on-premise side efficient. The CIRT MCP server I built automates builds, releases and multi-node deployments on that server, which cut deployments from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.

Our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS, while the validated core and our Azure DevOps Server stayed on-premise. So one release often touches both: the on-premise core and services on AWS. The risk is that the two sides drift apart.

I keep it safe with a few rules. One pipeline system: both sides are built and released from the same on-premise Azure DevOps Server, so there's one place for approvals, one release record and one audit trail. One release version: every component is tagged with the same release version, and we promote the exact same artifacts through FV, TechOps, UAT and production, never rebuilding in between. One order: the release plan says what goes first, usually database changes, then backend services on both platforms, then the UI, with backward-compatible changes so either side can go first safely. One configuration check: settings live in Azure DevOps variable groups for the on-premise side, and in Parameter Store and Secrets Manager for AWS, so before each deployment we compare the required keys on both sides. And one verification: after deployment, every on-premise node and every ECS service reports its version, and they must all match the release tag.

Approvals stay human, with named approvers in Azure DevOps for controlled environments. The CIRT MCP server I built runs these steps and checks, which is how one person can now do what took six, in 2 hours instead of 6.

It comes from our history. Our IRT platform started as CIRT, Cenduit's system, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS. But the builds, releases and validated deployments stayed on our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, because moving them means re-validation.

That on-premise work was the slow part. A release deployment took about 6 hours and needed about 6 people. Someone triggered builds, someone created the release and checked variable groups for each environment, someone watched approvals, someone ran and checked multi-node installs, and someone copied logs into chat. The steps were spread across the Azure DevOps web UI, scripts, servers and checklists.

AI assistants like Copilot and Cursor could help with code, but they couldn't reach our on-premise server. The ready-made integrations target Azure DevOps Services in the cloud, and our on-premise server runs older API versions behind the company network. So I built the CIRT MCP server in C#, with the official MCP SDK. It runs locally on each engineer's machine, inside the network, and exposes about 77 typed tools: builds, releases, approvals, variable group checks, multi-node deployments and environment checks.

Safety was designed in. It uses each engineer's own access token, so actions run with their permissions and show their name. Read tools are separate from write tools, risky steps need confirmation, every call is logged, and production approvals stay with named people in Azure DevOps.
The result: deployments went from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.

Situation: Our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services were built on AWS, while releases still ran from our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. That split configuration across two places: Azure DevOps variable groups for the on-premise side, and Parameter Store and Secrets Manager for the AWS services. In 2024, after a UAT release, errors rose to about 8 percent. A new required setting had been added, but it was missing in the UAT Parameter Store, because the checklist only covered variable groups.
Task: I rolled back within 15 minutes, and then took on the real problem: making sure configuration could never drift between the two platforms unnoticed.

Action: I did three things. First, the services validate their options at startup with ValidateOnStart, so a missing setting fails the deployment instead of the first user request. Second, I added a configuration manifest to each service's repository, listing every required key per environment. Third, I added a configuration parity check to the CIRT MCP server: before each deployment, it reads the manifest, checks the Azure DevOps variable groups and the AWS Parameter Store and Secrets Manager paths for that environment, and reports any missing keys, without ever showing secret values. It became a standard pre-deployment step.

Result: Since then, we've had no configuration-related release failures, and the check caught missing settings several times before deployment. It also made the transition feel safer for the teams, because both platforms are checked the same way.

Our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services went to AWS, while our Azure DevOps Server and the validated core stayed on-premise. So a release day touches both, but it's driven from one place.

It starts in Azure DevOps. YAML build pipelines, on every merge, build and test the .NET code, run SonarQube, and publish versioned artifacts. For AWS services, they also build Docker images and push them to Amazon ECR. Everything is tagged with the release version.

Then the release pipeline promotes those exact artifacts through FV, TechOps, UAT and production. For the on-premise core, a release stage runs Ansible, Python and Shell install scripts across the 4 to 6 nodes of that environment, using the environment's variable group. For AWS services, a stage assumes an IAM role through a service connection, runs Terraform for any infrastructure changes, registers a new ECS task definition with the new image, and updates the service, which does a rolling deployment with health checks. Configuration comes from Parameter Store and Secrets Manager.
Controlled environments need approval by named people before the stage runs, and release evidence, like test results and the change record, is attached, because it's GxP.

Finally, verification: every node and every ECS service must report the release version and pass health and smoke checks. Today the CIRT MCP server I built drives these steps, which cut a deployment from 6 hours to 2, and from 6 people to 1.

I work with both, because our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, with an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS. So I often translate between them.

For DevOps: Azure DevOps variable groups map to AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store for settings, and Secrets Manager for secrets. Azure Key Vault maps to Secrets Manager, with KMS for encryption keys. Build pipelines map to CodeBuild, and release pipelines, with their stages, map to CodePipeline, with CodeDeploy doing the actual deployment. Release approvals and gates map to manual approval actions in CodePipeline. Service connections map to IAM roles that the pipeline assumes. Agent pools map to CodeBuild's managed build environments, or self-hosted runners. And TFS version control, TFVC, and Azure Repos map to Git, hosted on GitHub or CodeCommit.

For the platform: App Service maps to Elastic Beanstalk or App Runner, containers map to ECS or EKS, and virtual machines map to EC2. Azure Monitor and Application Insights map to CloudWatch and X-Ray. Azure Service Bus maps to SQS for queues and SNS for publish and subscribe. ARM templates and Bicep map to CloudFormation and the CDK, while Terraform works on both.

The concepts are the same: store settings and secrets outside code, build once, promote through stages with approvals, use identities instead of keys, and monitor everything. In practice, we still use Azure DevOps to deploy into AWS, and my AlertWatchDog monitoring tool runs on Azure Functions, which would map to Lambda, EventBridge Scheduler, SQS and Step Functions on AWS.
