s: Both answer the same question: where do environment-specific settings and secrets live, outside the code? We use both, because our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, on an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS.

A variable group in Azure DevOps is a named set of variables, like UAT-Shipments, that pipelines link to. Values are injected into the pipeline at run time, and secret variables are masked in logs. They can also be linked to Azure Key Vault. Access is controlled by Azure DevOps security, and changes are recorded in its history. The key point is that variable groups are a pipeline feature: the values exist at deploy time, and the pipeline has to push them into the application's configuration.

In AWS, Systems Manager Parameter Store holds configuration as a hierarchy of paths, like /irt/uat/shipments/timeout, with versions, and SecureString values encrypted with KMS. Secrets Manager is for real secrets, like database passwords, with automatic rotation. The big difference is that the application reads them at run time, using its IAM role, so the pipeline doesn't need to know secret values at all.

So the mapping is: plain variables to Parameter Store, secret variables and Key Vault to Secrets Manager, and Azure DevOps permissions to IAM policies. During our transition, a setting once existed in a variable group but was missing in UAT Parameter Store, so I added a parity check to the CIRT MCP server that compares both before each deployment.

Our releases run in an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, inherited from CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, before IQVIA acquired Cenduit, and they deploy to both on-premise nodes and AWS. So I know the Azure DevOps side deeply, and how it maps to native AWS tools.

In Azure DevOps, a build pipeline produces an artifact, and a release pipeline deploys it through stages, one per environment, like FV, TechOps, UAT and production. Each stage has tasks, variables from variable groups, and pre- and post-deployment approvals and gates, like requiring named approvers or a successful health query.

In AWS, CodeBuild is the build service: it runs the buildspec file, tests, and produces artifacts or Docker images. CodePipeline is the orchestrator: a pipeline with stages, like source, build, and deploy per environment, and actions in each stage. Approvals map to manual approval actions, which pause the pipeline until a person approves, often with an SNS notification. CodeDeploy does the actual deployment, to EC2 instances, on-premise servers with an agent, Lambda, or ECS, with rolling or blue-green strategies and automatic rollback on alarms.

The ideas match one to one: build once, promote the same artifact, approvals before controlled environments, and automated rollback. The differences are mostly about tooling and identity: AWS uses IAM roles instead of service connections. We haven't moved our releases to CodePipeline, because our release history and approvals in Azure DevOps are part of our validation evidence, so we deploy to AWS from Azure DevOps instead.

Our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and its code lived in Team Foundation Server, using TFVC, Team Foundation Version Control. It moved to Git, in Azure DevOps Server, after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, as part of modernising before new services went to AWS.

The core difference is centralised versus distributed. TFVC is centralised: there's one server copy, you check files out and in, branches are heavy server folders, and many operations need the server. Git is distributed: every developer has the full history locally, branches are cheap and fast, and work happens offline, with pull requests to review and merge. Git made pull requests with policies, like required reviewers, a passing build and a SonarQube quality gate, the normal way of working, which fits GxP well, because every change is reviewed and traceable.
A TFVC-to-Git migration needs some care: deciding how much history to bring, mapping branches, handling large binary files, and retraining people on branching and merging.

On the hosting side, Azure Repos is Git inside Azure DevOps. In AWS, the native option was CodeCommit, but AWS stopped offering it to new customers in 2024, so most AWS teams host Git on GitHub or GitLab and connect it to AWS pipelines. In our case, the Git repositories still live in our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, next to the pipelines, while the services they build run on AWS.

Agents are the machines that actually run pipeline jobs. Our pipelines run on an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, inherited from CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, before IQVIA acquired Cenduit, so we use self-hosted agents.

In Azure DevOps, an agent pool is a group of agents, and a job asks for a pool, and optionally capabilities, like having Docker or a certain .NET SDK. Microsoft-hosted agents exist for the cloud service, but with an on-premise server, you run your own agents on your own machines. You patch them, install tools, and scale them yourself.

In AWS, the closest match is CodeBuild. Each build runs in a fresh, managed container, with the image and compute size you choose, so there are no servers to patch and no leftovers from previous builds, and it scales automatically. You pay per build minute. The other option is self-hosted runners on EC2, for example for GitHub Actions or for Azure DevOps itself, often in an Auto Scaling group, which gives full control over tools and network access.

In our setup, the agents that deploy to AWS run on EC2 inside our AWS account and are registered with our on-premise Azure DevOps Server. That way they're close to ECR and ECS, and they can use IAM roles instead of stored access keys, while agents for the on-premise core stay inside the company network, near the nodes they install to.
Whichever option, I treat agents as disposable and defined as code, with only the permissions their jobs need.

Both are how a pipeline proves who it is to the target platform, so it can deploy. We deploy from an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, inherited from CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, into AWS, where IQVIA runs new services, so I work with both.

In Azure DevOps, a service connection stores how to connect to an external system, like Azure, a Docker registry, Kubernetes, or AWS. Pipelines reference it by name, and access to it is controlled, so only approved pipelines can use a production connection. The weak version stores long-lived secrets, like a client secret or an access key, inside it. The better version uses workload identity federation, with OpenID Connect, so no secret is stored.

In AWS, the equivalent identity is an IAM role. The pipeline, or the build agent, assumes a role and receives short-lived credentials, valid for maybe an hour. The role's trust policy says who may assume it, like a specific OIDC identity or a specific EC2 instance profile, and its permission policy says exactly what it can do, like pushing to one ECR repository and updating specific ECS services. Every call is recorded in CloudTrail.

So the mapping is: a service connection becomes a role that the pipeline assumes, plus a trust policy. The principles I follow are the same on both sides: no long-lived keys, one identity per environment, least privilege, and production identities usable only by approved pipelines.

Both keep secrets out of code and configuration files, with strict access control and auditing. We use both worlds, because our product began as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, on Microsoft tooling, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS.

Azure Key Vault is one service for three things: secrets, like passwords and connection strings, cryptographic keys, and certificates. Access is controlled with Azure role-based access, apps use managed identities to read it, and Azure DevOps variable groups can link to it, so pipelines read secrets without copying them.

In AWS, those jobs are split across services. Secrets Manager stores secrets, with versioning and automatic rotation, which is built in for databases like RDS. KMS manages encryption keys: it encrypts data in other services, like S3, RDS and Parameter Store SecureString values, and keys never leave it. Certificates are handled by ACM, the AWS Certificate Manager, for load balancers and API Gateway. Access is through IAM policies, apps use their IAM roles, and every access is logged in CloudTrail.
So the mapping is: Key Vault secrets to Secrets Manager, or Parameter Store SecureString for simpler values, Key Vault keys to KMS, and Key Vault certificates to ACM.

In our AWS services, database credentials and vendor SFTP keys are in Secrets Manager, with rotation for RDS, and the application reads them at run time with its IAM role, so no secret ever sits in a pipeline variable or an image.

Both give you logs, metrics, alerts and tracing. Our product began as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, on Microsoft tooling, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS, where we use CloudWatch with Grafana dashboards.

In Azure, Azure Monitor is the overall platform: metrics, logs stored in Log Analytics workspaces and queried with KQL, and alert rules. Application Insights is its application performance part: requests, dependencies, exceptions, response times, and distributed tracing across services, with an application map.

In AWS, CloudWatch covers most of that. CloudWatch Logs stores logs, queried with Logs Insights. CloudWatch Metrics holds numbers, like CPU, request counts and custom metrics, and CloudWatch Alarms alert on them, through SNS. Dashboards show them, though we use Grafana on top. For tracing, AWS X-Ray, or OpenTelemetry with the AWS Distro, follows a request across services, like Application Insights does. CloudWatch Application Signals and Container Insights add APM-style views for ECS.
So: Log Analytics to CloudWatch Logs, KQL to Logs Insights queries, Azure Monitor metrics and alerts to CloudWatch Metrics and Alarms, and Application Insights to X-Ray or OpenTelemetry tracing.

I've used both: our AWS services report to CloudWatch, while AlertWatchDog, the monitoring tool I built on Azure Functions, reports its own health to Application Insights. Whatever the tool, the key is in the code: structured logs, and a correlation id on every request. In 2024, I added a correlation-id middleware across our 4 services, so one search shows a request's whole journey, which cut triage from about an hour to minutes.

Both are managed messaging services for decoupling systems. Our product began as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, on Microsoft technology, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS, so it helps to map the two.

Azure Service Bus offers queues, for one consumer processing each message, and topics with subscriptions, for publish and subscribe, all in one service. It has rich features: sessions for ordered processing per key, dead-letter queues, scheduled messages, duplicate detection, and transactions.

In AWS, those are split. SQS provides queues. Standard queues give nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, and FIFO queues give strict ordering per message group and deduplication, which is like Service Bus sessions. Dead-letter queues are built in. SNS provides topics for publish and subscribe, and the common pattern is SNS fanning out to several SQS queues, one per consumer, which matches a Service Bus topic with subscriptions. EventBridge adds event routing with rules, and Amazon MQ runs RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ as a managed broker.

In our platform, we actually use RabbitMQ for work queues and Kafka for business events, with the outbox pattern, rather than SQS or Service Bus. But the same rules apply on any of them: idempotent consumers, because delivery is at least once, dead-letter queues with alerts, and confirmations on publish. I added publisher confirms to RabbitMQ after an outage in mid-2024.

All of these are infrastructure as code: you describe cloud resources in files, review them in pull requests, and apply them through pipelines, instead of clicking in a console. We work across both worlds, because our product began as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, on Microsoft tooling, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS.

In Azure, ARM templates are the native JSON format, and Bicep is a cleaner language that compiles to ARM. Deployments are declarative, and what-if shows changes before applying. In AWS, CloudFormation is the native equivalent, with templates in YAML or JSON, stacks, and change sets to preview changes. The CDK lets you write infrastructure in a programming language, like C# or TypeScript, and generates CloudFormation. So ARM maps to CloudFormation, Bicep is closest in spirit to cleaner CloudFormation or the CDK, and what-if maps to change sets.

Terraform is the cross-cloud option: one language, HCL, providers for Azure, AWS and many others, a readable plan before every change, and a state file that must be stored safely, like in S3 with locking.

In our platform, the core AWS stacks, like networking, are in CloudFormation, owned by the platform team, and newer service infrastructure, like queues and alarms, is in Terraform. Both run from our Azure DevOps pipelines, with plan or change set review before apply.

These are the compute options, from fully managed to full control. Our product began as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, on Microsoft servers on-premise, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS, mostly as containers on ECS.

At the most managed level, Azure App Service runs web apps and APIs without managing servers: you deploy code or a container, and it handles scaling, patching and deployment slots. The AWS equivalents are Elastic Beanstalk, which deploys code onto managed EC2 instances, and App Runner, which runs a container from an image with almost no configuration. Deployment slots map to blue-green deployments in Beanstalk.

For containers, Azure Container Apps and AKS map to ECS and EKS. ECS is simpler and AWS-native, and with Fargate there are no servers at all. EKS is managed Kubernetes, matching AKS. For virtual machines, Azure VMs map to EC2, and scale sets map to EC2 Auto Scaling groups. Azure Functions map to Lambda.

My rule is to choose the most managed option that meets the need. For our .NET microservices, that's ECS on Fargate: we build images in Azure DevOps, push them to ECR, and ECS runs them across two availability zones with rolling deployments. VMs, or EC2, make sense when you need full control of the operating system, which is why the validated core, with its multi-node installs, still runs on servers rather than containers.

Not really, and I'm glad you asked, because it's an easy thing to misread. Our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS, IQVIA's standard cloud. What stayed on Microsoft is mainly our build and release tooling: an on-premise Azure DevOps Server. So the pipelines are Azure DevOps, but the services I design, build, deploy and support run on AWS.

On AWS, I work hands-on every week. Our .NET services run as Docker containers on ECS with Fargate, with images in ECR, behind an Application Load Balancer, across two availability zones. Data is in RDS SQL Server, with DynamoDB for some high-volume lookups, and ElastiCache Redis for caching. Secrets are in Secrets Manager, settings in Parameter Store, and each service has its own IAM task role. I write and review Terraform for new infrastructure, like queues and alarms, and I've changed CloudFormation stacks. And I debug production through CloudWatch Logs Insights, alarms and Grafana. For example, I fixed a Lambda that was timing out on a DynamoDB stream, by adding timeouts to a slow downstream call and tuning memory.
Where I have Azure depth is Azure DevOps, which is CI/CD rather than cloud hosting, plus some Azure Functions work, like the AlertWatchDog monitoring tool I built, and Azure OpenAI.

And honestly, I think in cloud concepts rather than vendor names: compute, identity, secrets, queues, infrastructure as code and observability. The names change between clouds, but the design decisions don't, so I'm productive on either.

Very hands-on, on the application side of AWS. Some context first: our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS. Our build and release tooling is still an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, but what it deploys, the services I build, runs on AWS.

Here's what I've done myself. I containerised .NET services with Docker, pushed images to ECR, and deployed them to ECS on Fargate, with task definitions, health checks, autoscaling and rolling deployments with the circuit breaker. I set up configuration through Parameter Store and secrets through Secrets Manager, read at run time with IAM task roles, so nothing secret sits in images or pipelines. I wrote Terraform for service infrastructure, like queues, alarms and IAM policies, with plan review in pull requests. I worked with RDS SQL Server, including the query tuning that took a shipment report from 8 to 12 seconds to under 300 milliseconds. I fixed a timing-out Lambda on a DynamoDB stream. And for operations, I use CloudWatch Logs Insights with correlation ids, CloudWatch alarms through SNS, and Grafana dashboards, which is how I root-caused our RabbitMQ outage.

What I haven't owned is the account-level platform: the landing zone, organisation policies and core networking belong to a platform team, though I understand and work within them, like VPC endpoints and security groups.

When I need something new, I ramp up the same way every time: official documentation and the Well-Architected guidance, then a small proof of concept in a sandbox account, then a review with someone who has run it in production.
I'd say about 7 out of 10, and I'll explain what's behind that number, so it's honest.

Context first: our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS, IQVIA's standard cloud. Our build and release tooling is still an on-premise Azure DevOps Server, but the services I build and support run on AWS, so I use it every week.

The strong part, around eight, is application workloads on AWS. Running .NET services on ECS with Fargate and ECR, RDS SQL Server and DynamoDB, Lambda, Secrets Manager and Parameter Store with IAM task roles, Terraform and CloudFormation for service infrastructure, and CloudWatch with Grafana for monitoring and root-cause analysis. I've deployed, tuned and debugged all of these in production.

The lower part, around five or six, is the account-level platform: designing the landing zone, organisation policies, multi-account networking, and services we don't use, like EKS in production or Kinesis. A platform team owns those, so I know the concepts but haven't designed them myself.

I don't stop at that number, though. I think in cloud concepts, like compute, identity, secrets, queues, infrastructure as code and observability, so new services come quickly. My way of ramping up is the official documentation, a small proof of concept in a sandbox, and then a review with someone experienced. I'd also happily take an AWS certification, like the Developer Associate, to formalise it.

AlertWatchDog is a monitoring and alerting tool I built for our IRT team, using Azure Functions. Its job is to notice problems in our background work before users do, and tell the right people quickly.

Some context: our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, new services moved to AWS, while our build and release tooling stayed on an on-premise Azure DevOps Server. A lot of important work in IRT happens in the background, like scheduled jobs that calculate site resupply, vendor files arriving over SFTP, messages flowing through RabbitMQ, and release pipelines. When one of those silently stops, nobody notices until a site calls or a shipment is late.

AlertWatchDog watches exactly those things. Every five minutes, a timer-triggered function runs a set of checks: has each scheduled job succeeded within its expected window, has each vendor file arrived on time, are any queues growing or any dead-letter queues non-empty, did a release pipeline fail, and are the services' health endpoints answering. Each finding goes onto a queue, and a queue-triggered function applies rules: thresholds, deduplication and quiet periods, so the team isn't spammed. Then it notifies a Microsoft Teams channel and email, and a Durable Functions orchestration escalates to the on-call person if nobody acknowledges.

It's read-only and sits outside the validated product, so we could build it without GxP re-validation. The result was that background failures were detected in minutes instead of hours, often before any user noticed.

AlertWatchDog is the monitoring and alerting tool I built for our IRT team. Our product started as CIRT, Cenduit's IRT, and after IQVIA acquired Cenduit, the services moved to AWS, while releases stayed on an on-premise Azure DevOps Server. The tool watches our background jobs, vendor files, queues and pipelines, and alerts the team.

I built it in C#, with Azure Functions on the .NET isolated worker model. There are three parts. First, a timer-triggered function, every five minutes, loads the list of checks from a configuration file in the repository, and runs them in parallel: querying job status, the RabbitMQ management API for queue depth and dead letters, health endpoints, and the Azure DevOps API for failed releases. Each check has a timeout, so one slow target can't block the rest. Second, every finding is written to a storage queue, and a queue-triggered function evaluates it against rules: severity, thresholds, deduplication by a key, and a 30-minute suppression window. Failed messages retry and then land in a poison queue, which itself raises an alert. Third, a Durable Functions orchestration handles escalation: notify the channel, wait 15 minutes for an acknowledgement, then escalate to the on-call person.

For security, it uses a managed identity, and secrets are in Key Vault. It runs on a Premium plan with network integration, so it can reach internal endpoints and has no cold starts. And it watches itself: if its own heartbeat stops, an Application Insights alert fires.
It's deployed through our Azure DevOps pipelines, like everything else.

Azure Functions is Microsoft's serverless compute service: you write small functions, and Azure runs them when an event happens, scaling them automatically, without you managing servers. It's the Azure equivalent of AWS Lambda. I've used it to build AlertWatchDog, a monitoring and alerting tool for our IRT team.

Every function has exactly one trigger, which is what starts it. Common triggers are HTTP, for small APIs and webhooks, timer, for schedules written as CRON expressions, queue triggers, for Azure Storage queues or Service Bus, blob triggers, when a file is uploaded, and Event Grid or Event Hubs triggers, for events and streams. The trigger also passes in the data, like the queue message.

Bindings are a declarative way to connect to other services without writing client code. An input binding reads data, like a blob or a table row, and an output binding writes data, like putting a message on a queue or saving a document, just by returning a value or setting a parameter. They remove boilerplate, though for complex logic I still use the normal SDK clients with dependency injection.

Functions live inside a Function App, which shares configuration, the hosting plan and scaling. In .NET, the isolated worker model is the current approach: functions run in their own process, with normal dependency injection, middleware and logging.
In AlertWatchDog, a timer trigger runs the checks, a queue output binding writes each finding, a queue trigger evaluates rules, and Durable Functions handles escalation.

Durable Functions is an extension of Azure Functions for writing stateful workflows in code. Normal functions are short and stateless, but some processes need to run many steps, wait for events, or take hours. Durable Functions lets you write that as an ordinary-looking C# method, and the framework saves its progress, so it survives restarts and doesn't pay for waiting time.

There are three kinds of functions. An orchestrator function describes the workflow: call this activity, then that one, wait for an event, set a timer. Activity functions do the actual work, like calling an API or sending a message. And a client function starts orchestrations, for example from an HTTP or queue trigger. Under the hood, it uses event sourcing: the orchestrator replays its history to rebuild its state, which is why orchestrator code must be deterministic. No direct I/O, no DateTime.Now, and no random numbers inside it; those go in activities, or use the context's own time.

Common patterns are function chaining, fan-out and fan-in to run work in parallel and combine results, async HTTP APIs for long jobs, monitors that poll until a condition is met, and human interaction, waiting for an approval with a timeout. Durable entities hold small pieces of state.

I used the human interaction pattern in AlertWatchDog, our monitoring tool. When an alert fires, the orchestration notifies the team channel, waits 15 minutes for someone to acknowledge, and if nobody does, escalates to the on-call person. On AWS, the equivalent is Step Functions.

A cold start is the extra delay when a function runs on a fresh instance: the platform has to allocate it, start the runtime, load your code and initialise dependencies. For .NET, that can be a second or more. It matters for user-facing HTTP functions, much less for timers and queues.

The hosting plan decides cost, scaling and cold starts. The Consumption plan is pure serverless: you pay per execution, it scales to zero, and it scales out automatically, but it has cold starts, execution time limits, and no private network access. The Flex Consumption plan is the newer version, with faster scaling, virtual network integration, and the option of always-ready instances to avoid cold starts. The Premium plan keeps pre-warmed instances, so there are no cold starts, supports virtual network integration and longer runs, but you pay for the minimum instances all the time. And the Dedicated plan runs functions on an App Service plan, like a normal web app, which suits predictable load or existing spare capacity.
To reduce cold starts in code: keep the package small, avoid heavy work at startup, reuse clients like HttpClient as singletons, and use the isolated worker model with ready-to-run compilation.

For AlertWatchDog, our monitoring tool, I chose the Premium plan, mainly because it needed private network access to reach internal endpoints, and pre-warmed instances meant alerts were never delayed by a cold start. On AWS, the matching ideas are Lambda's provisioned concurrency and VPC configuration.

AlertWatchDog is the monitoring and alerting tool I built for our IRT team on Azure Functions. Our services run on AWS, IQVIA's standard cloud, so the natural next step is to run it there too, and the design maps across almost one to one.

The timer trigger becomes an EventBridge Scheduler schedule, every five minutes, invoking a Lambda function that runs the checks in parallel: scheduled job status, RabbitMQ queue depth and dead letters, health endpoints, and failed releases. Each finding goes to an SQS queue, instead of a storage queue. A second Lambda is triggered by SQS, using an event source mapping, and applies the rules: severity, thresholds, deduplication and a suppression window, with the dedupe state in a small DynamoDB table with a time-to-live. Failed messages retry and then go to a dead-letter queue, which has its own alarm. Escalation, which is Durable Functions today, becomes a Step Functions state machine: notify through SNS, wait for an acknowledgement with a task token and a timeout, then escalate to on-call.

Security maps too: a managed identity becomes the Lambda execution role, Key Vault becomes Secrets Manager, and the functions run inside the VPC to reach internal endpoints. Many checks get simpler on AWS, because CloudWatch alarms can watch metrics directly, and EventBridge can react to events, like an ECS task stopping.
And the watchdog watches itself: a CloudWatch alarm on its own heartbeat metric. I'd define all of it in Terraform and deploy it through our pipelines.

nodes.label: Azure → AWS
nodes.detail: each box: Azure name, AWS below

s: They're the same idea: event-driven, serverless functions that scale automatically and charge for what you use. I've built AlertWatchDog, our monitoring tool, on Azure Functions, and I work with Lambda in our AWS services, so I know both.

The programming models differ a bit. Azure Functions has triggers and bindings: one trigger starts the function, and input and output bindings connect to other services declaratively. Lambda has a simpler model: a handler receives an event, and other services connect through event source mappings, like SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB streams, or invoke it directly, like API Gateway, S3 or EventBridge. Outputs are written with the SDK. Azure groups functions in a Function App that shares settings and scaling; in Lambda, each function is its own unit, with its own memory, timeout, concurrency and IAM execution role.

On limits and scaling: Lambda runs up to 15 minutes per invocation, and memory, from 128 MB to 10 GB, also sets the CPU. Azure Functions' limits depend on the hosting plan. For cold starts, Lambda has provisioned concurrency and SnapStart, while Azure has Premium pre-warmed instances or always-ready instances on Flex Consumption. For workflows, Durable Functions is code-first, and Step Functions defines a state machine.
Identity maps cleanly: a managed identity in Azure is the execution role in Lambda. Monitoring is Application Insights versus CloudWatch and X-Ray.
My view: the concepts transfer directly, so I'd pick whichever cloud the rest of the system lives on.

Both run code on a schedule, without a server running cron. I use a timer trigger in AlertWatchDog, our monitoring tool, which runs its checks every five minutes, and on AWS the equivalent is EventBridge Scheduler.

In Azure Functions, a timer trigger is defined on the function itself, with a CRON expression that includes seconds. It runs in the function app's time zone, UTC by default. The runtime makes sure only one instance runs each scheduled occurrence, even when the app scales out, and there's an option to run on startup, which should stay off in production. If the app was down, it can catch up on a missed run.

In AWS, EventBridge Scheduler is a separate service that invokes a target on a schedule. The target is often a Lambda function, but it can also be an ECS task, an SQS queue, a Step Functions state machine, or many other AWS APIs directly. It supports cron and rate expressions, time zones with daylight saving, one-time schedules, a flexible time window to spread load, retries, and a dead-letter queue for failed invocations. The older way was EventBridge scheduled rules, which still work but have fewer features.
So the main difference is that in Azure the schedule belongs to the function, while in AWS it's a separate resource that can trigger many kinds of targets.
Whichever I use, the job itself must be idempotent and safe to run twice, because any scheduler can occasionally retry.

Both let a function process messages from a queue automatically, with retries, so the producer and the consumer stay decoupled. In AlertWatchDog, our monitoring tool, every finding goes onto a queue, and a queue-triggered function applies the alert rules. On AWS, that would be SQS triggering Lambda.

In Azure Functions, a queue trigger listens to an Azure Storage queue, or a Service Bus queue. The runtime polls the queue, fetches messages in batches, and calls the function once per message. If it throws, the message becomes visible again and is retried, five times by default, and then it's moved to a poison queue, which you must monitor.

In AWS, Lambda uses an event source mapping on the SQS queue. Lambda polls the queue for you and invokes the function with a batch of messages, up to a batch size and batching window you configure. If the function fails, the whole batch returns to the queue after the visibility timeout, unless you report partial batch failures, which I always enable, so only the failed messages are retried. After the maximum receive count, SQS moves the message to a dead-letter queue. You can also cap concurrency for the mapping, to protect a downstream database.

The same rules apply on both: handlers must be idempotent, because delivery is at least once, the visibility timeout must be longer than the function's timeout, and the dead-letter or poison queue needs an alarm.

Both orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows reliably: they keep state between steps, retry failures, wait for events or people, and survive restarts. I used Durable Functions in AlertWatchDog, our monitoring tool, for escalation, and on AWS the equivalent is Step Functions.

The biggest difference is how you define the workflow. Durable Functions is code-first: the orchestrator is a C# method, with normal loops, conditions and try-catch, and the framework replays it from its history to rebuild state. That's natural for developers, but the code must be deterministic. Step Functions is definition-first: you describe a state machine in Amazon States Language, as JSON or with the visual designer, with task, choice, parallel, map and wait states. Each step can call Lambda or, directly, over two hundred AWS service APIs, like DynamoDB, SQS or ECS, often without writing a function at all. Its console shows each execution visually, which is great for support.

For waiting on people, Durable Functions uses external events with a timer, and Step Functions uses a task token with a heartbeat or timeout. Step Functions has two modes: Standard, for long workflows up to a year with exactly-once steps, and Express, for high-volume, short workflows.

In AlertWatchDog, escalation notifies the team, waits 15 minutes for an acknowledgement, then escalates to on-call. In Step Functions, that's an SNS notification, a wait with a task token and timeout, and a choice state.

Both turn telemetry into notifications when something is wrong. AlertWatchDog, the monitoring tool I built on Azure Functions, uses Application Insights for its own health, and our AWS services use CloudWatch alarms, so I use both.

In Azure, alerts are part of Azure Monitor. An alert rule watches a signal: a metric, like failed requests or response time from Application Insights, a log query, written in KQL, that runs on a schedule, or an availability test that pings an endpoint. When the condition is met, the rule calls an action group, which defines who is notified and how: email, SMS, Teams through a webhook, a function, or a logic app. Smart detection can also flag unusual failure rates.

In AWS, a CloudWatch alarm watches a metric, with a statistic like average or p95, a threshold and a number of evaluation periods, and has three states: OK, ALARM and insufficient data. On a state change, it typically publishes to an SNS topic, and SNS fans out to email, chat, a paging tool or a Lambda. Metric filters or Logs Insights turn log patterns into metrics, composite alarms combine conditions to reduce noise, and anomaly detection learns normal patterns.
So an alert rule maps to an alarm, an action group maps to an SNS topic with subscriptions, and KQL log alerts map to metric filters or Logs Insights.
The principle is the same: alert on symptoms users feel, make every alert actionable, and always alert when a monitor goes silent.

Situation: AlertWatchDog is the monitoring tool I built on Azure Functions for our IRT team. It watches our background work, like scheduled jobs, vendor files, queues and release pipelines, and alerts us. In early 2025, on a Saturday morning, it raised an alert: the shipment-status file from one depot vendor hadn't arrived within its expected two-hour window. Those files update shipment tracking, and sites rely on them to know when kits will arrive.
Task: I was on call, so my job was to find the cause and fix it before it affected sites or the next resupply run.

Action: The alert already told me which vendor, which file, and when the last one arrived, so I didn't start from zero. I checked our SFTP integration logs in CloudWatch, filtered by the correlation id, and saw our scheduled pull was connecting fine, but the vendor's folder was empty. The vendor had moved their output to a new folder during maintenance, without telling us. I contacted their support with the evidence, they confirmed it, and we pointed our pull to the new path through configuration, without a code change. The delayed files were then processed, and I checked that the shipment statuses were updated correctly.

Result: It was fixed within about two hours, before Monday, and no site saw stale shipment data. Before AlertWatchDog, we'd typically have found out from a site call days later. Afterwards, I added a check for an unexpected empty folder, and we agreed with the vendor to announce path changes in advance.
